I wonder when they last saw him.

contexts.subject: A volunteer says Mr. Fuji had been praying alone for Cubone's mother.

LavenderTown_VolunteerPokemonHouse_Text_.text: MR. FUJI had been praying alone\nfor CUBONE's mother.$

replies.text: He made time for someone who could no longer ask for it. That matters.
His action shows sustained concern beyond what could be fixed practically.
He did not forget her just because the danger had passed.
It is a gentle thing to do in a place with so much grief.
Remembering someone quietly is still a form of care.
A private act with no audience to reward it. That tells us something.
Some kindness is simply refusing to let a life vanish without being mourned.
Not every worthwhile act solves a problem. Some acknowledge what happened.
He kept a little space open for a life that was gone.
There is care in choosing to remember without needing anyone to watch.
I wonder whether Cubone knew someone was thinking of its mother.

contexts.subject: A volunteer explains that Fuji welcomes abandoned and orphaned Pokemon into his home.

LavenderTown_VolunteerPokemonHouse_Text_.text: This is really MR. FUJI's house.\pHe's really kind.\pHe looks after abandoned and\norphaned POKéMON.$

replies.text: A house that keeps saying there is room for one more. That is a wonderful use of a house.
Stable care can provide a crucial refuge after abandonment or loss.
He is doing work that matters. Day after ordinary day.
It is lovely that the welcome lasts beyond the first rescue.
A safe place needs someone willing to do the daily work. He does.
The remarkable thing is not the rescue scene but the home maintained afterward.
A room full of small lives that no longer have to be unwanted.
Practical, ongoing support. The unglamorous part is often the most important.
A door that opens kindly can change the rest of a life.
He makes room in his own everyday life. That says more than a grand promise.
I wonder which resident took the longest to feel at home.

contexts.subject: A child delights in the warmth of hugging a Pokemon.

LavenderTown_VolunteerPokemonHouse_Text_.text: It's so warm!\nPOKéMON are so nice to hug.$

replies.text: A tiny report from the department of excellent cuddles.
Warmth and familiar contact can make a safe interaction especially comforting.
Good to see them comfortable together.
A simple happy moment. I am glad this house has those too.
Warm company can make an ordinary room feel like the best place to be.
A glowing review delivered with no need for elaborate adjectives.
Something soft and alive making the world less severe for a moment.
Positive interaction, no complicated apparatus required. Excellent.
A little warmth shared without needing words.
Comfort looks rather lovely on both of them.
I wonder whether this is part of their everyday routine here.

contexts.subject: After giving the Poke Flute, Mr. Fuji explains that it wakes sleeping Pokemon.

LavenderTown_VolunteerPokemonHouse_Text_.text: Upon hearing the POKé FLUTE,\nsleeping POKéMON will spring awake.\pTry using it on POKéMON that are\nsleeping obstacles.$

replies.text: A gentle-sounding answer to a very large sleeping obstacle. Useful gift.
He describes a clear effect and a practical situation in which to use it.
Useful. Give the waking Pokemon room instead of crowding it.
I would like to hear what kind of breath brings it to life.
A kind gift with a real purpose for the road ahead.
The old caretaker sends us onward with an instrument suited to a new beginning.
A small sound can open a road that force would only make angry.
A specific acoustic tool for a specific problem. Elegant.
A sleeping path may only need the right little song.
He chose something helpful without making the gift about himself.
I wonder how he first came to have the flute.

contexts.subject: Mr. Fuji asks whether his Poke Flute has been useful.

An inherited interest with very durable souvenirs.
I'd ask whether their collections focus on the same kinds of material.
The same road can leave different stones in two pockets.
Sharing a hobby still leaves room for individual taste.
I'd ask who first took the younger collector out looking.

contexts.subject: The stair guard angrily questions how Devon was robbed.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_1F_Text_HowCouldW.text: It's beyond stupid.\nHow could we get robbed?$

replies.text: Shock is understandable. Calling the whole situation stupid won't recover the parcel.
A failed security process needs examination rather than disbelief.
Work out how it happened. Anger alone won't stop a repeat.
He sounds shaken enough to put it all into one sharp sentence.
I'd rather hear whether the person carrying it is all right.
The institution has discovered its impressive name does not repel thieves.
Disbelief remains an ineffective lock.
They should review the actual route and access points.
A place that felt secure has acquired a crack in its certainty.
He can be upset without turning it into blame for the victim.
I'd ask what they know for certain before guessing at fault.

contexts.subject: The greeter blames a staff member for being robbed of a parcel.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_1F_Text_StaffGotR.text: One of our research staff stupidly\ngot robbed of an important parcel.$

replies.text: The thief did the stealing. That seems like the important detail.
Being targeted does not establish negligence by the victim.
Blame the robber. Check on your coworker.
I'd hate to come back shaken and hear people say that about me.
Someone had a bad enough day before the office started judging them.
The account has curiously assigned the villain's work to the victim.
An unpleasantly efficient way to make a frightened colleague feel worse.
They need facts about the failure, not a convenient person to insult.
A stolen parcel should not cost somebody their dignity as well.
That is a poor way to speak about someone who needed help.
I'd ask whether anyone has actually listened to the staff member's account.

contexts.subject: The greeter welcomes visitors to Devon and describes its products.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_1F_Text_WelcomeTo.text: Hello and welcome to the DEVON\nCORPORATION.\pWe're proud producers of items and\nmedicine that enhance your life.$

replies.text: A company that makes useful things is happy to tell us about every one of them.
Their products span several applications rather than one narrow field.
A clear welcome. We can ask where we need to go.
It's nice to have someone make the large building feel less daunting.
I'd ask which everyday item people use without knowing it came from here.
The welcome contains a brisk tour of the company's ambitions.
A pleasant introduction with a brochure quietly folded inside.
I'd like to know how they decide which problems are worth solving next.
A building can send small useful things into many different lives.
They want us to know the work has a purpose beyond the walls.
I'd ask what the greeter is most proud to see people using.

contexts.subject: After the goods return, the guard warmly welcomes the player.

replies.text: The door has changed its opinion of us quite dramatically.
Our earlier actions have established trust with the staff.
Good to know. Let's respect the welcome.
A familiar face being glad to see us makes the building feel warmer.
It's a nice thing to hear after a difficult errand.
The former obstacle has become a particularly agreeable host.
Authorization has acquired a smile. An improvement.
We should still ask before entering an active work area.
A closed place can become somewhere that remembers us kindly.
A thank-you sometimes takes the form of being comfortable when you return.
I'd take a moment to say hello instead of simply rushing past.

contexts.subject: A researcher is struggling to develop a new PokeNav feature.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_2F_Text_DevelopNe.text: I'm trying to develop a new feature\nfor the POKéNAV…\pBut it's not going well.$

replies.text: The idea sounds smaller when you say feature than when you try making it work.
Integrating a new function often creates constraints beyond the function itself.
Better to test it properly than hurry out something unreliable.
I know the feeling of something clear in your head refusing to come out right.
A difficult day doesn't mean the whole idea is bad.
The promised improvement has reached the obstinate middle of its development.
A new feature has discovered several innovative ways to be unfinished.
I'd ask which test keeps failing. That would give us something useful to discuss.
A small light can need a great deal of work before it stays lit.
They may need a patient listener more than another bright suggestion.
I'd ask what they tried most recently and what it taught them.

contexts.subject: An engineer appreciates Devon freedom to pursue new inspirations.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_2F_Text_WhatToWor.text:
Well, now what shall I work on
developing next?\pOur company allows us to make our
inspirations into reality.\pOne couldn't ask for a better
environment as an engineer.$

replies.text: Finishing one invention has apparently opened twelve doors in his head.
Support for exploratory work can make uncertain but valuable projects possible.
Good situation. Pick a useful problem and give it proper attention.
It's nice hearing someone happy about the possibilities in their work.
Room to try things is worth appreciating. So is time to finish them.
The engineer stands before the blank page with an unusually supportive publisher.
A blank project list producing excitement instead of dread. Remarkable.
I'd ask which everyday frustration he's most tempted to tackle.
A place can offer shelter to thoughts that aren't useful yet.
Freedom is nicest when the people doing the work actually feel it.
I'd love to hear the strange idea he hasn't decided to say aloud yet.

contexts.subject: A researcher recognizes the PokeNav and recommends learning its features by trying it.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_2F_Text_WowThatsA.text:
Oh, wow!
That's a POKéNAV!\pIt came about as a result of our
PRESIDENT's desire to learn about\lthe feelings of POKéMON.\pWould you like me to describe its
features in detail?\pNo, no. I think you'll find out just by
trying the POKéNAV out.$

replies.text: He almost gave us the entire explanation, then trusted us to poke the useful buttons.
Direct exploration can teach an interface when its functions are discoverable.
Try it somewhere calm before relying on it in a hurry.
I appreciate being allowed to learn at a quieter pace.
I'd start with the feature we actually need for the next trip.
The lecture has graciously transformed into a practical demonstration by the visitor.
A description spared. The device may yet describe itself.
A tool should help people discover its functions without a long speech.
Curiosity can learn the shape of a useful thing through ordinary use.
He notices our experience matters more than his complete explanation.
I'd come back with one question after trying it rather than guess at everything.

contexts.subject: The fossil scientist reports a working regenerator; this label alone does not mean a fossil was submitted.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_2F_Text_DevelopDe.text: I've been trying to develop a device\nthat resurrects POKéMON from fossils…\pAnd, it's working!$

replies.text: A machine that can turn a very old trace into a living introduction!
Reconstructing a living Pokemon from a fossil is an extraordinary technical claim.
Impressive work. Be careful with whatever comes back.
The idea of meeting something from so long ago feels enormous.
A living creature will need more than a successful machine waiting for it.
The distant past has been offered a door into the present.
Prehistory has apparently become available by appointment.
I'd want to understand how they confirm the result is healthy and stable.
Something once held by stone may breathe again.
That is a tremendous responsibility as well as an achievement.
I'd ask what the first living result did when it looked around.

contexts.subject: The player declines fossil regeneration and the researcher affirms Devon expertise.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_2F_Text_OhIsThatS.text: Oh, is that so?\pDEVON's technological expertise\nis outstanding, I tell you.$

replies.text: He's still proud of the machine, even when we aren't using it today.
Our refusal does not evaluate the technology's actual capability.
We can wait until we're ready to make that decision.
It is a big choice. I'm glad nobody forced a quick answer.
Bringing a creature into our care deserves a little thought first.
The inventor accepts a declined demonstration while preserving the sales pitch.
His confidence has survived our lack of participation.
We can ask more questions about the process before committing a fossil.
An old remnant can remain quiet while we decide what follows.
We don't owe curiosity a decision before we're comfortable.
I'd ask what the process requires after the Pokemon is revived.

contexts.subject: A student is trading Pokemon with a friend.

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_TradingR.text: I'm trading POKéMON with my friend\nright now.$

replies.text: An actual lesson happening right in the middle of being excited.
They are learning an exchange process through a real transaction with a peer.
Let them finish. They need to pay attention.
They seem pleased to share something with each other.
A friend makes learning a new thing less intimidating.
The practical portion of the curriculum has acquired a personal audience.
A school activity with unusually interesting passengers.
They should check the exchange details before confirming.
Two little journeys are about to change who walks beside them.
Knowing the other Trainer makes it easier to ask about the Pokemon's habits.
I'd ask what made them choose this particular trade afterward.

contexts.subject: A student is excited to receive a long-wanted Seedot.

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_AlwaysWa.text: I always wanted a SEEDOT, and\nI'm finally getting one!$

replies.text: A long-standing wish is about to arrive wearing an acorn hat.
A particular interest can make the first chance to care for a Pokemon memorable.
Good. Now comes learning how to look after it.
I like the feeling in finally. It carries a lot of waiting.
I'd ask what they have learned about keeping Seedot comfortable.
A much-anticipated character is finally due to make an entrance.
An exceptionally small dream with a very satisfactory shape.
Enthusiasm is a good start. Preparation will help the first days go well.
A wish can be small enough to sit quietly beside you.
They already have a place for that Pokemon in their imagination.
I'd love to hear why Seedot became the one they hoped for.

contexts.subject: A student explains involuntary self-injury under battle confusion and recovery after leaving battle.

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_Confused.text:
You know how some POKéMON moves can
confuse a POKéMON?\pA confused POKéMON will sometimes
attack itself without meaning to.\pBut once it leaves battle, it will
return to normal.$

replies.text: That's awful for the Pokemon. It isn't choosing to hurt itself.
Confusion changes control of an action rather than reflecting a deliberate intention.
Pull a confused partner out if it needs help. Don't blame it.
It must be frightening to have your own movement stop making sense.
We should give it a calmer moment, not another shouted demand.
A cruel complication in which the actor loses command of its own actions.
One more reason not to mistake every action for a choice.
Switching out can remove the problem. Keep that option ready.
A body can become unfamiliar for a moment. Kindness should remain familiar.
The partner needs us to notice the condition before judging the result.
I'd watch closely for those signs instead of waiting for it to happen twice.

contexts.subject: The teacher gives a Quick Claw while jokingly warning inattentive students; bag-full failure invalidates the gift offer.

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_Students.text: Students who don't study get a little\ntaste of my QUICK CLAW.\pWhether or not you are a good student \nwill be evident from the way you use\lthis item.$

replies.text: That lesson came with a claw and a surprisingly pointed attendance policy.
She intends its use as a practical assessment of what a student understands.
We can learn the item without endorsing the threat in that introduction.
I think I would sit very straight in this classroom.
A demonstration will teach more than making students nervous.
The teacher has selected an unusually tactile metaphor for poor study habits.
An educational accessory with a rather alarming disciplinary reputation.
I'd ask what decisions she expects the holder to make differently.
A lesson should leave understanding, not just an anxious silence.
The useful gift doesn't need the intimidating flourish to matter.
I'd ask a student how the teacher actually explains its use.

contexts.subject: Scott introduces his Trainer scouting and recommends obtaining Cut in Rustboro.

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_ScottMet.text:
Hello? Didn't we meet before?
I think back in PETALBURG CITY.\pLet me introduce myself.
My name's SCOTT.\pI've been traveling everywhere in
search of outstanding TRAINERS.\pMore specifically, I'm looking for
POKéMON battle experts.\pSo, what brings you to this SCHOOL?
Are you a TRAINER, too?\pThe first thing you should do is to
have a POKéMON learn the move CUT.\pIf I remember correctly, someone in
this town has CUT.$

replies.text: He is looking for battle experts, and we're still collecting useful lessons.
He has offered a concrete local lead alongside his introduction.
Cut is useful. We can follow up without trying to impress him.
Being noticed by someone looking for experts makes a classroom feel different.
I'd rather learn the next useful thing than hurry to look accomplished.
The talent scout interrupts the first chapter with a sensible errand.
Potential expertise has been assigned some preliminary tree work.
We should ask the local resident for the HM and learn its limits.
A larger future can begin with one small obstacle understood.
He sees a Trainer to assess; we still get to choose our own pace.
I'd ask what he notices in the decisions of a good beginner.

contexts.subject: Scott recognizes the Stone Badge but says it cannot show how the player actually battles.

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_ScottMet.text:
Hello? Didn't we meet before?
I think back in PETALBURG CITY.\pLet me introduce myself.
My name's SCOTT.\pI've been traveling everywhere in
search of outstanding TRAINERS.\pMore specifically, I'm looking for
POKéMON battle experts.\pOh, what's that?
It's a STONE BADGE, isn't it?\pThat's pretty impressive, I'd say, for
a starting TRAINER like yourself.\pBut, you know, I would've loved to see
you in battle.\pIt's hard to tell what you're like as
a TRAINER from a LEAGUE BADGE.$

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_ScottSto.text:
SCOTT: Oh, what's that?\pIt's a STONE BADGE, isn't it?
That's pretty impressive, I'd say.\pBut, you know, I would've loved to see
you in battle.\pIt's hard to tell what you're like as
a TRAINER from a LEAGUE BADGE.$

replies.text: The badge tells him we did it. It doesn't tell him how many nervous faces I made.
An outcome records success without revealing the process that produced it.
Fair point. A Trainer's choices matter more than the shine in the case.
It's nice that he wants to see more than the finished result.
A badge doesn't show the practice, the mistakes, or how the team was treated.
The review acknowledges the award while requesting access to the actual performance.
A certificate has declined to become a full biography. Sensible.
Watching a battle would reveal far more about planning and adaptation.
A mark can remember a moment without holding its whole shape.
He treats the badge as a beginning to the conversation rather than its answer.
I'd ask which parts of a battle he watches most carefully.

contexts.subject: Scott sees student potential but does not yet know their talent levels.

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_StudentT.text: SCOTT: Hmm…\pThe talent levels of the students here\nare unknown. The potential's there.$

replies.text: A classroom full of people who haven't become their future selves yet.
He is distinguishing possible growth from currently observed ability.
Give them time and proper teaching before judging the result.
I like that not knowing still leaves room for hope.
People learn better when they aren't treated as finished products.
A cast of unwritten futures, mercifully spared a final review.
Potential: the respectable scientific term for wait and see.
The teaching environment matters as much as the first signs of aptitude.
A seed does not need to resemble a tree to be worth tending.
I'd want every student to get room to try, not only the obvious standouts.
I'd ask what the quietest student is excited to learn.

contexts.subject: The coin purchase has completed successfully.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_ThankYouHer.text: Thank you very much!\nHere are your COINS!$

replies.text: Our money has become smaller money with a much more specialized address.
The purchase completed. The coins are now available in the case.
Set aside what we're willing to spend before starting.
I would rather decide a stopping point while everything is still quiet.
Let's keep enough ordinary money for the rest of the trip.
The admission tokens have been acquired; the evening need not become an epic.
Our funds have changed costume. Their finite quantity remains.
We should check the balance and keep a simple limit in mind.
A small handful can still represent a great deal of work.
A budget is easier to keep before the room gets exciting.
I'd remember what we came to enjoy rather than chase every machine.

contexts.subject: The clerk cannot sell coins because the player lacks a Coin Case.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_NeedCoinCas.text: Okay, you wanted some COINS for\nthe games?\pBut you don't have a COIN CASE for\nstowing the COINS.$

replies.text: We arrived at the coin shop without anywhere to put the shop's particular coins.
The missing case prevents the transaction before any money changes hands.
Need the proper container first. Clear enough.
At least the problem is something small we can sort out.
Better to know before handing over the money.
The preliminary errand has acquired a preliminary errand of its own.
Special currency, special pocket. Administrative elegance.
We can locate the case before returning to buy anything.
Even a small pastime has its particular threshold.
The clerk gave us a useful reason rather than simply refusing.
I'd ask where visitors usually get a case in town.

contexts.subject: The requested coin purchase fails because the player lacks money.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_DontHaveEno.text: Um… You don't appear to have\nenough money…$

replies.text: The purse has voted to keep this visit short.
The requested amount exceeds our available funds. No purchase occurred.
Leave it for now. We have other things to pay for.
There is no need to feel embarrassed or keep trying the same answer.
Food and travel should come before more game coins.
Our financial narrator has closed this particular subplot.
A remarkably clear spending limit has presented itself.
We can choose a smaller plan instead of trying to force this one.
An empty hand can also be an instruction to pause.
The room's excitement doesn't get to decide what we can afford.
I'd find something else in town to enjoy today.

contexts.subject: The player cancels buying coins and the clerk wishes them well.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_DontNeedCoi.text: Oh… You don't need COINS, then?\nGood luck on your adventure!$

replies.text: A polite goodbye, and all our ordinary coins stayed ordinary.
The transaction was canceled without changing our funds.
We're done here for now. Good time to move on.
I'm glad deciding not to buy something can be this simple.
Sometimes keeping the money for another day is the pleasant choice.
The proposed purchase exits quietly, leaving no financial cliffhanger.
A successful encounter with the word no. Refreshing.
We can come back with a clearer plan if we want to play later.
A hand can close around what it chooses to keep.
The welcome didn't vanish when the purchase did.
I'd say thanks and see what else this afternoon offers.

contexts.subject: The coin purchase cannot complete because the Coin Case is full.

replies.text: We have reached the official edge of how many tiny round things fit.
Capacity, rather than funds, is the limiting condition. No additional purchase occurred.
Enough coins already. We don't need to buy more.
That seems like a useful point to stop at the counter.
A full case is a good reminder to use what we have thoughtfully.
The treasury has declared itself physically complete.
Abundance has met the zipper. A decisive opponent.
Check the actual balance before making another purchase request.
A container can know when enough has arrived.
There is no need to treat every limit as something to work around.
I'd decide what we actually want from this visit before using any.

contexts.subject: The player exits the prize-selection session without a new selection.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_OhIsThatSo.text: Oh, is that so? \nYou need to save some COINS before\lcoming back here.$

replies.text: The prize can stay on its shelf while we decide what matters to us.
The selection session has ended. This farewell does not establish a purchase.
No rush. Keep the coins until we know what we want.
I prefer leaving undecided to choosing because somebody is waiting.
A prize is nicer when you have a real place or use for it.
The display remains an assortment of possibilities rather than an obligation.
The dolls will endure another evening of remaining merchandise.
We can compare the options away from the counter.
A wanted thing need not become ours today.
Walking away is part of choosing, too.
I'd look at the whole visit before deciding what souvenir belongs to it.

contexts.subject: A patron explains that the games require coins.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_CoinsAreNee.text: COINS are needed to play here\nin the GAME CORNER.$

replies.text: The games have their own little money ecosystem.
The local currency separates play spending from ordinary purchases.
We know the requirement. We can decide if we want to take part.
It helps when someone explains the small thing everybody else assumes you know.
I'll keep our meal money separate from whatever we choose to spend here.
Every institution has a ritual; this one's is converting perfectly usable money.
A room with a currency and remarkably few essential goods.
We should learn the costs before turning the first coin into a game.
A threshold can be made of small metal circles.
A simple explanation can make an unfamiliar room feel less awkward.
I'd ask which game they actually enjoy, apart from the prizes.

contexts.subject: A patron describes roulette outcomes as luck rather than reliable skill.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_RouletteOnl.text: This ROULETTE thing…\nIt's rather demanding.\pWin or lose, it's only by luck.$

replies.text: The wheel has declined to become predictable just because somebody asked nicely.
A streak does not supply control over a chance-based outcome.
Then don't count on it paying for anything important.
I wouldn't want the next spin to decide how I feel about the whole day.
A little entertainment is easier to enjoy when dinner doesn't depend on it.
The wheel is an indifferent critic with no obligation to admire persistence.
Chance is notorious for not accepting complaints.
We can set a limit without needing to predict a winning pattern.
A turning circle is not a promise to return what it takes.
It's useful that he says so plainly amid all the excitement.
I'd ask whether he still enjoys the game when nothing comes back.

contexts.subject: The doll owner wants another prize but cannot win the jackpot.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_CantWinJack.text: There's a prize I want, but I can't win\nthe jackpot.$

replies.text: That prize has become very good at making the next attempt sound tempting.
Wanting the reward does not improve the probability of obtaining it.
Don't let a shelf decide how long the day lasts.
It sounds as if the waiting has stopped being much fun.
I'd take a break before deciding whether one more try is really worthwhile.
A coveted object has appointed itself the author of an increasingly long afternoon.
The jackpot continues its distinguished career as something not happening.
Compare the time and coins already spent with what the prize actually means.
A small longing can stretch a room until it has no visible end.
It is all right to like the prize and still choose to leave it.
I'd ask what drew her to that particular doll in the first place.

contexts.subject: The offered spare starter doll cannot be accepted because decoration storage is full.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_YouWantItBu.text: Huh?\nYou want it, but not right now?$

replies.text: The doll has been offered a home that is temporarily all furniture and no room.
The transfer failed for lack of decoration capacity. It remains with her.
We can return once there's space. No need to cram it in.
I'm glad she leaves the offer open without sounding hurt.
A nice gift deserves somewhere better than the edge of a pile.
The prospective new resident has encountered a housing shortage.
Our decor has developed a remarkably firm admissions policy.
We should organize storage before trying the gift again.
A welcome can remain warm while a place is being made.
She understood that the practical problem wasn't a rejection.
I'd thank her for keeping it safe in the meantime.

contexts.subject: The girl presses the spare doll offer after the player declines; this branch gives no doll.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_DontBeNegat.text: Oh, don't be so negative!\nYou can have this!$

replies.text: She is still offering, but our answer hasn't quietly turned into yes.
Her insistence does not complete a transfer. The doll remains unreceived.
We said no. That doesn't need to become a negotiation.
It is difficult when a kind offer doesn't leave room to refuse.
Not wanting another doll doesn't mean we dislike her generosity.
The rejected gift has returned for an unscheduled second audition.
An offer determined to outlive its answer.
She can keep the spare for someone who actually wants it.
A freely given thing needs a freely opened hand.
Calling a refusal negative is an unfair little push.
I'd thank her warmly while keeping the answer clear.

contexts.subject: A patron points the player to the neighboring woman for a Coin Case.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_NeedCoinCas.text: Hey, kid, if you want to play here,\nyou need a COIN CASE.\pI think the young lady next door\nhad one. Go see her!$

replies.text: A missing piece of equipment with an address conveniently attached.
He has supplied a nearby lead rather than only naming the problem.
Next door. We can ask without wandering town.
It's kind of him to notice a beginner might need directions.
We should ask the woman what she wants before assuming it's free.
The obstacle has been reduced to a very short side quest.
At last, advice whose destination is within ordinary walking patience.
Useful local knowledge saves a lot of unnecessary searching.
Someone nearby may hold the small thing that opens the next door.
He gives us enough information to approach her politely.
I'd ask whether he knows how she came to have a spare.

contexts.subject: A patron calls the Game Corner his favorite part of Mauville.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_MauvilleSom.text: MAUVILLE has something for\neveryone.\pFor me, it's the GAME CORNER.$

replies.text: He has found his particular corner of Mauville, very literally.
Different local amenities serve different preferences. This is his.
Fine place to enjoy himself, if he knows when to stop.
It's nice to hear where someone feels pleased to spend an ordinary afternoon.
I'd make sure the rest of his day still gets a turn too.
The town receives a glowing review from one carefully chosen seat.
A city judged by a single favorite room. Honest methodology, at least.
I'd ask what he enjoys about the place beyond the possibility of winning.
A person can find belonging in an unlikely small routine.
His favorite doesn't have to become everyone's favorite for the town to work.
I'd ask what else he would show a first-time visitor.

contexts.subject: An old man advises checking different roulette table costs against available coins.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_RouletteTab.text: The ROULETTE tables have different\nrates.\pCheck your COINS if you're going to\npick a table.$

replies.text: The tables look similar, but the little numbers have different appetites.
The rate determines how quickly a fixed coin supply can be spent.
Check the cost first. Easy rule to remember.
I would rather understand the choice before sitting down.
A little arithmetic keeps the evening from surprising the purse.
The furniture is identical; the financial consequences are not.
An excellent reminder to read the expensive little details.
We should compare cost per play rather than just the appearance of the table.
The same circle can take a different toll.
Knowing the price makes the choice properly ours.
I'd ask which rate he prefers and how he limits the visit.

contexts.subject: A cook realizes the games have distracted him from returning to work.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_EasyToLoseT.text: It's easy to lose track of time in here. \nI should get back to work.$

replies.text: The clock has kept doing its job while he forgot about his.
Attention-heavy activities can distort a person's sense of elapsed time.
He knows he needs to go. Best stand up now.
Thinking about leaving can take longer than leaving if you keep postponing it.
As one cook to another: go before somebody has to cover the whole kitchen.
The working day has returned to interrupt an absorbing subplot.
The phrase one more minute has apparently developed several sequels.
A reminder set before playing would make the next visit easier to manage.
A turning game can make the rest of the day feel still. It isn't.
He has noticed the problem. I hope he follows the thought through to the door.
I'd offer a quick goodbye instead of another reason to stay talking.

contexts.subject: A patron explains the maximum three-coin slot wager.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_UpTo3CoinsC.text: Up to three COINS can be used to play\nthe SLOTS.$

replies.text: Three is the ceiling, not an instruction to use the whole ceiling.
A permitted maximum does not establish an optimal personal choice.
We can spend less. The machine won't be offended.
It's useful to know the limit before the room makes everything feel hurried.
I'd decide the total for the visit before choosing the amount for one turn.
The game permits a flourish; our budget may prefer restraint.
A small maximum repeated often remains a potentially large total.
Track the cumulative spending, not only the cost of one play.
Many small circles can make a very long chain.
The option should serve what we want, not choose for us.
I'd ask which part of the game changes with the number used.

contexts.subject: A patron describes the difficult seven stop and Reel Time bonus.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_DifficultTo.text: It's very difficult to make it stop\nright on “7.”\pIf it stops on “7” during the REEL TIME\nbonus game, you'll receive extra COINS.$

replies.text: That seven has a very tiny doorway and very good evasive manners.
A difficult timing condition does not become reliable through wishing.
Try it for fun. Don't make a plan that needs the bonus.
I can imagine feeling the missed moment long after it passes.
A near miss is still a miss. Best remember that before trying all afternoon.
The elusive mark has been assigned a suspenseful supporting role.
A symbol with an impressively successful avoidance strategy.
We should understand the timing without treating a close attempt as a guarantee.
Almost can keep a person waiting far longer than never.
I'd enjoy a good attempt without making the next one a debt to it.
I'd ask whether he remembers his good stops more clearly than the misses.

contexts.subject: A patron explains lightning bolts, Reel Time chances, and a rare large bonus sequence.

MauvilleCity_GameCorner_Text_HeresSomeSl.text:
Here's some information for you
about the SLOTS.\pThe more lightning bolts you stock,
the more REEL TIME chances you get.\pIn a game with the maximum five
REEL TIME chances…\pIt is possible to receive four regular
bonuses, then a big bonus.\pThat would total 660 COINS, but it's
very difficult to get.$

replies.text: That's a very long ladder of maybes before the big pile of coins.
The maximum reward requires a specific sequence. Its size says little about its likelihood.
Rare bonus means don't count on it. Keep the visit sensible.
All those possibilities could make waiting for the best one feel endless.
I would enjoy an ordinary bit of play rather than make the rare result the whole point.
A spectacular ending is described in enough detail to tempt an unwary audience.
An elaborate chain of conditions wearing the cheerful face of a prize.
The sequence is useful to understand, but we should keep probability separate from possibility.
A far light can be real without being a promise to reach it.
She includes how difficult it is. That part deserves equal attention.
I'd ask what a normal visit looks like instead of only the most exciting one.

contexts.subject: The bard is disappointed that the player declined to hear his song.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_BardF.text: Oh…\nYou've left me feeling the blues…$

replies.text: The song hasn't started, and we've already reached the sad verse.
His disappointment doesn't mean our refusal was inappropriate.
He can offer. We can decline without needing a reason.
I understand feeling shy about sharing something, but an audience needs a choice.
Maybe another listener will have more time for it.
The performance has been canceled; the lament has regrettably continued.
A musical refusal has produced an unrequested emotional encore.
He could ask a little later instead of treating this as a final verdict.
A closed ear today is not a judgment on every note.
I would be kind without pretending we promised to stay.
I'd wish him a good afternoon and let the moment pass.

contexts.subject: The bard is disappointed when the player declines or cancels writing lyrics.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_BardF.text: Oh…\nYou've left me feeling the blues…$

replies.text: Enjoying a song and having spare lyrics in your head are rather different talents.
Declining to write doesn't establish a negative assessment of his music.
We aren't obliged to fix the song just because we heard it.
Sometimes I can listen carefully and still not know what words belong there.
Creative help is better when somebody actually wants to give it.
The audience has been invited to become staff and politely refused.
The lyrics remain his problem. A surprisingly healthy arrangement.
He can keep experimenting without making a stranger responsible for the result.
A word arrives more freely when it isn't pulled by the wrist.
Listening was already a bit of our time. It doesn't owe the next bit.
I'd thank him for singing without inventing a contribution we don't have.

contexts.subject: The bard accepts the approved new lyrics and will keep performing the song.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_IllSi.text: Okay! That's it, then.\nI'll sing this song for a while.$

replies.text: Our words have acquired legs in the form of someone else's singing.
The revised lyrics are confirmed and saved as his continuing version.
Good. We helped him make something he'll actually use.
It's a lovely feeling when somebody gives your words a voice.
A little shared work can keep making somebody happy after you leave.
The collaboration has reached publication by repeated public performance.
Our contribution has been sentenced to a hopefully pleasant life in song.
Hearing the trial version before approving it was useful.
A few words can travel on breath farther than their author.
He wants to stay with the version we made together. That's a warm compliment.
I'd enjoy hearing what it sounds like after he's lived with it a while.

contexts.subject: After the song has been changed, the bard wishes more people could hear it.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_WishI.text: Oh, what a moving song…\nI wish I could play it for others…$

replies.text: He likes the song enough to want the room around it to grow.
A satisfying result often creates an impulse to share the work.
A good audience can start with one person who listens.
I understand wanting a song to find the person who might need it.
Something enjoyed is often something you want to pass along.
The performer has become the strongest advocate for a wider engagement.
A song searching for a larger room. At least it can pack lightly.
He could start by asking people nearby whether they want to listen.
A small voice can wish for a wider piece of air.
I'd keep the invitation welcoming rather than make listening feel compulsory.
I'd ask where he most enjoys singing when people are around.

contexts.subject: The hipster has already taught the player and wants to share the word with others.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_IAlre.text: But, hey, I taught you what's hip and\nhappening already.\pI'd like to spread the good word to\nother folks.$

replies.text: Our lesson is over. The fashionable word has other appointments.
He has no additional lesson for us in his present state.
Fair enough. Other people can have a turn.
I like that he wants to spread the conversation beyond one visitor.
A little novelty is easier to enjoy when nobody keeps serving the same helping.
The linguistic evangelist moves on to a promising new audience.
We have received our ration of being current.
We can use what we learned instead of waiting for another announcement.
A little saying travels by finding another willing ear.
I wonder whether the next person will use it quite differently.
I'd listen for the word turning up somewhere unexpected later.

contexts.subject: The hipster finds the player already knows his available trendy sayings.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_IveGo.text: But, hey, you already know a lot about\nwhat's hip and happening.\pI've got nothing new to teach you!$

replies.text: We have accidentally become too up-to-date for the update desk.
His available vocabulary contains no new entry for us.
Then we're set. No need to force another lesson.
It's pleasant when someone can just admit they've nothing to add.
Knowing enough for today is a perfectly comfortable place to stop.
The student has overtaken the fashionable syllabus.
Our cultural currency remains valid for at least this conversation.
A useful system recognizes an empty update rather than pretending there is one.
A small cup can be full without needing to overflow.
He doesn't turn the lack of a new saying into a competition.
I'd ask what he finds interesting beyond the latest phrase.

contexts.subject: The hipster teaches a phrase but tells the player to ask their parents what it means.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_HaveY.text: Hey, have you heard about\n“{STR_VAR_1}”?\pWhat's it mean? Well…\nAsk your daddy or mommy, okay?$

replies.text: He delivered the word and outsourced the explanation to our family.
Knowing a term's sound is not the same as understanding its meaning.
I would rather know what I'm saying before repeating it.
That is an awkward amount of mystery to place inside a small word.
A useful lesson should include what the new thing is actually for.
The language instructor has abruptly transferred the final chapter to another author.
A definition conspicuously absent from the lesson. How fashionable.
I'd ask someone who can explain the context clearly.
A word can leave a mouth before it finds a meaning. Better to wait.
Being current isn't worth accidentally saying something you don't understand.
I'd ask where he heard it used, then work out whether it belongs in our speech.

contexts.subject: The decoration trader is disappointed that the player declines his initial offer.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Trade.text: Oh…\nYou've left me feeling the blues…$

replies.text: We declined the furniture, not his entire existence. An important distinction.
A rejected proposal isn't a rejection of the person offering it.
No trade today. He can put the guilt away.
I wish he didn't make a simple answer sound like we hurt him.
Maybe another visitor will want exactly what he's brought.
The opening offer has been declined; the emotional negotiation persists.
An unexpectedly melancholy introduction to used furniture.
An exchange works best when both people have a clear use for it.
A door can remain friendly even when it doesn't open to barter.
His disappointment is real, but it doesn't become our obligation.
I'd keep the farewell kind and the answer steady.

contexts.subject: The decoration trader reminds the player that their allowed trade is already complete.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_WeveA.text: But we've traded decorations already,\nyou and I.$

replies.text: He remembers our furniture transaction better than I remember my own pockets.
The existing trade record prevents another exchange in this state.
Already done. We can leave him to it.
It's nice that he recognizes the earlier meeting.
One fair exchange is a perfectly good result for a visit.
The completed bargain declines to be cast as a recurring scene.
The furniture has moved on. We should perhaps do the same.
We can work with the decoration we received instead of trying to repeat the process.
Some meetings leave a single object behind and are complete.
He is setting a clear limit without turning it into a dispute.
I'd ask how the decoration we gave him is working out.

contexts.subject: The player cancels selecting a decoration, and the trader feels unwanted.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_YouDo.text: You don't want anything?\nI feel unwanted…$

replies.text: His collection didn't fit our plans. That isn't a verdict on the man carrying it.
No preferred item was selected. That does not imply a personal judgment.
We're allowed to look and leave. No need for this.
I might like him better if choosing nothing felt safer.
A room only has so much space, and tastes differ.
The catalog has failed to produce a sale and taken it rather personally.
A rejected desk is apparently a rejected soul now.
We should choose for an actual use, not to avoid disappointing the seller.
A thing can be lovely without belonging in our home.
I would reassure him briefly without pretending to want something.
I'd thank him for showing the collection and let that be enough.

contexts.subject: The trade cannot proceed because the player owns no decorations to exchange.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_YouDo.text: Uh… Wait a second. You don't have a\nsingle piece of decoration!$

replies.text: We have arrived at the swap with an extremely minimalist contribution.
An exchange requires an item from both parties. We have none eligible to offer.
Nothing to trade. We'll come back when that changes.
I suppose a bare room leaves a lot of room for future plans.
No sense promising something we don't have.
The barter scene is missing half its essential props.
Our impeccable lack of clutter has become temporarily inconvenient.
We need to obtain a decoration before this service can apply.
An empty shelf is a beginning, not a failure.
It's an understandable mistake for a first visit.
I'd ask where beginners usually find something worth exchanging.

contexts.subject: The player cancels offering their own decoration, and the trader is disappointed.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_YouDo.text: You won't trade with me?\nI feel unwanted…$

replies.text: Wanting his decoration didn't mean we had to stop liking our own.
The player declined the proposed outgoing item. No exchange was completed.
Keep what matters to us. A trade has to be worth both sides.
Sometimes you don't notice an attachment until someone asks you to give it away.
We can appreciate the offer and still want to keep our familiar things.
A coveted acquisition has failed to defeat an existing attachment.
The furniture has successfully appealed against relocation.
It's useful to compare the real cost before confirming a change.
A familiar object can hold a place no new thing quite fills.
He can be disappointed without turning our preference into a personal slight.
I'd ask ourselves which decoration we'd genuinely be comfortable parting with.

contexts.subject: The decoration trade fails because its category storage is full.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Youve.text: You've got all the {STR_VAR_2}S that can\nbe stored. You've no room for this.$

replies.text: Our collection has shut the door before the new decoration could introduce itself.
The relevant category is at capacity. The exchange did not complete.
Sort the storage first. No reason to lose track of what we have.
I would rather make a deliberate place than hurry something out of the way.
A roomful of things should still leave room to use them.
The proposed new resident has been declined by the housing office.
Abundance has once again become an administrative problem.
We should check category capacity, not just the total number of objects.
A collection can ask us to pause and look at what is already there.
Wanting one more thing is a good time to reassess the whole arrangement.
I'd choose what to keep before coming back to bargain.

contexts.subject: The decoration exchange has completed and the trader sends the new decoration to storage.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_SendD.text: Then we'll trade!\nI'll send my decoration to your PC.$

replies.text: Two decorations get new homes, and two people get a little change of scenery.
The completed exchange updates both collections as agreed.
Done. Let's remember what we traded away.
I wonder how the familiar room will feel with that one detail changed.
It's nice when two people can each make use of the other's spare thing.
The cast has traded props, and both sets can begin their redesign.
A successful rearrangement without carrying furniture down the street. Civilized.
We can inspect the received decoration and plan where it fits.
A once-familiar thing will begin a different little history elsewhere.
The best exchange feels chosen on both sides.
I'd enjoy seeing how the decoration changes the room once it's placed.

contexts.subject: The storyteller is disappointed that the player declines or cancels hearing a tale.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Story.text: Oh…\nYou've left me feeling the blues…$

replies.text: A story can wait until the ears have time to sit down properly.
Choosing not to listen now is not a judgment on the tale's quality.
We can leave. An audience isn't something he's owed.
I'd rather hear a story when I can actually give it my attention.
Good company lets a person have somewhere else to be.
The narrator has found a listener with an inconveniently independent schedule.
The legend will have to survive another hour without our assistance.
He could offer a shorter version instead of treating the refusal as a disaster.
An untold story can remain safe for another day.
A disappointed host can still accept a kind farewell.
I'd ask when he is usually here if we want to return.

contexts.subject: The storyteller judges the player supplied accomplishment insufficiently legendary.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_NotWo.text: Hmm…\nI'm not satisfied…\pI wish you would bring me news worthy\nof being called a legend.$

replies.text: Our day was still ours, even if it doesn't fit his enormous story hat.
His threshold for legend is a preference, not a measure of our experience's value.
We don't need to turn the trip into a performance for him.
Small stories matter to the people who were there too.
An ordinary good day doesn't have to become an epic to be worth having.
The editor requests a larger explosion of significance. I respectfully disagree.
A perfectly adequate life has failed the dramatization requirements.
I'd ask what qualifies before trying to satisfy a vague target.
A quiet moment can remain dear without becoming a monument.
He can want a grand tale. We can still value the one we brought.
I'd rather hear why the event mattered than how impressive the count sounds.

contexts.subject: The storyteller enthusiastically turns a buffered player activity count into a new legend.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_YouDi.text:
What's that?!
You… You…\p{STR_VAR_2}
{STR_VAR_1} time(s)?!\pThat is indeed magnificent!
It's the birth of a new legend!$

replies.text: An ordinary habit has put on a cape while we weren't watching.
The count is real; the interpretation as a legend is his embellishment.
Glad he's enjoying the story. We still know what the days actually felt like.
It's odd hearing a little routine described as something enormous.
There must be a lot of ordinary effort tucked inside that number.
Our daily life has acquired a narrator with a generous scale of importance.
A statistic has escaped its ledger and become folklore.
I'd keep the measurement separate from the more colorful conclusion.
Many small moments can gather into a shape we never noticed forming.
His delight is real, even if the grand title is a bit much.
I'd tell him one detail the number doesn't capture.

contexts.subject: After telling a recorded tale, the storyteller wonders about other undiscovered Trainer stories.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Could.text: It gets me thinking, could there be\nother TRAINERS with more impressive\llegends awaiting discovery?$

replies.text: Somewhere, another Trainer is doing something ordinary that he could make enormous.
A limited collection should invite further observation rather than a claim of completeness.
Plenty of people out there. Ask them what they've done.
There are probably quiet stories nobody has thought to ask about.
I'd listen to people who don't expect their day to sound impressive.
An anthology has discovered the excellent problem of having more possible chapters.
The world contains a regrettable surplus of untapped anecdotes.
He could gather accounts from different towns instead of only comparing large totals.
A road can hold stories that have never needed an audience.
His curiosity might be kinder if it leaves room for modest lives too.
I'd ask whose story surprised him most when he first heard it.

contexts.subject: Giddy is disappointed that the player declines his opening story invitation.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Giddy.text: Oh…\nYou've left me feeling the blues…$

replies.text: His story wanted a listener, but our afternoon hasn't signed the agreement.
Declining the invitation is a normal limit, not evidence of unkindness.
Not today. We can say it gently and still mean it.
I don't like disappointing people, but sometimes I need a quieter moment.
A friendly offer needs room for a friendly no.
The forthcoming anecdote has encountered a scheduling conflict.
We have spared ourselves an unknown quantity of scintillation.
He could ask whether another time would suit us better.
A story can wait beside its teller without being abandoned.
I'd keep the farewell warm without pretending we can stay.
I'd leave him free to find someone who actually has time to listen.

contexts.subject: Giddy finishes his variable anecdotes and warmly invites another conversation.

MauvilleCity_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_WeSho.text: That's about it, I think…\pWe should chat again!\nBye-bye!$

replies.text: He found the end of his thoughts! I was beginning to wonder where it lived.
The exchange has reached a clear closing without requiring agreement on every detail.
A friendly goodbye. Good place to leave it.
I like that he enjoyed simply having someone listen.
A chat can be a good part of the day without needing to solve anything.
The wandering monologue has discovered a cheerful exit.
The final sentence has arrived. I welcome it warmly.
We can appreciate the conversation and still make room for the rest of our plans.
A few shared words can leave a small warmth after the voices stop.
His invitation sounds sincere, even if his sense of a short chat is adventurous.
I'd wave goodbye and remember which thought made us smile.

contexts.subject: The Fan Club chairman brother explains how affection affects Return and Frustration after a TM gift.

PacifidlogTown_House2_Text_ExplainReturn.text: If a POKéMON likes you a lot, RETURN's\npower is enhanced.\pIf it doesn't like you, FRUSTRATION's\npower goes up.$

replies.text: A move can show how things are going between partners. That's worth listening to.
The two moves depend on opposite ends of the friendship measure.
I'd rather build trust than build a plan around a partner resenting us.
A feeling becoming power doesn't make the unhappy feeling something to seek.
Keep the relationship healthy. The battle plan should work around that.
A relationship becomes a mechanic, without ceasing to be a relationship.
An effective grievance is still a grievance.
We should choose moves that fit a well-treated partner rather than manipulate distress.
Power can come from a feeling without telling us that feeling is good to cultivate.
The explanation is useful. The partner's comfort matters beyond the number.
I'd watch how our Pokemon feels about us outside battle too.

contexts.subject: The weekly TM recipient is told how many days remain before another suitable TM is available.

PacifidlogTown_House2_Text_GetGoodTMInXD.text: Oh, yes. In about {STR_VAR_1} or so days,\nI should be getting a good TM or two.\pYou should come see me then.\nI'll give you a TM that's suitable for\lyour POKéMON.$

replies.text: His supply schedule is slower than our ability to ask again.
A timed interval gates the next gift. The stated wait is the relevant constraint.
We'll come back later. No point standing over him.
It's nice to have a reason to stop by again after some time has passed.
We have plenty else to do while he waits for the next supply.
The next installment has a release date rather than a second copy today.
The calendar has declined an encore.
We can note the wait without repeatedly checking the same visit.
Some things arrive with days, not persistence.
He's offering a future kindness, not promising an endless handful now.
I'd plan another visit around the trip rather than make the wait the whole purpose.

contexts.subject: The chairman brother judges the player Pokemon bond moderate and asks for more effort.

PacifidlogTown_House2_Text_PutInSomeMore.text: Hmm…\nIt's not bad, but it's also not good.\pYou, as the TRAINER, need to put in\nsome more effort.$

replies.text: We don't need a grand trick. We need to keep showing up kindly.
The assessment suggests an ordinary middle range, not hostility.
Spend good time together. No need to panic over a middling report.
There is room to get closer without making the present sound terrible.
A dependable meal and a gentle routine are useful effort.
The reviewer requests development rather than a dramatic rescue.
Neither disaster nor triumph. A suspiciously normal result.
We can learn which parts of the routine our partner actually enjoys.
A bond can be growing before it looks remarkable.
I'd take the useful suggestion without turning affection into an exam.
I'd notice the small signs of comfort before looking for a bigger verdict.

contexts.subject: An Azurill interaction ends with an observation that it is friendly with its Trainer.

PacifidlogTown_House2_Text_VeryFriendlyW.text: It appears to be very friendly with the\nTRAINER.$

replies.text: That little Azurill has a familiar person it is very glad about.
Its behavior suggests comfort and a strong association with its Trainer.
Good. A small partner should feel safe beside its person.
You can hear a little warmth even in a short meeting.
I like seeing the result of ordinary care in a place like this.
A small cast member provides the most convincing reference for its companion.
A content little creature. An adequately persuasive argument for kindness.
It's useful to notice these small signals, not only obvious distress.
A little body can carry a great deal of trust.
Comfort often shows in how little someone feels they need to guard.
I'd watch how it turns toward the person it knows.

contexts.subject: An Azurill interaction ends with an observation of low affection for its Trainer.

PacifidlogTown_House2_Text_DoesntLikeTra.text: It doesn't appear to like the TRAINER\nvery much.$

replies.text: That little one doesn't seem comfortable with the person who should be helping.

I'd give it space instead of asking it to be friendly for us.
The next useful thing is a gentler routine, not blaming the Azurill.

Unhappiness is not improved by calling the unhappy one difficult.
We don't know the whole history, but the signal deserves a response.
A small guarded creature can make a room feel suddenly less warm.

contexts.subject: A resident admires the player Pokedex and the varied Pokemon encounters behind it.

PacifidlogTown_House3_Text_IsThatAPokede.text: Is that a POKéDEX?\pDid you get to meet a lot of different\nPOKéMON?\pI wish I was like you.$

A small page can point toward a very wide world.
We can share the interesting parts without making their own life sound smaller.

contexts.subject: The birthday Pokemon owner awkwardly insists he is not desperate after the player declines a trade.

PacifidlogTown_House3_Text_NotDesperateO.text: Oh, so you're not going to go through\nwith this?\pThat's cool. I'm not desperate to make\na trade or anything.$

replies.text: That was an impressively casual sentence carrying a rather heavy disappointment.

Let him keep his dignity. No trade is fine.
I know the voice people use when they hope nobody noticed the sting.
We can be kind without reopening the bargain out of guilt.
A wounded salesman has attempted to disguise himself as an uninterested bystander.
Absolutely unconcerned, as announced at extraordinary length.

A wish can retreat behind a deliberately careless voice.
I'd let the recovery stand rather than tease him about it.
I'd ask about the birthday catch if he still wants to chat.

contexts.subject: The trader refuses the wrong species for the Bagon request.

PacifidlogTown_House3_Text_WontAcceptAny.text: No, no, no! I won't accept any\nless than a real {STR_VAR_1}!$

replies.text: Our perfectly real Pokemon is simply real in the wrong category.
The selected species does not meet the exchange condition.
Wrong species. We can stop here or return with the requested one.
I would rather not make our partner stand there feeling unwanted.
He has a specific wish. This one isn't it.
The candidate is genuine, but has arrived for a different role.
An authentic Pokemon has failed an authentic species check.
We should verify the request before choosing another partner.
A refusal to exchange does not diminish the creature beside us.

contexts.subject: The trade completes and the recipient compares the new Pokemon with his previous one.

PacifidlogTown_House3_Text_ItsSubtlyDiff.text: Oh, so this is a {STR_VAR_1}?\pIt's sort of like a {STR_VAR_2},\nand yet it's subtly different.\pThank you!$

replies.text: He's already noticing the new partner instead of treating the trade like a finished errand.

A familiar outline can hold a very different presence.

contexts.subject: After trading, the recipient explains he especially wanted a Bagon raised by another Trainer.

PacifidlogTown_House3_Text_ReallyWantedT.text: I know I could go looking for one\non my own, but…\pBut I really wanted to get a BAGON\nthat another TRAINER caught…$

contexts.subject: A woman wonders where the high-flying Pokemon rumored over Hoenn rests.

PacifidlogTown_House4_Text_PeopleSawHigh.text: People were saying they saw a POKéMON\nflying high above HOENN.\pIs it flying around all the time?\nDoesn't it need to rest somewhere?$

replies.text: Even a very grand sky Pokemon probably appreciates somewhere to put its feet.

A creature can be impressive and still need a peaceful place to rest.

contexts.subject: A child excitedly repeats the idea of a sky Pokemon.

replies.text: Two words, and the whole ceiling feels too low for the excitement.

I like hearing a little voice make the world feel enormous.

contexts.subject: An elder recounts Pacifidlog ancestors spending entire lives aboard boats while searching for something.

PacifidlogTown_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Anc.text: The ancestors of the people in\nPACIFIDLOG were said to have been\lborn on boats and then lived and died \laboard them.\pI understand that they lived that way\nbecause they were searching for\lsomething.$

replies.text: An entire life on a boat makes finding land sound like a major change of furniture.
The account preserves a lifestyle clearly, but leaves the search target unspecified.
That takes endurance. I wonder what kept them going.
Born and growing old with the water always just beneath you.
They must have known the work of making a small space into home.
A generational voyage whose destination has fallen out of the surviving account.
A lifetime at sea. I would have several strongly worded concerns.
I'd compare family accounts to see whether any preserve the missing purpose.
A home can move for years while the same question travels inside it.
The search mattered enough to shape how whole families lived.
I'd ask which parts of that boat life still show in the town today.

contexts.subject: A resident presents the claim that Pacifidlog rests on a Corsola colony.

PacifidlogTown_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_OnC.text: PACIFIDLOG TOWN floats on top of\na colony of CORSOLA.\pIf I told you that, would you believe\nme?$

replies.text: Our downstairs neighbors might be an entire colony with very important structural duties.
That claim would make the settlement's ecology particularly important to understand.
If it's true, they need to look after what's supporting them.
It makes every ordinary step feel a little more connected to something living.
A whole town should be careful about what it sends into the water below.
The foundation may have a much larger cast than the population records suggest.
A living foundation. I would like the maintenance agreement explained.
I'd want to know how the platforms are supported without harming the colony.
A home may rest on many small lives that go unseen.
It's a lovely story, and one that deserves practical care if it is true.
I'd ask whether anyone can show us where the Corsola gather.

contexts.subject: A girl proudly says her Trainer Card is copper and asks about the player card.

PacifidlogTown_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Wha.text: What color is your TRAINER CARD?\nMine's copper!$

replies.text: She sounds proud enough of copper to make it look shiny from here.
The card color provides a compact symbol of recorded accomplishments.
Good for her. Ask what she did to earn it.
I would rather hear the story than compare which color is ahead.
A little mark can stand for a lot of work somebody remembers.
The credentials have become a pleasantly portable conversation starter.
A social introduction conducted through metallic stationery.
I'd ask which achievement changed it most recently.
A small color can hold a long stretch of effort.
She wants to share pride. We can receive that without making it a ranking.
I'd ask which part of earning it she enjoyed most.

contexts.subject: A resident describes the exceptionally skilled Trainers gathering at the distant League.

VerdanturfTown_House_Text_TrainersGather.text: Far away, deep in EVER GRANDE CITY,\nis the POKéMON LEAGUE.\pThe TRAINERS who gather there are\nall frighteningly well skilled.$

replies.text: A faraway room full of people who've also done a lot of walking and practicing.
A selective challenge attracts competitors with substantial experience.
Then we prepare seriously before going.
It sounds distant in more than just miles.
Strong Trainers still need ordinary good habits to keep their teams well.
A formidable cast assembled at the far end of a very long introduction.
An intimidating concentration of people with excellent battle plans.
We can work toward the specific skills needed instead of fearing a vague reputation.
A distant gate grows less mysterious one learned lesson at a time.
Their skill can be something to learn from, not only something to fear.
I'd ask whether the speaker has seen a League battle firsthand.

contexts.subject: A resident argues that successful Trainers need faith in their Pokemon.

VerdanturfTown_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Fai.text: You can't consider yourself a real\nTRAINER if you don't have faith\lin your POKéMON.\pOnly those people who can believe\nin their battling POKéMON can win\lthrough to the very end.$

replies.text: Trusting a partner also means noticing when it needs help, not just cheering louder.
Trust is useful when grounded in knowledge of the partner's actual abilities.
Believe in them, and make decisions that protect that trust.
I like confidence that leaves room for a partner to be tired.
Faith should come with the daily care that makes it reasonable.
A stirring principle, improved considerably by the practical work underneath it.
Belief is welcome. It should not be used as a substitute for a healing item.
Knowing the partner well makes trust more than optimistic guessing.
To believe in a creature is also to believe what its distress tells us.
They deserve support before the final battle as much as during it.
I'd ask what the speaker does when a trusted plan still goes wrong.

contexts.subject: A resident assumes visitors come for the Battle Tent, then considers a personal visit.

VerdanturfTown_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Vis.text:
The reason why anyone would visit
VERDANTURF…\pIt's the BATTLE TENT. It goes without
saying.\pOr is there somebody here that you
came to see?$

replies.text: The town's biggest attraction has competition from simply wanting to see somebody.
Public attractions and personal connections both explain travel.
Could be either. People are a good reason to come somewhere.
Sometimes one familiar person makes a whole town feel worth the trip.
A visit and a shared meal can be the entire plan.
The tourist brochure makes a gracious concession to the existence of relationships.
An itinerary featuring a person instead of a building. Sensible.
It's useful to ask rather than settle on the first assumption.
A place can become important because someone waits there.
I like that they leave room for the quieter reason in the end.
I'd ask who they would travel to another town to see.

contexts.subject: Wally aunt fears being unable to face his parents if he is hurt.

VerdanturfTown_WandasHouse_Text_IfAnythi.text: If anything were to happen to WALLY,\nI would never be able to look his\lparents in PETALBURG in the eye…$

replies.text: She is carrying worry for Wally and the weight of someone else's trust.
Responsibility to family can intensify uncertainty when a young person travels alone.
She needs reliable news about him, not another frightening guess.
It is hard to let someone grow when you promised to keep them safe.
I'd help her get a clear message rather than tell her simply not to worry.
His adventure has left a second story of anxious waiting at home.
An absent child can fill a room with very loud possibilities.
A regular way to check in could help without taking his independence away.
Love can hold fear in both hands and still wish to let go.
She wants to do right by him and by his parents. That's a difficult balance.
I'd ask when she last heard directly from Wally.

contexts.subject: Wally uncle learns that he has left on his own.

VerdanturfTown_WandasHouse_Text_WallySli.text: WALLY's gone away…\nHe slipped off on his own…$

replies.text: Wally has made a decision, and the news is only now catching up with home.
The lack of advance notice is a separate concern from his ability to travel.
Find out where he went before assuming the worst.
That first moment of realizing someone isn't where you expected is awful.
A short message would spare the people at home a lot of guessing.
The young adventurer has left the supporting cast without its next scene.
Independence has neglected to file its departure notice.
We should gather a recent location and a way to contact him.
An empty place can suddenly feel like a question.
He can be capable and still owe his family a little notice.
I'd ask who saw him most recently and what he said about his plans.

contexts.subject: After Victory Road, Wally aunt marvels that his parents would be astonished by his journey.

VerdanturfTown_WandasHouse_Text_WallyWas.text: WALLY was in EVER GRANDE?\pHis parents in PETALBURG would be\nastonished to hear that!$

replies.text: That is going to be a very interesting family conversation when the news arrives.
His demonstrated range has exceeded the family's earlier expectations.
They should hear it from Wally if possible. He earned the telling.
I imagine their surprise making room for a great deal of pride.
Someone should make sure the news reaches them before the rumors do.
The family's quiet child has returned in the account as a seasoned traveler.
An expedition large enough to disturb several relatives' expectations.
I'd help get a clear message to his parents, with the useful details.
A long road can change the way home imagines the one who left.
It is lovely when pride catches up with somebody's real growth.
I'd enjoy hearing which part Wally chooses to tell them first.

contexts.subject: The boy sends Wingull out on its mail errand.

replies.text: The little courier is off, with considerably less packing than we need.
A trained messenger can connect two places without a human escort.
Hope the route is clear. Give it room to leave.
There's something sweet about watching a familiar bird start a familiar task.
Somebody at the other end may be looking forward to that arrival.
A brief instruction launches a journey whose other chapter waits elsewhere.
A remarkably concise dispatch. The bird appears to know the paperwork.
I'd like to know how they taught the route reliably.
A small pair of wings carries a thread between homes.
The boy trusts it to know where it belongs and how to return.
I'd ask who is waiting at the far end of the errand.

contexts.subject: The returned Wingull carries a Mental Herb that its non-Trainer owner offers; failed receipt invalidates the offer.

FortreeCity_House4_Text_WelcomeWingullTa.text:
Good!
Welcome back, WINGULL!\pHuh? What is this?
What is it holding?\pA MENTAL HERB?
It must have picked it up somewhere.\pBut I'm not a TRAINER, so you can
have it.$

replies.text: Wingull brought home a little extra, and the boy found someone who might use it.
He distinguishes what he owns from what he has a practical use for.
Kind offer. Make sure the bird gets its welcome too.
I like that his first reaction was being glad Wingull came back.
A returning friend and an unexpected useful thing. A good afternoon.
The courier has added an unscheduled botanical subplot to the delivery.
A small bird has returned with an inexplicably excellent gratuity.
I'd check the herb's use before assigning it to a partner.
A journey can bring back something no one thought to ask for.
He shares the find without trying to make it more important than the homecoming.
I'd ask whether Wingull often returns carrying surprises.

contexts.subject: A girl mentions her brother past marine research.

SootopolisCity_House5_Text_BrotherUsedTo.text: My big brother used to study the sea.$

replies.text: Her brother studied a subject bigger than the view from the window.
Past work can remain part of how a family knows someone.
Sounds like someone worth asking about these waters.
I wonder which part of the sea he used to come home talking about.
A family remembers the ordinary person behind somebody's research.
A whole professional chapter, introduced by a much shorter family sentence.
The sea offers enough material to keep a sibling talking for years.
I'd ask what he investigated before assuming every sea question was his specialty.
A former pursuit can leave its tide in a person's life.
She says it with the familiarity of a story she has heard many times.
I'd ask what discovery she remembers him being excited about.

contexts.subject: A former researcher describes studying a connection between Sootopolis and Mt Pyre.

SootopolisCity_House5_Text_SootopolisMtP.text: There appears to be some connection\nbetween SOOTOPOLIS and MT. PYRE.\pMy friends and I did some research on\nit at the lab where I used to work.$

replies.text: Two places that seem separate may have a longer conversation underneath them.
A proposed connection calls for comparing evidence from both sites.
Worth hearing what they actually found.
I like discovering that a familiar place has another history beneath it.
I'd ask what brought the research group to that question.
Two distant settings may turn out to share a much older chapter.
A suggestive connection. I trust the evidence is less vague than the introduction.
I'd want to know which observations support the link and which remain uncertain.
Water and mountain can keep different parts of one old memory.
He sounds interested in the work even after leaving the lab.
I'd ask whether there is a record we can look at together.

contexts.subject: The visitor declines the Wailmer Doll and its owner expresses surprise.

SootopolisCity_House6_Text_DontWantThisD.text: Are you sure?\nYou don't want this DOLL?$

replies.text: Declining a very large Wailmer is still a perfectly ordinary kind of no.
The offer was declined. No decoration has been received.
We can say no kindly. We don't need to fill the room to prove gratitude.
I hope she knows we enjoyed visiting even without taking something home.
A warm welcome is already a good thing to give someone.
The prospective guest has declined to adopt the plush supporting cast.
The doll has survived another proposed relocation.
A gift needs a willing recipient, not just available storage.
A kind visit can leave no object behind and still matter.
I'd reassure her about the visit without changing an answer we meant.
I'd ask about the dolls she has kept, if she still feels like talking.

contexts.subject: The Wailmer Doll gift succeeds after this request; later storage failures replace it.

replies.text: A large soft new friend is joining the furniture. I think it will be good at sitting.
The transferred decoration comes with a simple request to preserve it well.
We'll give it a proper place. Kind of her to share it.
She sounds attached enough to want it comfortable in its new home.
A clean, dry spot and no crushing it under the supplies. Simple care.
The plush newcomer arrives bearing a modest condition of continued kindness.
A Wailmer with refreshingly manageable feeding requirements.
We should place it where it won't get caught on rough edges.
A small kindness can leave in the shape of a large soft creature.
It will look best where it feels deliberately welcomed, not squeezed into a gap.
I'd tell her where we plan to put it when we visit again.

contexts.subject: The Wailmer Doll gift cannot fit, so its owner agrees to keep it for later.

SootopolisCity_House6_Text_IllHoldItForY.text: Oh, you want it, but not right now?\nOkay, then I'll hold it for you.$

replies.text: The Wailmer is patiently waiting for our room to become less crowded.
The decoration remains with her because storage prevented the transfer.
We'll make room before coming back. No need to rush her.
It's kind of her to make the delay feel easy.
A soft gift should get a better welcome than being jammed into the last corner.
