contexts.subject: The Fortree trader welcomes the new partner and bids the traded Pokemon farewell.

FortreeCity_House1_Text_MonYouTakeCare.text: Oh, yeah, right on!\p{STR_VAR_1}, welcome!\n{STR_VAR_2}, you take care!$

replies.text: That was a proper little goodbye. Even a happy swap deserves one.
He welcomed one partner while acknowledging the other. A considerate transition.
Good. He remembered to say goodbye, too.
His excitement softened when he spoke to the one leaving. I noticed that.
A warm welcome and a kind goodbye. Both sides of the trade needed those.
He found room for enthusiasm and manners in the same breath. Excellent work.
One new arrival, one small farewell. Neither was treated like spare luggage.
The exchange is complete. Now both trainers get to learn somebody new.
A welcome can face two directions. His nearly did.
I liked that he addressed both Pokemon. Nobody disappeared into the transaction.
I'd ask him later how they're getting along. That welcome sounded promising.

contexts.subject: Sidney accepts defeat and enthusiastically sends the player onward.

EverGrandeCity_SidneysRoom_Text_PostBatt.text: Well, listen to what this loser has\nto say.\pYou've got what it takes to go far.\nNow, go on to the next room and enjoy\lyour next battle!$

replies.text: He lost and still wants us to enjoy ourselves. That's a remarkably sturdy good mood.
His assessment survived a result he disliked. I respect that intellectual flexibility.
A clean loss, a straight answer. Onward.
He didn't make his disappointment our burden. That's kind.
No bitter aftertaste from that battle. He sends us off well.
He introduced himself as the loser and somehow kept command of the room.
Defeat seems to have injured neither his humor nor his hair.
He's already thinking about our next challenge. We should do the same.
He knows when a closed door should become an open one.
He wears defeat comfortably. That takes more confidence than boasting.
I'd enjoy hearing him describe a match he won. This was already lively.

contexts.subject: Phoebe recognizes the bond behind the player team and accepts her mistake.

EverGrandeCity_PhoebesRoom_Text_PostBatt.text:
There's a definite bond between you
and your POKéMON, too.\pI didn't recognize it, so it's only
natural that I lost.\pYup, I'd like to see how far your bond
will carry you.\pGo ahead, move on to the next room.$

replies.text: She spotted what mattered, even if it took a battle to get a good look.
She revised her explanation after observing us. That's a useful habit in an expert.
She gives the whole team credit. Fair assessment.
Being understood after all that effort feels good. Even by an opponent.
She noticed how everyone worked together. That's worth more than a simple compliment.
A gracious correction from someone perfectly capable of making defeat sound mysterious.
She sees the bond now. Apparently it required a fairly forceful introduction.
She found the thing her first assessment missed. Better than defending a bad assumption.
Some ties become visible only when pulled tight. She recognized ours.
She looked past the result and noticed the relationship. I appreciate her eye.
I'd ask what tipped her off. Those little moments between partners interest me.

contexts.subject: Glacia sends the victor onward to test the strength of the League.

EverGrandeCity_GlaciasRoom_Text_PostBatt.text: Advance to the next room.\pAnd there, confirm the truly fearsome\nside of the POKéMON LEAGUE.$

replies.text: She makes the next room sound like a very serious second opinion.
Her conclusion is deliberately provisional. The remaining battles will supply more evidence.
She says there's more ahead. Let's prepare before we walk in.
She still sounds composed. I think that makes the warning land harder.
A victory here doesn't refill anyone's strength. Let's check how the team feels.
She concedes the room without conceding the entire League. Quite precise.
The welcome grows colder as the compliments grow warmer. Efficient arrangement.
Another stage of the challenge remains. We have a moment to assess our resources.
Her warning points onward. It would be foolish to mistake it for empty pride.
She hasn't lost her poise. That lends the next opponent a little extra weight.
I'd like to hear her assessment after we've seen the rest. For now, onward.

contexts.subject: Drake credits a virtuous heart and sends the victor toward the Champion.

EverGrandeCity_DrakesRoom_Text_PostBattl.text:
You deserve every credit for coming
this far as a TRAINER of POKéMON.\pYou do seem to know what is needed.\pYes, what a TRAINER needs is a
virtuous heart.\pPOKéMON touch the good hearts of
TRAINERS and learn good from wrong.\pThey touch the good hearts of
TRAINERS and grow strong.\pGo! Go onwards!
The CHAMPION is waiting!$

replies.text: That's a big compliment from a man with very big dragons. I'll hold it carefully.
He considers a trainer's conduct part of a Pokemon's education. A substantial responsibility.
Strong partners learn from what we do. He's right to remind us.
He spoke about kindness at the end of such a hard battle. I liked that.
They learn our habits along with our commands. We ought to give them good ones.
After all those dragons, the final lesson is decency. I find that rather satisfying.
A good heart survives the room full of teeth. Encouraging news.
He's judging how we guide the team, not merely which moves we selected.
Strength takes the shape of the hands guiding it. His warning is gentle, but serious.
He gives character the same attention as ability. That's a compliment worth keeping.
I'd remember that advice even outside this League. Our partners notice the small things.

contexts.subject: A trainer discovers being strongest among friends does not assure Frontier success.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_BestOutO.text: I'm the best out of all my friends.\nBut here…\lI've been useless!$

replies.text: Being the biggest fish at home doesn't stop this pond from having very large fish.
A stronger comparison group changes the ranking, not the value of earlier progress.
New opponents, new lessons. He isn't useless.
It must feel lonely when the thing everyone knows you for suddenly isn't enough.
He's found people who can teach him something. Once the sting wears off, that's useful.
His title survived the journey. Its jurisdiction turned out to be rather small.
The local champion has discovered a much larger locality. Painful, but educational.
Now he has better benchmarks. He can find the specific things holding him back.
A familiar hill can hide a mountain. It doesn't make the climb up the hill worthless.
He's comparing himself so harshly that he's erased the friends he used to impress.
I'd ask what surprised him most in those matches. There's probably a starting point there.

contexts.subject: An eager visitor is still too seasick to begin battling.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_GotSeasi.text: I wanted to take a challenge as soon\nas I arrived here.\pBut on the way, I got seasick…\nUrrrrp…$

replies.text: The boat won the first match. Let's give him some room to recover.
His enthusiasm arrived before his equilibrium did. A quiet rest seems sensible.
Battles can wait. He needs a steady place to sit.
I won't keep him talking. He looks like every extra word costs effort.
Fresh air, a quiet seat, and no grand challenge for a little while.
His opening opponent was apparently the sea. A notoriously poor sport.
The island is holding still. His stomach has yet to accept the evidence.
He shouldn't have to start a challenge just because he planned to arrive ready.
Even firm ground takes a while to feel trustworthy again.
I think the kindest greeting right now is a little more personal space.
I'll ask about the voyage later. Right now he needs fewer questions.

contexts.subject: A visitor describes the Frontier invitation system and its limited reputation.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_OnlyToug.text:
It's not as if just anyone can come
here, you know?\pOnly those TRAINERS who've been
recognized as tough are brought here.\pThat's why many TRAINERS don't even
know about the BATTLE FRONTIER.$

replies.text: A whole island that some trainers haven't heard of. Scott keeps a very peculiar guest list.
Selective invitations would explain why knowledge of this place spreads unevenly.
Getting here proves an invitation. What happens next still needs earning.
I wonder how many good trainers simply haven't been noticed yet.
Being invited is exciting. I wouldn't let it make us rude to people outside the list.
An exclusive gathering announcing its exclusivity. The invitation is doing double duty.
A secret known by this many boastful people must require constant maintenance.
Scott's scouting network must cover a lot of ground. Finding people is real work.
Recognition is a gate with somebody else's hand on the latch.
He seems almost as proud of knowing about the place as of being invited.
I'd be curious how each visitor first heard about it. Probably quite a few Scott stories.

contexts.subject: One visitor reassures another that the Factory provides rental Pokemon.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_BigGuySa.text: Uh…\nI'm sure it'll be okay.\pI think…\pBut remember that big scary guy?\nHe said, “I'll lend you POKéMON!”$

replies.text: They came without Pokemon and brought enough nervousness for an entire team.
The rental arrangement resolves their practical concern. Their confidence is catching up slowly.
They should confirm the rules at the desk. Better than reassuring each other indefinitely.
He sounds frightened too, but he's trying to help his friend stay brave.
Asking the staff would settle it. Neither friend has to pretend to know everything.
A reassuring promise delivered with several audible cracks in its foundation.
Two uncertain people have pooled their uncertainty. Somehow it looks a little warmer.
They have the right lead. Next step is confirming how the rental selection works.
Borrowed partners, borrowed courage. Both can be treated carefully.
The scary man's helpful offer seems to be struggling against his first impression.
I'd go ask with them. A clear answer could save a lot of nervous whispering.

contexts.subject: A visitor wonders who raises the Factory rental Pokemon.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_WhosRais.text: That's the BATTLE FACTORY.\nYou can rent strong POKéMON there.\pBut it makes me wonder.\nWho's raising those rental POKéMON?$

replies.text: Somebody must do the work before the impressive entrance. I'd like to meet that somebody.
A rotating rental roster implies substantial husbandry and training behind the facility.
Good question. Strong Pokemon don't prepare themselves for strangers overnight.
I wonder if they have favorite people among the staff.
Feeding that many trained partners must be a serious daily operation. Respect to the crew.
At last, someone has noticed that the impressive attraction requires actual people to run it.
The mysterious unseen worker. Usually found doing all the work.
I'd love to see the preparation routine. A rental system depends on much more than a counter.
Someone knows each one well before a visitor learns its name.
The finished experience hides a lot of care. I'm glad he thought to ask.
That's the person I'd want to interview. They probably know a hundred excellent details.

contexts.subject: A visitor wants to challenge everything despite fear of Seviper and the Pike building.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_ScaredOf.text: I'm scared of going into the BATTLE\nPIKE because of SEVIPER…\pB-but I came all the way here, so I will\ntry to conquer everything!\l…Shudder…$

replies.text: That's a lot of giant snake to walk toward when you're already afraid of snakes.
The architecture is an unusually intense introduction to the subject of her fear.
She can take her time. The building isn't going anywhere.
She admitted she was scared and still wants to try. That counts for something.
Coming this far doesn't mean she owes anybody a panic. A pause is allowed.
The architect certainly committed to the theme. Perhaps a little too successfully for her.
An enormous snake-shaped invitation. Subtlety was presumably unavailable.
She could look at the entrance first and decide afterward. Smaller steps still move forward.
Courage can shudder. I've never understood why people expect it to stand perfectly still.
She wants to go in, but she's allowed to choose the pace of her own entrance.
I'd walk with her if she wanted company. No need to turn it into a spectacle.

contexts.subject: Winning rock-paper-scissors persuades a visitor to attempt the Pike.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_WonIllTa.text: Yay! I won!\nI will take the BATTLE PIKE challenge!$

replies.text: One tiny victory has opened the gates of the giant snake. A busy pair of scissors.
An unrelated game has supplied confidence. It hasn't supplied a prediction of the challenge.
She's decided. Now she still needs to prepare.
That little win seems to have made starting feel easier.
A cheerful start helps. I'd still check the team before heading in.
The grand campaign begins with a small, decisive hand gesture.
Fate has apparently submitted its opinion through rock-paper-scissors.
Confidence acquired. Practical preparation remains a separate task.
A small omen, freely chosen. The next door will offer its own answer.
She looks much happier now that she's given herself permission to begin.
I'd ask how the challenge went afterward. This is an entertaining beginning.

contexts.subject: Losing rock-paper-scissors persuades a visitor to postpone the Pike.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_LostIllP.text: Oh, no…\nI lost.\pI guess I'm not very lucky today.\nI'll put off my BATTLE PIKE challenge\luntil tomorrow.$

replies.text: The scissors have canceled an entire day's plans. That's a lot of authority for two fingers.
That result doesn't establish her future luck, though postponing is still her choice.
She can try tomorrow. I'd put more weight on whether her team is ready.
Maybe she wanted a reason to wait. The game gave her one.
If she feels unsettled, a break might help more than another prediction.
An administrative decision issued by a hand game. I question the department's qualifications.
Tomorrow has been asked to provide better luck. A demanding appointment.
A different result wouldn't change the Pike's rules. Preparation gives her something firmer.
An omen can become an excuse very quietly. She still gets to choose.
She seems to need certainty before starting. I don't think this game can really offer it.
I'd ask what worries her about the Pike itself. That might be easier to talk through.

contexts.subject: A visitor prefers fishing and is disappointed the Frontier offers no catches.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_ChooseFi.text: I believe I'm the only person here who,\nfor some unknown reason, would choose\lfishing over battling.\pHuh? You can't catch anything here?\nThat's disappointing…$

replies.text: An island full of challenges and not one is the patient little fishing kind.
His preferred activity isn't supported here. Competitive density doesn't equal variety.
Fair preference. Not every trip needs a battle.
He came somewhere exciting and couldn't find the quiet thing he enjoys.
I'd help him find a better fishing stop after the visit. Everyone needs their own good day.
Hundreds of formidable opponents, yet no one has arranged an appointment with a fish.
The sea surrounds him in a particularly unhelpful manner.
A place can be excellent at its purpose and still miss someone's favorite pastime.
He can hear the water everywhere. That must make the disappointment rather pointed.
He sounds more surprised by his own preference than he needs to be.
I'd ask about his favorite fishing spot. He probably has much better stories from there.

contexts.subject: A gentleman wishes the player luck and hopes to meet as opponents.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_YoureOff.text: Oh? You're off to challenge\nthe BATTLE DOME?\pI'll wish you the best of luck.\nLet us both win our way up and meet\lin challenges.$

replies.text: He wants us both to do well enough to become each other's problem. That's lovely.
A mutually successful path would eventually create a direct competition. He welcomes both parts.
Good manners. I'd be glad to meet him across the field.
He made being an opponent sound like a friendly appointment.
A little goodwill before a hard challenge. There's room for both.
A courteous invitation to a future disagreement conducted entirely through Pokemon.
A promising acquaintance. Potentially dangerous, but very polite.
He's picturing both of us progressing. That's an encouraging way to frame the bracket.
Two wishes for success can share a path until the path narrows.
That was a graceful way to make a rival feel welcome.
I'd remember him if we met again. That greeting gives a match a little history.

contexts.subject: A trainer intends to keep battling until earning a Symbol today.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_KeepBatt.text: Today, I'm going to keep battling, no\nmatter what, until I get a Symbol.$

replies.text: That's a determined plan. I wonder if the Symbol knows it's on a deadline.
Persistence helps, but fatigue can reduce the value of repeated attempts.
Keep the goal. Take breaks before mistakes become habits.
I like the determination. The phrase no matter what makes me a little uneasy.
A whole day of battling still needs meals and water somewhere in it.
An admirable refusal to surrender. I would reserve the right to surrender briefly to lunch.
The Symbol has acquired a pursuer. Hopefully one who remembers to sit down.
A specific goal is useful. Reviewing each attempt would make the effort more useful still.
Resolve burns well. It also needs tending if it's meant to last.
He sounds as though stopping would feel like failure. A break doesn't have to mean that.
I'd ask what he's learned between attempts. That tells me more than the number of battles.

contexts.subject: An older trainer vows to beat the gentlemen but cannot locate the Dome entrance.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_WontLetG.text: Ah, so this here is the BATTLE DOME?\nI won't let GENTLEMEN beat me!\pBut where is the entrance?$

replies.text: His rivals are in serious danger as soon as he defeats the problem of the door.
His competitive plan currently depends on resolving a modest navigation problem.
First, the entrance. Then the gentlemen.
He sounded so fierce until he asked where to go. It was rather endearing.
Let's point him toward the entrance before the rivalry gets cold.
A formidable declaration, brought to a temporary halt by architecture.
The first opponent is the building. It appears to be defending competently.
Clearer entrance signs might prevent a surprising amount of wasted competitive energy.
Ambition is pointing straight ahead. His feet require slightly better directions.
I like his confidence. I'd quietly help with the part he hasn't mastered yet.
He'll have a much better story once he's actually found the way in.

contexts.subject: A visitor marvels at the new Frontier and wants to bring their mother.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_NothingH.text: There used to be nothing here not all\nthat long ago.\pBut, now look at this place! Amazing!\nI'll bring my mother out to see this.$

replies.text: His first thought after seeing all this was bringing his mother. That's my favorite detail.
Rapid development is impressive. I'd be curious what the site looked like before construction.
He wants to share the surprise. Good reason for another trip.
Some places make you wish a particular person were beside you. He knows who.
A visit with his mother sounds like a good next plan. Plenty here to talk about afterward.
An entire Frontier, and he immediately begins arranging a family outing. Sensible priorities.
A spectacular island has been promoted to somewhere Mother ought to see.
I'd love to compare the construction plans with what stood here before. That's a huge change.
He remembers the empty space. Bringing her will let him tell the story of its filling.
He wants to share the experience instead of simply saying he got here first.
I'd ask whether she enjoys battles too. Either way, he'd have plenty to show her.

contexts.subject: An arriving trainer expects their looks and ability to attract attention.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_FinallyA.text: I've finally arrived at the BATTLE\nFRONTIER!\pI'm sure to grab attention with\nmy looks and ability!$

replies.text: They've brought two kinds of confidence. Let's see how both handle the Frontier breeze.
Ability can be tested here. The amount of attention is a less controllable variable.
They're here. Now comes the part that earns the attention.
It's brave to arrive expecting to be noticed. I'd rather settle in quietly first.
A bright arrival. They'll still need a good routine once the excitement wears off.
They've announced an entrance without requiring anyone to announce it for them. Efficient.
The confidence has arrived ahead of the evidence. It looks quite comfortable.
Enthusiasm is useful starting energy. I'm curious what their team can actually do.
Being seen and being known are different wishes. They seem to want both.
Presentation and skill can work together. Neither guarantees what the crowd will do.
I'd ask which challenge they're most eager to try. That's where the interesting details begin.

contexts.subject: A visitor surveys the formidable crowd while eating.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_SquareFi.text: Munch, munch…\pIt looks like this square's filled with\ntough people.\pMunch, munch…$

replies.text: They've assessed the whole square without pausing the snack. Excellent jaw coordination.
A plausible observation, though the invitation system already selects a strong sample.
Eat first. Size up the competition afterward.
They sound comfortable here. Even all these tough trainers haven't spoiled the snack.
A sensible spectator has brought provisions. I'd ask what they're having.
An intimidating crowd receives its verdict between two unhurried bites.
The square is full of danger. The snack remains the immediate priority.
They're taking in the environment before jumping into a challenge. That seems useful.
A formidable gathering becomes a little less solemn with someone quietly munching through it.
They seem impressed without feeling obliged to compete with everyone in sight.
I'd like to know who caught their attention first. They've had time to look around.

contexts.subject: A snacking trainer recalls being defeated by a girl annoyed at their eating.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_MetOlder.text:
Crunch, munch…\pA while back, I met this older girl
at the BATTLE PIKE.\pShe had these eyes that were scary
in a real ornery way.\pCrunch, munch…\pShe got all furious: “Will you quit
eating!” Then she whaled on me.\pIt was a hair-raising kind of
scary experience, sure enough.\pCrunch, munch…$

replies.text: That was a frightening lesson. The snack seems to have declined to learn it.
The defeat changed his account of the opponent, but apparently not his eating schedule.
He lost. He can still choose a better moment for the snack next time.
Being frightened didn't make him stop eating. I can't tell whether that's brave or distracted.
I respect a good snack. I also respect putting it down when somebody needs your attention.
His terrible experience is interrupted by the exact habit that helped make it terrible.
Fear has passed through him. The appetite appears structurally untouched.
I'd separate what he learned about her team from what he learned about her patience.
He remembers the eyes very clearly. Perhaps the rest of the lesson is still arriving.
She wanted his attention. He seems to have given her only the part between bites.
I'd ask about the battle itself once he finishes chewing. That part is still missing.

contexts.subject: A fan insists shared eye contact with the Dome Ace meant sparks flew.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_LastTime.text: Huh? Will you listen to yourself?\nThat's nothing!\pWhy, the last time I cheered for him,\nour eyes met and sparks flew!$

replies.text: Their eyes met, and now the poor moment has to support an entire argument.
Eye contact is observable. The proposed significance is considerably less certain.
They can enjoy the memory without making it a competition.
A glance can feel important. I'd be embarrassed to argue over whose it was.
That memory clearly makes them happy. No need to turn it into a contest at the seats.
A brief glance has been asked to provide sworn evidence of mutual devotion.
Sparks, allegedly. No damage to the seating has been reported.
From a crowded arena, it's hard to establish exactly where somebody was looking.
A small bright moment can grow strange thorns when someone starts defending it.
They want the experience to feel personal. The argument is making it less pleasant.
I'd ask what they enjoyed about the match itself. There must have been more than one glance.

contexts.subject: A rival fan claims the Ace looked toward their especially loud cheering.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_DomeAceL.text:
Whaaaaaat?!
Pfft!\pThat only happened because
I happened to be sitting next to you!\pThe DOME ACE only looked our way
because my cheering was so loud!$

replies.text: They've promoted volume into proof of affection. My ears request a second opinion.
A loud sound can attract attention. That alone doesn't establish personal preference.
He heard the cheering. That's plenty. No need to shout down the neighbor.
I feel a bit sorry for whoever sat between them.
Cheering should make the day better for the people around you, too.
The argument now measures devotion in volume. A difficult system for everyone nearby.
The loudest person claims victory. A familiar and exhausting method.
They may well have attracted his attention. That doesn't tell us what he thought.
A voice can fill a room and still fail to make its owner feel seen.
They've turned a shared happy moment into a dispute over who owns it.
I'd rather hear why they admire him than hear the cheering reenacted at this distance.

contexts.subject: A longtime fan dismisses others and claims exclusive devotion to the Dome Ace.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_DomeAceI.text:
Oh, shush!
Keep that racket down!\pYou fair-weather fans should stick
to cheering for some GYM LEADER!\pThe DOME ACE is mine!
The only idol for me!$

replies.text: I don't think cheering comes with a deed of ownership. Someone should mention that gently.
Longer admiration doesn't confer exclusive access to the person being admired.
They can support him without treating other fans as trespassers.
It would be hard to enjoy a match with somebody deciding whether I belonged there.
There should be room for another person to discover something you love.
A fan club of precisely one, currently objecting to an alarming membership increase.
The idol has been claimed as private property. I doubt he signed the paperwork.
New fans could make the cheering stronger. They're treating a possible benefit as a threat.
Affection becomes a rather narrow room when only one person is allowed inside.
Calling everyone else insincere won't make their own admiration look warmer.
I'd like to hear how they became a fan, if we can get past the gatekeeping first.

contexts.subject: An observer explains that defeated accomplished trainers became devoted fans.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_FansOver.text:
Those people squabbling over there…\pIt's hard to believe, but they once
were TRAINERS, and good ones, too.\pThey used to be incredibly tough,
and they were famous, too.\pBut they were obliterated by this
certain TRAINER at a tournament.\pThey were so thoroughly whipped,
they became smitten by the TRAINER.\pNow they're just fans of the TRAINER.
They go cheer for their idol at the\lBATTLE DOME every day now.$

replies.text: He beat them so thoroughly they changed which side of the arena they wanted to stand on.
The defeat appears to have transformed their interest rather than extinguished it.
They know enough to recognize what beat them. Credit where it's due.
They found something to love inside a hard loss. I like that part.
At least the loss didn't drive them away from Pokemon altogether. They're still excited.
That must have been a spectacular defeat. It apparently recruited the entire opposition.
A crushing loss with an unusually successful fan-club enrollment afterward.
Experienced trainers can notice impressive choices a casual audience might miss.
They left the battle carrying admiration instead of only a bruise to their pride.
Their expertise makes the admiration interesting. Their squabbling makes it harder to hear.
I'd love their separate accounts of that match. They probably remember different turning points.

contexts.subject: A visitor delays challenges to seek a rumored long-tailed Pokemon.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_MonWithL.text: I heard a rumor that someone saw\na POKéMON with an unusually long tail\lsomewhere in the BATTLE FRONTIER.\pIt must be adorable. I'm sure of it…\pOh, challenges can wait. I feel driven\nto find the delightful creature!$

replies.text: One unusually long tail has defeated the whole challenge schedule. It must be very persuasive.
A report of tail length doesn't establish temperament or appearance. Still, curiosity is reasonable.
Look carefully. Cute is a guess, not permission to grab it.
I understand putting a crowded challenge aside for a chance to see something small and unusual.
A quiet search could be a good break. I'd keep a respectful distance if we find it.
The Frontier prepared seven grand attractions and has been upstaged by a rumored tail.
An unseen creature has already acquired an admirer. A powerful debut.
We could ask where it was seen before wandering around the entire island.
A rumor has tugged them away from the crowd. Long tails are apparently useful for that.
They've imagined the cuteness already. The real Pokemon deserves a chance to surprise them.
I'd ask the person who saw it where they were standing. Specific details would help.

contexts.subject: A visitor is impressed by the size and distinct presence of the Tower.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_BattleTo.text: Wow!\nIt's huge!\pThe BATTLE TOWER feels special.\nIt's different from the others.$

replies.text: It does seem determined to be visible from every possible direction.
Its vertical scale gives it a different visual presence from the surrounding facilities.
Big building. Still one battle at a time once we're inside.
I think I'd feel very small walking toward it alone.
It makes an impressive landmark. At least getting lost near it would be difficult.
The Tower has declined any invitation to blend into the neighborhood.
A building with no apparent fear of being called conspicuous.
I'd love to know how they planned the structure for that height and all those visitors.
It asks the eye to keep climbing. The feet may have other opinions.
It looks like the centerpiece, even among all these places competing for attention.
I'd want to see how it looks from the far side of the grounds, too.

contexts.subject: A visitor wants to conquer the League and Frontier before asking Mimi for friendship.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_ConquerL.text: My grand ambition is to conquer both\nthe BATTLE FRONTIER and the POKéMON\lLEAGUE.\pAnd if my dream comes true…\pI… I'm going to ask MIMI next door\nif she will be friends with me!$

replies.text: That's an enormous errand before saying hello to the neighbor. We could probably shorten it.
Those achievements aren't a necessary prerequisite for asking someone to be friends.
He can ask her now. A no wouldn't erase anything he's earned.
I understand finding excuses to wait. His are much more ambitious than mine.
Maybe start with a greeting. Friendship usually needs conversation more than trophies.
He has placed an extraordinary amount of competitive bureaucracy between himself and hello.
Two mighty institutions stand between him and the girl next door. Neither knows this.
That's a very elaborate dependency chain. I'd try the smallest step first.
He wants enough glory to make a simple question feel safe. It may never work that way.
Mimi might prefer getting to know him before hearing the complete victory list.
I'd ask what they already have in common. There may be an easier opening right next door.

contexts.subject: A frustrated trainer jokes about climbing the outside of the Pyramid.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_PyramidT.text: The BATTLE PYRAMID's too harsh!\nI just can't make it to the top!\pSince I'm out of options, maybe I can\nclimb the outside…$

replies.text: The outside route seems to have fewer trainers and significantly worse handrails.
External climbing wouldn't solve the actual challenge and introduces rather different hazards.
Bad plan. Rest, rethink, use the entrance.
He sounds worn down enough to make an absurd shortcut feel tempting.
Maybe he needs a proper break before another attempt. Frustration isn't good climbing equipment.
An ingenious attempt to avoid the problem by acquiring a much taller problem.
The walls have been mistaken for an alternate admissions policy.
We should review where his attempts fail. Moving the problem outside won't fix the strategy.
A hard path can make every nearby wall look like a door. Usually it isn't.
He wants a way around feeling stuck. I think he needs a fresh plan inside.
I'd ask which part keeps stopping him. The answer might be more useful than a ladder.

contexts.subject: A Hex Maniac enthusiastically welcomes the Pyramid darkness and desperation.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_ThriveIn.text: I thrive in darkness…\nYes… What is worthy of me?\lNone other than the BATTLE PYRAMID…\pWhat say you to wandering in darkness\nand in utter and total desperation?$

replies.text: She says total desperation the way other people say complimentary breakfast.
Her preferred environment differs markedly from the average visitor's comfort requirements.
She likes the dark. I still want a way to see where we're stepping.
Darkness can be peaceful. I'm less sure about the desperation part.
I'd pack carefully before accepting that invitation. Enthusiasm won't find a misplaced supply.
A wonderfully candid advertisement. Absolutely no effort to soften the word desperation.
I appreciate the darkness. I usually prefer to schedule desperation separately.
Low visibility changes how you navigate. I'd plan for it rather than trust the mood.
Darkness has its comforts. She and I may disagree about which ones.
She's found a challenge that suits her whole presentation. That's an impressive match.
I'd be curious what she notices down there that visitors miss while worrying.

contexts.subject: A trainer claims a sleepless week produced an unbeatable Arena team.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_PutToget.text: I didn't sleep for a week, but then\nI put together the ultimate team!\pI can't see myself losing, no joke.\nWe're storming the BATTLE ARENA!$

replies.text: The team might be ultimate. The trainer sounds one blink away from meeting the floor.
Sleep loss is unlikely to improve the decisions needed to use that team effectively.
A week's preparation deserves a rested trainer. Go sleep.
I can't tell how much of that confidence is excitement and how much is exhaustion.
I'd feed him something simple and point him toward a bed before the Arena.
He has perfected every component except the person currently issuing the commands.
The ultimate team has a very tired weak link standing in front of us.
Testing a design while exhausted makes the results harder to trust. Rest first, then assess it.
He's poured the entire week into a future victory. He should keep some strength for arriving there.
He's proud of the work. Resting would protect that effort rather than diminish it.
I'd rather hear his team plan after he's slept. He might even spot an improvement himself.

contexts.subject: A trainer promises Zigzagoon favorite treats if it wins.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_BelieveI.text: ZIGG!\nI believe in you, little buddy!\pI'll make my little ZIGG any favorite\ntasty treats you like if you win!$

replies.text: Zigg has a personal cheering section and a very specific reason to win.
The promised reward is clearly tailored to the individual. He knows his partner's preferences.
Good to hear him backing his little partner. Keep that up after losses, too.
He sounds so fond when he says the name. Zigg must hear that.
Favorite treats are serious business. I'd ask Zigg which ones top the list.
A heartfelt address, followed by a highly practical incentive package.
The stakes are high. Possibly crunchy. We haven't established the menu.
He's made the reward concrete. Now the battle still needs a sensible plan.
A small creature has someone's whole faith placed gently beside it.
That nickname makes the encouragement feel like theirs alone.
I'd love to hear how Zigg earned its name. He sounds ready to tell us.

contexts.subject: A compulsive intervenor worries about merely observing at the Palace.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_PeopleCa.text:
People call me a busybody,
but I can't help it.\pYour hat's on crooked!
Oh, no, trash on the ground!\lOops, it's almost dinnertime!\pI don't know if I can stand to just
watch at the BATTLE PALACE…$

replies.text: He fixed our hat, found some trash, and scheduled dinner before finishing one thought.
A format that removes direct commands may be especially uncomfortable for him.
He'll have to let his Pokemon act. That's the Palace rule.
He notices every small thing. Letting go must take a lot of effort.
Remembering dinner is useful. Correcting everybody else's evening may be less welcome.
A man attempting to supervise the entire island has encountered a no-supervision challenge.
Even the litter has received instructions. The Palace should be educational.
He could practice observing without correcting. Start with something smaller than a battle.
Still hands can be harder work than busy ones. He's about to discover how much.
Helpful attention can feel intrusive when nobody asked for the help.
I'd ask what he notices when he gives himself a minute without acting on it.

contexts.subject: An older trainer considers returning to competition after a past Gym victory.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_OnceBeat.text: I may not look that impressive now,\nbut I once beat a GYM LEADER.\pWho knows, maybe I should give it\nanother shot at glory.$

replies.text: A victory doesn't expire just because the trainer has acquired more birthdays.
His past success is relevant experience, though a return would test his current preparation.
Give it a try if he wants. No need to apologize for being older.
That old win still makes him brighten. A new attempt might mean a lot.
He can return at his own pace. There's no need to recreate his younger self exactly.
He has a perfectly good achievement and is considering another. An excellent use of history.
The retired glory appears to be considering part-time employment.
I'd start by seeing what his team can do now. Experience gives him a useful foundation.
An old fire has stirred. It needn't burn exactly as it once did.
I dislike that he feels obliged to explain his appearance before his achievement.
I'd ask about that Gym match. People remember remarkable little details after years.

contexts.subject: A cyclist boasts of speed both riding and winning battles.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_FastOnBi.text: I'm fast on my BIKE, and that goes for\nthe way I battle, too.\pI win matches in the blink of\nan eye!$

replies.text: Fast wheels, fast wins. I wonder if he takes his victory lap before anyone notices.
Quick wins suggest decisive matchups. Speed alone doesn't explain the underlying choices.
Quick is useful. Knowing when to slow down is useful, too.
I might need him to describe one of those matches more slowly.
A quick match leaves more time for a proper meal afterward. Sensible scheduling.
He appears committed to giving both opponents and scenery very little time with him.
A man in a hurry, even while boasting about being in a hurry.
I'd like to know which decisions let him finish so efficiently.
Speed makes a clean promise. A difficult opponent may ask him to amend it.
He's made quickness his signature. It's a memorable introduction.
I'd ask for one specific match story before he speeds off again.

contexts.subject: A girl confidently says she is better at Pokemon than her father.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_BetterTh.text: I'm better than my daddy\nat POKéMON.$

replies.text: She has measured the family rankings and sees no need for a committee.
She sounds confident in that comparison. I'd be interested in how they practice together.
Good for her. He seems proud enough to survive it.
She says it so simply. No grand speech required.
A child getting better than her parent can be a happy milestone for both.
A concise family assessment. Father has apparently lost the deciding vote.
The household hierarchy has been updated. Daddy seems likely to receive a notice.
Teaching someone who eventually surpasses you is a successful result.
Growing past someone's reach needn't mean leaving their affection behind.
She's comfortable taking credit for her skill. I'm glad she can.
I'd ask whether they battle each other often. It sounds like an entertaining household.

contexts.subject: A father cheers his daughter and compares her skill to her mother.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_GoRackUp.text: Go on, my baby sweetie!\nGo rack up some wins for Daddy!\pYou're just like your mother,\nso you'll be dominating!$

replies.text: He's cheering for the next generation and complimenting the previous one at the same time.
He sees a family resemblance in ability. His enthusiasm seems quite genuine.
He knows she's good. He's not pretending otherwise to protect his pride.
It must feel good to know he believes in her that openly.
That's a proud dad. I bet he'll remember every match more loudly than she does.
A family with one very enthusiastic supporter and apparently two formidable competitors.
He sounds thoroughly outmatched at home and delighted about it.
Recognition from somebody who knows her well can help steady the nerves.
His pride has room for both of them. A warm sort of inheritance.
He makes the resemblance to her mother sound like the highest possible compliment.
I'd ask whether her mother came along. This sounds like a whole family of stories.

contexts.subject: A visitor observes that Scott spots talent but has never been seen battling.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_DidScott.text:
Did SCOTT bring you here, too?
What is it with that guy?\pIt sounds like he really does know
how to spot talented TRAINERS, but…\pI've never seen him battling in person
ever.$

replies.text: Scott has found all these trainers without once demonstrating how he handles a tackle.
Recognizing expertise and performing it are related but distinct abilities.
He recruited the talent. That doesn't tell us what he can do in a battle.
I hadn't realized how little we know about that part of him.
Some people are better at bringing a team together than taking the field themselves.
He has assembled a remarkable guest list while leaving his own entry strangely blank.
A man surrounded by battle records who has supplied none of his own. Neat trick.
Scouting skill is evident. His competitive skill remains untested evidence.
He's very good at opening doors for others. His own door remains shut.
He directs attention toward everyone else's ability. People are starting to notice the gap.
I'd ask him if he enjoys battling. A simpler question than guessing at a secret history.

contexts.subject: A visitor complains the Arena crowd differs from the attractive girl he expected.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_HeardPre.text:
It wasn't easy getting here,
but I'd heard about this knockout\lpretty girl at the BATTLE ARENA.\pInstead of her, do you know what
I found?\pA whole teeming mob of sweaty,
stinky, and primitive martial artists!$

replies.text: He traveled all this way and forgot the battle part of Battle Arena.
His expectation concerned one person's appearance rather than the purpose of the facility.
People are there to battle. They don't owe him a pleasing view.
Those martial artists didn't do anything wrong by being there.
He might enjoy the trip more if he gave the actual matches a chance.
A man disappointed that a martial contest contains martial artists. An ambitious complaint.
The Arena has failed to organize itself around one stranger's taste. Tragic, apparently.
He should check the event before planning a trip around a rumor.
He brought a narrow expectation. The crowd has politely refused to fit inside it.
He could have kept the insults to himself. Nobody here was hired to decorate his visit.
I'd rather talk to the people who came for the battles. They probably have better observations.

contexts.subject: A child describes a kind older Palace visitor with impressive Pokemon.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_Sometime.text: I sometimes see this really important-\nlooking old man going in there.\pHe has these really awesome POKéMON.\nHe seems really nice, though.$

replies.text: Awesome Pokemon and a nice person. That's a much better combination than awesome and unbearable.
The child separates his imposing presence from his actual manner. A useful distinction.
Strong doesn't have to mean unfriendly. Good that the kid has seen that.
He noticed the kindness after the impressive entrance. I like that.
A powerful team is easier to admire when its trainer treats people well.
An important-looking gentleman who hasn't let the appearance become an obligation to be unpleasant.
The formidable old man turns out to be nice. A welcome breach of expectation.
I'd be curious how he works with those Pokemon under the Palace rules.
Some people carry authority lightly enough that a child can approach it.
He made an impression without frightening the child. That's a good kind of presence.
I'd ask what made him seem nice. Children often remember exactly the thing adults overlook.

contexts.subject: A visitor improvises a Pyramid legend and admits it has no established meaning.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_LegendOf.text:
Do you know it?
The legend of the BATTLE PYRAMID?\pWhen there comes a confident TRAINER
reaching for the golden pinnacle,\lthere shall appear a man among men.\pDon't know that legend?
Well, of course not!\lI just made it up!\pWhat's it supposed to mean?
That, my friend, I can't say!$

replies.text: A freshly baked ancient legend. Still warm, and nobody knows what's inside.
He disclosed the invention immediately. At least the provenance is unusually transparent.
Fair enough. As long as he doesn't pass it off as history.
He sounded so solemn. Then he admitted it, and I nearly laughed.
He invented it on the spot and told us so. Harmless fun with honest labeling.
I admire the immediate confession. Most invented legends insist on several centuries of dignity first.
An ancient tradition born moments ago and already unsure of its purpose.
He's testing an idea aloud. It clearly still needs a few design decisions.
A new tale has no roots yet. He seems content to let it wander.
The delivery was grand enough to make the admission much funnier.
I'd ask him again tomorrow. He may have invented an entirely different meaning by then.

contexts.subject: A previously unbeaten trainer reels from a crushing loss and an insult to his talent.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_GotWiped.text:
Man! Oh man!
I've never lost once before!\pBut I got wiped out with no saving
grace at all!\pAnd then I'm told I don't have any
talent?! Man!$

replies.text: Losing for the first time is hard enough without somebody stamping an insult on top.
One defeat disproves invincibility. It doesn't establish an absence of talent.
He lost a battle. Whoever called him talentless was adding noise.
He sounds hurt underneath all that anger. I wouldn't make him explain it twice.
Let him cool off before picking apart the match. Right now everything feels personal.
The result was clear enough without an unsolicited verdict on his entire future.
An undefeated record has broken. The person attached to it is still intact.
He can examine the decisions later. First he needs to separate the result from the insult.
One fallen certainty can sound like the whole world falling. It isn't.
He had never practiced being the person who loses. That part takes learning, too.
I'd ask about one turning point once he's ready. A whole career is too much to judge at once.

contexts.subject: An observer warns that a nearby trainer suffered a difficult Tower defeat.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_ToughTra.text: This guy ran into a horribly tough\nTRAINER while he was on the BATTLE\lTOWER challenge.\pNow look at him…\pYou need to be cautious if you ever\ndecide to go to the BATTLE TOWER.$

replies.text: The warning is useful. Pointing at the poor fellow adds a little too much demonstration.
His account establishes a difficult opponent exists, though not how often we would meet them.
We'll prepare. He should give his friend a minute to recover.
It's hard enough losing without becoming the example everyone points at.
A warning can help us without making the other trainer feel smaller.
A cautionary tale is standing right there, apparently without being asked to participate.
The Tower is dangerous. So is becoming the local public-service announcement.
Knowing a tough opponent exists is useful. Learning how they battled would help more.
Someone else's wound is being used as a signpost. A gentler warning would do.
He may mean well, but his friend's embarrassment probably doesn't need an audience.
I'd listen to the trainer's own account if he wanted to share it.

contexts.subject: A visitor has earned enough points for another giant plush doll.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_EnoughBa.text: Yes!\nI've finally got enough Battle Points!\pI guess I'll trade for another giant\nplush DOLL!$

replies.text: All that fierce battling has produced a very large, very soft objective. Excellent.
A tangible personal goal can sustain effort better than an abstract ranking.
Earned enough for something they want. Good for them.
They sound genuinely excited. I'd like to see which one they choose.
A giant plush seems like a comfortable reward after so many hard battles.
The campaign concludes in upholstery. I thoroughly approve of this ambition.
A formidable trainer is about to acquire another extremely huggable dependent.
They planned for a specific reward and reached the point total. Satisfying work.
A hard-earned softness. There are worse things to carry home.
Another giant one? I need to know how they've arranged the first ones.
I'd ask about the collection. That word another is doing interesting work.

contexts.subject: A trainer wants a lasting place in the Ranking Hall.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_LikeToHa.text: Oh, yeah, okay!\nSo this is the RANKING HALL!\pI'd like to go down in history as\na super champ and have my name\lrecorded here for posterity.$

replies.text: A name on a wall is a fine goal. First it needs a few very busy battles underneath it.
The record would document a specific performance. Longevity depends on what later challengers do.
He's found the goal. Now he needs the work that gets him there.
Wanting to be remembered feels bigger than simply wanting to win.
It could be something lovely to show people later. He'll have to earn the entry first.
Posterity has a reception desk here. Apparently it requests excellent battle results.
Immortality, with competitive admission requirements.
He could pick a facility and measure his progress toward its listed records.
A name can stay on a wall while its owner keeps changing. I wonder which part he wants preserved.
He already imagines how the name will look. I wonder which achievement he wants beside it.
I'd ask why being remembered matters to him. There's usually a good story behind that wish.

contexts.subject: One partner expresses absolute confidence from being beside the other.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_CanDoAny.text: With you by my side, I can do anything.$

replies.text: That's sweet. I'd still bring a plan for the things affection can't tackle directly.
A trusted partner can improve confidence. Unlimited ability is a more poetic claim.
Good to have someone you trust. Stay ready to help them, too.
They said it so easily. I think I'd need a moment before answering.
Being on the same side matters. I like hearing them say it out loud.
A magnificent promise. I trust neither has been asked to move the Tower by hand.
Together they can do anything. Presumably including accepting reasonable exceptions.
Trust makes cooperation easier. The details of the plan will still matter.
Some hands make the next step feel possible before anything else has changed.
It sounds less like showing off and more like telling one person they matter.
I'd be curious how they first became partners. They seem very comfortable together.

contexts.subject: An enthusiastic partner expects their love to conquer the Multi Battle challenge.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_PowerOfO.text:
Ooh, darling, you are so wonderful!\pOoh, I just can't wait anymore!\pLet's go to a MULTI BATTLE ROOM
right this instant!\pIf we get together in the BATTLE SALON,
the power of our love will overcome\leveryone we meet.\pWhy, before us, darling, everything
will topple like dominoes!$

replies.text: Love has entered the tournament and is making very bold predictions about the bracket.
Mutual trust should help their coordination. Opponents will still require specific responses.
They'd better talk tactics as enthusiastically as they talk about each other.
They really don't mind everyone hearing. I'm a little impressed.
They sound happy. I'd also check that both of them know the plan.
A romantic declaration with collateral damage promised to every team in the building.
Affection has become a competitive hazard. Nearby dominoes should seek shelter.
The shared enthusiasm is excellent. They'll need to account for their partners' moves together.
They see a straight path because they're looking toward the same thing. The arena may bend it.
They're enjoying being a pair. A difficult match will test how well they listen, too.
I'd ask afterward whether the teamwork matched the prediction. They're making it memorable.

contexts.subject: A visitor speculates that the variety of invited talents reflects a larger purpose.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_Frontier.text:
The BATTLE FRONTIER isn't exclusively
for tough TRAINERS.\pMany people with special abilities
have been invited, it seems.\pThat man SCOTT…\pHe may have built this place to serve
a bigger objective…$

replies.text: There are plenty of unusual talents here. Scott's guest list is more interesting than a win chart.
The varied invitations are observable. His proposed larger objective remains speculation.
Maybe Scott has a bigger plan. We can ask before inventing one.
I like that there might be room here for more than the loudest battlers.
A gathering works better with people who bring different things to it.
A mysterious objective is possible. So is a man who simply enjoys assembling interesting people.
The suspicion has a promising shape and no confirmed contents yet.
Different specialties make the whole place more capable. That part needs no secret explanation.
A place can serve more than one purpose. We haven't been handed its hidden one.
I'm glad someone noticed the people whose talents don't fit a battle score.
I'd ask what special abilities they've actually seen. That gives us something firmer to explore.

contexts.subject: An older visitor asks whether an unusual tree is really moving.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_OddTreeH.text: Excuse me, young one.\nHave you good eyesight?\pThere is an odd tree past here, and to\nmy tired eyes it seems to wiggle.$

replies.text: If the tree is wiggling, I don't think her eyes are the part causing trouble.
Independent observation could distinguish actual movement from a visual impression.
We can look. Give the odd tree some space until we're sure.
She asks so gently. I'd like to help her check.
No reason to dismiss her just because she's tired. Let's see what she noticed.
A tree behaving suspiciously is a perfectly respectable reason to request a second witness.
I dislike vegetation that makes eye contact with my doubts.
We should observe it for a moment before deciding whether the movement is real.
Some things seem rooted only because we haven't stood quietly enough beside them.
She noticed something odd and asked for another opinion. Sensible, really.
I'd ask when she first saw it move. Then we can watch the same spot.

contexts.subject: After the unusual tree is gone, the visitor asks whether her memory is accurate.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_OnceAnOd.text: Excuse me, young one.\nHave you a good memory?\pI have this feeling there once was\nan odd tree past here.$

replies.text: Now the tree's gone and she's doubting a different part of herself. Poor thing.
A changed location doesn't invalidate a previous observation. Memory and present evidence differ.
She remembers something real. We can reassure her about that.
I'd tell her she didn't imagine it. That seems important.
A simple answer could put her mind at ease. No need to make a mystery out of it.
The tree has departed and left its former observer to defend the evidence alone.
An absence with unusually poor manners. It could at least have left a note.
We can confirm that the place changed rather than making her question her memory.
An empty patch can make a clear memory feel very small. It shouldn't have to.
She deserves a straightforward answer instead of a joke about getting older.
I'd tell her what we know. There's no reason to leave her wondering whether she imagined it.

contexts.subject: A camper describes a sticky long-tailed Pokemon hiding beneath a boulder.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_StickyMo.text:
I…
I saw it!\pThere was a sticky sort of a POKéMON
with a long tail up ahead!\pIt was hiding under a boulder, and
it kept staring at me!$

replies.text: A sticky stranger under a rock was staring back. That's a very good reason to blink first.
We have a location and several physical observations. More useful than the earlier rumor alone.
Look from a distance. Don't reach under a boulder after something startled.
It might have been as surprised to see him as he was to see it.
If it's hiding, I'd give it room. Curiosity doesn't require pulling it out.
The rumored tail now comes with a boulder and a rather pointed stare. Details are accumulating.
The hidden observer has been observed. Neither party appears pleased by the arrangement.
I'd check the surroundings before approaching. That boulder may conceal more than the Pokemon.
It chose shelter and still kept an eye on the world. A familiar compromise.
He sounds startled, which is fair. An unexpected stare can make a small encounter feel enormous.
I'd ask which boulder and how far away he stood. Quiet observation seems the best next step.

contexts.subject: The expert calls the assessed stat relatively good.

BattleFrontier_Lounge1_Text_StatRelative.text: That stat is relatively good.\n…Hm… That's how I call it.$

replies.text: A good quality in that stat. Small praise still deserves a little smile.
That assessment applies to the particular stat he identified. It isn't an overall verdict.
Useful to know. One trait doesn't decide the whole partner.
He found something good there. I'd keep the rest of the Pokemon in mind, too.
A useful strength to work with. No need to turn it into a demand for perfection.
A modest compliment, delivered with the gravity of a royal proclamation.
Relatively good. The elder has opened the smallest drawer in his praise cabinet.
That's one useful detail for planning. It doesn't replace checking the rest of the team.
One good thread in a larger weave. The whole creature is still there.
It's a measured compliment. We don't have to make it smaller by comparing endlessly.
I'd ask how that strength shows itself in practice. Numbers become interesting when they matter.

contexts.subject: The expert calls the assessed stat quite impressive.

BattleFrontier_Lounge1_Text_StatImpressi.text: That stat is quite impressive.\n…Hm… That's how I call it.$

replies.text: That stat got a proper nod from the expert. Nicely done, little partner.
He rates that particular attribute highly. A useful distinction from his overall assessment.
A real strength. Let's use it well.
I like that he sounds pleased to find something impressive.
That's something to feel good about without making every other quality a competition.
The expert has moved beyond polite approval. His eyebrows may even have participated.
Impressive enough to earn an entire sentence of approval. A generous day.
Now we know a strong part of the design. The plan can account for it.
A bright quality noticed by an old eye. It was there before he named it.
Specific praise feels better than a vague compliment. This gives us something clear.
I'd be interested to see when that quality makes a difference in a close match.

contexts.subject: The expert calls the assessed stat outstanding.

BattleFrontier_Lounge1_Text_StatOutstand.text: That stat is outstanding!\n…Hm… That's how I call it.$

replies.text: That stat has earned the big compliment. I think it can stand a little taller now.
An excellent assessment of the identified attribute. It doesn't imply every attribute matches it.
Strong trait. Good information to have.
He sounds certain. I think our partner deserves a quiet bit of praise, too.
That's a lovely strength. It still belongs to a whole Pokemon we care about.
Outstanding, pronounced with all the ceremony the word seems to require.
One stat has distinguished itself from the crowd. Quietly smug behavior is now understandable.
That's a significant strength to factor into training and battle choices.
Something exceptional has been seen clearly. Naming it doesn't create it, but it can help.
It's good to have the compliment aimed at something specific instead of just a ranking.
I'd ask what surprised him about it. An expert's small observations can be fascinating.

contexts.subject: The expert calls the assessed stat flawless, without implying all stats are perfect.

BattleFrontier_Lounge1_Text_StatFlawless.text: It's flawless! A thing of perfection!\n…Hm… That's how I call it.$

replies.text: A perfect mark for that stat! Even the stern little grading pencil seems pleased.
That attribute meets his highest standard. We should keep its scope precisely in mind.
Can't improve that particular mark. Plenty else still matters.
That's such emphatic praise. I'd probably be smiling at our partner for a while.
A perfect mark is lovely. Being cared for never depended on earning one.
The expert has reached the ceiling of his vocabulary. A memorable occasion.
One flawless stat. The universe has allowed a small exception to its usual untidiness.
That's the upper limit for this assessment. Now we can plan around that confirmed strength.
A small perfection in a living, changing creature. No need to ask the rest to imitate it.
An excellent quality, clearly recognized. We can celebrate it without demanding eleven more.
I'd remember the look on the trainer's face when he said that. Good news lands visibly.

contexts.subject: The breeder scolds the player for declining his assessment.

BattleFrontier_Lounge1_Text_NoTimeForMyA.text: What?\nYou have no time for my advice?\pYou should always be eager to learn\nfrom the experiences of your elders!$

replies.text: I can respect seventy years of experience and still have somewhere else to be.
His expertise deserves consideration. It doesn't make every declined consultation disrespectful.
We said no to advice, not to his entire life.
I didn't mean to upset him. I just wasn't ready to show a Pokemon.
A useful offer is still an offer. There's no need to season it with guilt.
A consultation politely declined has somehow become a referendum on respect for one's elders.
The advice has been canceled. The lecture has proved less cooperative.
We can return when an assessment would actually help us make a decision.
An open hand feels different once it closes around your sleeve.
I wish he'd let the invitation stay welcoming. We might have come back more readily.
I'd rather ask when we're curious than pretend to listen just to avoid a scolding.

contexts.subject: A trainer is pleased that careful raising received the expert praise.

BattleFrontier_Lounge1_Text_SaidMyMonIsO.text: He said my POKéMON is outstanding!\nI'm glad I raised it carefully!$

replies.text: That compliment has found someone who will be smiling about it all day.
The assessment reassures her, though it doesn't measure every aspect of her care.
She's proud of her partner and the work. Fair enough.
She sounds relieved as well as pleased. The effort mattered to her.
Being attentive every day rarely comes with applause. Nice that she got a moment of it.
A short expert opinion has supplied a very long-lasting grin. Efficient generosity.
The quiet daily work has received one loud little reward.
It's encouraging to have a strength recognized after putting real care into a partner.
She held something carefully, and someone noticed its brightness.
I like that her pride goes straight back to the Pokemon.
I'd ask what routines they enjoy together. Care is often hidden in ordinary details.

contexts.subject: A trainer is surprised by an outstanding rating despite no special raising method.

BattleFrontier_Lounge1_Text_DidntDoAnyth.text: He said my POKéMON is outstanding!\nBut I didn't do anything special\lraising it…$

replies.text: Sometimes a little partner arrives with surprises already packed inside.
Innate variation can explain a strong assessment without an unusual training method.
Doesn't need a secret method to be worth celebrating.
He looks almost apologetic about the good news. He can just be happy.
Ordinary care can still be good care. Nothing special doesn't mean nothing kind.
Excellent news has arrived without the expected heroic backstory. How refreshing.
An outstanding Pokemon has neglected to require an elaborate origin story.
The result may reflect qualities he didn't create. Recognizing them is still useful.
Not every lovely thing announces the work of becoming lovely. Some simply arrive.
He doesn't have to invent an impressive routine to deserve enjoying his partner.
I'd ask what surprised him most about the assessment. He seems ready to reconsider a few assumptions.

contexts.subject: A student admires the Frontier Maniac ability to gather news.

BattleFrontier_Lounge2_Text_NewsGatherin.text: What amazing news-gathering power!\nMy mentor's like none other!$

replies.text: His mentor gathers news. He gathers opportunities to tell us how impressive that is.
Collecting timely information is a real skill. I'd also ask how the sources are checked.
Useful talent. Accurate matters as much as fast.
He's very proud of his teacher. It's nice when admiration is that uncomplicated.
Keeping up with this whole island must take a fair amount of conversation.
The mentor has acquired an enthusiastic publicity department of one.
Every rumor enters. Presumably some facts emerge. I'd ask about the sorting process.
An information network needs dependable contacts. I'm curious how he maintains them.
News travels from mouth to mouth. Its shape can change on the way.
He praises the skill instead of claiming it as his own. That's rather sweet.
I'd ask which discovery impressed him most. That would make a good introduction.

contexts.subject: A student admires the mentor powers of observation.

BattleFrontier_Lounge2_Text_AmazingPower.text: What amazing powers of observation!\nMy mentor's like none other!$

replies.text: He watches his mentor watching things. That's a surprisingly busy little arrangement.
Careful observation is teachable. I wonder what his mentor asks him to notice first.
Seeing details helps. Checking what they mean comes next.
I like teachers who help people notice what was already beside them.
Noticing a small problem early can save everyone a large headache later.
A keen observer, now observed by an extremely approving observer.
The noticing has become recursive. We may be watching its third generation.
I'd ask for a specific example. The method interests me more than the praise.
Some eyes make an ordinary room seem crowded with things we missed.
He's impressed enough to look more closely himself. That may be the real lesson.
I'd compare what each of them noticed in the same match. That could be fascinating.

contexts.subject: A student praises the mentor persuasive ability.

BattleFrontier_Lounge2_Text_AmazingPower.text: What amazing power of persuasion!\nMy mentor's like none other!$

replies.text: He's convinced me that he's convinced. The mentor's work is traveling well.
Persuasion can communicate good evidence or conceal weak evidence. The distinction matters.
A convincing voice still needs a sound point.
I hope he feels free to disagree with the person he admires.
Getting people to listen is useful. Leaving them room to decide matters, too.
The mentor's greatest proof of persuasion appears to be standing directly in front of us.
A very persuasive man has obtained a very persuaded audience.
I'd like to know how he explains things. A clear method can be learned.
Some voices open a path. Others quietly remove all the forks.
Admiration is warm. I'd still want to hear the idea before agreeing with it.
I'd ask for an example of an opinion the mentor changed. The details would tell us more.

contexts.subject: A visitor is unnerved by the intense Frontier Maniac room.

replies.text: A room full of matching enthusiasm can be more unsettling than an actual ghost.
The concentrated admiration may feel socially disorienting to someone outside the group.
They can step outside. No need to stay uncomfortable.
I understand. Sometimes a room feels as though everyone learned a rule except you.
Let's give them a little space. They don't need another person asking what's wrong.
The atmosphere appears to have become slightly more organized than comfort allows.
No hauntings confirmed. The enthusiasm alone seems to be managing.
A quiet break outside might make the room less overwhelming when they return.
A room can be crowded with certainty. It's difficult to breathe between all of it.
Being the only uncertain person in a very certain group is uncomfortable.
I'd ask whether they want company outside. We don't need to make a scene.

contexts.subject: The gamblers brusquely dismiss the player before considering a wager.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_CantYouSeeWe.text: …What's that you want?\pCan't you see we're kind of busy here?\nCan't your business wait till later?$

replies.text: He could have said busy without wrapping it in quite so many elbows.
Their activity doesn't excuse the discourteous response. We can leave them to it.
Fine. Plenty of better company elsewhere.
I wasn't trying to interrupt anything important. We can go.
No need to stand around waiting for someone determined to be unpleasant.
A spectacularly unwelcoming welcome from a room that could have simply said later.
The atmosphere has declined our company. I accept on behalf of both sides.
We don't have a reason to keep interrupting. Let's use the time elsewhere.
A closed door without the courtesy of an actual door.
He made the room smaller with one greeting. I wouldn't fight for a place in it.
I'll save my questions for somebody who feels like answering them.

contexts.subject: After paying a successful wager, the gambler invites another challenge.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_ThinkOfMeFor.text: If you're up for another challenge,\nplease do think of me!$

replies.text: He's paid up and would love another appointment with our points. Naturally.
The previous payout is settled. It doesn't change the risk of the next wager.
One settled deal. We don't owe him another.
He sounds friendly again now that everything went well. I'd remember both moods.
We can enjoy getting the points back without immediately putting them at risk again.
A business relationship that survives success is now eagerly requesting a sequel.
The points returned home. Their former host is already sending invitations.
Any new arrangement needs a fresh decision. The previous result shouldn't make it automatic.
A returned handful can make the next open hand seem safer than it is.
He's pleasant when he's pleased. That doesn't tell us how the next bet will go.
I'd rather choose our next challenge first, then decide whether this arrangement belongs in it.

contexts.subject: After a failed wager, the gambler says the staked points cannot be returned.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_NiceTryCantR.text:
Oh, it's you…
Nice try…\pI hate to break it to you, but I can't
return your Battle Points…\pI guess we'll have to let it motivate
us to try harder next time!$

replies.text: The points are gone, and his consolation has arrived with completely empty pockets.
The loss is now realized. Another wager isn't required to justify the previous stake.
Lost points. Stop and think before risking more.
His softer voice doesn't make the missing points feel much better.
We don't need to chase the loss today. Let's do something that doesn't require another stake.
He offers motivation with admirable generosity, given that it costs him none of the missing points.
The consolation is free. Everything useful has remained elsewhere.
We should assess the arrangement on its actual cost before repeating it.
An empty hand can itch to reach out again. It doesn't have to.
Calling the loss motivation puts a flattering ribbon around an unpleasant result.
I'd rather review what happened than hear another promise about next time.

contexts.subject: The gambler calls the player afraid after a declined wager.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_NotIntereste.text: Not interested?! You shouldn't be\nso afraid to take a chance!$

replies.text: My points don't have to jump off a cliff to prove they aren't afraid of heights.
Declining a wager may reflect preference or judgment. Fear isn't the only explanation.
We said no. He can live with it.
That makes me less inclined to change my mind, honestly.
A good offer shouldn't need an insult to push someone into it.
He has mistaken an attempt to preserve our points for a personal character flaw.
The offer has grown teeth now that we stopped feeding it.
Pressure after a refusal is useful information about the person making the offer.
A choice stops feeling free when refusal becomes an accusation.
He's trying to make sensible caution look embarrassing. That doesn't improve his proposal.
I'd rather spend time with someone who can hear no without inventing a story about it.

contexts.subject: An observer disapproves of trainers gambling instead of taking challenges.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_ShouldBeTaki.text: Those TRAINERS…\nWhat are they doing?\lThey should be taking challenges.$

replies.text: An island full of actual battles, and they've built a small argument about other people's battles.
They prefer wagering to direct competition. That may explain the activity without endorsing it.
Their choice. Just don't let them rope unwilling people in.
Maybe being a spectator feels easier than being judged themselves.
I'd rather use my own effort to earn points, too. Less waiting on somebody else.
They have found a way to make other people do the battling while they supply the tension.
A battle facility has developed a secondary industry in standing around.
The challenges offer direct feedback. Watching a wager doesn't teach quite the same things.
Some people prefer to place their hopes in another person's hands.
I understand his frustration. I'd also leave room for people to enjoy different parts of a visit.
I'd ask the gamblers what they like about it. The answer might be more revealing than the game.

contexts.subject: A repeated losing bettor considers returning to ordinary battles.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_BackedWrongT.text: I backed the wrong TRAINER again!\pMaybe I should be battling normally\nlike everyone else…$

replies.text: His own Pokemon might enjoy being promoted from audience to actual participants again.
Repeatedly unsuccessful predictions are a reasonable basis for reconsidering the method.
Sounds sensible. Put effort into a result he can influence.
He sounds tired of waiting for someone else to win for him.
Battling himself could give him something useful even when he loses: practice.
He has discovered that choosing the winner is harder than simply announcing one.
The fortune-telling department is considering a practical career change.
Direct participation would give him more information about his own decisions.
His attention is beginning to return to the path beneath his own feet.
He seems ready to choose a different way to spend the afternoon. Good.
I'd ask which challenge he used to enjoy. That could be a nicer place to restart.

contexts.subject: A bettor confidently claims to recognize winners on sight.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_KnowWinnerWh.text: Giggle!\nI know a winner when I see one!$

replies.text: I wonder if the winners know they've been identified. It might save them some suspense.
That claim would be interesting to compare against a recorded prediction history.
Everyone can spot the winner after the result. Before it is the hard part.
She sounds very sure. I wouldn't borrow that certainty without knowing why.
A confident smile doesn't make a stake any less costly if she's wrong.
A bold claim, conveniently unaccompanied by the results ledger.
The smile is certain. The future has declined to comment.
I'd ask what evidence she uses. A repeatable method is more useful than confidence.
Eyes can find what they expect very easily. The next match may be less obliging.
She certainly knows how to make the prediction feel reassuring. That's its own skill.
I'd ask her before a match and check afterward. Memory is kinder to winners than to misses.

contexts.subject: An observer says a skilled trainer struggles with pressure at the Dome.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_TrainerGoodB.text: That TRAINER…\pHe's good, but he gets rattled too\neasily to survive the BATTLE DOME…$

replies.text: Knowing the right move and remembering it while everyone's staring are different little beasts.
Performance under pressure is a separate skill from understanding the strategy.
Then he needs practice with pressure. Calling him doomed won't help.
I understand getting rattled when people expect you to do well.
He might do better with a calm supporter than another person measuring every wobble.
A sound assessment could become useful advice if delivered with considerably more kindness.
Talent has encountered nerves. They have a well-established disagreement.
He could rehearse decisions under smaller amounts of pressure and build up gradually.
A steady hand is sometimes learned one shaking attempt at a time.
Everybody watching him seems to have an opinion. That may be part of the difficulty.
I'd ask the trainer what helps him settle. The spectator can't answer that for him.

contexts.subject: A cook sees a restaurant opportunity among the Frontier visitors.

BattleFrontier_Lounge4_Text_IfIOpenedRes.text: If I opened a restaurant here,\nit'd make money for sure.$

replies.text: A crowd of hungry battlers. That's a business plan with several rumbling endorsements.
Visitor volume suggests demand. Costs and daily demand variation still need checking.
People need to eat. He should work out the numbers before opening.
I'd like somewhere quiet to sit after a challenge. Maybe he could make that.
I'd ask what he'd serve first. Feeding a rushed crowd takes a menu that works hard.
