Seven facilities have produced an eighth challenge: finding lunch. He's noticed the vacancy.
A profitable ambition. The island's stomachs are probably willing to negotiate.
He needs a supply plan as well as customers. An island adds complications.
A place built around striving could use somewhere that simply welcomes hunger.
The room itself might matter as much as the menu. People will want a breather.
I'd ask who he imagines sitting at the first table. That usually makes a plan more vivid.

contexts.subject: A resting trainer continues planning strategies despite exhaustion.

BattleFrontier_Lounge4_Text_NeedBreather.text: Whew…\pI need to take a breather after\nsome intense battles…\pBut even now, I never take a break\nfrom plotting strategy and combos.$

replies.text: His feet are resting. The rest of him has started another tournament.
Mental fatigue can persist even when physical activity stops. A genuine pause may help.
Take the breather properly. The next combination can wait.
Sometimes thoughts keep moving because going quiet feels harder.
I'd give him a drink and a few minutes without asking about the next match.
He has granted his body a recess while keeping his mind under full interrogation.
A rest with all the restful parts carefully removed.
Writing the idea down might let him stop rehearsing it for a while.
A mind can pace the room long after its owner has sat down.
He sounds proud of never stopping. I wonder whether it's still helping him.
I'd ask about something besides battling for once. He might enjoy remembering the island exists.

contexts.subject: A viewer hopes to see interviews with strong trainers on television.

BattleFrontier_Lounge4_Text_WonderIfInte.text: I wonder if they'll be airing interviews\nwith tough TRAINERS today?$

replies.text: The battles show what they do. I'd like to hear what they thought they were doing.
Interviews can reveal reasoning unavailable from observing the battle alone.
Could be useful. Depends whether they ask about the actual decisions.
I'd be curious what they're like once nobody needs to look fearless.
I like hearing the ordinary routines behind somebody's big achievement.
A chance for the formidable trainers to reveal whether they can also survive a question.
After the battle comes the difficult task of explaining yourself in public.
I'd want them to explain one choice that didn't work. That's often the useful part.
A voice after the spectacle can bring a distant person a little closer.
Interviews show how people carry attention. That can be as revealing as the answers.
I'd love to know which questions the interviewer chooses. Follow-ups make all the difference.

contexts.subject: The girl refuses to read an Egg because it is asleep.

BattleFrontier_Lounge5_Text_NatureGirlEg.text: That's silly! An EGG is asleep!\nI can't talk to it!$

replies.text: The Egg has declined the interview by being extremely busy becoming a Pokemon.
An unhatched Pokemon doesn't provide her the same basis for a reading. Sensible boundary.
Fair enough. Let the little Egg be.
I like that she thinks of it as sleeping. She sounds very certain about being considerate.
No need to wake a guest who hasn't even arrived yet.
The smallest guest has secured an exemption from all conversation. Enviable.
The Egg is unavailable for comment. A dignified response.
She knows a case her method doesn't cover. That's useful to acknowledge.
Some closed things deserve time before questions.
She may be blunt, but she isn't going to pretend to hear something just to impress us.
We can ask again after it hatches. Then there will be a new little personality to meet.

contexts.subject: The girl pouts after the player declines to show a Pokemon.

replies.text: We've been charged one small pout for keeping our Pokemon to ourselves.
Disappointment doesn't create an obligation to participate in her reading.
She can be disappointed. We can still say no.
I feel a little bad. I still wasn't ready to show anyone.
A no doesn't have to spoil the whole visit. She'll find another thing to do.
A devastating review from a customer who was never actually our customer.
The consultation has ended in a highly compact protest.
No Pokemon was selected, so there's no reading to assess. We can return another time.
A small disappointment can make a loud little shadow. It passes.
She wants to show what she can do. I understand the pout without needing to give in.
I'd give her a moment rather than turn it into an argument.

contexts.subject: A gentleman is charmed by a girl who claims to understand Pokemon.

BattleFrontier_Lounge5_Text_LadyClaimsSh.text: How charming!\nThat little lady claims she can\lunderstand POKéMON!$

replies.text: He finds it charming. I'd like to hear the Pokemon's review before we settle the question.
He reports her claim, rather than independently demonstrating its accuracy. A useful distinction.
Interesting claim. Let's listen before deciding what to make of it.
He sounds pleased just watching her enjoy herself.
If she pays close attention to them, that part alone is worthwhile.
A charming claim with a conveniently difficult interview process for its other witnesses.
The gentleman is convinced of the charm. The translation remains under review.
I'd compare the reading with observable behavior. That gives us a place to start.
Understanding another creature begins with noticing it. Whatever else she does, that matters.
He isn't mocking her. That's a gentler response than she might get elsewhere.
I'd ask what he's seen her notice. A specific example would be interesting.

contexts.subject: A Black Belt suspects the girl Pokemon readings are profound.

BattleFrontier_Lounge5_Text_GirlSayingSo.text: I have this feeling that the little girl\nis saying something profound.$

replies.text: He's searching for deep meaning. The girl may just be having a very direct conversation.
A feeling of profundity isn't evidence of accuracy, though it can prompt closer attention.
Maybe ask her what she means. No need to guess forever.
I know that feeling when something simple seems bigger than I can explain.
A good question might get him farther than looking impressed from across the room.
He has discovered mystery and is treating it with admirable seriousness.
The depth remains unmeasured. He has wisely declined to announce a number.
He could ask for clarification. That's often the quickest route through a mysterious idea.
A small voice can make a large silence around it. He seems to be listening to that.
He wants to understand, which is a warmer response than simply dismissing her.
I'd ask which part stayed with him. That might be more revealing than the word profound.

contexts.subject: A boy says the girl often plays at the red house.

BattleFrontier_Lounge5_Text_GirlPlaysAtR.text: I know something!\pThat little girl plays at the red house\na lot!$

replies.text: A grand mystery has acquired a very ordinary detail: she has a favorite place to play.
A specific repeated observation. That helps place her daily routine.
Good to know. Still her choice where she goes.
I like hearing about the ordinary part of her day.
Even somebody with an unusual talent needs somewhere familiar to spend time.
A useful reminder that the mysterious young oracle also has afternoons to fill.
The intriguing child has been discovered committing ordinary childhood.
He knows where she spends time. That doesn't tell us everything about why she likes it.
A favorite house can anchor a very strange little day.
He's noticed her routine without making a grand claim about it. Refreshing.
I'd ask whether they play together. He seems glad to share the detail.

contexts.subject: The Frontier trader promises care after exchanging Meowth for Skitty.

BattleFrontier_Lounge6_Text_PromiseIllBe.text: Oh, it's adorable!\nThank you!\lI promise I'll be good to it!\pOh! I hope you'll be good to\nmy {STR_VAR_2}, too!$

replies.text: Two new partners, and she remembers to wish both of them well.
The exchange is complete. Her promise concerns the ongoing care that follows it.
Good promise. Now both trainers need to keep it.
She sounds delighted and a little protective at the same time.
A new home starts with getting to know what the little one actually likes.
The exchange ends with mutual responsibilities. A much better conclusion than merely calling it a bargain.
A small creature has arrived to enthusiastic reviews and a promise of kindness.
Now comes the learning: habits, preferences, and how each partner communicates.
A parting wish reaches after the one leaving. A welcome waits for the one staying.
She's delighted without forgetting the partner she handed over. I appreciate that.
I'd ask her later how Skitty settled in. That first welcome sounds warm.

contexts.subject: The trader graciously accepts a declined exchange and invites another visit.

BattleFrontier_Lounge6_Text_WellThatsFin.text: Oh, you won't?\nWell, that's fine, too.\lPlease come visit us again.$

replies.text: A declined trade, and we're still welcome. Nice when a conversation keeps its manners.
She separates the proposed exchange from the social visit. A considerate response.
No argument. Good way to handle it.
I'm glad she didn't make saying no feel unkind.
We can enjoy visiting without having to make an exchange.
A gracious refusal of any need to be offended. Admirably economical.
The trade has vanished. The hospitality remains.
We can reconsider later without being pushed into a decision now.
A door stays open after a hand is drawn back.
She left room for us to visit as people instead of only potential traders.
I'd happily come back just to ask how her partner is doing.

contexts.subject: The trader declines a Pokemon of the wrong requested species.

BattleFrontier_Lounge6_Text_DontTradeFor.text: Oh, I'm sorry!\nI don't intend to trade for anything\lbut a {STR_VAR_1}.$

replies.text: She's looking for one particular little face. Our offer hasn't changed the shopping list.
The proposed Pokemon doesn't meet the species requirement. The exchange hasn't occurred.
Wrong species. At least she's clear about it.
She apologized first. That makes a small refusal easier to hear.
Wanting a specific partner isn't a criticism of the one we showed her.
A precise request has received a precise correction. No diplomatic incident required.
The specification survives contact with an alternative. A firm little boundary.
We need the requested species if we want to proceed. The condition hasn't changed.
One creature cannot stand in for another merely because we offered it.
She knows what she wants and says it politely. That's fair.
I'd ask why that species caught her interest. There might be a nice story behind it.

contexts.subject: After the trade, the delighted trader says Skitty exceeds her expectations.

BattleFrontier_Lounge6_Text_SkittySoMuch.text: Giggle!\nA SKITTY is so much cuter than I had\limagined. I'm delighted!$

replies.text: The real Skitty has defeated the imaginary Skitty in a decisive cuteness contest.
Direct experience exceeded her expectation. A rather pleasant revision.
She's happy with the partner. Good to see.
She still sounds surprised by how much she likes the little one.
That welcome seems to have lasted past the first excitement. Lovely.
An excellent result for Skitty, whose mere presence has outperformed advance publicity.
Reality has briefly been kinder than imagination. Skitty should receive appropriate credit.
She had a clear wish and is pleased by the actual partner, not just the idea.
Sometimes the thing we waited for arrives with more life than our wanting could invent.
She's delighted by the individual in front of her. That matters more than the original picture.
I'd ask what Skitty does that she finds funniest. She looks ready to tell us.

contexts.subject: A move tutor accepts cancellation and invites the player back.

BattleFrontier_Lounge7_Text_YouDontWantT.text: What's that?\nYou don't want to…\pIf you want to see how skilled I am,\nyou come see me anytime!$

replies.text: We can come back when the team is ready. Her confidence will clearly keep until then.
No lesson was completed. The option remains available for a later decision.
Fine. Better to choose a move carefully than spend points in a hurry.
She sounded disappointed, but she still invited us back.
A lesson can wait until we know which partner actually needs it.
She has preserved both the invitation and her unshaken opinion of her own skill.
The demonstration has been postponed. The confidence is already fully assembled.
We can compare the move choices before committing our points.
Knowledge can wait without becoming less useful.
She wants to impress us, but she left the choice with us.
I'd come back with a specific question. That would make the visit more useful.

contexts.subject: The tutor finishes a successful lesson and takes the agreed Battle Points.

BattleFrontier_Lounge7_Text_IllTakeBattl.text: Do you see how skilled I am now?\nI'll take your Battle Points, thanks!$

replies.text: New skill learned, agreed fee paid. Her victory speech comes included.
The lesson succeeded and the quoted cost is now collected. A completed transaction.
Learned the move. Paid the price. Let's practice using it well.
She's so pleased to prove herself. Our partner did some learning, too.
Worth giving the new move a little thought before trying it in a serious match.
Service rendered, fee collected, modesty still notably absent. A complete experience.
The lesson is complete. Her self-esteem required no additional instruction.
Now the team has another option. I'd work out where it fits with the existing moves.
An old skill has found a new pair of hands. Or paws.
She earned the payment. I think she enjoyed the recognition almost as much.
I'd ask our partner how that new move feels. The teacher has certainly given her review.

contexts.subject: An observer suspects the bickering tutors remain together because they are friends.

BattleFrontier_Lounge7_Text_ThinkLadiesD.text: Those ladies, the way they bad-mouth\neach other, you probably think that\lthey don't get along.\pBut if that were true, they wouldn't\nstay out here together, would they?$

replies.text: They've found someone willing to stay nearby through an impressive amount of complaining.
Their continued company supports his interpretation, though it doesn't settle every disagreement.
Could be fond of each other and still argue. Happens.
They seem to know exactly which things will make the other react.
Some people fuss at each other the way other people offer another cup of tea.
A friendship conducted almost entirely through objections. The longevity is persuasive.
They have apparently agreed to remain together and disagree about everything else.
A long working partnership can include friction. I'd look at how they actually treat each other.
Some roots twist around one another. Pulling apart would be the stranger shape.
He notices the choice to stay together underneath the noisy performance.
I'd like to hear how they met. They might even interrupt each other with matching corrections.

contexts.subject: An old admirer praises the tutors increasing skill but laments aging.

BattleFrontier_Lounge7_Text_LadiesWereSt.text:
When I was just a wee YOUNGSTER,
those ladies were strong and beautiful.\pThey were idols among us TRAINERS.\pEven now, age hasn't dulled their
abilities.\pIn fact, their POKéMON moves have
grown even more polished.\pBut… For some reason, I can't help
but feel this…\pTime is so cruel…$

replies.text: Their moves keep improving. Time seems to have handed them at least one decent gift.
He reports their skill has advanced with experience. That deserves attention in its own right.
Still strong, still teaching. Nothing cruel about that part.
I wish he could say all the kind things without making the years sound like an apology.
They've kept learning and sharing it. That's a good way to carry a long life.
He praises everything the years have added, then files a complaint against the years.
Time has improved the moves and offended the admirer. The ladies seem busy regardless.
Decades of refinement would explain the polish. Experience keeps producing useful work.
A long life changes the vessel. What it holds can grow richer.
He remembers their beauty so strongly that he's overlooking the people standing here now.
I'd ask the tutors what they're proudest of learning lately. They're the better people to answer.

contexts.subject: A boastful visitor lists every trainer virtue but does not know what Pokemon are.

BattleFrontier_Lounge8_Text_WhatATrainer.text:
What a TRAINER needs…\pKnowledge…
Strategy…\lLuck…\lGuts…\lSpirit…\lBravery…\lAnd ability…\pWell, I'm all set in every way!
I'll be unstoppable at every building!\pHuh? POKéMON?
What's that?$

replies.text: He's packed every possible quality and somehow left out the Pokemon. That's a special kind of light travel.
His checklist omits the defining participant in the activity. A substantial conceptual gap.
He might want to start with the basic question before challenging anything.
I thought he was joking. I'm still not completely sure.
That's like planning a whole meal and asking what food is. We should begin again.
A magnificent inventory of qualifications, missing only the central premise of the entire profession.
Perfectly prepared, apart from a small disagreement with the meaning of prepared.
The requirements list needs one major revision before any practical testing.
He has gathered every key except the one belonging to the door.
His confidence survived not knowing the central detail. That's almost a talent by itself.
I'd ask one careful follow-up. I really need to know whether he's serious.

contexts.subject: A visitor explains Scott title for the seven facility leaders.

BattleFrontier_Lounge8_Text_KnowAboutFro.text: Do you know about the FRONTIER\nBRAINS?\pThat's what SCOTT calls the seven\nspecial TRAINERS that run the seven\lfacilities in the BATTLE FRONTIER.$

replies.text: Seven Brains running seven buildings. I wonder who gets called when they disagree.
The title identifies the seven facility leaders. Useful terminology for the local hierarchy.
Seven specialists. Each place has someone responsible for its challenge.
That makes the big buildings feel a little more personal. Somebody shaped each one.
Seven very different challenges must need seven very different kinds of attention.
A grand collective title. Considerably more memorable than facility management.
An island with seven Brains and apparently no shortage of opinions.
I'd like to know how much each leader helped design their facility's rules.
Seven houses, seven minds. Each will leave a different shape on the people entering.
Scott understands a memorable title. People will remember that one after hearing it once.
I'd ask which leader they've met. The official title tells us less than an actual encounter.

contexts.subject: A boy distinguishes his battle talent from his stronger interest in Contests.

BattleFrontier_Lounge8_Text_ToldMeIHaveT.text: At the BATTLE TOWER, an older girl\ntold me that I have a lot of talent\lfor battling!\pI like POKéMON CONTESTS more!\pBut I'm no good at CONTESTS!\pI guess having talent and liking\nsomething aren't the same.$

replies.text: Being good at one thing doesn't mean it gets to confiscate the thing you love.
Aptitude and interest are separate variables. Practice can still improve the preferred activity.
He can like Contests. Talent isn't an order.
I'd rather hear what he loves about Contests than tell him to give them up.
He doesn't have to turn his easiest skill into his whole life. Enjoyment is worth something.
A talent has arrived and attempted to appoint itself his future. He may decline the position.
A gift doesn't get to issue instructions simply because it arrived early.
He can build Contest skills deliberately. Starting behind doesn't make the project pointless.
The easy path isn't always the one that calls your name.
I like that he knows the difference. Other people may need reminding more than he does.
I'd ask which part of Contests he enjoys most. That's where I'd start talking about practice.

contexts.subject: The attendant introduces the hall honoring Frontier records.

BattleFrontier_RankingHall_Text_ExplainR.text: This is the RANKING HALL.\pThis is where we recognize the immortal\nTRAINERS who left great records in\lBATTLE FRONTIER events.$

replies.text: A room full of names that earned a little extra space in people's memories.
The hall records exceptional results across facilities. A useful comparative archive.
Those names earned their place. Ours would need to do the same.
I'd read slowly. Each name probably means a great deal to someone.
A lot of ordinary practice must sit behind every extraordinary number.
Immortality has been reduced to a conveniently readable list. Efficient institution.
A hall of people who have defeated the reasonable stopping point.
I'd compare the categories before deciding which record to pursue.
The wall keeps the name. The person keeps the cost of reaching it.
Recognition matters. I like that the achievement stays beside the name.
I'd want to hear one story from each person, though that might take a very long visit.

contexts.subject: A boy realizes he cannot appear in the records before attempting a challenge.

BattleFrontier_RankingHall_Text_MyNamesN.text: Hmm…\nMy name's not up there…\pWell, it's only natural since I haven't\ntaken any challenges yet.$

replies.text: He checked just in case the wall had done the battling for him. Sensible to confirm.
He has correctly identified the missing prerequisite. Participation precedes a result.
At least he's honest. First attempt comes before the record.
Maybe seeing the empty place will make starting feel a little more real.
Everyone on that list had a first attempt. He can have one, too.
An unexplained omission has received an exceptionally straightforward explanation.
The records office has declined to invent his career. Harsh but fair.
Now he can choose a challenge and establish a starting result.
An unwritten name isn't a rejected one. Sometimes the story hasn't begun.
He's able to laugh at the gap between wanting it and having tried. That's healthy.
I'd ask which challenge he wants to attempt first. That's the interesting next question.

contexts.subject: The boy admires the player listed record and feels motivated to improve.

BattleFrontier_RankingHall_Text_WowThats.text: Wow, that's super!\nI'll have to try harder, too!$

replies.text: Our name gave him a little push forward. That's a nice thing for a name to do.
An example has become a concrete source of motivation. A constructive comparison.
Good. Let it encourage him to try.
He sounds happy for us without making himself smaller.
A shared achievement can give someone else a place to start.
An accolade has escaped the wall and become useful to another person. Excellent.
The record has successfully reproduced ambition. The hall should be pleased.
He has a benchmark now. Smaller goals can build toward it.
A name on a wall has opened a door in someone else's day.
His congratulations felt warm. I like that he made room for his own hopes, too.
I'd ask him to tell us when he sets his first record. I'd like to hear about it.

contexts.subject: The boy suggests a friend name in the records could encourage harder effort.

BattleFrontier_RankingHall_Text_WorkHard.text: Oh, is that right?\pIf you saw your friend's name up here,\nI bet it would make you work harder!$

replies.text: A familiar name might make the big wall feel a little closer to home.
Peer examples can motivate effort, though people respond differently to comparison.
Friendly competition can help. It shouldn't become resentment.
I'd mostly be happy to see someone I knew. The harder work could come later.
A friend's success is worth celebrating before making it our next assignment.
He proposes borrowing ambition from a familiar name. A plausible arrangement.
Friendship, now available as a gentle competitive nuisance.
A specific example can make a target seem reachable. The next step still needs planning.
A familiar name can turn a distant achievement into a path someone we know has walked.
I'd want the friend to feel celebrated, rather than immediately treated as the next rival.
I'd ask how they earned it. Knowing their route could be more useful than copying the goal.

contexts.subject: Grandparents accompanying their grandson decide to shop for souvenirs.

BattleFrontier_Mart_Text_ChaperonGrandso.text: We came here to chaperon our\ngrandson.\pBut since we're here, we thought\nwe should get some souvenirs.$

replies.text: They came as chaperons and have discovered the side quest of bringing something home.
A supporting visit can still include interests of their own. Sensible use of the trip.
Good. They should enjoy the visit, too.
I like that this has become a little outing for all of them.
A small souvenir can make the journey feel like theirs as well as his.
The official chaperoning mission has expanded to include a modest shopping operation.
Responsible supervision, with optional commemorative purchases.
I'd choose something easy to carry for the return journey.
They followed his adventure and found a small piece of their own.
They deserve something they actually like, rather than just a token of being good grandparents.
I'd ask what they enjoyed most so far. The answer might surprise their grandson.

contexts.subject: A grandparent mistakes the Pokemon supplement Protein for an appetizing gift.

BattleFrontier_Mart_Text_ProteinMakeNice.text: Dear, what do you think of this?\nWouldn't this make a nice gift?\pIt's…PRO…TE…IN?\nIt sounds delicious, doesn't it?$

replies.text: It sounds tasty to her. I think we should check the label before anyone sets out a plate.
That's a Pokemon supplement rather than an ordinary snack. The label deserves a closer look.
Ask the clerk what it is before buying it as food.
She wants to choose something nice. A little explanation would help more than laughing.
I admire the gift instinct. I'd redirect the menu before anybody samples it.
A generous purchase is approaching a small but important category error.
The gift may be useful. The proposed tasting notes are less well supported.
Packaging should make the intended use clearer. This confusion is quite understandable.
A kind thought has taken a wrong turn at an unfamiliar word. Easy enough to guide back.
She wants the gift to feel like a treat. We can help her find something that fits.
I'd ask the clerk to explain it kindly. She's choosing with care, just missing a detail.

contexts.subject: A shopper notes item restrictions make Frontier battles more difficult.

BattleFrontier_Mart_Text_FacilitiesDontA.text: A lot of the BATTLE FRONTIER's\nfacilities don't allow the use of items\lduring battles.\pThat rule makes things tougher than\nthey already are!$

replies.text: The bag can't rescue every problem here. It may have to enjoy being luggage for once.
Restricting in-battle items shifts more weight onto preparation and move selection.
Know the rules before packing a plan around items.
I'd miss having one more way to help when a partner struggles.
Then preparing well beforehand matters even more. Shopping isn't the whole plan.
The emergency supplies have been politely informed that they are not on the team sheet.
An impressive bag is about to discover the indignity of being irrelevant.
We'll need plans that work within each facility's restrictions.
A familiar safety net has been folded away. Best to notice before stepping out.
The same team can need a different approach when one familiar option disappears.
I'd ask which restriction surprised them most. That could save us an avoidable mistake.

contexts.subject: A trainer plans to take every challenge with a cherished Skitty.

BattleFrontier_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Goi.text: Giggle… I'm going to go through every\nchallenge with just this baby!$

replies.text: One Skitty, an entire Frontier, and enough confidence to fill the rest of the team slots.
A highly focused ambition. Facility rules and matchups may complicate the implementation.
Bold plan. She'll still need to respect each facility's entry rules.
She calls the little one her baby. There's so much affection in that.
I like the faith in her partner. I'd keep the challenges at a pace they both enjoy.
A tiny partner has been assigned a very large itinerary.
The Frontier has seven grand facilities. Skitty has one enthusiastic advocate.
I'd start by checking which challenge formats allow the team she intends to use.
One small companion can make a huge place feel like a shared adventure.
She isn't shopping for a more impressive-looking partner. She's proud of the one beside her.
I'd ask which challenge they're excited about first. That pair clearly has plans.

contexts.subject: A student encounters a Pokemon absent from their school lessons and wonders about its habitat.

BattleFrontier_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Nev.text:
There was someone here using a 
POKéMON I've never seen before.\pI never learned about it at
TRAINER'S SCHOOL at least.\pI wonder where you can catch POKéMON
like that.$

replies.text: School has run out of Pokemon before the world has. That's a rather exciting discovery.
A curriculum is necessarily incomplete. Direct observation has supplied a new question.
Good question. Ask the trainer where they met it.
I like that not knowing made them curious instead of embarrassed.
There's always something new beyond the lessons. A polite question could tell them plenty.
The world has failed to stop expanding at the end of the textbook. Excellent news.
An educational omission with a face. Much more interesting than a missing paragraph.
They could note its features, ask the trainer, and compare the information afterward.
A lesson ended. The creature beyond it did not.
They're comfortable admitting they haven't seen it before. That makes learning much easier.
I'd ask what detail caught their eye first. A good observation begins there.

contexts.subject: A trainer chooses suitable partners from storage before visiting the Arena.

BattleFrontier_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_Nex.text: Okay! Next stop, the BATTLE ARENA!\nI'd better get the right POKéMON from\lthe PC Storage System.$

replies.text: An enthusiastic destination, followed by a sensible pause to choose who actually comes.
Selecting for the facility's specific rules should improve the relevance of the team.
Good. Prepare before walking into the challenge.
I like hearing someone sound excited and still take time to think.
Picking the right partners is kinder than expecting everyone to handle every situation.
The grand declaration has been followed by the practical work. A rare and pleasing sequence.
Ambition remembered to stop at the planning desk. Promising behavior.
Order matters in the Arena. I'd check the whole sequence, not only the first partner.
A choice made quietly here will shape what happens in the bright room ahead.
Being ready can look quite ordinary from the outside. This is part of it.
I'd ask why they chose each partner. The reasoning would tell us a lot about their plan.

contexts.subject: The ferry attendant refuses boarding because the player has no ticket.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_MustHave.text: {PLAYER} doesn't have the TICKET…\pI'm terribly sorry.\pYou must have a TICKET to board\nthe ferry.$

replies.text: A whole ferry is being held back by one missing little rectangle. Rules do love rectangles.
The required ticket is absent, so boarding cannot proceed. A clear administrative barrier.
Need the ticket. Arguing won't put one in the bag.
At least the attendant explained it kindly.
We should check where the ticket belongs before making another trip to the dock.
The ship may float, but the paperwork has declined to budge.
The sea is open. The boarding policy is not.
We have a specific missing requirement. That's easier to solve than an unclear refusal.
A short crossing can wait behind a very small missing thing.
They're apologetic without making the rule confusing. I appreciate the clear answer.
I'd ask where to sort out the ticket. Better than guessing around the harbor.

contexts.subject: The attendant warmly accepts a canceled ferry trip.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_SailWith.text: Please sail with us another time!$

replies.text: The boat is staying without us, and nobody has made it awkward. A fine cancellation.
The journey was declined without consequence. The service remains available later.
We can sail another time. No hurry.
I'm glad changing our mind didn't become a whole conversation.
A trip is more pleasant when we actually feel ready to take it.
A cordial end to an expedition that never quite became an expedition.
The sea has been postponed. It seems likely to remain available.
We can finish what we're doing here before deciding on a destination.
A departure can wait. The shore isn't going to resent us for staying.
That was an easy, gracious goodbye. Good service includes letting people leave the counter.
I'd rather sail with a clear plan for where we're going. We can take a little time.

contexts.subject: The Tower attendant ends the visit by inviting another challenge, regardless of result.

BattleFrontier_BattleTowerLobby_Text_Loo.text: We look forward to seeing you on\nanother challenge!$

replies.text: The Tower will still be here when we feel like trying again. Rather hard to misplace it.
That invitation follows multiple outcomes. It doesn't itself specify a win or loss.
A clear stopping point. We'll decide when to return.
It's nice to be welcomed back without another judgment attached.
Time to regroup and see what everyone needs before another attempt.
A courteous farewell from a building with an inexhaustible supply of opponents.
The Tower remains optimistic about our future availability.
We can review the visit before choosing another challenge.
An open invitation can stay open while we rest.
I appreciate a goodbye that leaves the next visit up to us.
I'd return with a fresh plan and see what changes.

contexts.subject: The Dome guide closes the visit without specifying the tournament result.

BattleFrontier_BattleDomeLobby_Text_Hope.text: We hope to see you again.$

replies.text: The Dome has said goodbye without asking for one more round of applause.
A general farewell. The tournament outcome must be established by other information.
Visit finished. Good time to take stock.
I like leaving on a quiet, kind note after all the competition.
We can get something to eat before considering another tournament.
A pleasant closing line that wisely makes no promises about our next opponent.
The bracket has released us back into ordinary conversation.
We have time to reconsider team choices before another visit.
A crowded contest can end with a very small goodbye.
The invitation is warm without being pushy. That helps.
I'd be curious what the tournament looks like on a different day.

contexts.subject: The Factory attendant ends the rental challenge visit.

BattleFrontier_BattleFactoryLobby_Text_L.text: We look forward to your next visit.$

replies.text: Next visit, a new set of unfamiliar faces to get to know. That's quite a greeting policy.
A later visit may offer a different rental selection. Adaptation remains central here.
We're finished for now. Review what worked before going back.
I wonder which rental partners we'll remember longest.
Learning somebody else's habits quickly takes attention. A break sounds good now.
The Factory parts politely with its temporary workforce of visiting strategists.
The next visit is waiting. Presumably beside several unpredictable teammates.
I'd note which combinations worked while the details are fresh.
A borrowed partnership can leave a surprisingly lasting impression.
A neat end to a visit built around quick introductions.
I'd ask the staff how often the rental lineup changes.

contexts.subject: The Palace guide asks the visitor to return when trainer and Pokemon are fortified.

BattleFrontier_BattlePalaceLobby_Text_Re.text: When you have fortified your heart\nand POKéMON, you must return.$

replies.text: A little stronger, a little steadier, and perhaps a little less tempted to shout advice.
The Palace asks us to prepare both the team and our expectations of direct control.
We'll return when we're ready. Both parts of the partnership.
I like that the farewell includes us as well as our Pokemon.
A good rest belongs in that preparation. Strength isn't only earned by pushing.
A polite invitation to improve one's inner resources before disturbing theirs again.
The Palace recommends fortification. I support the version involving a quiet chair.
We can consider how the moves suit each partner before another attempt.
Some strength is built by learning when to loosen your grip.
The farewell sounds serious without shutting the door on us.
I'd return after noticing more about how our partners choose to act.

contexts.subject: The Arena attendant invites a later challenge after the visit concludes.

BattleFrontier_BattleArenaLobby_Text_Awa.text: We await your challenge on\nanother occasion!$

replies.text: Three-turn decisions can be tiring. I'm glad the goodbye isn't also being judged.
The visit has reached its endpoint. The invitation doesn't distinguish the preceding result.
Enough for now. We can prepare the next team order later.
I'm happy to have a moment where nobody has to act quickly.
A breather first. Then we can talk through what the Arena taught us.
A gracious farewell from an institution that gives indecision very little room to stretch.
The judges have no jurisdiction over our leisurely walk outside. Reassuring.
We can revise the sequence before entering another challenge.
The short battles are over. We can let the next few moments take their time.
They keep the invitation courteous, whatever kind of visit we had.
I'd like to compare our expectations with what actually mattered there.

contexts.subject: The Pike guide closes the visit and invites a return without promising luck.

BattleFrontier_BattlePikeLobby_Text_Look.text: We look forward to seeing you\non another occasion…$

replies.text: The snake has politely let us go. I won't ask it to predict our next visit.
The farewell is an invitation, not evidence that a future route will be fortunate.
We're done for now. No need to test one more door immediately.
I'm glad there's no choice hidden inside the goodbye.
We can sort ourselves out before another trip through those rooms.
A courteous conclusion from a place whose hospitality varies considerably by doorway.
The Pike wishes to see us again. Its rooms have submitted no separate statement.
I'd review which preparations helped across the different room outcomes.
An uncertain path has a certain exit, at least for this moment.
The calm goodbye feels welcome after so many unpredictable possibilities.
I'd ask other visitors which surprises caught them out. There may be something useful to learn.

contexts.subject: The Pyramid guide ends the expedition visit and invites another.

BattleFrontier_BattlePyramidLobby_Text_L.text: We look forward to your\nnext challenge!$

replies.text: Back to ground-level plans for a little while. My feet approve.
The expedition is concluded. A future attempt can be planned from the available results.
A good point to stop and check the whole team.
It's nice to have a simple way out after all those uncertain passages.
I'd settle somewhere comfortable before planning another climb.
The guide is already looking forward to an expedition our legs have not yet agreed to.
Another invitation to upward mobility. We may consider remaining horizontal first.
We can review navigation and supplies before taking the next challenge.
The climb has ended. There is no need to keep climbing inside our heads.
A warm welcome back makes even a difficult trip easier to leave behind.
I'd ask which part of the expedition stays clearest in everyone's memory.

contexts.subject: The fortune teller ends by allowing disbelief and saying the future can change.

BattleFrontier_BattlePyramidLobby_Text_B.text: Whether you believe my fortunes\nor not, the choice is yours…\pThe future can be changed anytime…\nI wish you safe passage…$

replies.text: A fortune that leaves us room to disagree. I like having some elbow room in the future.
She explicitly allows uncertainty and change. More responsible than presenting inevitability.
We'll use the warning without surrendering our judgment.
The safe-passage wish matters more to me than sounding certain.
Advice should leave room for what we choose next. Hers does.
An oracle willing to release the audience from compulsory belief. Excellent manners.
The future has been allowed to revise its appointment. Civilized arrangement.
Treat the warning as preparation information, then respond to what actually happens.
A glimpse needn't become a chain. She understands that.
She doesn't need us to agree in order to wish us well. I appreciate that.
I'd remember the caution and keep observing. Those can work together.

contexts.subject: A trainer learns that using only defensive moves hurt the Arena judgment.

BattleFrontier_BattleArenaLobby_Text_Bad.text: I lost on the REFEREE's decision…\pI don't think it was a good idea to only\nuse defensive moves and not attack…$

replies.text: A very sturdy defense has discovered the judges wanted an actual attack somewhere.
The Arena evaluates aggression as one criterion. Pure defense can therefore score poorly.
He identified the problem. Change the plan for these rules.
It must be frustrating when surviving still isn't enough.
A safe-looking choice can cost you under different rules. Good lesson to carry forward.
An excellent fortress has lost an argument about whether it did anything.
The defense held. The judges remained unimpressed.
The strategy needs to account for the scoring system as well as damage prevention.
A shelter can keep you safe without taking you anywhere.
He's willing to question his own choice. That gives him something useful after the loss.
I'd ask which defensive move he'd replace first. That's a practical starting point.

contexts.subject: A trainer credits consistent successful attacks for a judging victory.

BattleFrontier_BattleArenaLobby_Text_Lan.text: I won in judging!\pLanding hits consistently on\nthe opponent's POKéMON worked!$

replies.text: A plan built around actually landing the hits has received a favorable review.
Successful moves support the Skill criterion. His result is consistent with that rule.
Reliable hits did the job. Useful lesson.
He sounds pleased to understand why it worked.
Something dependable paid off. That's a satisfying kind of win.
The humble successful attack has triumphed over more elaborate forms of wishful thinking.
Hitting the opponent. An unfashionably direct method, vindicated.
Consistency mattered under the judging rules. I'd keep that in mind when choosing moves.
Small certainties can add up to a deciding weight.
He gives credit to a repeatable choice instead of calling it magic.
I'd ask what he changed from his previous attempt. That could explain the improvement.

contexts.subject: A trainer describes a timed Arena match ending in a draw with similar HP.

BattleFrontier_BattleArenaLobby_Text_Mat.text: Our match was declared a draw.\pWhen we ran out of time, both my\nPOKéMON and the opponent's had about\lthe same amount of HP left.$

replies.text: They both reached the finish with almost the same amount of stubbornness left.
Similar remaining HP alone doesn't explain every scoring factor, but he remembers a close contest.
Close match. Worth looking at what could have broken the tie.
A draw must feel strange after trying so hard to separate the result.
Neither side quite pulled away. There's probably a useful detail to learn from it.
Two opponents spent the match arguing and arrived at an inconveniently balanced conclusion.
A very thorough disagreement that failed to select a winner.
I'd review the other judging factors as well as the remaining HP.
Two paths met at the same edge and neither crossed it.
He isn't inventing a grand excuse. Just describing how close it felt.
I'd ask which turn he would change if he could replay one.

contexts.subject: A trainer recommends arranging Arena partners to handle weaknesses in sequence.

BattleFrontier_BattleArenaLobby_Text_Ord.text:
In the BATTLE ARENA, the order of
POKéMON is totally important.\pFor example, if your first POKéMON
has certain type disadvantages,\ltry making your second POKéMON one\lwith moves that are super effective\lagainst the first one.\pI think that will be a good way of
making an effective team.$

replies.text: The next partner needs to know how to clean up the kind of trouble the first one attracts.
Sequential coverage matters when switching is unavailable. His advice addresses that constraint.
Build for the whole line, not three separate strong choices.
I like thinking about how one partner can make things easier for the next.
Planning the order now can spare someone a very uncomfortable entrance later.
A queue with consequences. The second arrival should have a useful answer to the first disaster.
Even standing in line has become a tactical responsibility.
We can map likely weaknesses across the order before selecting the final team.
Who comes next matters most when the first door closes behind you.
He's thinking about the relationship between choices. That tends to get overlooked.
I'd ask for an example from his own team. Concrete matchups make the advice clearer.

contexts.subject: A trainer regrets leaving the needed partner in reserve and advises checking opponents.

BattleFrontier_BattleDomeLobby_Text_Need.text: I would've won if I'd kept this POKéMON\nheld in reserve.\pYou need to check your opponent's\nPOKéMON carefully before choosing\lyour battling POKéMON.$

replies.text: The perfect answer was nearby, having a very unhelpful afternoon off.
Preselection information can improve the matchup. Hindsight may still overstate certainty of victory.
Check the opponent before choosing. He learned that the expensive way.
It hurts when the choice you regret was made before the battle even started.
A minute spent looking carefully can save a lot of wishing afterward.
The reserve partner has become an undefeated champion in the tournament of what might have happened.
The absent solution is enjoying a very flattering reputation.
We should compare the available information before committing our selections.
A closed choice can grow very bright in memory. It still can't be reopened today.
He has useful advice. I wouldn't assume the alternative was a guaranteed win, though.
I'd ask which opposing partner changed his mind. That detail matters.

contexts.subject: A trainer was eliminated early after drawing a tournament favorite.

BattleFrontier_BattleDomeLobby_Text_Tras.text: I ran into one of the tournament\nfavorites in the very first round.\pOf course I got trashed…$

replies.text: A first round can still contain somebody's final-boss-sized problem.
Early elimination doesn't imply a weak opponent. The draw affects the route considerably.
Tough draw. Still worth learning how they beat him.
He sounds as though he stopped believing he had a chance before it began.
A hard opponent first doesn't make the whole effort worthless. Let the sting settle.
The tournament placed the intimidating part at the front for his convenience. Unkind arrangement.
A short visit with a very concentrated amount of defeat.
I'd separate the unfavorable matchup from decisions he can improve next time.
A difficult beginning can make the path seem shorter than the work behind it.
He expected the favorite to win. I wonder whether that changed how he approached it.
I'd ask whether there was a moment that felt closer than he'd expected.

contexts.subject: A visitor explains repeated Dome victories attract stronger challengers.

BattleFrontier_BattleDomeLobby_Text_Winn.text:
When a TRAINER chains tournament
wins at the BATTLE DOME, he or she\lgains a reputation as a star.\pTough TRAINERS are drawn by that
reputation to the BATTLE DOME.\pA true superstar is a TRAINER who
can keep winning tournaments.$

replies.text: Win enough and your reward is more people determined to ruin the winning part.
Reputation creates a feedback loop that attracts stronger opposition. Sustaining success gets harder.
A title draws challengers. Keeping it takes work.
Being known sounds exciting until everyone arrives expecting something from you.
I'd rather build a routine that lasts than spend every day trying to look unstoppable.
Fame has arranged its usual prize: a growing queue of people eager to contradict it.
The reward for winning is an increasingly inconvenient guest list.
A strategy needs to adapt as the opponents get stronger and learn what to expect.
A bright name calls distant eyes toward it. Some arrive carrying a challenge.
Keeping a reputation can ask more of a person than earning the first bit of attention.
I'd ask a frequent winner what changed once other trainers started recognizing them.

contexts.subject: An adult admits difficulty interpreting the Factory hints.

BattleFrontier_BattleFactoryLobby_Text_C.text: You know how the staff here give you\na few hints about your next opponent?\pWell, I'm a full-grown man, but I have\ntrouble figuring out their hints.$

replies.text: Being grown-up doesn't automatically install the hint decoder. Mine certainly didn't arrive.
Age doesn't guarantee familiarity with specialized clues. He needs a clearer interpretive method.
Ask what the hint means. Being an adult doesn't forbid questions.
I'm glad he admitted it. I'd probably be wondering the same thing quietly.
I'd rather ask twice than pretend I understood and waste a whole attempt.
Adulthood has failed to supply an honorary degree in cryptic receptionist remarks.
A full-grown man has discovered a perfectly ordinary gap in the instructions.
He could compare a hint with the opponent afterward and build a useful reference.
A clue is only helpful when someone can find the handle.
He shouldn't have to apologize for needing the explanation to be clearer.
I'd ask which hint confused him. We might work it out more easily together.

contexts.subject: A trainer warns that rental teams still require extensive battle knowledge.

BattleFrontier_BattleFactoryLobby_Text_N.text:
Hi!
You, there!\pAre you thinking that the events here
are easy since you don't need to have\la raised team of POKéMON?\pI wouldn't be too sure about winning
that easily.\pIf you don't have thorough knowledge
about POKéMON and their moves,\lit will be tough to keep winning.$

replies.text: Borrowing the Pokemon doesn't come with borrowing somebody else's understanding of them.
Removing the raising requirement leaves team assessment and move knowledge fully relevant.
A ready team still needs a trainer who knows what it's doing.
Meeting a partner for the first time before a challenge sounds difficult in its own way.
Somebody else did the raising. We still have to pay attention to the Pokemon in front of us.
The rental agreement includes the Pokemon, regrettably without a transferable lifetime of expertise.
The team is provided. Competence remains a bring-your-own requirement.
We should inspect the moves and team interactions before deciding how to battle.
A borrowed tool still asks the hand to learn its weight.
He's warning against an easy assumption. Better to hear it here than discover it mid-match.
I'd ask what unfamiliar move caught him out. Specific mistakes can teach a lot.

contexts.subject: An unsuccessful trainer advises studying opposing Pokemon during rental battles.

BattleFrontier_BattleFactoryLobby_Text_N.text: Things haven't been going my way\nat all.\pYou need to check your opponent's\nPOKéMON during battle to see if\lthey're any good.$

replies.text: An opponent can be a future teammate. That's a good reason to pay attention before the handshake.
Observed battle behavior provides information for the later swap decision.
Watch what they actually do before deciding they're worth a swap.
It must be odd choosing someone who was trying to beat you a moment ago.
A familiar species can still carry surprises. Better to learn before making the exchange.
The opposing team is conducting an extremely aggressive job interview.
Today's enemy may become tomorrow's coworker. Take useful notes.
We can track revealed moves and how they complement the existing team.
A hard encounter may leave something useful besides the memory of being hit.
He's looking for better information rather than just another lucky choice. That helps.
I'd ask which detail he wishes he'd noticed earlier. That's usually the useful clue.

contexts.subject: A trainer regrets choosing a rental partner based on species rather than its actual strengths.

BattleFrontier_BattleFactoryLobby_Text_S.text: I swapped for a weak POKéMON…\nI thought it was a good kind to have…\pThey wiped the floor with us…$

replies.text: The species looked like the answer. The actual battle filed a rather firm objection.
Species reputation alone doesn't describe the individual moveset or fit within the team.
Check the actual partner, not just the name.
He sounds disappointed in the choice. I'd avoid making the Pokemon the whole blame.
Sometimes a good partner is a bad fit for the plan. That distinction matters.
A promising label has failed to perform the work of a careful inspection.
The name was reassuring. Reality proved less interested in the name.
He needs to compare the role and known moves, not only the species.
An imagined strength can hide the creature actually standing there.
Calling it weak may be easier than explaining why it didn't suit the team.
I'd ask what the swap was supposed to solve and what happened instead.

contexts.subject: A trainer is surprised by a docile partner fierce behavior in the Palace.

BattleFrontier_BattlePalaceLobby_Text_Mo.text: My POKéMON is usually very docile.\pBut when it's in a BATTLE HALL,\nit sometimes seems to become\ltransformed into something wicked!\pIt becomes totally intimidating.\nIt's shocking, even.$

replies.text: The quiet one apparently had a very forceful opinion saved up for battle.
Behavior changes with context. A docile everyday manner doesn't exclude competitive aggression.
Gentle at home doesn't mean helpless in a fight.
Maybe this is a side they hadn't needed to show before.
I like learning that a familiar partner still has surprises. I'd pay attention rather than panic.
The supposedly mild partner has submitted a dramatic correction to its public description.
Quiet creatures are under no obligation to remain convenient little mysteries.
The Palace reveals choices the trainer usually makes on the Pokemon's behalf. Useful information.
A still pond can hold a very determined current.
They're meeting a less familiar part of someone they thought they knew completely.
I'd ask what it did that looked so different. That sounds worth describing carefully.

contexts.subject: A trainer advises matching a partner moves to its nature for the Palace.

BattleFrontier_BattlePalaceLobby_Text_Na.text:
Hmm…\pIt appears that the nature of POKéMON
and the moves that they have been\ltaught are the keys to battle here.\pTo be more precise, it's how well
the moves match the nature of\lthe POKéMON.\pIf your POKéMON is in trouble and
unable to live up to its potential,\lyou may need to examine how well\lits moves match its nature.$

replies.text: A fine move won't help much if the little expert carrying it refuses to use it.
The rule set makes individual move preferences strategically important. Fit matters.
Build for how the partner acts here. Wishing won't change the rules.
I like that the answer starts with understanding the Pokemon instead of blaming it.
It's easier to work together when you know what someone is comfortable doing.
A brilliant plan must first survive consultation with the creature expected to execute it.
The Pokemon has preferences. The strategy has been asked to accommodate this inconvenience.
We should compare move categories with the nature's behavior before entering.
A path fits better when it follows the shape of the feet walking it.
Sometimes improving the match means changing the plan instead of pushing the partner harder.
I'd ask what adjustment made the biggest difference for their team.

contexts.subject: A visitor doubts the correct guess that a Lax nature favors indirect interference.

BattleFrontier_BattlePalaceLobby_Text_Wh.text: I wonder what sort of nature a POKéMON\nwould have if it favored enfeebling its\lopponents and chipping away slowly.\pI'd be surprised if it was a LAX nature.\pBut, nah, that can't be right.$

replies.text: He found a possibility and talked himself away from it before anyone could answer.
The nature's name alone isn't a reliable guide to its behavior under Palace rules.
Check the rule instead of arguing with the label.
I know that feeling of distrusting the answer that came to mind first.
A question is easier to settle when you ask someone who knows the system.
An idea has been proposed, cross-examined, and dismissed by a committee of one.
His guess has failed its interview before the evidence arrived.
We can test the preference or consult the relevant data rather than infer it from a name.
A name can point the imagination down entirely the wrong little corridor.
He seems worried the answer sounds silly. That isn't the same as it being wrong.
I'd ask the guide. A direct answer could rescue him from quite a long internal debate.

contexts.subject: A visitor abandons a battle discussion to praise the girl who reads Pokemon thoughts.

BattleFrontier_BattlePalaceLobby_Text_La.text:
For a hardy fellow like me,
hardy POKéMON are the best.\pOffense is the best defense!
A relentless attack is the ultimate!\pBut that's not what I wanted to chat
about.\pEvery so often a really cute lady
swings by here.\pShe says that she can tell what
POKéMON are thinking.\pI don't know about that part,
but she is really cute.\pHuh?
Why are you looking at me like that?$

replies.text: He took the scenic route from battle tactics to admitting he likes seeing her visit.
His attraction doesn't establish whether her readings are accurate. Two separate questions.
He can like her. He could also listen to what she's actually saying.
I think he realized halfway through how much he'd said out loud.
He remembers her looks very clearly. I'd ask whether he remembers any of her advice.
A tactical lecture has wandered off and become a rather obvious personal confession.
A formidable offense has encountered a complete failure of subtlety.
I'd rather hear whether her observations helped him understand his team.
He sees the visitor brightly and her words only dimly. Perhaps that can change.
Complimenting her appearance is easy. Taking her thoughts seriously would tell me more.
I'd ask him one question about what she said. He might discover he was listening after all.

contexts.subject: A visitor reports ten completed Pike challenges without a trainer battle.

BattleFrontier_BattlePikeLobby_Text_Neve.text: I've completed the challenge 10 times\nnow, but I've never had to battle\la TRAINER once.$

replies.text: Ten trips and no trainer battles? The trainers must keep choosing a different corridor.
An unusual reported sequence. It doesn't guarantee the same outcome for the next visitor.
Lucky route history. I wouldn't plan around repeating it.
I wonder whether that made the rooms feel calmer or stranger each time.
Good for them. I'd still bring a team ready for the battle they haven't met yet.
A remarkable campaign of successfully failing to meet one's opponents.
The battle facility has provided a prolonged absence of battles. Impressive specialization.
Past routes don't remove the need to prepare for other possible rooms.
An empty path ten times can still have someone waiting on the eleventh.
That's a memorable streak. I hope they're enjoying it without expecting the place to owe them more.
I'd ask what they encountered instead. No trainers doesn't mean nothing happened.

contexts.subject: A trainer lost one room from the Pike goal and warns about status conditions.

BattleFrontier_BattlePikeLobby_Text_OneR.text: Arrgh! I blew my chance!\nI was one room away from the goal!\pIn this place, you'd better watch out\nfor poison, freezing, and so on.$

replies.text: One room short is a particularly pointy place to lose.
Status conditions can accumulate into a decisive constraint. Proximity to the goal doesn't remove them.
Hard loss. Take the warning seriously before our next entry.
I think the almost part is hurting more than the loss itself.
A near finish can leave you replaying every small choice. Rest before doing that endlessly.
The finish was close enough to be irritatingly specific. A cruel feature of almost.
The last room has become much larger in memory than any room deserves.
We should account for condition protection when choosing partners and held items.
A threshold can be visible and still remain out of reach. That hurts.
He has turned the frustration into one useful warning. That part is generous.
I'd ask which condition caused the turning point once he's ready to talk about it.

contexts.subject: A visitor suggests Pokemon abilities may be especially useful in the Pike.

BattleFrontier_BattlePikeLobby_Text_Thin.text: Listen! Listen!\pDon't you think that the special\nabilities of POKéMON will be useful\lhere?$

replies.text: The little things a Pokemon does without being asked might become very big advantages here.
Passive abilities can affect hazard resilience and encounters. A sound avenue to examine.
Yes. Choose for more than attacks.
I like noticing the strengths that don't need a shouted command.
A partner may help the whole trip simply by being the kind of Pokemon it is.
A sensible reminder that the team contains more useful features than the move list.
The quiet advantages would like a moment of recognition.
We should review each ability against the possible room effects.
Some gifts work quietly enough that people forget to thank them.
It's good advice for anyone focused only on what looks impressive in a battle.
I'd compare notes with someone who used an ability to avoid a difficult room effect.

contexts.subject: A distraught explorer lost accumulated Battle Bag items after a failed expedition.

BattleFrontier_BattlePyramidLobby_Text_L.text: Awaaaaaaarrrrgh!\pI had a whole lot of items, but I lost\nthem all when I lost!\pAwaaaaaaarrrrgh!$

replies.text: That wasn't only a loss. It was a whole collection of useful little hopes falling out at once.
The Battle Bag loss rule makes accumulated supplies vulnerable when an expedition fails.
Rough. Let him be upset before offering another plan.
I don't think he wants advice yet. I think he wants someone to understand how much was there.
I'd find somewhere quiet for him to sit. Counting everything again won't make this easier right now.
An inventory has become a lament, with every missing item apparently joining the chorus.
The expedition took the supplies and left him with a very thorough explanation of grief.
Once he's ready, we can look at what led to the failure and how to protect the next run.
A bag holds more than things once you've struggled to gather them.
He lost the work those items represented as well as the items themselves.
I'd let him tell us what happened at his own pace. The shouting sounds like real frustration.

contexts.subject: A visitor advises quiet movement to avoid attracting Pyramid trainers.

BattleFrontier_BattlePyramidLobby_Text_T.text: Did you know?\pIf you run fast, TRAINERS may notice\nand come after you for a battle.\pSo, if you want to avoid TRAINERS,\ndon't catch their eyes, but sneak\lcautiously and quietly past them.$

replies.text: The Pyramid notices an enthusiastic pair of feet. Mine will attempt to become boring.
Running changes how trainers detect the explorer. Movement speed becomes a tactical choice.
Slow down if we're trying to avoid a battle. Simple enough.
Quiet steps feel sensible in a place where we can't see far ahead.
No need to hurry into a fight we meant to avoid.
A useful case in which making a dramatic entrance is explicitly the wrong approach.
The floor has no interest in our athletic ambitions. Walk politely.
We can trade speed for lower attention when preserving resources matters.
A quiet foot can leave a larger distance between us and trouble.
Small habits can announce us before we've decided whether we want company.
I'd ask how close they got before being noticed. That could help us judge the spacing.

contexts.subject: The exchange clerk closes shopping and welcomes a later visit with saved points.

BattleFrontier_ExchangeServiceCorner_Tex.text: Thank you very much.\pPlease visit us when you have\nsaved up Battle Points.$

replies.text: A whole counter of lovely things, and we are allowed to leave without adopting them all.
The shopping session has ended. This farewell doesn't specify whether a purchase occurred.
Done shopping. We can decide what to save for next.
I like having time to think instead of choosing just because the list is open.
I'd save for something we'll actually use, or something that genuinely makes us happy.
The clerk releases us from the menu and sends us back into the economy of effort.
The prizes remain. Our impulse to own every cushion may hopefully subside.
We can compare the point costs with our priorities before returning.
Wanting something can wait without spoiling it.
A polite goodbye gives us room to decide what belongs in our life.
I'd ask everyone which prize they remember afterward. The favorites usually become clear.

contexts.subject: A decoration exchange fails because decoration storage is full.

BattleFrontier_ExchangeServiceCorner_Tex.text: I'm so sorry…\nYour PC appears to be full…$

replies.text: The new decoration has reached the border of an already very decorated life.
Storage capacity prevented the exchange. The decoration wasn't delivered.
No room. Sort what we have before trying again.
It's a little disappointing to choose something and find nowhere for it.
We should make space deliberately instead of clearing something we still like in a hurry.
The collection has become so successful that it now objects to further collecting.
The dolls have apparently occupied all available territory.
We need a free decoration slot before this transaction can succeed.
A crowded shelf is also a record of earlier wishes. Choose carefully what moves.
I would look through the collection before deciding another piece has to fit.
I'd like to see what's already there. We may rediscover something worth displaying.

contexts.subject: An item exchange fails because the player cannot carry it.

BattleFrontier_ExchangeServiceCorner_Tex.text: I'm so sorry…\nYou don't have space to hold it…$

replies.text: We've earned the choice but failed the carrying portion of the examination.
The item was not received because carrying capacity prevented delivery.
Make room first. The points aren't a substitute for space.
At least we found out here instead of dropping something outside.
Time to sort the bag before asking for more things to put in it.
A promising purchase has encountered the implacable physics of a full bag.
The bag has exercised its right to refuse further responsibility.
We can reorganize and return. No need to force the transaction now.
Even a useful thing needs somewhere to arrive.
I'd rather make space thoughtfully than discard the first thing we touch.
We should check what we've been carrying around without using. There may be an easy fix.

contexts.subject: A man defensively tells the player to obtain their own plush doll.

BattleFrontier_ExchangeServiceCorner_Tex.text:
Hah?
What are you gawking at?\pI don't like you staring at my plush
doll like that.\pIf you want it, go get one yourself!
Isn't that right, SMOOCHUM?$

replies.text: I admired the doll. I hadn't realized it needed a personal security detail.
Looking at an object doesn't establish an intention to take it. His reaction is disproportionate.
We're looking. The doll is safe.
I didn't mean to make him uncomfortable. I just thought it was nice.
He can enjoy his doll. There's no need to bark at somebody for noticing it.
An innocent glance has triggered a full defense of the plush estate.
The doll has acquired an unusually aggressive legal representative.
If he dislikes attention, pointing it out to everyone may be counterproductive.
A soft thing is being guarded with rather sharp words.
He doesn't have to justify loving a plush. I wish he knew that before going on the attack.
I'd leave him to enjoy it. No reason to turn a passing glance into a feud.

contexts.subject: A sailor expects the exchange items to strengthen his Pokemon.

BattleFrontier_ExchangeServiceCorner_Tex.text: If I can get hold of the items here,\nmy POKéMON will get tougher.\pYou bet they will!\nNo question about it!$

replies.text: He has found the shopping list of his dreams. The actual training may still want a word.
Suitable items can help, but their value depends on the partner and intended use.
Useful gear helps. It won't replace a sound plan.
I hope he keeps seeing his partner underneath all the improvements he's imagining.
I'd choose what suits the Pokemon, rather than whatever sounds most powerful on the shelf.
A confident forecast issued before the items have even left the counter.
The merchandise has been assigned responsibility for an entire future victory.
He should match each item's effect to a specific need in the team.
A useful gift fits the creature receiving it. The wish alone isn't enough.
He sounds eager to help his Pokemon. A more specific choice would serve that wish better.
I'd ask which item he wants first and what problem he expects it to solve.

contexts.subject: A mother promises to overcome anything to obtain the prize her child wants.

BattleFrontier_ExchangeServiceCorner_Tex.text: Leave it to your mommy!\pIf it's anything you want, I'll go\nthrough anything to get it, honey!$

replies.text: That's a devoted promise. I wonder which plush has persuaded her to take on the island.
Her affection is clear. A specific goal and manageable effort would make the promise more practical.
She wants to make the kid happy. She can still set a limit.
It's sweet hearing somebody feel that supported. I hope she enjoys the visit herself, too.
A gift is lovely. She doesn't have to wear herself out proving how much she cares.
An innocent prize counter has received a declaration of unlimited maternal determination.
Somewhere on the shelf, a doll has no idea what it's started.
She could set a point target and work toward it without turning the visit into an ordeal.
Love can make a small wish feel worth a very long journey.
I'd like the child to know her company is a gift before the prize ever arrives.
I'd ask which prize caught their eye. She's certainly ready to hear the answer.

contexts.subject: A shopper wants every size of doll and cushion on display.

BattleFrontier_ExchangeServiceCorner_Tex.text: Oh, they're so nice!\nI wish I had them!\lCute cushions!\lBig plush DOLLS!\lLittle plush DOLLS!\lI wish I had them all!$

replies.text: Big dolls, little dolls, cushions. His wish list has discovered categories and refuses to stop.
The desire concerns the entire assortment. Prioritizing one choice may be more manageable.
Pick a favorite first. A room still needs somewhere to walk.
I understand wanting several soft things. All of them sounds difficult to carry home.
I'd start with the one that makes him smile most when he looks back at the shelf.
A collector surveying an empire he intends to acquire one extremely soft province at a time.
The ambition is vast. The proposed population is entirely plush.
He should measure the available space before assigning every doll a future address.
A wish can grow until it fills the room before a single thing has arrived.
The big and little pieces could look wonderful together. We'd still need an arrangement.
I'd ask whether he already has a collection. That level of enthusiasm suggests a story.

contexts.subject: A visitor explains that longer facility records increase Battle Point awards.

BattleFrontier_ExchangeServiceCorner_Tex.text: Did you know?\pIf you stretch your record at any of\nthe BATTLE facilities, they start\lgiving you more and more Battle Points.$

replies.text: The longer the streak, the more the prize shelf starts looking reachable.
Rewards increase with extended records. The expected effort still varies by facility and skill.
Useful to know. Chasing more points still needs a sensible stopping point.
I'd rather build up steadily than make every match feel like a shopping deadline.
A bigger award is nice. Resting before mistakes pile up is nice, too.
Success has acquired a loyalty program. Predictably, it requires more success.
The winning streak receives encouragement to become even more of itself.
We can account for the reward structure when choosing a facility goal.
A growing reward can make a tired person forget how far they've walked.
I like knowing the system before setting a goal. It makes the choices less hazy.
I'd ask which facility they found most rewarding for the time they actually enjoyed spending.

contexts.subject: The gambler urges the player toward Tower Singles because the wager depends on it.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_GetToBattleT.text: Get to the BATTLE TOWER's\nSINGLE BATTLE ROOMS pronto!\pIt's a must-win situation!\nDon't blow your chance!\lBoth of our futures depend on you!$

replies.text: His future has apparently climbed into our Tower appointment without asking for a seat.
The instruction identifies Tower Singles. His urgency doesn't change the challenge requirements.
Tower Singles. We heard him. The pressure isn't helping.
Both our futures sounds like an awful lot to put on one visit.
I'd rather prepare calmly than carry his panic through the Tower door.
A wager has become an extravagant prediction about the fate of two entire lives.
The Tower is tall enough without him adding emotional floors.
We'll need a Singles plan. His shouting contributes no useful part of one.
He has tied his hopes to our climb. We still have to choose each step.
That urgency is his feeling. We don't need to wear it as our own.
I'd confirm the event, then step outside for a quieter moment before starting.

contexts.subject: The gambler demands success in the Tower Double challenge.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_GetToBattleT.text: Get to the BATTLE TOWER's\nDOUBLE BATTLE ROOMS pronto!\pIt's a must-win situation!\nDon't blow your chance!\lBoth of our futures depend on you!$

replies.text: Two Pokemon at once, plus one very demanding voice we'd best leave in this room.
Tower Doubles requires coordination. Anxiety about the wager supplies no tactical advantage.
Doubles, then. We should check how the partners work together.
I'd like a little quiet before making a decision with two partners depending on it.
His points are invested. Our attention still belongs with the team.
He has volunteered us for a rescue mission in the doubles division. How generous of him.
Two active partners are enough company. His panic needn't become the third.
We should review paired moves and avoid interfering with our own partner.
Two paths must move together. A stranger's urgency won't align them.
He makes the wager sound personal. The practical work is still ours to do.
I'd rather talk through our pairings than listen to another warning about blowing it.

contexts.subject: The gambler sends the player to the Tower Multi challenge with exaggerated urgency.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_GetToBattleT.text: Get to the BATTLE TOWER's\nMULTI BATTLE ROOMS pronto!\pIt's a must-win situation!\nDon't blow your chance!\lBoth of our futures depend on you!$

replies.text: We're finding a battle partner while he auditions to be an entire crowd of pressure.
Multi Battles add another trainer's decisions. His demand can't control that variability.
Need a good partner. Not a louder gambler.
I hope the person beside us feels easier to talk to than he does.
A calm conversation with our partner will help more than his dramatic instructions.
He has invested in teamwork and expressed it by speaking as though nobody else has a choice.
A team event, burdened with a spectator who has mistaken himself for management.
We should understand our partner's team before attempting a coordinated challenge.
Trust grows between the people doing the work. His wager stands outside that circle.
He wants a result from people whose cooperation he isn't helping.
I'd ask the battle partner about their plan first. We need a conversation that goes both ways.

contexts.subject: The gambler insists the player win the Dome Singles tournament for the bet.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_GetToBattleD.text: Get to the BATTLE DOME's\nSINGLE BATTLE Tourney pronto!\pIt's a must-win situation!\nDon't blow your chance!\lBoth of our futures depend on you!$

replies.text: The tournament bracket apparently contains our opponents and his entire peace of mind.
Dome Singles involves selection against known opponents. That deserves more attention than his urgency.
We'll inspect the opponents. Rushing the selection won't help.
It's harder to think when somebody keeps announcing how much depends on you.
A breath before choosing is worth more than a hurried promise.
He has turned a tournament entry into a personal emergency without consulting the tournament.
The bracket has enough branches without his worries growing extras.
We need to select the right pair from the information available at the Dome.
A chart can show the route. It cannot promise who reaches the end.
He's trying to make certainty out of insistence. The match won't work that way.
I'd focus on the first matchup rather than try to carry the whole tournament at once.

contexts.subject: The gambler pressures the player to enter the Dome Double tournament.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_GetToBattleD.text: Get to the BATTLE DOME's\nDOUBLE BATTLE Tourney pronto!\pIt's a must-win situation!\nDon't blow your chance!\lBoth of our futures depend on you!$

replies.text: A doubles tournament and double the urgency, somehow from the same single man.
The requested event is Dome Doubles. Pair compatibility and opponent information remain essential.
Prepare the pair. His impatience can stay here.
I'd like the two partners to feel settled before everybody starts expecting a grand result.
We should choose carefully instead of treating his worry like a countdown.
He is remarkably eager for us to perform a strategy he has contributed nothing toward.
An entire tournament has been reduced to please fix my bet. Concise, if unpleasant.
The pair needs to function against the selected opponents, not merely look strong together.
Two companions will carry the work. His hope adds weight without adding strength.
He keeps saying chance as though it becomes safer when spoken loudly.
I'd check the matchup information before agreeing with any of his predictions.

contexts.subject: The gambler urgently assigns the Factory Singles rental challenge.

BattleFrontier_Lounge3_Text_GetToBattleF.text: Get to the BATTLE FACTORY's\nBattle Swap Single Tourney pronto!\pIt's a must-win situation!\nDon't blow your chance!\lBoth of our futures depend on you!$

replies.text: He trusts us with his future before we've even met the Pokemon supposed to help carry it.
The rental roster is not yet known. A guarantee would be particularly unjustified here.
We need to see the rentals before making a plan.
New partners and somebody else's expectations. That's quite an introduction.
We'll take time to understand the rentals. They deserve more attention than his deadline.
