An abandoned family subplot appears long enough to deliver one strangely specific detail.
An unfamiliar name can briefly become a room full of things you never agreed to enter.
Identity hypothesis rejected by the speaker. No need to preserve it as a fact about us.
A red thread has been mentioned, but not tied to the person standing here.
He has made a private detail sound like an accusation. Unpleasant.
I wonder what made that thought occur to him just now.

contexts.subject: Lawson keeps returning to the same cave spot and suspects the boulder count is a clue.

FiveIsland_LostCave_Room1_Text_LawsonPos.text: I'm trying to get out of here, but\nI always end up at the same spot.\pMaybe the number of boulders is\na hint…$

replies.text: The cave has a very strict return policy. Counting the rocks sounds worth trying.
Repeated returns suggest a rule in the route structure. The boulder pattern is a testable lead.
Track the turns and count. Better than repeating the same frustrated walk.
It must be unnerving when a path seems to refuse to become somewhere new.
A calm note of the layout can help when the scenery keeps repeating.
The maze has trapped the explorer in an unusually literal recurring scene.
A pattern may be hiding inside what first looked like an empty room.
A loop with possible encoded guidance. Time for a careful controlled test.
The stone keeps returning the same face until someone notices its small difference.
A useful observation. Frustration had not stopped him seeing the clue.
I wonder which turns he has already tried from this room.

contexts.subject: Laura reports that a woman went deeper into Lost Cave.

FiveIsland_LostCave_Room4_Text_LauraPost.text: Earlier, a lady went into the caves\nahead.$

replies.text: A useful sighting in a place particularly good at making ahead difficult to define.
The observation suggests another person is in the deeper passages. Her condition is unknown.
Keep an eye out. A confusing cave is a bad place to end up tired and alone.
I hope she knows the way back better than the walls suggest.
A calm check on someone farther in could be worthwhile.
The maze's cast may include one more person beyond the next uncertain doorway.
Someone else's footsteps have left a little worry in the dark.
Presence reported, location approximate. Follow the route carefully.
Another small life has passed between these silent walls.
A clear sighting is more helpful than a dramatic guess about what happened.
I wonder how long ago Laura saw her go by.

contexts.subject: Milo mentions flying onward to Four Island.

FiveIsland_MemorialPillar_Text_MiloPostB.text: You can fly to FOUR ISLAND from\nhere.$

replies.text: A clear next destination, with the sea kept pleasantly beneath the route.
Aerial travel is an available route between these locations under the appropriate conditions.
Useful option if the flying partner is ready for the trip.
It is nice hearing a complicated bit of geography become a simple way onward.
A safe crossing still means checking the partner's condition first.
The itinerary offers a skyward transition to the next setting.
A far shore is sometimes closer from above.
Alternative transport route noted. Verify readiness before departure.
The water can lie quietly between two places the wings already know.
Helpful directions, especially when the ground route is not obvious.
I wonder which island Milo most likes arriving at from the air.

contexts.subject: Chaz points out a somber man nearby.

FiveIsland_MemorialPillar_Text_ChazPostB.text: There was a really somber guy\nover that way.$

replies.text: Then we should approach gently, if we approach at all. A sad person is not an attraction.
The description concerns an apparent mood, not the cause of it. We should avoid assumptions.
Give him room. He may have a good reason to want quiet.
I would not want my expression made into somebody else's sightseeing tip.
A little consideration is more useful than curiosity about the sadness.
The local observer points toward a scene that may not need an audience.
A quiet sorrow can be noticed without being investigated.
Observation does not grant access to the person's private history.
A lowered voice is enough of a reason to lower our own.
Somebody looking sad does not owe strangers an explanation.
I wonder whether Chaz knows him well enough to offer company kindly.

contexts.subject: Harold delights in his birds' playful begging.

FiveIsland_MemorialPillar_Text_HaroldPos.text: It fills me with happiness when\nbird POKéMON beg playfully…$

replies.text: A very persuasive little feathered lobbying group. They know their audience.
Familiar play behaviors can become a rewarding part of the partnership.
Good to enjoy the small things between battles.
It is lovely how much happiness fits inside a tiny familiar habit.
Birds can negotiate very effectively when they think a snack is available.
The devoted audience appears delighted with an entirely improvised avian performance.
A little silliness keeping a strong bond pleasantly ordinary.
Positive interaction that both sides recognize. Excellent feedback.
Small bright movements making a familiar afternoon warmer.
The partner's personality is what he remembers first. Nice.
I wonder whether each bird has a different way of asking him.

contexts.subject: Daisy realizes her paint tubes have spilled everywhere.

FiveIsland_ResortGorgeous_Text_DaisyPost.text: Uh-oh, my paint tubes have\nscattered everywhere!$

replies.text: The painting supplies have attempted an unscheduled still life. Better gather them.
A scattered kit can be damaged or lost quickly outdoors. Recovery first.
Pick them up before someone slips or a tube rolls away.
That sinking little moment when the things you need are suddenly everywhere.
A cloth and a little patience are better than stepping through the mess.
The art department has distributed its materials across the entire set.
A small colorful catastrophe. Fortunately, an ordinary one to put right.
Contain the spill, retrieve the small parts, then inspect the damage.
The colors have gone wandering before reaching the page.
An organized bag can save a lot of this particular kind of drama.
I wonder whether any of the tubes opened when they fell.

contexts.subject: Celina immediately resumes directing Gillian's pose for her art.

FiveIsland_ResortGorgeous_Text_CelinaPos.text: GILLIAN?\nPlease tilt your head slightly…\lThere! That's the look I want!$

replies.text: The battle has ended; the important head angle is back on the schedule.
A small pose adjustment can change the composition considerably.
Fair enough. Make sure Gillian is comfortable holding it.
It is interesting watching someone recognize the exact little look they wanted.
A patient model deserves a break as much as the artist needs the right angle.
The artist returns to directing the more cooperative scene.
A small tilt can make a familiar face feel suddenly different.
Fine adjustment requested. Check the model's comfort before a long hold.
One face turns slightly, and the light finds another place to rest.
She has a precise eye. Kind direction makes that eye easier to work with.
I wonder what changed in the expression when the head moved.

contexts.subject: Rayna finds the changing sky and sea difficult to capture in art.

FiveIsland_ResortGorgeous_Text_RaynaPost.text: The sky and the sea…\nThey are so fickle.\pTheir changing expressions make\nthem difficult to capture.$

replies.text: The scenery keeps changing its mind faster than the paint can dry. Unfairly talented scenery.
Changing light and moving surfaces make a single fixed representation challenging.
Pick the moment worth keeping. Cannot hold the whole sea still.
I understand wanting to catch a feeling just before it becomes another one.
A little of the change can be part of what makes the finished thing alive.
The two grandest models in the room refuse to hold a pose.
A restless subject may ask for a little restlessness in the picture.
Dynamic input, fixed output. Choose which properties to preserve.
The light keeps crossing a threshold no hand can quite follow.
An honest little impression can be more striking than pretending nothing moved.
I know that feeling. Sometimes one clear moment says more than trying to keep every wave.

contexts.subject: Jacki enjoys relaxed battles in the gentle sea breeze.

FiveIsland_ResortGorgeous_Text_JackiPost.text: I find it pleasurable to leisurely\nbattle in the gentle sea breeze.$

replies.text: A match with a nice breeze has fewer complaints from the hair department.
Comfortable conditions can make a familiar activity feel pleasantly different.
Good to enjoy it without turning every result into a crisis.
A battle can be a happy shared moment instead of a grand judgment.
A calm pace and a lovely place make the outing easier on everyone.
The competitive scene has chosen a rather agreeable natural venue.
A little challenge, a little wind, no need to make the afternoon cruel.
Suitable conditions, positive experience. A good recreational setup.
The air has left room for the game to stay light.
Enjoying the setting is part of choosing the outing well.
I wonder whether Jacki comes here at the same time to catch this breeze.

contexts.subject: Gillian imagines the relative pleasures of a pool and a sunroom.

FiveIsland_ResortGorgeous_Text_GillianPo.text: A pool would be nice, but I must\nsay, a sun-room may be sublime.$

replies.text: A difficult choice between two exceptionally comfortable ways to stay in one place.
They offer different conditions. The preference depends on how the room would actually be used.
Either is fine if she enjoys it. The view is already doing plenty of work.
A little room for quiet daylight sounds lovely to me.
A sunroom with a comfortable seat would make a good place for a slow meal.
The leisure itinerary has expanded into a property-development proposal.
A room full of light is a quiet sort of luxury.
Glazing, ventilation, shade. Sublime still needs a practical design.
Somebody is imagining a little place to sit inside the weather.
The sunroom has atmosphere. The pool has a much more demanding maintenance list.
I wonder which view she would want the windows to frame.

contexts.subject: Destin enjoys running with the wind and imagines flying.

FiveIsland_ResortGorgeous_Text_DestinPos.text: When I run with the wind, it feels\nlike I could fly!$

replies.text: The wind is a very encouraging running partner, provided it is on the correct side.
A following wind can make movement feel unusually effortless.
Enjoy the pace. Keep enough energy to return.
That small feeling of lightness sounds worth the run.

contexts.subject: An older man contrasts human aging with the sea's enduring life.

LilycoveCity_Text_SeaRemainsForeverYoung.text: Even as we grow old and wrinkled,\nthe sea remains forever young with\lthe vivid brilliance of life…\pFwohoho fwohohohoho…$

replies.text: The sea keeps finding new little lives to brighten its old blue coat.
A changing living system can appear enduring across one person's lifetime.
Good to keep noticing what still feels alive.
It's lovely when a familiar view can keep surprising someone.
A place can stay comforting without staying exactly the same.
An old setting can remain full of unwritten beginnings.
The sea has an excellent method of avoiding stale dramatic material.
I'd compare the details that change with what makes the view feel constant.
A long life can keep meeting the world as something still arriving.
Age doesn't stop a person having a bright eye for beauty.
I'd love to hear what he sees here now that he missed when he was young.

contexts.subject: An older woman remembers her husband proposing here sixty years ago.

LilycoveCity_Text_SixtyYearsAgoHusbandPr.text: It was sixty years ago that my husband\nproposed to me here.\lThe sea remains as beautiful as ever.\pMufufufu mufufufufufu…$

replies.text: A single place has been keeping a very lovely memory warm.
A familiar setting can retrieve an event with remarkable emotional detail.
Good place to remember. Let her enjoy it.
I wonder which small detail of that day still feels closest.
It's lovely having somewhere ordinary you can return to with that warmth.
A beloved scene has survived sixty years of changes around it.
A long-running romance with an exceptionally reliable backdrop.
I'd be interested in what changed here and what she immediately recognizes.
A shared promise can leave its light in a place for many years.
The view is beautiful partly because of what it means to her.
I'd remember her smile at the memory as much as the water behind it.

contexts.subject: A resident criticizes Aqua modifying a natural cave while claiming to love nature.

LilycoveCity_Text_TeamAquaRenovatedCaver.text:
Hm, you know of the peculiar cavern
in this cove?\pThat had been a natural formation,
but then that TEAM AQUA lot came\lalong and made their renovations.\pThey call themselves
the “nature-loving TEAM AQUA”!\pBut what they do and what they say
don't match at all!$

replies.text: The slogan and the building work seem to be having different conversations.
The discrepancy is a useful reason to judge actions rather than labels.
He's right to question it. Words don't repair the place.
It's unsettling when care gets used as the name for control.
The lives around the cave should matter in the decision.
The proclaimed theme has failed to survive contact with the actual scene.
An environmental love letter delivered with a very large hammer.
We should inspect effects instead of granting the group its preferred description.
A thing can be admired without being remade into our own convenience.
A stated aesthetic means little if the work ignores what was already there.
I'd compare the remembered cave with what their changes actually did.

contexts.subject: The resident notices Aqua's cave is empty and assumes they left permanently.

LilycoveCity_Text_TeamAquaLotGoneForGood.text: That cave in the cove…\pI didn't notice it right away,\nbut it's completely empty now.\pThat TEAM AQUA lot, they must\nhave gone away for good.$

replies.text: An empty cave is welcome news, though forever is a long inspection period.
Their absence is observable; permanence remains an inference.
Good they're gone. Still keep an eye on the place.
It must feel different walking past without expecting them.
The town can have some room to settle again.
An unwelcome cast has left the set, though the narrator has guessed at the sequel.
A conclusion with one useful fact and one ambitious prediction.
We can notice what remains without assuming every effect vanished with them.
A quiet place can begin recovering before its whole future is known.
The absence matters more than making a triumphant final claim.
I'd like to see what ordinary use the cove returns to now.

contexts.subject: A sailor repeats a report of Sky Pillar on the sea routes.

LilycoveCity_Text_HeardTowerCalledSkyPil.text: I heard there's a tower somewhere out\non the sea routes.\pIt's called the SKY PILLAR, I hear.$

replies.text: A tower has entered the conversation before anybody supplied an address.
A report is a useful lead if we keep its uncertainty clear.
Ask where the sighting came from. Don't sail on a guess.
The name alone makes it feel very tall in my imagination.
A careful plan should come before making it the next destination.
A striking title has introduced a setting still mostly off the page.
An architectural rumor with excellent atmosphere and poor directions.
We need location and access details before investigating.
An unseen place can begin as a small question carried between people.
A memorable name can make a vague report feel more certain than it is.
I'd want to hear from someone who actually saw it.

contexts.subject: A traveler wonders whether a tower seen near Route131 is Sky Pillar.

LilycoveCity_Text_SawTallTowerOnRoute131.text: I saw this tall tower somewhere\naround ROUTE 131.\pCould that possibly be…?$

replies.text: A very tall maybe has appeared near Route131.
A firsthand location helps, while the identification still needs confirmation.
Useful sighting. Check the route before exploring.
It must stand out strangely against all that open water.
A trip there needs a return plan as much as curiosity.
The rumor has acquired a visible outline and a much better setting note.
A promisingly specific piece of architecture-related uncertainty.
We can compare the shape and location with reliable descriptions.
A distant outline can give a familiar sea an unfamiliar depth.
A distinctive silhouette is a good beginning, not the whole explanation.
I'd love to know which angle made it suddenly visible to them.

contexts.subject: Newlyweds saw a Dragon Pokemon high in the sky on arriving in Hoenn.

LilycoveCity_Text_JustArrivedAndSawRareP.text:
We just arrived here on our
honeymoon vacation.\pWe happened to see a DRAGON-type
POKéMON flying way up in the sky.\pDo cool POKéMON like that live in
the HOENN region?$

replies.text: The honeymoon has received an unusually impressive welcome committee.
A memorable first sighting can make a new place feel immediately distinctive.
Great start. Enjoy the sight without chasing it blindly.
It's lovely having a little surprise they can remember together.
A good trip can turn one ordinary arrival into a favorite story.
A grand entrance has happened above the travelers rather than in front of them.
An excellent opening scene for a holiday with ambitious expectations.
I'd record what they actually saw before settling on the identity.
A shared glimpse can make two people carry the same small wonder.
A striking arrival doesn't need to be owned to become part of the trip.
I'd remember how they looked at each other when they realized both had seen it.

contexts.subject: The couple is delighted their wish to see rare Pokemon was met immediately.

LilycoveCity_Text_HoneymoonVowToSeeRareP.text: On our honeymoon, we vowed to see as\nmany rare POKéMON as we can.\pSo we were delighted to see a rare\nPOKéMON as soon as we arrived.\pI mean, we are totally happy!$

replies.text: Their holiday wish has arrived before the luggage finished settling.
An early encounter can encourage curiosity throughout the rest of the visit.
Good memory already. Let the rest of the trip unfold too.
I love that they're happy about having noticed it together.
A shared little celebration can be more lasting than another purchase.
The hoped-for theme has appeared in the very first chapter.
A holiday itinerary receiving an unexpectedly efficient response.
They can keep looking while leaving room for ordinary surprises.
A wish fulfilled can make the unfamiliar feel welcoming.
Their happiness is the part that makes the whole sighting lovely.
I'd enjoy hearing what unexpected ordinary thing becomes their next favorite memory.

contexts.subject: On a repeat interaction the Aqua trainer commands Wailmer to leap.

LilycoveCity_Text_WailmerLeapOutOfWater.text: There! WAILMER!\nLeap out of the water now!$

replies.text: A very large performer is being asked for another entrance.
A repeated command doesn't tell us whether the Pokemon needs a break.
Watch how Wailmer's doing, not just the jump.
I wonder whether it enjoys the practice or just keeps following.
A proper pause belongs in training too.
A spectacle is only worthwhile when its performer is cared for.
An impressive amount of splash is being requested on schedule.
Observe the response rather than treating obedience as the whole result.
A willing movement can look different from a tired one.
A big presentation shouldn't make the actual Pokemon disappear from attention.
I'd watch what Wailmer does in the moment after landing.

contexts.subject: The Wailmer trainer rudely tells us to leave the training alone.

LilycoveCity_Text_GetLostMessingUpTraini.text: Hunh? What do you want?\pYou're messing up our training,\nso can you, like, get lost?$

replies.text: His training has already occupied rather more than his personal space.
A need to concentrate doesn't justify dismissing the people affected.
We can give room and still question the blockage.
It's uncomfortable being treated like the only interruption here.
The other harbor users deserve some consideration too.
A disruptive guest has become very protective of his own scene.
A remarkable claim to peace from someone monopolizing the setting.
The practical effects matter more than the defensive tone.
A boundary should leave room for the lives around it.
He wants space while giving everyone else less of it.
I'd notice the Wailmer and the harbor behind him, not only the demand.

contexts.subject: An Aqua grunt imagines grand opportunities without understanding the boss.

LilycoveCity_Text_ChanceToDoBigThings.text:
I'm just a GRUNT, so I don't know what
the BOSS is thinking…\pBut being on TEAM AQUA, I know I'll get
the chance to do big things!\pWh-who are you?!
I was just talking to myself!$

replies.text: Big things is a very roomy phrase for not knowing what you're doing.
Ambition needs an understood purpose, not only promised significance.
Ask what the big things are before helping them happen.
He sounds like he wants his life to feel important.
Meaningful work should make room for the people it affects.
A supporting character wants a larger role before reading what the role requires.
A dream of importance with a suspiciously blank job description.
We should separate his personal hope from evidence about the organization.
A wish to matter can be met without surrendering judgment.
An impressive title doesn't make the conduct underneath it worthwhile.
I'd be interested in what he actually values once the group stops supplying the words.

contexts.subject: An Aqua grunt demands obedience about the cave based only on being an adult.

LilycoveCity_Text_DontGoNearCaveInCove.text: Hey, you!\pDon't go near the cave in the cove!\pWhy? You don't need a reason why!\nI'm an adult, so you just listen to me!$

replies.text: An adult ought to have room for at least one actual reason.
Age doesn't substitute for a justified restriction.
Being older doesn't make every order right.
It's hard to trust a warning that refuses to explain itself.
A responsible person can care about safety without using it to silence questions.
Authority has attempted to enter the scene without its supporting evidence.
A title borrowed directly from having been around longer.
We can assess visible risks without accepting his entire claim.
A larger voice needn't make our own judgment smaller.
The age argument doesn't fit better just because he says it firmly.
I'd notice what he's trying to keep from being seen.

contexts.subject: An Aqua member claims their control of the world will make Pokemon happier.

LilycoveCity_Text_IfWorldBecomesOurs.text: If this whole wide world becomes ours,\nTEAM AQUA's, it will be a happier\lplace for POKéMON, too.$

replies.text: The Pokemon should get a say before the whole world is assigned new owners.
A claimed benefit doesn't justify assuming control over everyone affected.
Look at what the Pokemon actually need. Not the slogan.
It's frightening hearing care described as a reason to own everything.
A happy world should include people being allowed to question the plan.
A grand ending has been promised without asking the existing cast.
An enormous claim with an exceptionally convenient judge.
We need consequences and evidence, not merely possession relabeled as kindness.
A life can be protected without the protector claiming the whole sky.
A beautiful promise doesn't excuse an overbearing design.
I'd compare their treatment of the Pokemon nearby with the happiness they're advertising.

contexts.subject: May treats our declined battle as evidence of inadequate training.

LilycoveCity_Text_MayNotRaisingPokemon.text: MAY: Oh, why? {PLAYER}{KUN}, haven't you\nbeen raising your POKéMON?\pThat's not a very good showing as a\nTRAINER…$

replies.text: The invitation has again mistaken no for a complete report card.
Refusing the match doesn't establish how much care or practice we've given.
Can choose not to. Doesn't make the team neglected.
It's tiring having the real answer replaced by somebody else's guess.
A quiet day can be part of good care too.
The missing scene doesn't require an unfavorable rewrite of the character.
A small refusal has somehow been assigned an entire moral appendix.
Readiness and timing deserve a question before a conclusion.
A choice can stay simple without becoming a verdict.
A friendly invitation should leave the other person room for their own reason to say no.
I'd rather let the honest answer stand than battle to defend an image.

contexts.subject: Brendan assumes we lack confidence when we decline his Lilycove challenge.

LilycoveCity_Text_BrendanNoConfidence.text: BRENDAN: Oh, what's the matter?\nDon't have the confidence?$

replies.text: Confidence is allowed to have other plans for the afternoon.
The decision doesn't reveal a single reliable motive on its own.
We can say no and still trust the team.
It would be easier if the invitation left room to decline comfortably.
Another match can wait until it suits everyone.
A refused performance needn't become a crisis of character.
My schedule is not a confession about my deepest inadequacies.
Ask whether and when we're ready instead of diagnosing the answer.
A small pause can belong to a steady relationship.
A confident choice sometimes looks exactly like choosing not to perform.
I'd want a future meeting to feel welcoming rather than corrective.

contexts.subject: May contrasts our badge journey with her competitive Pokedex plans.

LilycoveCity_Text_MayYouGoingToCollectBa.text: {PLAYER}{KUN}, what are you going to do?\pCollect all the GYM BADGES and take\nthe POKéMON LEAGUE challenge?\pWell, while you're collecting BADGES,\n{PLAYER}{KUN}, I'm going to work on my\lPOKéDEX. I'll complete it before you!\pSee you!$

replies.text: Different homework, same remarkably competitive goodbye.
Our goals can differ while both involve learning about Pokemon.
Good for her. We'll choose our own pace.
It's nice that the friendship has room for different directions.
A journey shouldn't become only a race to finish the list.
Two characters can carry different plots without leaving the shared story.
The rivalry has branched into separate departments.
We can compare discoveries instead of forcing identical progress markers.
Different paths can still meet with something worth sharing.
A personal goal fits better than copying somebody else's itinerary.
I'd enjoy hearing about one new discovery instead of only who is ahead.

contexts.subject: May asks our next goal while promising to complete her Pokedex first.

LilycoveCity_Text_MayYouGoingToPokemonLe.text:
{PLAYER}{KUN}, what are you going to do?\pAre you taking the POKéMON LEAGUE
challenge?\pOr, are you going to complete your
POKéDEX?\pI might've lost to you in battling,
but I'll finish my POKéDEX before you!\pSee you!$

replies.text: She has relocated the rematch to the pages of a very ambitious notebook.
A battle result needn't decide which other activities someone enjoys.
Let her chase the Dex. We'll plan our next challenge.
It's nice she can stay excited after losing.
The people and Pokemon along the way matter more than the finishing date.
A defeated rival has given herself a perfectly valid new plot.
A competition now measured in more than the result that just annoyed her.
We can choose the next task by what the team is ready for.
A long road can hold more than one kind of growth.
Changing the goal isn't the same as changing the whole friendship.
I'd like to see which encounter becomes her favorite, even if it adds nothing rare.

contexts.subject: After our Championship May contrasts Frontier challenges with her Pokedex ambition.

LilycoveCity_Text_MayYouGoingToBattleFro.text:
{PLAYER}{KUN}, what are you going to do?\pAre you taking the BATTLE FRONTIER
challenge?\pOr, are you going to complete your
POKéDEX?\pI might've lost to you in battling,
but I'll finish my POKéDEX before you!\pSee you!$

replies.text: A very grand next challenge and a very determined book project.
The options ask for different preparation; neither needs to be chosen automatically.
We'll decide what suits the team now.
It's lovely that finishing something big still leaves different good ways forward.
The next chapter can have ordinary restful days too.
A completed title has opened several possible sequels rather than one required ending.
An impressive amount of homework waiting on both sides of that farewell.
We can compare the new format with what we actually want to learn.
A destination reached can reveal space for a different kind of path.
A new achievement doesn't have to become a uniform we keep wearing.
I'd like the next journey to include a surprise beyond another race.

contexts.subject: Brendan considers following our badge path and encourages us.

LilycoveCity_Text_BrendanYouGoingToColle.text: {PLAYER}, what are you going to do?\pCollect all the GYM BADGES and take\nthe POKéMON LEAGUE challenge?\pMaybe I'll do that, too…\pWell, anyway, hang in there!$

replies.text: Our route has apparently become somebody else's suggested itinerary.
He can use our example without needing an identical journey.
Good luck to him. Needs his own plan too.
It's nice having the encouragement underneath the competitive talk.
A good route should fit the team actually traveling it.
A companion's story can inspire another without becoming a script to copy.
The rivalry has paused long enough for a fairly kind goodbye.
He should compare his team's needs with the next challenge, not only our result.
An example can point without deciding every step.
Borrowing inspiration works better than borrowing the entire look.
I'd be interested in what he changes once he tries the path himself.

contexts.subject: Brendan encourages our League goal while imagining he could become stronger.

LilycoveCity_Text_BrendanYouGoingToPokem.text: {PLAYER}, what are you going to do?\pSince you're that strong, are you\ntaking the POKéMON LEAGUE challenge?\pHeh, even me--if I trained my POKéMON\na bit more, I should be stronger than\lyou, {PLAYER}.\pWell, anyway, hang in there!$

replies.text: A warm goodbye has left one competitive foot on the doorstep.
His possible improvement doesn't invalidate what either team has done.
Let the next work speak. We still have choices to make.
I think the encouragement is real even when he adds the little boast.
A partner needs steady care, not only a future comparison.
The recurring rival has insisted on one final optimistic revision of his ranking.
Hypothetical strength remains unusually undefeated.
He could test a new method instead of merely promising more training.
A friendly bond can hold a little pride without following it everywhere.
The confidence lands better when he also leaves us a genuine good wish.
I'd remember the hang in there as well as the claim around it.

contexts.subject: Brendan suggests the Frontier and imagines his own future growth.

LilycoveCity_Text_BrendanYouGoingToBattl.text:
{PLAYER}, what are you going to do?\pAre you taking the BATTLE FRONTIER
challenge?\pOr, are you going to complete your
POKéDEX?\pSince you're that strong, you should
consider the BATTLE FRONTIER.\pHeh, if I train my POKéMON a bit more,
I'll get stronger than you, {PLAYER}.\pMaybe I should go to the BATTLE
FRONTIER.\pWell, anyway, hang in there!$

replies.text: The future has acquired both a new venue and another confident comparison.
A different format can reveal strengths the previous journey didn't test.
Learn what it asks before choosing it.
It's nice knowing there are possibilities without having to begin immediately.
A rested team should get room in the plan too.
A long story has opened a new setting without closing every alternative.
A sequel proposal with the rivalry carefully preserved in the footnotes.
We can assess the rules and goals before treating the recommendation as a perfect fit.
A next path can be chosen for interest instead of obligation.
A fresh challenge deserves preparation that actually suits it.
I'd enjoy hearing what surprised him if he tries it before we meet again.

contexts.subject: A resident explains coordinated faster blending improves Pokeblocks.

LilycoveCity_Text_FasterSpinBetterPokebl.text: People have to work together to get it\nto spin faster.\pThe faster you can make it spin, the\nbetter {POKEBLOCK}S you can get, I've heard.$

replies.text: The snack apparently needs a small cooperative athletics team.
Shared timing can affect the quality of the process.
Work together. No point rushing in different directions.
It's nice having a little task where listening changes the result.
Good coordination is part of making something well.
The ensemble has a practical reason to follow the same beat.
A machine thoughtfully designed to absorb some of the social awkwardness.
I'd start with a clear rhythm before trying to increase speed.
Several small efforts can become one steadier motion.
A good group activity gives everyone a way to contribute.
I'd watch when the group stops reacting separately and starts anticipating each other.

contexts.subject: A resident introduces Pokeblocks as candy improving Pokemon condition.

LilycoveCity_Text_ExplainBerryBlender.text: It's used for making a kind of candy\ncalled a {POKEBLOCK}.\pIf you give a good {POKEBLOCK} to a POKéMON,\nits condition will improve by a lot.$

replies.text: A little sweet with a very ambitious training résumé.
Preparation and individual preference matter alongside the intended benefit.
Choose what suits the Pokemon. Don't just collect sweets.
It's nice when care can include something enjoyable.
I'd pay attention to which flavors each partner actually likes.
A small prop can support a different kind of performance.
Candy with purpose is a tempting category.
We should learn what changes and how to make it consistently.
A useful treat can still be offered gently.
The best little finish is the one that fits its wearer, or eater.
I'd notice the Pokemon's reaction rather than only the promised result.

contexts.subject: The Cave of Origin guardian describes its tradition and asks us to leave.

SootopolisCity_Text_CaveOfOriginPleaseLe.text: Who might you be?\pThis is the CAVE OF ORIGIN.\pThe spirits of POKéMON, becalmed at\nMT. PYRE, are said to be revived here.\pPlease leave.$

replies.text: A mysterious place can still have an ordinary boundary to respect.
The tradition explains why access may be treated with care.
We'll leave it peaceful. No need to force a visit.
It's all right not knowing everything behind the door.
The people tending the place deserve consideration.
A significant setting needn't open its entire story to every visitor.
An invitation to remain outside can be accepted without becoming ominous.
We can ask elsewhere rather than treat a locked role as a puzzle to defeat.
A closed place can still be held kindly from a distance.
Respect doesn't require understanding every part of the tradition first.
I'd remember the guardian's care more than the frustration of not entering.

contexts.subject: The guardian describes Wallace's criteria for a capable trainer to be brought to the cave.

SootopolisCity_Text_LeadSuperiorTrainerT.text:
A person with a strong will and
superior talent…\pA TRAINER who has knowledge and
experience of many kinds of POKéMON…\pIf such a person were to appear, I was
instructed by WALLACE to lead that\lTRAINER to this CAVE.$

replies.text: That sounds like a request for judgment, not merely a larger attack.
The criteria combine experience, knowledge, and the ability to act with purpose.
Know what we're taking on before accepting the role.
It's a heavy description, but it doesn't require pretending we know everything.
A capable person still needs help and a ready team.
The role asks for a whole character, not one impressive entrance.
An unusually substantial qualification hidden in a brief introduction.
We should compare the actual task with what we can responsibly do.
A strong will can still leave room for listening.
Experience looks better when it can admit what remains uncertain.
I'd want to hear what Wallace needs rather than only whether we fit the description.

contexts.subject: The guardian says the cave rests after the crisis ends.

SootopolisCity_Text_CaveOfOriginSleepsTo.text: This is the CAVE OF ORIGIN…\pWith the passing of the crisis,\nthe cave, too, shall sleep…$

replies.text: Even a cave has earned a quieter afternoon.
The return to restricted quiet marks a changed role after the emergency.
Good. Leave the place some peace.
It's comforting when something stops needing urgent attention.
The people guarding it deserve rest as well.
A climactic setting can return to a life beyond the plot.
An unusually large location with a sensible recovery plan.
A period of calm lets us assess rather than keep intervening.
A still place can hold what happened without repeating it.
A quiet ending doesn't need another impressive disturbance.
I'd remember how different the same entrance feels when nobody is hurrying.

contexts.subject: The guardian reflects that a third awakened Pokemon ended the clash.

SootopolisCity_Text_AwakenedPokemonClash.text: Oh, my…\pThe clash between the two awakened\nPOKéMON was quelled by the awakening\lof a third POKéMON…$

replies.text: The fighting stopped without either side having to become the winner.
A new intervention changed a conflict neither participant was resolving.
Important part is the city gets to breathe again.
It must feel strange watching an old story happen so close.
The people here need time to feel safe after all that noise.
The resolution arrived from outside the duel's own two answers.
A dramatic ending whose best effect is the chance to stop being dramatic.
We should remember what actually changed rather than only the impressive scale.
A fierce argument can need a voice beyond itself.
The quiet afterward matters as much as the spectacular arrival.
I'd notice what the guardian looks at now that the movement has stopped.

contexts.subject: Kiri is frightened by the giant Pokemon fighting and asks someone to stop them.

SootopolisCity_Text_BigPokemonFighting.text: A big POKéMON is fighting with\nanother big POKéMON!\pPlease, someone make them stop!$

replies.text: She needs someone calm beside her, not a grand promise.
Her fear makes sense; we should help her stay with someone trusted and safe.
Keep her away from danger. Find who can stay with her.
I wish the city didn't have to sound this frightening to her.
A familiar person can help make the next few minutes less lonely.
A child shouldn't have to carry the catastrophe as a story about being brave.
This is no place for a clever line from us.
We can help with the immediate safe step without claiming to control everything.
A small frightened voice deserves to be heard beneath the larger noise.
She doesn't need to look composed for us to take her seriously.
I'd notice who is looking after her while everyone's eyes are on the fight.

contexts.subject: Kiri notices the beautiful Pokemon descending from the sky.

SootopolisCity_Text_PrettyMonCameFromSky.text: A pretty POKéMON came down from\nthe sky…$

replies.text: She found something beautiful to notice in a very frightening sky.
A striking appearance can draw attention before its role is understood.
Keep her safe while she watches.
It's lovely that wonder still has a little room beside the fear.
I hope a familiar adult is close enough for her to share the sight.
A child's first description has gone straight to the beauty of the entrance.
A remarkably gentle observation for such an enormous moment.
We should observe what happens rather than assign an intention from appearance.
A bright little wonder can enter a difficult day without asking permission.
She noticed the beauty before reaching for a title.
I'd remember the way her attention lifted when it appeared.

contexts.subject: Kiri wonders what wish our name contains.

SootopolisCity_Text_WhatKindOfWishInYour.text: I wonder what kind of wish is included\nin your name.$

replies.text: A name might be a tiny letter someone sent into our future.
A chosen name can carry hopes even when we don't know their exact origin.
Could ask whoever chose it. Good thing to wonder about.
It's a lovely way to think about a word you hear every day.
A hope for someone's good life can be very simple and warm.
A character's name may contain a small story from before their own memory.
My name has mostly contained people calling me back to things.
We can be curious without assuming every name has one clear intended meaning.
A little wish can remain close through being spoken often.
A name can fit in ways its giver never predicted.
I'd love to hear the story told by the person who first chose it.

contexts.subject: Kiri accepts our answer about seasons and says she has many questions.

SootopolisCity_Text_OhDoesntMatter.text: Oh…\nIt doesn't matter…\pThere's so much that I want to know…$

replies.text: A small no has failed to slow a very healthy question factory.
Curiosity can remain useful without every guess proving correct.
Good. Keep asking without needing every first idea to work.
It's nice that she doesn't make being wrong feel like the end.
There is plenty worth wondering about on an ordinary day.
An inquisitive character has kept room for several possible stories.
An excellent reason to keep a very small notebook handy.
Questions improve when we let the answers change the next question.
A little wonder can turn gently without needing to stop.
Being interested matters more than having the most polished first explanation.
I'd like to hear which new question caught her attention next.

contexts.subject: Kiri decides autumn is her favorite because she was born then and asks ours.

SootopolisCity_Text_ThenILoveAutumn.text: Then KIRI was born in the autumn,\nso I love the autumn!\pWhich season do you like?$

replies.text: Autumn has gained a very sincere little supporter.
A personal association can make a season meaningful without settling everyone's preference.
She can like it for her own reasons. Nice question.
I like the quiet feeling when the air starts to change.
Autumn makes me think of warming meals and things ready to harvest.
A season can be a setting and a piece of personal history together.
A very reasonable choice, particularly for the fading-light department.
I enjoy watching the changes that make one season become another.
The turning year gives familiar places another kind of life.
The colors are a strong argument, though I like the clothes too.
I'd enjoy hearing what she notices first when her favorite season returns.

contexts.subject: A resident recounts a sudden severe weather shift and wonders about the Pokemon.

SootopolisCity_Text_WeatherWentWild.text:
The weather was clear this morning,
but…\pAll of a sudden, dark clouds brewed up,
rain started falling in sheets, and\lthere was thunder and lightning, too.\pThe weather just went completely
wild!\pIs all of this because of those
POKéMON?$

replies.text: A normal morning changed faster than anyone could prepare for.
The timing suggests a connection worth examining without guessing every mechanism.
Find a safe place first. Questions can follow.
It must feel frightening when the familiar weather stops behaving familiarly.
People need shelter and clear help, not only an explanation.
The ordinary setting has changed beneath the characters' feet.
A day with entirely too much atmospheric ambition.
We should focus on observed changes and immediate conditions.
A sudden storm can make home feel temporarily unknown.
She doesn't need to make the fear look dramatic; the change already was.
I'd listen for what happened first and what people nearby need now.

contexts.subject: A resident credits us with bringing the flying Pokemon.

SootopolisCity_Text_YouBroughtFlyingMon.text: Oh?\pIt was you who brought that flying\nPOKéMON here?\pWell, aren't you amazing!$

replies.text: We helped, but that was more than a trick we could order on demand.
Our part matters without turning the Pokemon's action into our possession.
Glad it helped. The Pokemon deserves credit too.
It's lovely if the thanks means the city feels safer.
The people here deserve a quiet day after all that worry.
A supporting effort needn't claim the central character's whole achievement.
A generous review with a larger cast than the compliment names.
We should remember what the Pokemon chose, not only our route here.
A great moment can include our effort without belonging to us.
Gratitude looks best when it leaves room for everyone who helped.
I'd remember the relief in her face more than the praise directed at us.

contexts.subject: A man teasingly calls us neither ordinary nor extraordinary tourists.

SootopolisCity_Text_NoOrdinaryTourist.text: Hm!\nYou've come all the way to SOOTOPOLIS?\lYou're no ordinary tourist.\pBut I suppose that doesn't make you\nan extraordinary tourist, either.$

replies.text: Our tourism has been officially classified as somewhere in the middle.
He has supplied a category without much practical information behind it.
Fair enough. We're still free to look around.
That's an oddly careful way not to sound impressed.
The visit can be good without winning a title for it.
A grand introduction has been revised into an unremarkably nuanced review.
An extremely balanced appraisal of our ability to arrive somewhere.
The actual route and purpose tell us more than either label.
A journey needn't be exceptional to belong to the person making it.
An arrival doesn't have to look impressive to be worth making.
I'd rather hear what he thinks a visitor should notice next.

contexts.subject: A resident quietly notes the city is calm again.

SootopolisCity_Text_CityRegainedCalm.text: The city has regained its calm…$

replies.text: An ordinary quiet street has become very good news.
The change matters most in how people can resume their daily lives.
Good. Give the place time to recover.
That little sentence sounds like being able to breathe properly again.
A familiar meal and a safe evening can mean a lot now.
The best closing scene may be the return of an unremarkable day.
A welcome reduction in the local dramatic workload.
Calm gives us room to assess what still needs care.
A place can find its familiar shape again one small routine at a time.
Relief doesn't require a grand display to be visible.
I'd notice the first ordinary conversation that has nothing to do with the crisis.

contexts.subject: A resident loves the sky framed in a circle by the volcanic crater.

SootopolisCity_Text_SootopolisSkyBeautif.text:
SOOTOPOLIS sprang up as a town in
the crater of a volcano.\pIf you look up at the sky, the lip of
the crater is also visible.\lSo, all you see is the sky in a circle.\pBut that's what makes the sky above
SOOTOPOLIS the most beautiful.$

replies.text: The town has given the sky its own enormous picture frame.
A restricted view can make the visible shape more striking.
Good view. Easy to see why she keeps looking up.
I like how a familiar sky can feel completely different in one place.
A little pause outside can be its own good part of the day.
The setting has composed a scene before anyone adds a line.
An exceptionally ambitious window for the whole town.
I'd watch how the edge changes the way light reaches the streets.
A small visible piece can make the whole sky feel close.
A strong frame can make a simple color feel extraordinary.
I'd love to see how the same circle looks at different hours.

contexts.subject: A resident feels powerless before the enormous battling Pokemon.

SootopolisCity_Text_GiganticPokemonFight.text: When two POKéMON that gigantic\nare fighting that savagely, there's\lnot much that we can do.$

replies.text: Not being able to stop the whole fight doesn't make keeping people safe meaningless.
The scale limits intervention, but immediate protective actions still matter.
Help who we can. Keep clear of the danger.
It must be frightening watching something far beyond what you can change.
A safe place and a familiar person can still help someone.
An enormous scene needn't erase the value of every small action around it.
We are allowed to have limits without becoming useless.
Identify what is controllable instead of forcing an impossible direct response.
A small care can remain real beside a very large fear.
Nobody needs to look heroic to help an ordinary person get through this.
I'd notice the people who are being overlooked while everyone stares upward.

contexts.subject: A resident cherishes the stars framed by the crater at night.

SootopolisCity_Text_NightSkyFavoriteScen.text: A circle of a night sky framed by\nthe crater of a volcano…\pAnd in that ring, stars flicker and\nblink as if they were alive…\lIt's my favorite scenery.$

replies.text: A whole town with an exceptionally tasteful ceiling.
The crater provides a distinctive frame for a familiar night sky.
Sounds worth staying up a little for.
I'd love to sit quietly and watch the little changes in the stars.
A warm drink outside would make that a lovely evening.
A setting can hold a complete scene without needing anyone to speak.
An excellent night view with naturally controlled levels of unwanted daylight.
I'd compare the brightness at the rim with the open part above.
A circle of darkness can hold a very wide kind of wonder.
A restrained frame lets the tiny lights do the work.
I'd remember the stillness around the view as much as what fits inside it.

contexts.subject: A resident initially feared the descending third Pokemon.

SootopolisCity_Text_FearedWorstWhenPokem.text: When that third POKéMON flew down,\nI feared the worst.$

replies.text: After that much fear, even another arrival could look like more trouble.
Her reaction makes sense without advance knowledge of the outcome.
Good reason to be cautious. Nobody knew what came next.
It's hard to trust a new movement while the whole place feels unsafe.
She deserves time for the worry to settle.
A new character's entrance looked entirely different from inside the crisis.
A reasonable response to a day already far beyond its allotted spectacle.
We should judge with the information available then, not what we know afterward.
A startled heart can need longer than the storm to grow quiet.
Her first fear doesn't become foolish because the ending changed.
I'd remember how little anyone could be sure of in that first moment.

contexts.subject: A child reacts to the dangerous clash with excited awe.

replies.text: It looks enormous. We still need to keep him out of the way.
Excitement can obscure how close a child is to actual danger.
Make sure someone's watching him, not just the fight.
It's strange seeing wonder and risk in the same little expression.
A safe place to stay matters more than the view.
A spectacular scene can look like entertainment to someone inside it.
A lively reaction that needs a sensible adult nearby.
We can acknowledge the sight without encouraging a closer look.
A bright feeling can still need a careful hand beside it.
He doesn't need a better angle if it puts him where he shouldn't be.
I'd watch where he steps while his attention stays on the enormous movement.

contexts.subject: The child remains awestruck after the great clash ends.

replies.text: That is a very small review of a very large afternoon.
A child may remember the scale before understanding the consequences.
Glad he's safe. Let him talk it through.
It must be strange returning to ordinary streets after seeing that.
A familiar routine can help the day become manageable again.
An immense event has been compressed into one breathless closing line.
A concise review from the least cynical member of the audience.
I'd ask what he actually noticed before adding an explanation.
A little wonder can remain after the fear has passed.
An honest reaction doesn't need to sound polished.
I'd remember which detail he tries to describe with his hands.

contexts.subject: A lifelong resident wonders about life beyond the crater's round sky.

SootopolisCity_Text_WonderWhatWorldIsLik.text: I… I've never been out of this city.\pI wonder what the world is like on\nthe other side of this round sky?$

replies.text: The circle overhead has room for a very large question.
A familiar environment can leave much of the outside world difficult to imagine.
Can learn a little at a time. Doesn't have to leave tomorrow.
I'd love to hear which outside place he pictures first.
A visitor's ordinary story can make somewhere far away feel real.
A small setting has opened a character's thoughts onto an enormous unwritten map.
An excellent reason to ask travelers questions that aren't about winning.
We can share concrete details instead of only grand descriptions.
A home can be loved while the horizon beyond it remains curious.
A new view can begin in a conversation before it becomes a journey.
I'd tell him about one ordinary moment beyond the crater, not only the impressive sights.

contexts.subject: A child cannot understand why the giant newcomers are fighting instead of being friends.

SootopolisCity_Text_GiantPokemonSuddenly.text:
These giant POKéMON suddenly appeared
in the middle of the city!\pAnd, I've never seen them before!\pWhy are they smashing into each
other like that?\pWhy can't they be friends, those
POKéMON?$

replies.text: Wanting them to be friends is a gentler thought than the scene deserves.
The child is noticing conflict without having the information to explain it.
Keep him safe. Don't make up a simple answer.
It's hard when something frightening doesn't have a reason you can understand.
A trusted person nearby can help more than a grand theory.
A child's question has reached the point the spectacle can't answer for itself.
A plain wish for kindness beneath an exceptionally noisy day.
We should separate what can be observed from the motives nobody has established.
A small hope can remain gentle even when it cannot stop the world.
He doesn't need his concern turned into something silly.
I'd listen to the friendship question rather than only the astonishment at their size.

contexts.subject: A child asks about the strange green Pokemon.

SootopolisCity_Text_WhatIsThatGreenPokem.text: What? What? What?\nWhat is that green POKéMON?!$

replies.text: A remarkable new face has arrived before its name did.
We can describe what is visible without guessing beyond what we know.
Watch from somewhere safe first.
It's lovely and unsettling seeing something nobody around you can name.
The child deserves a calm answer rather than more frantic guesses.
The new arrival has changed the scene before receiving an introduction.
A very large mystery with an unusually distinctive color choice.
Observe its actions before deciding what the entrance means.
An unknown life can invite wonder without requiring an instant explanation.
The silhouette is unforgettable even before the name arrives.
I'd remember the first thing it did, not only how different it looked.

contexts.subject: A child worries Groudon and Kyogre may cause disasters elsewhere.

SootopolisCity_Text_WhereDidLegendariesG.text: GROUDON and KYOGRE…\nWhere did they go?\pWill they cause droughts or downpours\nsomewhere else?$

replies.text: Feeling safe here doesn't answer every worry about where they went.
It's a reasonable question, but we shouldn't invent certainty about distant events.
Keep to what we know. Don't promise what we can't check.
A frightening day can leave the mind looking for the next bad place.
A calm person can listen without feeding the worry.
The local ending hasn't answered every question the event opened.
An understandable concern with a much larger map than anyone can inspect at once.
We should distinguish reported conditions from imagined possibilities.
A worry can be heard without being handed another dark story.
He deserves honesty that doesn't make uncertainty sound like a new catastrophe.
I'd tell him what is actually known and leave room for asking again later.

contexts.subject: Steven marvels at Rayquaza making the rampaging Pokemon retreat.

SootopolisCity_Text_SoThatsRayquaza.text: STEVEN: So that's RAYQUAZA…\pIt's incredible how the two rampaging\nPOKéMON would flee from it in fear…$

replies.text: An enormous argument has found something both sides were willing to leave.
The response gives us an observation about its influence, not a complete explanation.
Glad the fighting stopped. People need the quiet.
It must feel strange seeing so much danger end in one movement.
The city deserves time to recover beyond the impressive moment.
A brief entrance has changed the course of a very long scene.
A remarkably efficient performance with unusually welcome consequences.
We should record what happened without pretending it explains every mechanism.
A great stillness can arrive on the other side of a great power.
The result matters more than making the arrival into a spectacle.
I'd notice how the people react when the space finally stops shaking.

contexts.subject: Steven believes we can help Wallace.

SootopolisCity_Text_KnowWhatsNeededToHel.text: STEVEN: I think you have what's\nneeded to help him…$

replies.text: Trust is encouraging. I still want to hear what help is actually needed.
We can assess the task without treating confidence as a full explanation.
Find out what he needs. Then choose the next step.
It's a little daunting, but being asked doesn't mean doing everything alone.
The team should be part of preparing, not forgotten in the urgency.
A vote of confidence should open a conversation, not replace it.
A very short sentence with a substantial amount of responsibility inside.
Clear requirements will tell us more than a broad assessment of our potential.
A hand offered help can still ask how best to hold it.
A capable person is allowed to need directions.
I'd want to hear Wallace's own account before deciding what our role should be.

contexts.subject: Steven speculates the two leaders went to return the Orbs at Mt. Pyre.

SootopolisCity_Text_MaxieArchieLeft.text: STEVEN: It looks like both MAXIE and\nARCHIE have gone away somewhere.\pPerhaps they've gone to MT. PYRE to\nreturn those ORBS…$

replies.text: That would be a useful act, though perhaps is still doing important work.
Their departure is known; the destination and intention remain a hypothesis.
Hope they do. Still need to make things right.
A small repair can matter after something that frightening.
The guardians deserve to have what was taken returned safely.
A possible act of restitution has entered the story without yet becoming fact.
An encouraging guess with a sensible amount of uncertainty attached.
We can check the outcome rather than treat an inferred intention as completed.
A returned thing can begin a repair without finishing every hurt.
A better choice should become visible through what they actually do.
I'd remember Steven's uncertainty instead of retelling it as a confirmed apology.

contexts.subject: Steven admits he has never visited Sky Pillar and does not know its location.

SootopolisCity_Text_NeverBeenToSkyPillar.text: STEVEN: The SKY PILLAR…\pI've never been there.\nI wonder where it could be?$

replies.text: Even the stone expert has places still missing from his map.
An honest gap is useful information when choosing whom to ask next.
Then find someone who knows. No need to guess.
It's reassuring when someone capable can simply say they don't know.
A reliable local direction would help more than a confident invented one.
A knowledgeable guide has left room for another character's expertise.
A very respectable refusal to manufacture an answer.
We should seek a confirmed location before planning the trip.
A known limit can become the beginning of a better question.
Confidence looks better when it doesn't cover uncertainty with decoration.
I'd be interested in which traveler first gives us a place we can actually check.

contexts.subject: A boy senses the giant Pokemon may lack control rather than feel anger.

SootopolisCity_Text_TwoPokemonArentAngry.text: I just get this sense somehow that\nthe two POKéMON aren't angry.\pI think… They probably can't control\ntheir own power…$

replies.text: A different reason for the danger doesn't make the danger less real.
It's a hypothesis about motive, and observation may help distinguish it.
Keep safe first. We don't need to decide their feelings from here.
It's kind that he wonders whether they are struggling too.
Living things can need help even while they cause harm.
The apparent antagonists may not understand the scene the way the audience does.
A more humane question than simply assigning villain roles.
We can note behavior without turning an impression into certainty.
A fierce motion can come from more than one hidden feeling.
The thought leaves room for care without excusing the damage.
I'd listen to the uncertainty in his words as much as the explanation he hopes for.

contexts.subject: The boy describes the flying Pokemon ending the rampage.

SootopolisCity_Text_FlyingMonStoppedRamp.text: That flying POKéMON came down from\nthe sky and stopped the rampaging\lPOKéMON…$

replies.text: The best part of that extraordinary entrance is everyone getting an ordinary tomorrow.
The observed effect is clear, even if much about it remains unknown.
Good. Give the city time to settle.
It's lovely hearing the word stopped after all that fear.
People can finally think about what they need next.
The final movement matters because it let so many other stories continue.
A spectacle whose greatest achievement is allowing the spectacle to end.
Now we can assess what requires care without the immediate disruption.
A shared quiet can arrive before anyone has words for the relief.
The memory needn't become glamorous to remain important.
I'd notice the people looking at each other again instead of only at the sky.

contexts.subject: A spectator asks the names of the battling Pokemon.

SootopolisCity_Text_DoYouKnowMonNames.text: … … … … … …\pHi, do you know the names of those\nPOKéMON fighting over there?$

replies.text: A name might make the enormous sight feel a little less unknowable.
Identifying them can help without explaining the whole event.
We'll keep to what we know. Stay clear while asking.
It's hard wanting a simple answer in such an overwhelming moment.
A calm answer is better than another shouted guess.
The audience is trying to find a familiar handle on a scene beyond its scale.
An understandable attempt to reduce a catastrophe to something pronounceable.
Names should follow reliable identification, not only a passing impression.
A thing can be named without becoming understood or safe.
The question deserves an answer that doesn't turn danger into a game.
I'd notice whether knowing the name actually helps the person feel steadier.

contexts.subject: A spectator is surprised that the green newcomer resolves the red-blue contest.

SootopolisCity_Text_GreenOneSettlesThing.text: I was wondering which one would win,\nthe red one or the blue one, but, oh no,\lit's the green one that settles things!\pTalk about a huge turn of events!$

replies.text: A fight can end without picking either side's winner.
The new intervention changed the situation rather than winning by the expected comparison.
Good outcome. Better than cheering for more damage.
I hope the surprise makes room for noticing the frightened people too.
The city needed peace, not a better sporting finish.
A third character has broken the false choice at the center of the scene.
An excellent argument against treating every conflict as a two-color contest.
We should remember what changed, not only how unexpected it looked.
A quarrel can be answered from beyond the terms that kept it going.
The most striking turn is the chance for ordinary life to resume.
I'd remember the change in the crowd when the outcome stopped being a prediction.

contexts.subject: A girl fears the city will be destroyed.

SootopolisCity_Text_SootopolisWillBeWrec.text: Oh, no!\nSOOTOPOLIS CITY will get wrecked!$

replies.text: She's looking at home, not just a scene in the distance.
Her fear concerns familiar people and places, not merely the scale of the event.
Get her somewhere safe with someone she trusts.
It must hurt seeing the place you know feel suddenly breakable.
The next safe step matters more than a big reassuring speech.
A threatened setting is somebody else's ordinary life.
This isn't a moment to make her fear sound excessive.
We can help with immediate needs without promising what we can't control.
A familiar doorway can hold a very large fear when home is at risk.
She doesn't have to look brave for the worry to deserve attention.
I'd notice what person or place she keeps looking toward.

contexts.subject: The girl is relieved her city survived.

replies.text: Home is still here. That is a very good small sentence.
Relief may arrive before the body fully settles after the danger.
Good. Let her find her people.
It's lovely hearing the same voice hold something gentler now.
A familiar safe evening can mean everything after that fear.
An ordinary street has become the most welcome possible ending.
A reassuringly intact setting with many ordinary stories still inside.
We can check what still needs help without taking away the relief.
A place can feel newly precious by simply remaining.
She doesn't need a more polished way to say she's glad.
I'd remember where she looks first now that she can believe it's still there.

contexts.subject: An enthusiast feels they are witnessing the ancient land-and-sea legend.

SootopolisCity_Text_SeeingLegendWithOwnE.text:
There's an ancient legend that claims
the land and sea were shaped by\la colossal battle between POKéMON.\pWell, I'm seeing that happen with
my very own eyes!\pWhoa! I never expected to be
witness to something this huge!$

replies.text: A legend happening nearby is much less comfortable than one told from a chair.
The resemblance is striking, but immediate safety comes before interpretation.
Keep clear. The city isn't an exhibition.
It must feel overwhelming when an old story becomes something you can hear.
The people living here need more than an interested audience.
A scholar has found the story becoming a setting with consequences.
A powerful observation in an exceptionally poor viewing environment.
Record what is actually visible rather than fitting every detail to the legend.
An old tale can feel suddenly alive without becoming ours to possess.
Wonder is understandable; consideration for everyone around it still matters.
I'd notice the moment fascination gives way to realizing how close it is.

contexts.subject: Afterward the enthusiast reflects on witnessing a legendary battle firsthand.

SootopolisCity_Text_SawLegendWithOwnEyes.text:
There's an ancient legend that claims
the land and sea were shaped by\la colossal battle between POKéMON.\pWell, I saw that happen with
my very own eyes!\pWhoa! I never expected to be
witness to something this huge!$

replies.text: An enormous story has become a memory that still has to settle.
A firsthand account should preserve uncertainty alongside vivid observations.
Glad he can tell it safely. Keep the details honest.
It might take time before the whole event feels real in memory.
The people who were frightened belong in the story too.
A witness now has the responsibility of telling more than the most spectacular scene.
A very large experience with no convenient final punctuation.
Separate what was seen from the explanation formed afterward.
A remembered wonder can hold care for the lives around it.
The event doesn't need extra flourish to be significant.
I'd listen for the ordinary little detail he remembers amid the immense movement.

contexts.subject: Wallace thinks the leaders meant no harm and suggests hearing them out.

SootopolisCity_Text_AquaMagmaDidntMeanHa.text: WALLACE: {PLAYER}{KUN}…\pThe leaders of TEAM MAGMA and AQUA,\nI don't think they meant harm.\pIt wouldn't hurt to hear what they\nhave to say for themselves.$

replies.text: We can listen without pretending the damage was only a misunderstanding.
Intent matters to understanding, but consequences still require accountability.
Hear them. Don't erase what happened.
A chance to speak should include listening to the people who were hurt too.
Making amends needs more than finding the gentlest explanation.
A character deserves a hearing, not an automatic rewrite of the earlier chapters.
A kind interpretation should still leave the facts intact.
We can compare their explanation with the choices and effects already observed.
A listening ear need not become an empty place where responsibility disappears.
Mercy looks stronger when it doesn't demand everyone forget.
I'd want to hear what they understand now, not only what they say they intended.

contexts.subject: Wallace explains Waterfall's Rain Badge requirement and points us to the Gym.

SootopolisCity_Text_ExplainWaterfallGoTo.text:
That HIDDEN MACHINE contains
WATERFALL.\pIf you have the RAIN BADGE, a POKéMON
that has learned that HM move can\lforce its way up waterfalls.\pAnd where does one get the RAIN BADGE?
You know, don't you?\pThat's right! You have to beat
the SOOTOPOLIS GYM LEADER.\pWhen you're all set to go, step through
that door.$

replies.text: A new way uphill comes with one very specific appointment first.
The move and field permission are separate parts of the route requirement.
Get ready for the Gym. No need to rush through the door.
It's nice having a clear next step after so much uncertainty.
The team deserves proper recovery before another demanding challenge.
The great crisis has given way to a much more manageable next chapter.
A practical obstacle with remarkably useful directions.
We can assess readiness rather than treat receiving the move as full preparation.
A path can wait while the travelers find their strength again.
A clear plan feels better than another grand expectation.
I'd remember the calm in this ordinary instruction after everything that came before.

contexts.subject: Wallace encourages us to reach Sky Pillar's top.

SootopolisCity_Text_HaventYouScaledSkyPi.text:
WALLACE: Oh?
{PLAYER}{KUN}?\pHaven't you scaled the SKY PILLAR
yet?\pI'm sure that you can make it to
the top of the SKY PILLAR…$

replies.text: His confidence is welcome. The climb still gets to be a careful one.
Encouragement doesn't remove the need to assess the route and conditions.
Go prepared. No point proving urgency by getting hurt.
It's a big thing to be trusted with, but the next step is still small.
A check on the team belongs before another difficult climb.
A mentor's belief should steady the protagonist rather than hurry the scene.
A remarkably ambitious errand with no need for additional theatrical pressure.
We should identify the actual obstacles instead of assuming determination solves them.
A tall path can be walked with care rather than answered all at once.
Confidence works best when practical judgment stays beside it.
I'd want to know which part of the climb needs the most patience.

contexts.subject: Wallace praises his mentor's elegant battle style.

SootopolisCity_Text_DazzledByMentor.text: WALLACE: I'm sure that you will be\ndazzled by my mentor's breathtakingly\lelegant battle style.$

replies.text: A glowing recommendation from someone who knows a dramatic entrance.
An experienced observer may notice a style's structure as well as its appearance.
Respect the opponent. Watch what the moves actually do.
I'm curious what makes the whole battle feel elegant to him.
A good performance still begins with a well-cared-for team.
A devoted student has given the next character an exceptionally flattering introduction.
The review is dazzling enough before the battle even starts.
I'd examine how the decisions fit together beneath the visual effect.
A practiced skill can become a kind of clear movement.
Elegance is lovely when it has real function underneath it.
I'd watch for the small choice that makes the style feel unmistakably theirs.

contexts.subject: Maxie pleads with Groudon after realizing the threatened scale of destruction.

SootopolisCity_Text_GroudonPleaseStop.text: MAXIE: G… GROUDON…\nPlease! Stop what you're doing!\pI know the extent of your power now!\pIf you keep going, all HOENN, not just\nSOOTOPOLIS, will be utterly ruined!$

replies.text: He finally sees the lives inside the plan he wanted.
Recognition of the risk is necessary, though it doesn't itself restore control.
Stop insisting it should obey. Look for real help.
He sounds frightened by what he thought he understood.
The people of Hoenn shouldn't have had to become the lesson.
The grand ambition has encountered the consequences omitted from its own script.
A sobering moment, with an entire region beyond his voice.
We need an effective response, not only a repeated command.
A power admired from afar can become a very different thing when it moves.
His fear matters, but so do the people who never agreed to this.
I'd remember the moment his language changed from wanting more to begging it to stop.

contexts.subject: Maxie bitterly contrasts his elaborate plans with one Pokemon's simple resolution.

SootopolisCity_Text_AfterAllOurScheming.text:
MAXIE: So the super-ancient POKéMON
weren't only GROUDON and KYOGRE…\pAfter all our fruitless scheming and
frantic efforts, that one POKéMON's\lsimple action puts everything right\lagain as if nothing had happened…\pFu…
Fuhahaha…$

replies.text: The simple ending doesn't make the harm before it imaginary.
His comparison exposes how little their elaborate effort actually controlled.
Learn from it. Don't turn relief into another excuse.
That laugh sounds more unsettled than happy.
The people who lived through it need care beyond his realization.
A complicated plot has been resolved outside the ambitions that created it.
A very unkind joke played on his theory, not on the people endangered by it.
He should examine the assumptions rather than only admire the contrast in effort.
A quiet result can leave a loud responsibility behind.
The ending looks simple because someone else did what their plans couldn't.
I'd listen for whether the realization changes what he chooses afterward.

contexts.subject: Archie cannot get Kyogre to respond to the Red Orb.

SootopolisCity_Text_KyogreCalmDown.text:
ARCHIE: KYOGRE! What's wrong?!
Look over here! It's the RED ORB!\lCalm down! KYOGRE!\p… … … … … …
… … … … … …\pIt's no good!
It's not responding at all!$

replies.text: The object is in his hand, but the control never was.
The failed response contradicts the assumption driving his plan.
Stop relying on what isn't working. Find another way to help.
He sounds shocked that the familiar command has no meaning here.
Everyone around him needs more than another desperate attempt.
The central prop has failed to guarantee the promised ending.
A very clear limit on the power he thought possession gave him.
Use the observed failure to revise the model, not repeat it louder.
A life cannot always be reached through the thing we think should speak for it.
His certainty has fallen away. Practical responsibility still remains.
I'd remember how long he looked at the Orb before admitting the Pokemon wasn't responding.

contexts.subject: Archie reflects that their grand plans may have meant little to the ancient Pokemon.

SootopolisCity_Text_TryingMeaninglessToP.text:
ARCHIE: KYOGRE and GROUDON both
flew off to who knows where.\pThe weather in HOENN has returned
to its normal state…\pHaha…
Hahaha…\pMaybe what we were trying to do was
something small, even meaningless,\lto POKéMON…$

replies.text: Their plans may have been small to the Pokemon. The danger wasn't small to people.
A difference in scale doesn't reduce the consequences of the choices made.
Then respect the limits. Start making things right.
It must feel strange having the whole purpose collapse into that thought.
The people affected still need care even if the ambition feels foolish now.
A grand narrator has discovered he was not directing the central characters.
A humbling thought that shouldn't become a way to dismiss the harm.
He can learn from the mismatch between intention, power, and outcome.
A small ambition can still cast a very large shadow.
The insight matters if it changes his next ordinary choice.
I'd want to hear what he is willing to do differently once the laughter stops.

contexts.subject: The Maniac identifies the mysterious Salon Maiden as the Tower leader.

BattleFrontier_Lounge2_Text_SalonMaidenI.text: Bet you didn't know this!\pOne of those top TRAINERS that SCOTT\ncalls the FRONTIER BRAINS is there.\pIt's this mysterious TRAINER called\nthe SALON MAIDEN that runs the place.$

replies.text: A mysterious trainer at the top of a very obvious tower. Interesting balance.
We have a title and a responsibility. Her battle methods remain unspecified.
She's responsible for the Tower. Worth remembering.
I wonder whether she enjoys being called mysterious or just doesn't talk much.
I'd rather meet her than build an opinion from the title alone.
A grand title, a tall building, and remarkably little personal information. A tidy introduction.
The mystery has been labeled. Apparently that counts as reducing it.
I'd like to know how she shaped the Tower's challenges.
A name can make a distant figure feel nearer without revealing much at all.
Mysterious might mean private. I'd give her room to introduce herself.
I'd ask someone who's actually met her what the conversation was like.

contexts.subject: The Maniac reports the Salon Maiden testing roster of Psychic, Fire, and Normal partners.

BattleFrontier_Lounge2_Text_SalonMaidenS.text: Have you battled the SALON MAIDEN?\pWhen she's measuring up her opponent,\nshe apparently uses these POKéMON:\pA PSYCHIC-type PSI POKéMON,\na FIRE-type VOLCANO POKéMON,\land a NORMAL-type SLEEPING POKéMON.$

replies.text: A thinking one, a blazing one, and a sleeping one. That last job sounds suspiciously attractive.
The reported Psychic, Fire, and Normal coverage gives us several distinct matchups to consider.
Don't underestimate the sleeping partner. Plan for all three.
I wonder how the quiet-looking one fits with the other two.
A calm appearance can hide plenty of strength. I'd prepare before deciding who's easiest.
An impressive spread of talents, including the highly refined art of looking asleep.
The sleeper has made the intimidating roster. A professional inspiration.
We can compare our coverage against the reported types before entering.
Stillness stands beside fire and thought. I wouldn't mistake it for absence.
It's useful information, though I wouldn't let the labels replace watching the actual partners.
I'd ask which of the three surprised his source most.

contexts.subject: The Maniac describes the Salon Maiden serious Dragon-Psychic, Electric, and Normal roster.

BattleFrontier_Lounge2_Text_SalonMaidenG.text:
Have you battled the SALON MAIDEN
when she's serious?\pWhen she's battling flat out,
she apparently uses these POKéMON:\pA DRAGON & PSYCHIC EON POKéMON,
an ELECTRIC-type THUNDER POKéMON,\land a NORMAL-type SLEEPING POKéMON.$

replies.text: She's changed the first two and kept the sleeper. Apparently naps survive every promotion.
That reported roster changes the coverage substantially. The Normal partner remains a constant.
Different threats now. Recheck the plan instead of replaying the old one.
The familiar partner might be the one I'd be most careful not to overlook.
A repeated partner probably has a good reason to stay. I'd respect that.
The serious roster has arrived, and the sleeping specialist has retained its position.
Lightning, dragons, and a nap. A surprisingly coherent threat.
We need answers to the new type combinations, not merely stronger versions of the old approach.
