A repeated headline can become familiar without becoming any less ugly.
The city deserves ordinary days that nobody needs to report.
Worth taking care as we approach rather than treating it as a distant story.
Newsprint carries an event lightly compared with the people who lived it.
Concern is a better response than treating the trouble as local colour.
I wonder which details never make it into the short newspaper account.

contexts.subject: A Lance admirer is frustrated that the fan club does not share their enthusiasm.

SaffronCity_Text_HowCanClubNotRecognizeL.text:
This FAN CLUB…
No one here has a clue!\pHow could they not recognize
the brilliance that is LANCE?\pHe stands for justice!
He's cool, and yet passionate!\lHe's the greatest, LANCE!$

replies.text: This fan has brought enough enthusiasm for the whole club and is annoyed about doing all the carrying.
Admiration is personal. The other members are not obliged to rank the same traits highest.
They can like Lance without starting an argument about everyone else's choice.
It can feel lonely when nobody shares an interest that means a lot to you.
Enthusiasm is easier to share when it is not served as a correction.
The passionate critic has declared the rest of the audience unqualified to appreciate the star.
A fan club can contain the astonishing complication of more than one favourite.
Explaining what they admire may work better than insisting the others lack judgment.
A bright devotion need not put out the lamps beside it.
The affection for Lance is charming; the contempt for the club rather less so.
I wonder what Lance did that made this fan feel so strongly about him.

contexts.subject: The Dojo master reminds the player not to take a second prize Pokemon.

replies.text: One generous offer does not turn the rest of the room into a take-home display.
The original offer covered one choice. The remaining Pokemon was not included.
We made our choice. Respect the limit.
A gift should not make someone feel they must give everything else, too.
Accepting something kindly includes knowing when to stop asking.
The awards ceremony has ended before the winner can annex the remaining cast.
Gratitude looks better when it leaves something on the table.
A clear limit keeps the original agreement from expanding after the fact.
An open hand need not empty itself to prove it was generous.
He should not have to defend the other gift after making the first.
I wonder how often a generous offer gets mistaken for an unlimited one.

contexts.subject: The Ruin Valley researcher claims discovery of the site.

SixIsland_RuinValley_Text_IFoundThisPlac.text: Let me tell you, I found this\nplace.\pDon't look so envious, will you?$

replies.text: He found the place. I suspect the stones had already noticed they were here.
Locating a site and establishing its history are different kinds of knowledge.
His discovery does not make the place his property.
I understand being excited to find something before you have the words to explain it.
A discovery deserves care before it deserves a victory speech.
The explorer has announced his claim to the opening credit.
An old place has become new to one person and immediately acquired an ownership problem.
Record the find carefully before letting excitement outrun the evidence.
The first person to name a threshold is rarely the first life to cross it.
Pride in noticing something is better than pretending it began with you.
I wonder what first caught his eye about this particular site.

contexts.subject: A trainer asks Slowbro to pay attention after it fails to follow a command.

replies.text: The instruction arrived, but Slowbro appears to have left its attention somewhere else.
A failed response can have several causes. Repeating the demand alone may not resolve it.
Try a calmer approach before raising the voice.
I wonder whether the trainer is noticing what Slowbro actually responds to.
A little patience might do more than another sharp instruction.
The intended scene has stalled because one performer is considering a different production.
Attention is an awkward thing to command by sounding increasingly annoyed.
Check whether the instruction is understood rather than simply increasing the volume.
Two lives are standing close while their thoughts remain rather far apart.
Frustration is understandable, but it is not an explanation Slowbro can follow.
I would watch what happens before the missed cue as carefully as what happens after.

contexts.subject: A trainer sharply blames Slowbro after another failed instruction.

replies.text: That sentence has a lot of blame and not much help packed inside it.
Naming failure does not identify its cause or show the Pokemon how to respond differently.
Blaming Slowbro again will not make the instruction clearer.
It is hard to learn when every mistake arrives with that voice attached.
A calmer reset would be more useful than serving the disappointment back at it.
The director has announced the failed take without offering any direction.
Again is a heavy little word to keep dropping on someone.
Change the approach and observe the result before repeating the same criticism.
A repeated sharp word can become the only thing a companion learns to expect.
It would look better to ask what went wrong than announce whose fault it was.
I wonder whether the trainer has ever tried a cue that matters to Slowbro.

contexts.subject: The toothless Warden gives an excited but unintelligible response after the player agrees.

FuchsiaCity_WardensHouse_Text_AhHowheeHo.text: Ah howhee ho hoo!\nEef ee hafahi ho!$

replies.text: I caught the enthusiasm. The actual words have escaped through a different door.
His articulation makes the response difficult to interpret. We should not pretend to have a translation.
Let him finish. Not understanding is no reason to laugh at him.
He sounds eager to be understood. That makes the missing words feel more frustrating.
A bit of patience is more useful than nodding confidently at something we did not catch.
The emotion is legible, even if the dialogue is temporarily unavailable.
There is a person trying quite hard behind the incomprehensible syllables.
Gestures or a written note might help where spoken words are not getting through.
A voice can carry intent even when the shape of the message is missing.
We can be honest about not understanding without making him feel foolish.
I would look at his expression before deciding what that answer means.

contexts.subject: The toothless Warden responds in frustration after the player declines.

FuchsiaCity_WardensHouse_Text_HeOhayHeHa.text: Ha?\nHe ohay heh ha hoo ee haheh!$

replies.text: We are having the sort of conversation where everybody has words and nobody has the same words.
The response remains unintelligible. Inferring detailed instructions would be unwarranted.
He is struggling to explain. Give him a moment.
It must feel awful to know exactly what you mean and have nobody else catch it.
Maybe a gesture or something to write with would make the exchange easier.
The communication problem has survived the attempted answer quite intact.
A misunderstanding is much less funny from inside the person it keeps happening to.
We need another way to exchange information rather than more guesses.
The message keeps reaching the edge of the mouth and losing its shape.
An awkward conversation still deserves decent manners from everyone in it.
I wonder what simple detail would let us stop guessing at what he needs.

contexts.subject: Oak's aide invites the player to return once the research requirement is met.

Aide_Text_GetEnoughMonsComeBackForItem.text: …Oh. I see.\pWhen you get {STR_VAR_1} kinds of POKéMON,\ncome back for the {STR_VAR_2}.$

replies.text: An errand with a research condition. We know what to work toward before returning.
The reward is conditional on a measured collection milestone, not merely accepting the offer.
We can come back when the requirement is met.
A clear goal makes the next visit feel less uncertain.
We can fit the research into the journey instead of rushing it for a prize.
The professor's assistant has supplied a future appointment with a measurable entrance condition.
An unfinished task has been given a rather practical bookmark.
We can compare the required milestone with the actual record before returning.
The next step is out on the road rather than in this conversation.
A straightforward explanation keeps a delayed reward from feeling arbitrary.
I wonder how many travellers have made this promise and arrived back proudly later.

contexts.subject: Oak's aide checks the Pokedex and finds the reward requirement is not yet met.

Aide_Text_HaventCaughtEnoughMonsForItem.text: Let's see…\nUh-oh! You have caught only\l{STR_VAR_3} kinds of POKéMON!\pYou need {STR_VAR_1} kinds\nif you want the {STR_VAR_2}.$

replies.text: The notebook has been inspected and asked to grow a little more before payday.
The measured record remains below the stated threshold. The check has not awarded the item.
Not enough yet. We can keep exploring and return later.
It is a little disappointing, but at least the goal is something we can understand.
No need to turn the next few encounters into a frantic shopping list.
The progress report has found the right direction and an unfinished distance.
Not yet is a smaller word than never, even if it is inconvenient today.
We know the remaining gap exists without needing to guess at the hidden criteria.
An empty place in the record can still be an invitation rather than a reproach.
The aide can be precise without making the shortfall a judgment of us.
I wonder which next discovery will make the return visit feel different.

contexts.subject: Oak's aide cannot give the promised reward because the Bag has no room.

Aide_Text_DontHaveAnyRoomForItem.text: Oh! I see you don't have any\nroom for the {STR_VAR_2}.$

replies.text: We have managed the research and been defeated by the luggage.
The reward condition is distinct from the capacity condition; the handover has not completed.
Make room before asking for the item again.
An awkward delay after the harder part was already done.
A little sorting can make the next visit much less frustrating.
The accomplished researcher has encountered a stern review of their packing.
Even a deserved prize needs somewhere physical to go.
Capacity is a separate practical constraint. We can resolve it directly.
A full bag can close a very small door at an inconvenient moment.
Better to notice now than pretend the reward somehow fitted.
I wonder what has been sitting untouched at the bottom of that Bag.

contexts.subject: The prize clerk requires a Coin Case before an exchange can begin.

replies.text: The prize counter has a prerequisite before it has a conversation about prizes.
A Coin Case is the specified access requirement for the exchange service.
We need the case first. No exchange happened.
At least the missing requirement is clear.
We can sort the practical part before getting attached to a particular prize.
The glittering display has been interrupted by a very ordinary equipment check.
An exciting reward can still come with distinctly unexciting preliminaries.
We should gather the required equipment before planning the exchange.
The counter has drawn its first small boundary around an absent object.
A direct explanation is easier to work with than a vague refusal.
I wonder how often the clerk has to stop an enthusiastic visitor at that first step.

contexts.subject: The restaurant patron asks for Bag space before handing over his Coin Case.

replies.text: A man trying to part with something has discovered our Bag is not cooperating.
His offer cannot complete until the item has space in the Bag.
Clear some room, then return. He has not given it yet.
I hope the delay does not make the conversation feel more awkward for him.
A practical bit of sorting will let the offer proceed without fuss.
The proposed transfer of a small regrettable legacy has stalled at the luggage.
A fresh beginning has been briefly obstructed by an overfull pocket.
The capacity problem is ours to fix before the handover can happen.
He is ready to let something go; we need to be ready to carry it.
We can make room without making him repeat the whole story.
I wonder whether handing it over will feel like relief when the practical part is done.

contexts.subject: The defeated Rocket cannot leave until there is space to return the stolen TM.

CeruleanCity_Text_MakeRoomForThisCantRun.text: Make room for this!\nI can't run until I give it to you!$

replies.text: He has found the one escape route that leads directly through our untidy Bag.
The attempted restitution has not completed because the item cannot fit.
Make room. He still needs to return what he stole.
His impatience does not make the missing item any less important.
We can sort the Bag without pretending he has already put things right.
The fleeing criminal has been detained by a remarkably domestic obstacle.
A man in a hurry has become dependent on somebody else's packing habits.
A free slot resolves the handover problem. His desire to leave is secondary.
A stolen thing waits at the narrow mouth of an overfull bag.
His predicament would be easier to sympathize with if he had not stolen the TM.
I wonder how much longer he imagined this encounter lasting before he met the capacity problem.

contexts.subject: The Magikarp seller cannot complete the sale because the party has no room.

Route4_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_NoRoomForMo.text: There's no more room for any more\nPOKéMON, it looks like.$

replies.text: Even the enthusiastic salesman has run out of room to keep the pitch moving.
The transaction has encountered the party-capacity requirement before completion.
No room, no sale. We can decide later whether to return.
A pause gives us time to think beyond the salesman's urgency.
We should choose responsibly rather than rearrange the team just to keep the pitch going.
The commercial momentum has been stopped by an unexpectedly full cast list.
A small administrative interruption can rescue a decision from a very fast talker.
The capacity check does not tell us whether the purchase is worth making.
An unopened place in the journey remains unopened for now.
We do not have to solve the seller's problem simply because he wants a sale.
I wonder how differently the offer will feel after we step away for a moment.

contexts.subject: The Magikarp seller refuses the sale because the player lacks the asking price.

Route4_PokemonCenter_1F_Text_YoullNeedMo.text: You'll need more money than that!$

replies.text: The special favour has a very firm minimum price attached to it.
The stated payment condition is unmet, so the sale has not completed.
We cannot afford it now. No reason to rush into finding the money.
It might be useful to think about whether we wanted the purchase or just felt pushed.
Keeping money for travelling needs is a fair reason to walk away.
The generous-sounding pitch has returned abruptly to its central concern.
A salesman has discovered the limits of persuading an empty pocket.
We should assess the value of the offer before treating the shortfall as a problem to solve.
An empty purse has said no more firmly than the conversation did.
A price is clearer than all the talk about doing us a favour.
I wonder how often the prospect sounds less urgent once the traveller has left the counter.

contexts.subject: The harbour sailor explains that the ship has already sailed.

replies.text: The harbour has reached the part of the story where the ship is elsewhere.
The response confirms departure rather than offering a current boarding option.
It has gone. We can make another plan.
An empty berth can feel oddly final when you came expecting a ship.
We can check the other travel options before spending the day waiting here.
The setting has retained the dock and removed the principal attraction.
Ships are inconsiderately committed to leaving once they have set sail.
We need current transport information rather than relying on the earlier schedule.
The water has closed the space where a departure used to be.
A clear answer is kinder than letting visitors keep hoping at the gate.
I wonder what the harbour feels like on the morning the ship arrives again.

contexts.subject: A harbour sailor welcomes the player to the S.S. Anne.

replies.text: A proper shipboard welcome. I feel slightly more nautical already.
A clear welcome helps a visitor know they have reached the correct entrance.
Friendly start. We can take our time looking around.
It is nice when someone makes a large unfamiliar place feel easy to enter.
A warm greeting does a lot before the visit has even begun.
The voyage's grand venue has appointed a pleasantly direct welcoming voice.
A little courtesy makes a threshold much less imposing.
Knowing where to begin saves wandering around the dock uncertainly.
A welcome can make a large hull feel briefly like a familiar doorway.
Simple hospitality suits a busy entrance rather well.
I wonder how many different journeys arrive at this same greeting.

contexts.subject: A local asks whether the player has noticed the S.S. Anne in the harbour.

VermilionCity_Text_DidYouSeeSSAnneInHarb.text: Did you see the S.S. ANNE moored\nin the harbor?$

replies.text: A ship large enough to become the neighbourhood's favourite opening question.
A prominent visitor can become a shared point of interest throughout a port.
Hard to blame the interest. It is quite a sight.
I like hearing people sound pleased about something arriving in their own town.
A busy harbour must have a different sort of energy while the ship is here.
The town has acquired an impressive guest and an immediate conversation starter.
A familiar place can still be surprised by what comes to rest beside it.
A large ship brings plenty of interesting movement into an ordinary dockside day.
The horizon has delivered something the whole town can point toward.
Shared excitement makes an ordinary local question rather charming.
I wonder which part of its arrival the people here look forward to most.

contexts.subject: A former trading partner asks whether the Pokemon they traded away has grown stronger.

Trade_Text_HasTradedMonGrownStronger.text: The {STR_VAR_2} that I traded you,\nhas it grown stronger?$

replies.text: The trade did not make them stop wondering how their old companion is doing.
A follow-up question shows continuing interest beyond the completed exchange.
They still care about the Pokemon. Good to hear.
It feels kind to remember the life that left with somebody else.
A handover does not have to end all interest in what happens afterward.
The former supporting character has requested news of an old cast member.
An exchange can finish while a small thread of concern remains.
We could describe actual progress without inventing improvements to be polite.
A familiar life has travelled away, but not entirely out of mind.
I like that the question is about the Pokemon rather than whether the deal was clever.
I wonder what little detail they would be happiest to hear about.

contexts.subject: A prospective trading partner accepts that the player does not want the exchange.

Trade_Text_WellIfYouDontWantTo.text: Well, if you don't want to…$

replies.text: The trade has stayed an offer instead of becoming an argument. Good.
A fair exchange requires willing agreement from both trainers. That condition was not met.
We can decline. No Pokemon needs to change hands.
A little disappointment is all right if the choice is still respected.
Better to keep the team we want than accept something to avoid an awkward moment.
The proposed cast exchange has been cancelled without requiring a second act.
An unwelcome deal is allowed to remain an unfinished sentence.
We can consider future trades separately from this decision.
Two roads may meet without exchanging the lives that travel them.
An accepted refusal is the most important courtesy in a negotiation.
I wonder how long they have been looking for a suitable willing partner.

contexts.subject: A trading partner thanks the player after a completed Pokemon exchange.

replies.text: A new chapter on both sides of a very small handshake.
The gratitude closes the exchange after the trade sequence has completed.
Deal settled. Time to get to know the new companion properly.
A simple thank-you makes the handover feel a little warmer.
The real part begins with caring for the Pokemon after the excitement of trading.
The exchange has concluded with a short and entirely satisfactory curtain call.
Two little journeys have changed direction with surprisingly few words.
Now we can learn how the new team member fits our actual plans.
A familiar path has been offered a new pair of footsteps.
A pleasant ending to the arrangement is a good beginning for what follows.
I wonder what each trainer will notice first about the companion arriving with them.

contexts.subject: A trading partner explains that the selected Pokemon is not the species requested and leaves the offer open.

Trade_Text_ThisIsntMon.text: Hmmm?\nThis isn't a {STR_VAR_1}.\pThink of me if you get one.$

Trade_Text_ThisIsNoMon.text: …This is no {STR_VAR_1}.\pIf you get one, trade it with me.$

replies.text: The introduction was a little off target. No exchange has happened.
The selected Pokemon does not match the stated species requirement.
Wrong match for this offer. We can leave it there.
It is good to have the mismatch explained without anyone treating the Pokemon as a mistake.
A specific request can remain unmet without anyone needing to feel insulted.
The casting call has received an enthusiastic but unsuitable audition.
The offer was narrow; the world of perfectly good Pokemon is much wider.
We should check the actual requested species before trying the selection again.
A closed exchange is not a closed future for the companion beside us.
There is no need to make a practical mismatch sound like a personal failure.
I wonder what makes that particular species so important to the person asking.

contexts.subject: A trader abruptly points out that the offered Pokemon is not the requested species.

replies.text: A mismatch has apparently startled the whole sales pitch out of them.
The species requirement is unmet. The surprised tone adds no further information.
Wrong selection. We can correct it without making a fuss.
I would rather the Pokemon not have to listen to that much disappointment about itself.
A clear request does not need a sharp response when somebody misses it.
The audition has gone off-script and the director has chosen volume over tact.
A small error has acquired an unnecessarily dramatic reception.
We can check the requirement again rather than reacting to the tone.
A thing can be wrong for a bargain and still entirely right in itself.
A little courtesy would make the correction easier to receive.
I wonder whether they hear how abrupt that sounds from the other side.

contexts.subject: A trader proudly asks whether their former Pokemon is impressive.

replies.text: That sounds like fondness trying to wear the disguise of a confident review.
They still take pride in the Pokemon even after the exchange.
A good sign that the former trainer remembers it warmly.
I like hearing someone sound pleased about a companion who went to another home.
A little praise can keep the handover from feeling purely transactional.
The former agent remains an enthusiastic publicist for the departed star.
Affection has survived the practical arrangement and returned as a boast.
Knowing what the previous trainer valued might help us notice useful traits.
Something once cared for is still shining in the memory that kept it.
It is charming when the pride feels generous rather than possessive.
I wonder which familiar habit they are picturing while they ask.

contexts.subject: A trader asks about their former Pokemon and says the received Pokemon is doing well.

Trade_Text_HowIsMyOldMon.text: How is my old {STR_VAR_2}?\nMy {STR_VAR_1} is doing great!$

replies.text: A little news exchanged after the Pokemon. The conversation has a life beyond the deal.
The update concerns both sides of the trade, which is a useful and considerate follow-up.
Good to hear the other Pokemon is settling in.
It is lovely to know the care continued after we stopped watching.
A reassuring update can make a trade feel like two good beginnings.
The exchanged cast members have prompted a brief reunion of their former managers.
An arrangement feels warmer when nobody forgets to ask how the lives involved are going.
A real report tells us more than simply assuming the exchange worked out.
Two paths can stay lightly connected by news of those travelling them.
The question makes room for care on both sides instead of only satisfaction with the bargain.
I wonder what story we would each choose first if there were time for a proper conversation.

contexts.subject: Wind drives blue fluid into an artificial whirlpool in a glass vessel.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Whir.text: A blue fluid is spiraling inside\na glass vessel.\p“This is an experiment to create a\nWHIRLPOOL artificially using wind.”$

replies.text: A little whirlpool with no boats to trouble. A surprisingly well-behaved version.
The contained model makes the effect of wind easier to observe. Elegant demonstration.
Good place to learn what the motion looks like. Better than from inside it.
I could watch that turn for a while. It's calmer with glass between us.
A large danger made small enough to understand over a quiet afternoon.
The sea's dramatic habits have been persuaded to perform in a jar.
A contained spiral. My preferred arrangement for things that pull you under.
I'd like to see how changing the airflow changes the shape.
The little current keeps circling a place it never quite reaches.
The blue makes the motion easy to follow. A good display choice.
I'd watch where the spiral starts and compare it with the air above it.

contexts.subject: A bobbing red ball demonstrates buoyancy in a waterfall model.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Wate.text: A red ball is bobbing up and down\ninside a glass vessel.\p“This is an experiment simulating a\nWATERFALL using the ball's buoyancy.”$

replies.text: That ball has a very busy afternoon and absolutely no progress to show for it.
Buoyancy provides a visible way to follow the flow. The red contrast helps.
A useful model. We can watch without getting swept anywhere.
It keeps coming back up. There's something quietly pleasing about that.
That little red ball is working harder than most of the visitors.
A hardworking performer, committed to the same entrance several hundred times.
An endless cycle, attractively presented and mercifully happening to a ball.
The tracer makes the forces visible. I'd like to examine the circulation.
Down and up again, with the water deciding the route.
They chose the red well. Nothing else competes for the eye.
I'd follow one full cycle rather than just catch the movement at a glance.

contexts.subject: Layered ocean sediment preserves remains that reveal the ancient past.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Ocea.text:
It's a sample of soil from the ocean
floor.\p“Over many years, the remains of
life-forms settle at the bottom of\lthe sea, making sedimentary layers.\p“By analyzing these layers, the
ancient past is revealed.”$

replies.text: A handful of seabed turns out to be an extremely untidy old diary.
Successive layers preserve different periods. Their order is part of the evidence.
Easy to overlook dirt. Harder once you know what it remembers.
I like the thought of a quiet layer keeping something small from being forgotten.
Something that looks ordinary can hold a very long story.
The past has filed its records under the sea, an inconvenient but effective archive.
History, compressed beneath water and considerable patience.
I'd want to see how they collect a sample without mixing the layers.
Small lives settle into the same dark, and time makes room above them.
The plain sample becomes more interesting after the label gives us a way to look.
I'd ask what this particular layer revealed, not just what samples can reveal generally.

contexts.subject: The sand display traces beach grains back to mountain rocks carried by rivers.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Beac.text: It's a sample of beach sand.\p“Stones from mountains are washed\ndown by rivers where they are\lchipped and ground down.\p“They are reduced to grains and end\nup as sand on beaches.”$

replies.text: The beach is full of extremely well-traveled bits of mountain. I owe it more respect.
Transport and abrasion connect the mountain material to these much smaller grains.
Long journey for something we usually shake out of a shoe.
I hadn't thought of sand as something that came all that way.
The river does a lot of preparation before the beach ever sees the result.
A mountain has spent years arriving at the shore in very small installments.
Even the sand has gone on a longer trip than it admits.
I'd compare the grain shapes with samples farther upstream.
A hard thing becomes small enough for the water to carry gently.
Texture has a history. That makes even plain sand feel less interchangeable.
I'd like to see the whole route, from the rocks to the beach, through a few careful samples.

contexts.subject: A museum panel explains the blue appearance of seawater through light passing through it.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Ocea.text:
“OCEANIC MINIFACT 1
Why is seawater blue?\p“Light is composed of many colors.\p“When light passes through water,
most kinds of light lose color.\p“However, blue light retains its
color, making the sea appear blue.”$

replies.text: The sea borrowed a whole lesson about light just to choose an outfit. Thorough.
The explanation concerns how light behaves in water. Color carries information about the medium.
Useful reminder that what we see depends on what the light passed through.
I like knowing a little more without having to stop finding it beautiful.
A familiar blue has a lot going on beneath it. Nice reason to look again.
The ocean's famous color has submitted an explanation instead of simply accepting compliments.
A beautiful effect with a perfectly serious mechanism underneath. Relatable.
I'd enjoy a display that lets us compare light through different depths of water.
A color can belong partly to the distance it traveled.
Knowing how the blue happens doesn't make me want to use it any less.
I'd watch how the water's color changes near shore after reading that.

contexts.subject: The panel describes dissolved salts carried from rocks into the sea.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Ocea.text:
“OCEANIC MINIFACT 2
Why is the sea salty?\p“Seawater contains dissolved salt in
the form of sodium and chlorine ions.\p“These ions leech out of rocks
and are carried out to sea by rain.\p“The concentration of dissolved salt
makes the sea salty.”$

replies.text: So the sea has been collecting tiny rock ingredients this whole time. No wonder it tastes ambitious.
The panel connects dissolved ions with material transported from land. A useful large-scale link.
Water carries things we can't see. Worth remembering.
It's strange how something invisible can change the whole taste of a place.
A little salt goes a long way. The ocean has been taking that advice very generously.
The rocks have contributed to the sea's seasoning over an impressively long preparation time.
A planetary collection of dissolved leftovers. Surprisingly photogenic result.
I'd compare samples where rivers enter the sea with samples farther out.
The land leaves a trace even in water that seems to have gone beyond it.
An invisible ingredient changes an enormous impression. I like that detail.
I'd ask what varies between the samples upstairs. This gives us a good question to carry there.

contexts.subject: The panel says sea covers about seventy percent of the planet.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Ocea.text:
“OCEANIC MINIFACT 3
Which is bigger? The sea or land?\p“The sea covers about 70% of
the planet, and the rest is land.\p“The sea is therefore more than twice
the size of land.”$

replies.text: All that land we've walked on is the smaller part. My feet are taking the news personally.
The stated proportion makes the ocean the dominant surface environment. Perspective changes quickly.
Most of the world is water. Good reason to respect the people who know it.
That makes the horizon feel a little farther away than it did before.
A small patch of dry ground can feel enormous until somebody shows the whole picture.
The land has been rather successful at making itself feel like the main attraction.
A mostly aquatic planet with a remarkably opinionated dry minority.
I'd like to compare the ocean coverage with a globe rather than a flat panel.
We stand on the smaller part and name the larger part the edge.
It's an easy proportion to read and a difficult scale to really imagine.
I'd love to ask a sailor what that number feels like after days beyond sight of land.

contexts.subject: Fossilized ripples preserve marks left by ancient flowing seawater.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Foss.text:
It's a fossil with wavy ridges on it.\p“Soil on the ocean floor gets scoured
by the tide.\p“The flowing seawater marks the soil
with small ridges and valleys.\p“If this soil becomes fossilized, it is
called a ripple mark.”$

replies.text: The water left, but its little wrinkles stayed behind. That's very stubborn evidence.
The preserved structure records a process, even without preserving the water itself.
You can learn what moved here from the mark it left. Useful.
It looks almost soft until I remember it's stone.
A moment of movement has lasted far longer than anyone standing in this room.
The ancient current has provided a signed impression in lieu of attending the exhibition.
A wave that finally agreed to sit still. It took becoming rock.
I'd want to compare the ridges with patterns forming in a shallow tray of moving water.
A passing thing can leave a shape that refuses to pass.
The repeated ridges make such a quiet pattern. Knowing their age gives it weight.
I'd look along the ridges from a lower angle. Their shape deserves more than a quick glance.

contexts.subject: An unidentified rotating machine under glass may measure depth.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_1F_Text_Dept.text: A strange machine is rotating under\na glass dome.\pMaybe it's for measuring the depth\nof something…$

replies.text: It looks very busy. I wish its explanation had clocked in for the same shift.
Depth measurement is only a guess here. We'd need a label or mechanism to identify its purpose.
Don't touch it to find out. Ask someone who knows.
I like watching it turn, even though I don't understand what it's doing.
Someone keeps it running. I'd ask them what we're meant to notice.
An industrious mystery, earning its place beneath glass through sheer commitment to rotating.
The mechanism remains secret. The rotation is very forthcoming.
I'd love a diagram showing what connects to what. The motion alone doesn't explain the job.
A little machine works inside a clear shell, keeping its purpose to itself.
The display catches attention well. It seems to have misplaced the next step of communication.
I'd ask the staff what it's measuring before deciding what the movement means.

contexts.subject: Regional seawater samples show that connected seas can have different water characteristics.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_Wate.text: “WATER QUALITY SAMPLE 1,” the\nlabel says.\pThe sea is all connected, but the\nwater seems to differ by region.$

replies.text: One connected sea, several different little personalities in jars.
Connection doesn't imply immediate uniformity. Local conditions can preserve differences.
Same sea doesn't mean the same conditions everywhere.
I like that a small sample can make a huge place feel less like one blank blue.
Different shores leave different things in the water. The samples make that easier to notice.
The sea has declined to become identical merely because the map gives it a connected shape.
A collection of water, each sample refusing to be simply more water.
I'd want the collection sites and sampling dates beside them for a useful comparison.
Things can touch for a long time and still keep traces of where they came from.
The plain jars ask us to notice differences instead of relying on a dramatic display.
I'd ask what difference they measured first. The label has made me curious enough to want details.

contexts.subject: The second water sample asks whether seawater saltiness varies by region.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_Wate.text: “WATER QUALITY SAMPLE 2,” the\nlabel says.\pDoes the saltiness of seawater differ\nby region, too?$

replies.text: I would like the answer without arranging a museum-wide tasting session.
Salinity can be compared by measurement. Sampling conditions would help interpret the result.
Measure it. Don't drink the exhibit.
I wonder how different two samples can be while looking so similar.
My tongue has opinions about salt, but I think the museum has a better method here.
An intriguing comparison that does not, I trust, require us to lick the evidence.
The water looks innocent. The proposed tasting experiment should remain theoretical.
I'd like the measurements displayed together rather than have visitors guess from appearance.
A small invisible difference can tell you where a current has been.
It's a good question. I wish the answer were beside it instead of leaving us to imagine.
I'd ask the staff how they compare the samples. That sounds worth learning.

contexts.subject: A changing rubber ball illustrates increasing pressure in deep water.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_Pres.text:
A rubber ball is expanding and
shrinking.\p“In the sea, the weight of water itself
exerts pressure.\p“In shallow water, the pressure is not
very heavy.\p“However, in extremely deep water,
the pressure can reach even tens of\lthousands of tons on a small area.”$

replies.text: That poor ball is trying on several sizes of itself for our education.
The deformation makes otherwise invisible pressure changes observable. A clear model.
Deep water is heavy. Good reason to trust proper equipment.
Watching it shrink makes the depth feel more real than a large number does.
I'm glad a rubber ball gets to demonstrate this instead of a living partner.
A humble ball has accepted the difficult role of making an enormous force look understandable.
An exhibit about being under pressure. The ball is handling the publicity better than expected.
I'd like to see the pressure scale synchronized with the change in volume.
The weight of all that unseen water finds a shape our eyes can follow.
A simple shape changing tells the story quickly. That's thoughtful display design.
I'd watch the ball through a full cycle before looking back at the numbers.

contexts.subject: A miniature Hoenn diorama prompts the player to locate Littleroot.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_Hoen.text: “MODEL OF HOENN REGION”\pIt's a miniature diorama of the\nHOENN region.\pWhere is LITTLEROOT TOWN on this?$

replies.text: Littleroot must be a very small little Littleroot from up here. I'll look gently.
The model trades detail for regional context. Finding a familiar location anchors the scale.
Find home first. Then the rest of the route starts making sense.
A place can look tiny on a model and still hold most of someone's beginning.
I'd trace the trip from Littleroot slowly. We've covered more ground than it sometimes feels like.
The entire region has agreed to fit inside a room, with modest reductions to everyone's importance.
A whole journey made small enough to inspect without acquiring new blisters.
I'd compare the elevation and transport routes. A model makes those relationships much clearer.
A little place stays large in memory, even when the map barely has room for it.
Finding somewhere familiar gives the whole display a more personal shape.
I'd ask each of us to point out the place that feels biggest in our own memory.

contexts.subject: Deep currents are driven by differences including temperature and salinity.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_Deep.text: It's a display on the flow of seawater.\p“Near the bottom of the sea, water\nflows due to differences in such\lfactors as temperature and salinity.”$

replies.text: The sea keeps moving down where the wind can't reach to give it a nudge. Industrious.
Temperature and salinity affect water density, providing a mechanism distinct from surface wind.
Deep water has its own currents. Surface calm won't tell the whole story.
It's strange imagining all that movement under something that looks still from a boat.
A quiet surface doesn't mean the whole place has settled. Worth remembering at sea.
The depths have their own arrangements, apparently requiring no assistance from the weather overhead.
Even the bottom of the sea has somewhere it insists on going.
I'd love to see the layers shown with different colors so the circulation becomes visible.
Below the light, small differences can keep an enormous darkness moving.
The display changes how I picture the sea. There are several motions under one surface.
I'd ask how people measure something moving so far below them.

contexts.subject: The display explains wind-driven currents near the surface.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_Surf.text: It's a display on the flow of seawater.\p“Toward the surface, seawater flows\nas currents driven by the winds.”$

replies.text: The wind doesn't stop at ruffling our hair. Apparently it has much larger chores.
Wind transfers motion to surface water. The display connects two familiar observations.
Watch the wind and the water together. Both affect a crossing.
I like seeing a connection between two movements I usually notice separately.
A pleasant breeze on shore might mean a harder trip for somebody farther out.
The wind has been pushing the scenery around while pretending to be merely atmospheric.
The sea has received instructions from something nobody can see. Very cooperative.
I'd compare the current direction with the airflow instead of looking at the water alone.
A passing breath can set a much heavier thing in motion.
The invisible force becomes easier to imagine once the water gives it a visible effect.
I'd ask a sailor how they recognize those patterns without a museum diagram.

contexts.subject: A scale replica depicts the S.S. Tidal, described as under construction at Stern shipyard.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_SSTi.text: “THE FERRY S.S. TIDAL\p“A scale replica of the ship under\nconstruction at STERN'S SHIPYARD.”$

replies.text: A little ship previewing a very big trip. It must be impatient to grow into its own plans.
The model represents the proposed vessel. Its construction label may precede the actual service status.
Good way to see the ship's shape before standing beside the real hull.
I like imagining all the people who might eventually travel on it.
A ferry means a lot of ordinary reunions as well as grand journeys.
The ship has arrived at the museum ahead of its larger, considerably less portable counterpart.
A sea voyage reduced to a convenient shelf-sized commitment.
I'd love to compare this with the yard plans and see what changed during construction.
A route can exist first as something small enough to lift in two hands.
The model gives the ship a presence before passengers have their own memories of it.
I'd ask the builders which part was hardest to capture at this scale.

contexts.subject: A replica shows the Submarine Explorer 1 designed for ocean-floor exploration.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_Subm.text: “SUBMARINE EXPLORER 1\p“A replica of the high-performance\nocean floor exploration submarine.”$

replies.text: A little submarine for a very deep idea. I'm glad the glass case isn't the ocean-sized version.
The replica presents a vessel intended for seafloor work, not an actual pressure-tested exhibit.
Real exploration depends on more than the impressive shape. Good crews matter.
I wonder what it feels like to leave daylight behind inside something that small.
I'd want to know how the people inside stay comfortable and supplied during a long descent.
A journey to the ocean floor, thoughtfully offered in a form that doesn't require us to descend.
The miniature version has a much more forgiving pressure requirement.
I'd like to see a cutaway showing the hull, controls, and occupied space.
A small shell is built so people can enter a place their bodies cannot bear alone.
The shape looks purposeful. I'd be curious which features came from the conditions below.
I'd ask what the first explorers most wanted to see from its windows.

contexts.subject: A model depicts an unmanned compact pod for exploring the seafloor.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_Sumb.text: “SUBMERSIBLE POD\p“A replica of a compact, unmanned\npod for seafloor exploration.”$

replies.text: A tiny underwater scout. It gets the first look without needing a packed lunch.
An unmanned design allows observation without placing an occupant in the same environment.
Send a purpose-built pod where people can't safely go. Sensible.
I'd like to see what comes back through its eyes.
Someone can learn about the deep and still come home to supper without the descent.
A compact envoy sent to endure the uncomfortable portion of scientific curiosity.
An excellent volunteer for a job nobody asked a person to fit inside.
I'd love to know how it sends information back and how they recover it.
A small made thing carries human curiosity where human breath cannot follow.
Being compact changes the whole silhouette. Nothing is shaped around a passenger.
I'd ask what its first images showed. The moment of seeing something new must be wonderful.

contexts.subject: A replica depicts the globe-circling luxury liner S.S. Anne.

SlateportCity_OceanicMuseum_2F_Text_SSAn.text: “S.S. ANNE\p“A replica of the luxury liner that\ncircles the globe.”$

replies.text: A ship that circles the world sounds like a very elaborate way to return something borrowed.
Its stated purpose combines long-distance travel with passenger comfort. Different priorities from the research models.
Luxury or not, I'd still check the weather before boarding.
I wonder how many different goodbyes the real ship has heard.
I'd be curious about the galley. A long voyage asks a lot from whoever feeds everyone.
A floating promise that distance need not prevent people from insisting on excellent chairs.
A voyage around the world, provided the world doesn't disturb the upholstery.
I'd compare how much space is devoted to passengers versus operating the ship.
A circle around the world must gather a strange collection of small homesicknesses.
The luxury details make this one feel very different from the working vessels beside it.
I'd ask a passenger which port stayed in their mind long after the trip ended.

contexts.subject: A painting shows an odd landscape with fantastic scenery.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_1F_Text_OddL.text: It's an odd landscape with bizarre\nand fantastic scenery.$

replies.text: I can't tell which way I'd walk through it. That may be the landscape winning.
The unusual forms make familiar spatial expectations unreliable. Interesting effect.
Looks strange. I'd need a better route before walking into a place like that.
I like that it feels like somewhere I haven't learned how to describe yet.
I'd want a familiar little place to sit inside all that strangeness.
A landscape that has declined most of geography's more restrictive suggestions.
An excellent place to get lost without leaving the room.
I'd like to see the first sketches. Those shapes must have developed in an interesting order.
It looks like a place remembered by something that dreams differently from us.
The unfamiliar shapes still feel deliberate. That's what keeps me looking.
I'd ask everyone which part they noticed first. I suspect we'd point in different directions.

contexts.subject: A realistic Berry painting looks delicious enough to provoke hunger.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_1F_Text_Pain.text: It's a delicious-looking painting\nof BERRIES.\pThis painting could make you hungry!$

replies.text: The artist has painted a very convincing argument for lunch.
The visual detail evokes a familiar taste expectation. An effective still life.
Good painting. Still need actual food if we're hungry.
I like how a quiet picture can make the room feel warmer.
That's dangerously good. I want to know which Berries they arranged and whether anyone ate them afterward.
A still life has successfully created a highly active appetite.
A painting that refuses to feed the hunger it caused. Art can be cruel.
I'd like to compare the colors they used for the shine with the actual Berry skins.
A painted harvest can offer the memory of sweetness, if not the sweetness itself.
The arrangement makes the shapes feel generous. It's difficult not to want one.
I'd look closer at the surface, then find something real to eat before visiting the next room.

contexts.subject: An old painting shows patches of peeling paint.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_1F_Text_Very.text: It's a very old painting.\nThe paint is peeling here and there.$

replies.text: It's coming apart in tiny places. I hope somebody here knows how to help it hold together.
The deteriorating paint warrants conservation. Age and physical condition aren't the same as artistic value.
Don't touch the loose parts. Let someone trained handle it.
I keep wondering what the missing little patches used to show.
It has lasted a long time. I'd like it to have the care it needs for a little longer.
The painting has survived history and is now losing a quiet argument with its own surface.
Time has developed an alarming interest in the edges.
I'd ask what conservation method suits the materials before attempting any repair.
A picture can fade unevenly, leaving some parts to remember the others.
The damage changes how we see it. I'd still want to know what the artist meant before it happened.
I'd ask whether an older photograph records the parts that are beginning to peel.

contexts.subject: A portrait shows a smiling woman with a Pokemon resting on her lap.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_1F_Text_Pain.text: It's a painting of a beautiful, smiling\nwoman with a POKéMON on her lap.$

replies.text: That lap looks thoroughly claimed. A very small throne with an unusually comfortable ruler.
The shared posture makes the relationship central to the portrait.
They look comfortable together. That tells a story by itself.
Her smile seems quieter because the Pokemon is right there with her.
I like pictures of ordinary contentment. Nobody has to be doing something impressive.
A formal portrait quietly taken over by the person occupying the best seat.
The companion appears to have negotiated excellent living conditions.
I'd look at how the artist positioned their hands and the Pokemon to show trust.
A small weight can make a person look more settled in the world.
The relationship makes the portrait warmer than a smile aimed only at the viewer.
I'd ask whether the artist knew them. The moment feels comfortably observed.

contexts.subject: A replica preserves the form of a famous ancient bird Pokemon sculpture.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_Text_BirdPok.text: It's a replica of a famous sculpture.\pIt depicts an ancient BIRD POKéMON.$

replies.text: A copy of a very old bird. Its migration route has apparently included several workshops.
The replica lets people examine the form without requiring the original object to travel.
A copy can still show good work. No need to pretend it's the original.
I wonder which detail made the first sculpture famous.
I'm glad more people can see it without risking the older piece on every journey.
The ancient bird has sent a competent representative rather than attend personally.
A replica with excellent credentials and much less historical anxiety.
I'd like to know which materials and methods were used to reproduce the surface.
A shape can travel farther than the stone that first held it.
I'd compare it with an image of the original. Small differences can change the whole feeling.
I'd ask where the original stands and what people see around it there.

contexts.subject: A painting depicts Grass Pokemon enjoying a gentle breeze.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_1F_Text_Pain.text: It's a painting of GRASS POKéMON\nswaying in a breeze.\pThey appear to be enjoying the wind's\ngentle caress.$

replies.text: They look as though the breeze told a very small joke and everyone leaned over to hear it.
The repeated postures imply a common direction of motion. A convincing effect.
Peaceful scene. Nice to see Pokemon simply enjoying the day.
I can almost feel the quiet around them. I'd stay beside this one a little longer.
That looks like an afternoon where nobody needs anything urgently. Lovely.
The painter has persuaded a still surface to spend the afternoon moving gently.
A peaceful day, preserved before anyone arrived with a schedule.
I'd look at the leaf angles and how the artist makes them share the same wind.
A breeze becomes visible in the little bodies that welcome it.
The shared movement ties the whole picture together without making every Pokemon identical.
I'd want to visit a place like that quietly, so the scene could keep happening around us.

contexts.subject: A large tablet depicts Pokemon beside dense unreadable ancient writing.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_1F_Text_Ston.text: It's a huge stone tablet inscribed\nwith POKéMON and dense text in the\lsmall characters of an ancient,\lunreadable language.$

replies.text: A huge message, and we don't know where to begin. Stone has excellent patience for confused readers.
We can describe the symbols without claiming a translation. Documentation comes before interpretation.
Don't guess the meaning and call it fact. The tablet can wait.
Someone worked so carefully to say something. It's sad not knowing what they wanted heard.
I'd like to know who can study the writing without damaging the surface.
An enormous statement from the past, currently refusing all requests for clarification.
The old words remain. Our understanding has failed to keep its appointment.
I'd compare repeated signs and the layout around the Pokemon figures. Patterns could matter.
Words can survive their voices and still wait for another one to reach them.
The dense arrangement is striking even before we understand what any of it says.
I'd ask what researchers have actually established and where the uncertainty begins.

contexts.subject: The artist imagined a legendary Pokemon from the distant past.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_1F_Text_Pain.text: It's a painting of a legendary POKéMON\nfrom long ago.\pThe artist painted this from\nimagination.$

replies.text: The artist hasn't met the Pokemon, but they've certainly arranged an impressive introduction.
This is an imaginative reconstruction, not evidence of the creature's exact appearance.
Enjoy the picture. Keep the distinction between imagination and a sighting.
I like seeing what someone hoped the creature would feel like to encounter.
A legend can give people something to imagine together, even when the details differ.
A portrait completed without the awkward business of persuading the subject to sit still.
The subject was unavailable. Imagination has supplied a remarkably confident replacement.
I'd be curious which details came from old accounts and which were the artist's choices.
An unseen thing can take many shapes in the space people leave for it.
The choices reveal the artist as much as the imagined subject. That's part of the interest.
I'd ask what detail the artist settled on first. It might explain the rest of the image.

contexts.subject: A large black-stone Poke Ball was apparently used in old festivals.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_1F_Text_BigP.text: It's a big POKé BALL carved from\na black stone.\pIt was apparently used in festivals\nin the olden days.$

replies.text: A Poke Ball with a very serious carrying problem. The festival must have supplied strong volunteers.
Its apparent ceremonial use differs from an ordinary functional ball. The material reinforces that.
Heavy object. I'd like to know how they moved it safely.
I wonder what it looked like with people gathered around it instead of museum walls.
A festival object makes me imagine the ordinary work of getting everyone ready for the day.
A Poke Ball intended to hold an occasion rather than a Pokemon. An intriguing promotion.
A festive symbol with an extremely un-festive lifting requirement.
I'd examine the carving marks and ask how they shaped such a large piece.
A dark stone has outlasted the voices that once circled it.
The familiar shape changes when the material gives it so much weight and permanence.
I'd ask whether any account of the festival survives. The object leaves a very large question.

contexts.subject: A pink-adorned picture frame waits without a painting.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_2F_Text_ItsP.text: It's a picture frame with pink-colored\nadornments.$

replies.text: An empty pink frame. It's already dressed for somebody's very cheerful arrival.
The frame supplies a visual tone before a subject occupies it. Interesting anticipation.
A place waiting for a picture. No need to invent what's inside.
The little pink details make the empty space feel less abandoned.
Someone has made a welcoming place before the guest is here. I like that.
A carefully dressed entrance patiently awaiting the thing meant to make it famous.
An absence with pink trim. Surprisingly optimistic.
The adornments establish the border. The future picture will need to work with them.
A soft edge can change the shape of waiting.
Pink sets an expectation without choosing the whole image. I'd keep the balance in mind.
I'd like to see how the room changes when something finally fills it.

contexts.subject: An empty frame has yellow-colored adornments.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_2F_Text_ItsY.text: It's a picture frame with\nyellow-colored adornments.$

replies.text: That's a remarkably sunny welcome for a picture that hasn't arrived yet.
The yellow border will affect how neighboring colors are perceived in a future composition.
Empty for now. The bright frame makes the space easy to notice.
I like the warmth around it. Even the blank center seems less cold.
A little yellow can make a waiting place feel ready instead of forgotten.
The frame has begun celebrating a guest whose invitation is still being arranged.
A blank space enjoying excellent weather at the edges.
I'd consider the intended lighting along with the yellow trim before choosing a picture.
Light has gathered around an unwritten little space.
Yellow is a bold choice for something meant to sit around another image. It needs confidence.
I'd compare it under daylight and the room's lamps. The color may feel quite different.

contexts.subject: A red-adorned frame has no painting yet.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_2F_Text_ItsR.text: It's a picture frame with\nred-colored adornments.$

replies.text: The empty frame has made a very firm announcement about the color red.
The strong border draws attention even before a subject is present.
Bold frame. Whatever goes inside will have to hold its own.
It feels expectant in a louder way than the others.
A bright welcome can be nice. I'd want the picture to feel at home in it.
An empty frame that has declined to be overlooked while awaiting its principal attraction.
Nothing inside yet. The edges have compensated with enthusiasm.
We'd need to consider how much contrast the future image should have against that trim.
A red boundary makes the silence inside it seem deliberate.
That border has presence. I'd want the picture and frame to share the attention gracefully.
I'd step back across the room to see how strongly it pulls the eye from a distance.

contexts.subject: An empty picture frame is adorned in blue.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_2F_Text_ItsB.text: It's a picture frame with\nblue-colored adornments.$

replies.text: The blue frame looks patient. I suspect it would wait more gracefully than I would.
A cool-colored border may establish a different mood from the warmer frames.
Quiet color. The empty space stands out without shouting.
This one feels calm enough that I don't mind the waiting.
I'd like a picture here that still gives your eyes somewhere to rest.
A dignified blue introduction, currently waiting for the person it was meant to introduce.
A very composed absence. It appears to have practiced.
The room's lighting will matter to how that blue relates to the eventual image.
A cool edge can make a little emptiness feel like open air.
I like how it changes the pace beside the brighter borders. The group needs that.
I'd compare where my attention lands in this frame and the red one.

contexts.subject: Green adornments border an empty place for a painting.

LilycoveCity_LilycoveMuseum_2F_Text_ItsG.text: It's a picture frame with\ngreen-colored adornments.$

replies.text: A little green border, waiting for something interesting to grow in the middle.
The frame establishes a color relationship that the eventual picture will need to answer.
A prepared space. We'll see what earns the place inside.
I keep imagining leaves around it, even though that's only the color suggesting things.
The green makes the empty space feel like a beginning rather than a gap.
A promising border has been installed before anyone has supplied its central argument.
A vacant plot, attractively landscaped at the edges.
I'd compare the trim with the surrounding wall before selecting colors for the picture.
Some waiting places resemble seeds more than holes.
Green can be quiet or sharp depending on what sits beside it. The image will decide a lot.
I'd be curious whether everyone imagines the same sort of picture for this frame.

contexts.subject: An imposing laboratory machine appears intended for Birch research, with no identified function.

LittlerootTown_ProfessorBirchsLab_Text_S.text: It's a serious-looking machine.\nThe PROF must use this for research.$

replies.text: That machine has a very serious face. I wonder whether it knows what all its buttons do.
The setting suggests research use, but appearance alone doesn't identify the apparatus.
Ask Birch what it does before putting a hand near it.
I think I'd feel as though it could tell I hadn't understood the label.
Something that complicated probably took a lot of ordinary patient work to make.
An imposing piece of equipment, looking fully prepared to disapprove of an uninformed question.
The machinery appears serious. Whether it has a sense of humor remains untested.
I'd love a diagram. A complicated exterior only makes me want to know the job inside.
A room can hold a large question in the shape of a machine.
It communicates importance very efficiently. Its purpose is less forthcoming.
I'd ask the professor what observation it helps him make.

contexts.subject: Birch research computer is left undisturbed.

LittlerootTown_ProfessorBirchsLab_Text_P.text: It's a PC used for research.\nBetter not mess around with it.$

replies.text: Important research is in there. My curiosity can survive a closed keyboard.
Unknown work may depend on its current state. Asking before using it is sensible.
His work. Leave it as we found it.
I'd feel awful if a curious glance changed something he'd spent hours doing.
We can ask about the research without treating the computer like a public toy.
An invitation to be curious, with the sensible restriction that we use our mouths first.
The research has survived us noticing it. Let's preserve that success.
I'd ask for a demonstration when he has time, so we understand the setup properly.
Other people's unfinished thoughts deserve a door we knock on.
A useful boundary. Interest doesn't make every workspace open for handling.
I'd rather hear the story from Birch than try to piece it together from a screen.

contexts.subject: A densely packed shelf holds books about Pokemon.

LittlerootTown_ProfessorBirchsLab_Text_C.text: It's crammed with books on POKéMON.$

replies.text: That's a lot of Pokemon knowledge. The shelf is doing a very strenuous amount of knowing.
A substantial reference collection. I'd start with a particular question rather than attempt every volume.
Plenty to learn here. Pick one useful book first.
I like a room where people keep things they might want to understand better.
I'd ask which volume gets used most. The worn one may be the best place to begin.
A great many answers have been placed shoulder to shoulder, awaiting the right troublesome question.
The shelf appears one new discovery away from requiring reinforcement.
I'd want an index. A useful collection needs a way to find what you're looking for.
A crowded shelf is a quiet gathering of people trying to leave something behind.
The variety matters more to me than the impressive quantity. I'd look at the subjects.
I'd ask Birch which book changed how he looked at Pokemon.

contexts.subject: A research book is beyond the player present understanding.

LittlerootTown_ProfessorBirchsLab_Text_B.text: It's a book that's too hard to read.$

replies.text: The book has defeated me without even using a move. I think it had several syllables equipped.
Difficulty often means prerequisites are missing. A simpler introduction could bridge the gap.
Not yet understood. That's different from impossible.
I'd like someone patient enough to explain the first page without making me feel foolish.
No shame in starting with a clearer explanation. Everybody learned the words somewhere.
An impressive defense made entirely from terminology. We may require a glossary to breach it.
The book has declined casual acquaintance and requested several years of preparation.
I'd identify the first unfamiliar term instead of trying to swallow the entire chapter.
An unopened understanding can still have a path leading toward it.
Hard to read can be a matter of experience, or of how clearly someone chose to write.
I'd ask the professor which easier book would help us approach this one.

contexts.subject: Devon display connects industrial work with everyday products, medicines, and trainer tools.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_1F_Text_ProductDi.text:
Prototypes and test products fill
the glass display case.\pThere's a panel with a description…\p“In addition to industrial products,
DEVON now markets sundries and\lpharmaceuticals for better lifestyles.\p“Recently, DEVON has begun marketing
tools for POKéMON TRAINERS, including\lPOKé BALLS and POKéNAV systems.”$

replies.text: Devon has found quite a few ways to make itself useful in our pockets.
The display describes diversification from industry into consumer and trainer products.
Wide range. I'd judge each thing by how well it does its own job.
It's interesting seeing the early versions of things people now use without thinking.
A useful product becomes part of a very ordinary day. That's a worthwhile ambition.
A company with a notably broad interpretation of the phrase we make things.
The prototype cabinet is full of objects hoping to become indispensable.
I'd love to compare the test pieces with the finished designs. What changed, and why?
A small object can carry a surprising amount of someone's time in its shape.
I'd look for the difference between something that attracts attention and something easy to use.
I'd ask a tester which product improved most between its first and final versions.

contexts.subject: Devon history began with quarried stone and iron obtained from sand.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_1F_Text_RocksMeta.text:
Samples of rocks and metal are
displayed in the glass case.\pThere's a panel with some writing
on it…\p“DEVON CORPORATION got its start as
a producer of stones from quarries.\p“The company also produced iron from
filings in the sand.\p“From that humble start as a producer
of raw materials, DEVON developed.\p“DEVON is now a manufacturer of a wide
range of industrial products.”$

replies.text: All that machinery began with rocks and sand. The sand has done very well for itself.
The exhibit connects raw-material production with the company's later industrial development.
Useful to remember where finished equipment actually begins.
I like seeing the plain beginning beside everything the company became.
A long chain of work sits between a handful of material and something useful in a home.
An impressive corporate history beginning with the modest discovery that the ground contains things.
The raw materials have escaped the ground and acquired a remarkable career.
I'd want to see the steps between these samples and the finished metal parts.
Something quiet underfoot can become the bones of an entire changing town.
Showing the material makes the company's story less abstract. It's a good choice.
I'd ask whether any of the oldest quarry workers' accounts were kept.

contexts.subject: The Devon president displays a personal rare-rock collection.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_3F_Text_RareRocks.text: It's a collection of rare rocks and\nstones assembled by the PRESIDENT.$

replies.text: He makes all sorts of complicated things and still leaves room to admire a good rock.
The collection reflects interest beyond the company's immediate production work.
A personal collection. Leave it where he arranged it.
I wonder which one he picked up himself instead of acquiring through someone else.
It's nice seeing something he keeps because it interests him, not because it has a job.
A room full of responsibilities has retained one respectable corner for interesting stones.
The president has provided evidence that a rock can succeed without becoming a product.
I'd ask how he chose the display order: origin, material, shape, or simple affection.
A stone can be rare in the world or simply rare in one person's memory.
I'd want to know whether the arrangement reflects his favorites or the specimens themselves.
I'd ask which piece has the best story attached to finding it.

contexts.subject: Steven keeps a collection of unusual rocks and stones at home.

MossdeepCity_StevensHouse_Text_Collectio.text: It's a collection of rare rocks and\nstones assembled by STEVEN.$

replies.text: A house with room for important rocks. I respect a host who gives his pebbles a proper address.
The selected specimens could reflect geology, appearance, or collecting history. I'd ask which.
Something he cares about. Handle it only if he offers.
The collection makes the room feel more like someone actually lives here.
I'd ask which stone he found on a good day and which one helped rescue a bad one.
A perfectly legitimate reason to return from a long walk carrying considerably more weight.
The stones appear comfortably settled. Travel evidently suited them.
I'd compare the textures and ask where each formed. There's a lot of variety to study.
He has gathered pieces of far places into one quiet room.
The choices tell us something about his eye. Not all rare things attract the same person.
I'd ask which one he'd show a first-time visitor and why.

contexts.subject: A promising glint in the ship turns out to be ordinary trash.

AbandonedShip_HiddenFloorRooms_Text_Brig.text: It's bright and shiny!\nBut it's just trash…$

replies.text: The sparkle had excellent publicity. The treasure itself has filed for a downgrade.
Reflectivity doesn't establish value. The inspection corrected our initial expectation.
Trash. Watch our footing and keep looking.
For a second I thought we'd found something. The light made it look special.
At least we checked. I'd leave the sharp bits alone while sorting what it actually is.
A brilliant entrance from an object with absolutely no qualifications for being treasure.
A reminder that rubbish can possess exceptional presentation skills.
We should identify the material before handling it. Shiny scrap can have sharp edges.
Light can make a discarded thing ask to be noticed again.
A strong first impression isn't the same as something worth carrying home.
I'd remember the difference between a glint and a find before calling everyone over next time.

contexts.subject: The storage key jams in the lock but opens the ship storage-room door.

AbandonedShip_Corridors_B1F_Text_Inserte.text: {PLAYER} inserted and turned the\nSTORAGE KEY.\pThe inserted KEY stuck fast,\nbut the door opened.$

replies.text: The key has decided to live here permanently. At least it remembered to let us through first.
The door opened despite the jammed key. The key is no longer available for reuse.
Door open. Don't wrench the stuck key and break something else.
That little moment when it stuck must have felt awful before the door moved.
One problem solved, and we don't need to force the mechanism any farther.
A successful entry, accompanied by the key's unexpected decision to retire in place.
The lock has accepted the key as a permanent resident.
The mechanism released before seizing. We should inspect the doorway rather than keep twisting.
A small thing stays behind so the way ahead can open.
I like a clear outcome, even if the key's departure from our plans was a little dramatic.
I'd check what the room contains before celebrating too loudly on an old ship.

contexts.subject: A room key sticks after unlocking one of the hidden ship doors.

AbandonedShip_HiddenFloorCorridors_Text_.text: {PLAYER} inserted and turned the\nKEY.\pThe inserted KEY stuck fast,\nbut the door opened.$

replies.text: Another key has developed a powerful attachment to its door. The ship seems to encourage commitment.
The unlocking succeeded. The jam means we should not plan on retaining that key.
Open now. Leave the key rather than damage the lock further.
I'm glad it worked before it stuck. I don't enjoy that uncertain pause.
No need to keep struggling with a problem the open door has already solved.
The key completed its assignment and promptly became part of the architecture.
A one-way career transition from useful key to very small door ornament.
The next useful check is the condition of the room beyond the threshold.
An old lock can hold one thing fast while finally releasing another.
We should remember which door opened rather than assume the key is still with us.
I'd take a moment to get our bearings before moving through another similar-looking room.

contexts.subject: A locked ship door is marked as storage.

AbandonedShip_Corridors_B1F_Text_DoorIsL.text: The door is locked.\p“STORAGE” is painted on the door.$

replies.text: The door has provided the room's job description and refused all introductions.
The label identifies the room, but not the means of access. A suitable key is still needed.
Locked storage. Find the key instead of forcing old wood.
I wonder what somebody thought was worth keeping behind it.
A locked room on a wreck may hold supplies, or simply more trouble. Carefully either way.
An informative welcome, followed by an extremely firm refusal of admission.
The room is storage. Our curiosity has nowhere to store itself yet.
We should look for the correct key before putting stress on the deteriorating structure.
A name on a closed door leaves plenty of room for wondering.
The faded purpose is still clear, even though the people using the room are gone.
I'd check nearby rooms for a clue rather than guess at what the lock wants.

contexts.subject: An overheating generator radiates heat from a distance and needs shutting down.

NewMauville_Inside_Text_GeneratorRadiati.text: The generator is radiating heat that\ncan be felt even at a distance.\pIt looks like it should be turned off\nas soon as possible.$

replies.text: If we can feel it from here, the generator is being much too generous with the warmth.
The heat is evident at a distance. We should follow the intended shutdown method rather than approach carelessly.
Keep back. Find the proper control.
The whole space feels tense around it. I'd like the heat to stop.
I'd check that our partners stay clear while we look for the control.
An unwanted demonstration of just how much warmth a machine can contribute to a conversation.
The generator has mistaken alarming for productive.
We need the designed shutdown control. Touching the housing is not a useful diagnostic step.
The air carries the machine's distress farther than we ought to walk toward it.
The warning is plain enough without leaning closer to prove it.
I'd keep track of the safe route out while we find the way to stop it.

contexts.subject: The generator has quieted after being switched off.

replies.text: That's a much better conversation with a machine. It has stopped shouting heat at us.
The reduced activity is consistent with shutdown. Residual heat may still remain.
Quiet now. Give the machinery space while it settles.
I didn't realize how tense I'd been until the sound changed.
A quieter room makes it easier to check how everyone's doing.
The generator has accepted a less demanding role in the local atmosphere.
A machine discovering the considerable social benefits of silence.
The immediate shutdown is complete. I'd still avoid the housing until it's cooled.
A harsh presence has loosened its hold on the room.
The difference is noticeable. It's good to have a result we can actually hear.
I'd take one last look from a safe distance, then tell Wattson what changed.

contexts.subject: A box identifies a Pokemon-branded moving and delivery service.

InsideOfTruck_Text_BoxPrintedWithMonLogo.text: The box is printed with a POKéMON logo.\pIt's a POKéMON brand moving and\ndelivery service.$

replies.text: Even the boxes have Pokemon on the job. I wonder whether the logo gets a rest break.
The logo identifies the delivery service. It doesn't tell us the contents of this particular box.
Delivery box. Best leave somebody else's packing sealed.
Moving boxes make a place feel temporary, even when everything inside matters.
I hope whoever packed it remembered where the everyday essentials went.
A branded promise that one's belongings will travel in a more organized fashion than one's nerves.
The box has a clearer travel plan than most of its passengers.
Good labeling should help identify the shipment without opening it.
A sealed box can hold a surprising amount of the place someone left behind.
A simple logo has to remain recognizable on a battered box. Practical design.
I'd ask where the delivery is headed before assuming the box has reached its final home.

contexts.subject: A faded old inscription hopes a future human visitor will be kindhearted.

FarawayIsland_Entrance_Text_Sign.text: The writing is fading as if it was\nwritten a long time ago…\p“…ber, 6th day\nIf any human…sets foot here…\lagain…et it be a kindhearted pers…\l…ith that hope, I depar…”$

replies.text: Most of the words are going, but the wish for kindness is still holding on.
The surviving fragments support that wish. They don't establish a complete date or author.
We can honor the clear part. Be gentle with what's here.
Someone left hoping a stranger would be kind. I want that part to be answered well.
A careful visit seems like the least we can give that old request.
Time has damaged the sentence without managing to erase the most important request.
An old warning with a surprisingly modest demand: try not to be awful.
I'd document the remaining marks without filling the missing text with guesses.
A stranger's hope has survived long enough to become our responsibility for a moment.
The missing words make the remaining ones feel more deliberate. I wouldn't embellish them.
I'd record exactly what's legible, then leave the place as gently as the writer asked.

contexts.subject: An island inscription links fading memories with keeping them in the heart.
