SouthernIsland_Exterior_Text_Sign.text: “Those whose memories fade seek to\ncarve them in their hearts…”$

replies.text: A sign about remembering. It has volunteered to do some of the remembering for us.
The inscription contrasts fading recall with enduring personal significance. A thoughtful metaphor.
Keep what matters. It doesn't all need to stay perfectly sharp.
I know how a small detail can fade while the feeling stays very clear.
Sometimes remembering means doing the kind thing again, rather than repeating every word exactly.
A brief inscription asking a much larger question than its surface has room to hold.
Memory is unreliable. Apparently the heart has been assigned supplementary storage.
A written marker can support memory without replacing the person who gives it meaning.
Some things become less clear and no less present.
I like that it leaves room for a personal answer instead of telling us what to remember.
I'd ask what place each of us remembers most clearly even when the details have softened.

contexts.subject: A simple description identifies the pale rock in Mossdeep.

replies.text: A white rock. It has supplied exactly one fact and refuses to become more mysterious for us.
We know its appearance, not its composition or origin. No further conclusion follows yet.
A rock. We can look without giving it a legend.
I like its plainness. Not everything has to ask for a grand explanation.
Something ordinary can still make a nice place to stop and look around.
A remarkably concise introduction from an object surrounded by our temptation to speculate.
White. Rocky. An exemplary commitment to giving no unnecessary information.
I'd examine the texture before guessing at the material. Color alone isn't enough.
Sometimes a pale stone is allowed to be only a pale stone.
Its contrast with the surroundings catches the eye. That's already something to notice.
I'd ask whether locals know where it came from, without assuming the answer will be extraordinary.

contexts.subject: The Fossil Maniac displays rocks with unusual shapes.

Route114_FossilManiacsHouse_Text_RocksFi.text: Rocks in peculiar shapes fill\nthe display case…$

replies.text: An entire case of rocks that refused the ordinary-rock silhouette.
Unusual shapes may reflect different formation or weathering histories. I'd want specimen details.
Interesting collection. Keep the case closed unless the owner offers.
I wonder which shape made him stop in the middle of a walk.
I'd ask which one took the most patience to find.
A gathering of stones selected for their ability to make a person say hang on a moment.
An exhibition of very slow, very committed eccentricity.
I'd compare the surfaces for clues about how each shape formed.
Water and time can leave a hard thing looking surprisingly uncertain of its own edges.
The different outlines make the whole case lively without any bright colors.
I'd ask what each one looked like before it was cleaned for display.

contexts.subject: Books about strata, rain-shaped land, and rocks fill the Fossil Maniac shelf.

Route114_FossilManiacsHouse_Text_Crammed.text: THE COMPOSITION OF STRATA…\nHOW RAIN SHAPES THE LAND…\lSTONES, SOIL, AND ROCK…\pIt's crammed with books.$

replies.text: He doesn't just collect rocks. He's collected several ways to ask the ground questions.
The subjects link material, layered deposits, and erosion. A coherent reference collection.
Good to learn what you're digging through before digging farther.
I like that the books make rain sound like something that can write on the land.
Understanding the place probably makes every find more meaningful to him.
A shelf prepared to explain why the landscape looks the way it does, given enough time.
The ground has a complicated biography. He appears to own the reference edition.
I'd start with the erosion book and compare its diagrams with the terrain outside.
Rain makes marks so slowly that a book helps us notice the hand.
The shelf makes his interest feel deeper than simply wanting unusual objects.
I'd ask which subject he thought was dull until he saw it happen outdoors.

contexts.subject: Bill praises Lanette storage-system improvements and encourages further research.

Route114_LanettesHouse_Text_EmailFromBil.text:
There's an e-mail from someone on
the PC.\p“… … … … … … …\p“Your Storage System offers more
convenience than mine.\p“It has a lot of user-friendly features
that make it fun and useful, too.\p“It makes me proud that I played
a part in its development.\p“Here's hoping that you'll continue
research in Storage Systems.\p“From BILL
… … … … … … … …”$

replies.text: A lovely message from someone pleased to see another person's work grow beyond his own part in it.
He credits the improved usability while acknowledging their shared development history. Collegial and precise.
Good to see someone proud of a colleague doing better work.
That kind of encouragement would make a difficult day feel much less lonely.
He remembered to say the work helps people. That's a useful compliment to carry back to it.
A predecessor has encountered an improvement and chosen pride over wounded importance. Admirable.
A professional message containing actual generosity. Worth preserving.
I'd love to hear which user-friendly features he noticed first. Good feedback can guide the next iteration.
A hand in the beginning needn't hold everything that grows afterward.
He recognizes her choices instead of only reminding her where the work began.
I'd ask Lanette which part of the message meant most to her.

contexts.subject: A student notebook summarizes catching, traveling with, raising, and battling Pokemon.

RustboroCity_PokemonSchool_Text_Students.text:
It's this student's notebook…\pPOKéMON are to be caught using
POKé BALLS.\pUp to six POKéMON can accompany
a TRAINER.\pA TRAINER is someone who catches
POKéMON, raises them, and battles\lwith them.\pA TRAINER's mission is to defeat
the strong TRAINERS who await\lchallengers in POKéMON GYMS.$

replies.text: A whole trainer's beginning, packed into a notebook. I hope there's room left for the surprising bits.
A concise outline of the conventional trainer role. The actual practice will add nuance.
Useful basics. How we treat the partners matters alongside the checklist.
I'd like to see the little notes the student adds after trying those things themselves.
The notes say how to begin. Everyday care will fill a lot of the space between the steps.
An entire profession has been compressed into a few determined lines of student handwriting.
The adventure fits on paper. The blisters are supplied separately.
It's a starting framework. Experience should help connect the listed tasks rather than leave them isolated.
A small page can point toward a much larger life without knowing all its turns.
I like seeing what someone chose to write down as important at the beginning.
I'd ask which lesson they've tried outside the classroom and what surprised them.

contexts.subject: The ship porthole frames the distant horizon.

replies.text: A tiny round window trying to hold an enormous straight line. Brave little window.
A fixed frame makes the scale beyond it particularly striking.
Good view. Keep the corridor clear for people walking through.
I could stand here a while. The distance makes my thoughts feel less crowded.
A quiet look outside can help settle a busy journey.
The ship has thoughtfully framed a landscape far too large to bring aboard.
A small circle containing an unreasonable amount of outside.
I'd watch how the line shifts with the ship's motion. A simple view reveals quite a bit.
The far edge keeps its distance while the whole room moves beneath us.
That round border changes the scene completely. It makes the open sea feel intimate.
I'd wait for a change in the light rather than hurry past the window.

contexts.subject: A posted board lists colored shards accepted in exchange for evolution stones.

Route124_DivingTreasureHuntersHouse_Text.text:
{CLEAR_TO 10}Wanted item{CLEAR_TO 124}Trade item
{CLEAR_TO 15}RED SHARD{CLEAR_TO 89}{LEFT_ARROW}{RIGHT_ARROW}{CLEAR_TO 123}FIRE STONE{CLEAR_TO 200}\p{CLEAR_TO 10}Wanted item{CLEAR_TO 124}Trade item
{CLEAR_TO 6}YELLOW SHARD{CLEAR_TO 89}{LEFT_ARROW}{RIGHT_ARROW}{CLEAR_TO 115}THUNDERSTONE{CLEAR_TO 200}\p{CLEAR_TO 10}Wanted item{CLEAR_TO 124}Trade item
{CLEAR_TO 12}BLUE SHARD{CLEAR_TO 89}{LEFT_ARROW}{RIGHT_ARROW}{CLEAR_TO 121}WATER STONE{CLEAR_TO 200}\p{CLEAR_TO 10}Wanted item{CLEAR_TO 124}Trade item
{CLEAR_TO 8}GREEN SHARD{CLEAR_TO 89}{LEFT_ARROW}{RIGHT_ARROW}{CLEAR_TO 123}LEAF STONE$

replies.text: A very colorful answer to the question of what those little bits are worth to somebody.
The board defines the exchange mapping. It doesn't indicate that any trade has occurred.
Check the color before offering a shard. Clear terms.
It's nice when a collection of little found things has a purpose you can actually read.
I'd choose the stone we need rather than trade every shard just because the board is there.
A neatly organized proposal to turn the sea's fragments into somebody else's next beginning.
The broken pieces have unexpectedly good career prospects.
The mapping is explicit. We can plan which shard to keep before making an exchange.
A small fragment can open a larger possibility when it reaches the right hands.
The colors make the matching easier to follow. Useful information presented well.
I'd ask which shards are hardest to find and how the hunter learned to identify them.

contexts.subject: The posted Seedot size record celebrates a giant specimen and invites larger examples.

SootopolisCity_LotadAndSeedotHouse_Text_.text: The biggest SEEDOT in history!\n{STR_VAR_2}'s {STR_VAR_3} giant!\pA SEEDOT bigger than a LOTAD\nalways wanted!$

replies.text: An exceptionally large little acorn. Seedot has found a wonderfully confusing career.
This is a recorded specimen measurement, not evidence that the player has just set a new record.
A big Seedot. Still needs treating like a partner, not a measuring trophy.
I wonder what its trainer first noticed about it before somebody reached for a ruler.
I'd be more curious about its habits than how much space its size takes on the sign.
A modest species has acquired a magnificently immodest entry in the local record book.
The acorn has outgrown expectations and several people's vocabulary for small.
I'd check how they standardize the measurement before comparing another specimen.
A small creature can become large in a room through size, or through what people make of it.
It's a memorable record. I'd want the individual to remain more than the number.
I'd ask the trainer how people react when they first see it.

contexts.subject: A posted record celebrates an unusually large Lotad and seeks a still larger one.

SootopolisCity_LotadAndSeedotHouse_Text_.text: The biggest LOTAD in history!\n{STR_VAR_2}'s {STR_VAR_3} colossus!\pA LOTAD bigger than a SEEDOT\nalways wanted!$

replies.text: That's a lot of Lotad. The leaf must cast a very respectable little patch of shade.
The record concerns the measured individual. It doesn't establish a new result from this inspection.
Impressive size. No need to chase a larger one just to keep the sign busy.
I wonder whether it knows how much conversation follows it around.
A very large partner still has ordinary preferences. I'd start by asking about those.
A colossus in the specific and delightful field of being a Lotad.
The pond's modest resident has become a considerable local event.
We'd need the same measurement method to compare another Lotad fairly.
A broad leaf can make a quiet little creature suddenly hard to overlook.
The competitive sign is funny. I'd want the trainer's affection to remain less competitive.
I'd ask where its trainer found it and what made them notice it first.

contexts.subject: The hall shelf contains multiple books organized around the current local trend.

DewfordTown_Hall_Text_BooksAboutTrend.text:
IDENTIFYING GOOD
“{STR_VAR_1}” &\lBAD “{STR_VAR_1}”…\pTHE LINK BETWEEN
“{STR_VAR_1}” AND\lPOKéMON…\pUSEFUL
“{STR_VAR_1}”…\pIt's neatly jammed with books about
“{STR_VAR_1}.”$

replies.text: They've filled an entire shelf already. That trend has a terrifyingly efficient publishing department.
The books repeat the current phrase across several subjects. Popularity doesn't establish a real connection.
A lot of books about one fad. I'd check what they actually say.
I wonder whether anyone still reads them after the town finds its next favorite thing.
A full shelf can still leave a simple question unanswered: is any of this useful?
The fashionable phrase has acquired scholarship with astonishing speed and questionable necessity.
A shelf full of certainty, all apparently printed before anyone asked why.
I'd compare the contents instead of assuming different titles mean different information.
A passing word has made itself a very permanent-looking little house.
The books make the trend look established. That's part of how the room keeps it alive.
I'd ask which one somebody has actually read. The answer might change how I see the shelf.

contexts.subject: The Tower sign challenges trainers to sustain a winning streak.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_BattleTo.text: This is the BATTLE TOWER!\nKeep the win streak as the toughest\lTRAINER!$

replies.text: A tall building asking for a long streak. It seems to appreciate matching proportions.
The stated goal emphasizes consecutive wins rather than a single impressive match.
Consistency matters here. Prepare for more than one good opening.
The sign makes the first battle feel like the beginning of a much longer thought.
I'd want a plan the team can sustain, not just one dramatic burst.
The Tower has chosen endurance with a competitive number attached.
A building advertising several opportunities to discover a flaw in your plan.
We should plan for varied opponents across the whole round.
A straight tower, a long chain of moments. Both can seem smaller from the bottom.
The emphasis is clear. Every match contributes to the impression, not just the first.
I'd ask a regular challenger which ordinary decision kept their streak alive.

contexts.subject: The Palace sign invites visitors to observe Pokemon battles.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_BattlePa.text: This is the BATTLE PALACE!\nKeep your eyes on POKéMON battles!$

replies.text: A battle sign asking us to keep our eyes open. Sensible advice before the rules get stranger.
Observation is emphasized here. We'd need the guide's explanation for the full battle format.
Look carefully. Knowing what the Pokemon choose matters.
I like an invitation that begins with paying attention.
Watching well can be a way of looking after the partners, too.
The Palace offers spectacle with a surprisingly useful instruction to actually notice it.
A sign politely recommending the underused skill of looking.
We should learn the exact format instead of inferring every rule from the slogan.
A quiet eye can find things a loud command would miss.
It's a restrained invitation compared with some of the island's louder promises.
I'd watch one match before deciding what to make of the place.

contexts.subject: The Arena sign calls for the toughest teams to gather.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_BattleAr.text: This is the BATTLE ARENA!\nLet the toughest teams gather!$

replies.text: A meeting notice for tough teams. I wonder whether anybody brings the quiet snacks.
The sign emphasizes team strength. The actual judging rules need separate explanation.
A tough team still needs the right order. Let's check the rules.
Gather sounds friendlier than prove yourselves, even on a battle sign.
A team is more than three individually impressive partners. I'd remember that here.
An open invitation to assemble the local competition in one conveniently intimidating room.
A gathering where the introductions may involve quite a lot of impact.
We should understand how the Arena evaluates a team before choosing ours.
Several strengths can share a direction without being the same strength.
I like that the sign names the team, rather than only the person leading it.
I'd ask what makes a team work well here beyond simply looking formidable.

contexts.subject: The Pyramid sign advertises an advancing Battle Quest.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_BattlePy.text: This is the BATTLE PYRAMID!\nAdvance through the Battle Quest!$

replies.text: A quest with its own very large roof. That's a confident amount of adventure to promise indoors.
The sign presents progression as exploration. The facility rules will define the constraints.
Learn the supply rules before starting a climb.
Quest makes it sound like there could be something around every corner.
I'd want everyone rested before accepting a challenge that might take a while.
A grand promise of adventure, helpfully stored in one conspicuously solid landmark.
A quest housed in a pyramid. Subtle invitations were apparently not available.
We should ask what resources remain with us during the exploration.
An upward path can hold many sideways uncertainties.
The name promises a journey instead of simply another room of matches.
I'd ask an explorer what they wish they'd known before the first floor.

contexts.subject: The sign directs visitors to exchange Battle Points for prizes.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_Exchange.text: BATTLE POINT EXCHANGE SERVICE CORNER\nExchange your Battle Points!$

replies.text: The place where all those difficult decisions become a very soft doll, if we want.
A designated point-redemption service. We should compare terms before selecting a reward.
Points for prizes. Decide what we actually want first.
I like having something to look forward to that isn't another opponent.
A useful item or a small joy can both be worth saving for.
The island's efforts conclude here in an admirably tangible selection of consequences.
A counter prepared to turn competence into cushions. Excellent civilization.
We can check the full list and prices without committing immediately.
Hard-won effort can change shape when it reaches a different pair of hands.
I'd pick one thing I truly wanted before the display persuaded me to need five.
I'd ask everybody which prize they noticed first. The answers could be entertaining.

contexts.subject: The Ranking Hall sign encourages new records.

BattleFrontier_OutsideEast_Text_RankingH.text: BATTLE FRONTIER RANKING HALL\nSet your sights on new records!$

replies.text: A sign asking us to improve the wall's reading material. Ambitious little sign.
The hall recognizes measurable results. A specific category gives that ambition clearer shape.
Set a realistic goal before chasing somebody else's number.
I wonder how it feels to find your own name where you used to read others.
A record is nice. I'd still want the work getting there to be something we can live with.
A public invitation to become somebody else's intimidating benchmark.
Posterity has installed directional signage. Very organized.
We can inspect the categories and compare them with our current results.
A name waits beyond a great many ordinary attempts.
The promise of being remembered is powerful. I'd choose what I wanted remembered for.
I'd like to hear a record holder describe the attempt before the successful one.

contexts.subject: The Dome sign promises a path toward becoming an invincible superstar.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_BattleDo.text: This is the BATTLE DOME!\nYour path to the invincible superstar!$

replies.text: Invincible superstar is quite a destination. I hope the path has somewhere to sit halfway.
The language is promotional. A tournament can establish a winner, not literal invincibility.
Good slogan. Still need to win the actual matches.
I'd rather learn the format before imagining all those eyes on us.
A good team can have an ordinary bad day. The sign doesn't get to forbid that.
A modest promise from a building devoted to the completely reasonable ambition of universal acclaim.
A path to invincibility, subject to several awkwardly capable opponents.
We should prepare for selection and matchups, not rely on the advertised feeling.
A bright word at the entrance doesn't light every difficult step inside.
The sign understands what people dream about. I wonder how the actual experience supports them.
I'd ask a visitor what surprised them once the grand first impression wore off.

contexts.subject: The Pike sign presents its defining choice among three paths.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_BattlePi.text: This is the BATTLE PIKE!\nChoose one of three paths!$

replies.text: Three paths. My uncertainty has been given a small but respectable menu.
The sign establishes the branching choice, not the consequences behind each route.
Three doors. Learn what hints are available before guessing.
I'd probably stand at the entrance longer than I meant to.
Whatever we choose, I'd like the team ready for more than one possibility.
A remarkably concise invitation to consider how little a doorway tells you.
Three opportunities to wonder whether the other two were better.
Preparation should cover different outcomes rather than depend on choosing a perfect door.
A choice can look simple when the walls are doing most of the hiding.
The sign is honest about the choice and very quiet about everything after it.
I'd ask how much information the attendants can actually provide.

contexts.subject: The Factory sign asks visitors to seek the toughest Pokemon.

BattleFrontier_OutsideWest_Text_BattleFa.text: This is the BATTLE FACTORY!\nSeek out the toughest POKéMON!$

replies.text: A tough-Pokemon search inside a factory. I hope they aren't all queued behind one enormous clipboard.
The slogan emphasizes selection. The rental and swap rules determine how that selection works.
Find the right partners, not just the strongest-looking ones.
I'd want to learn a little about the Pokemon before deciding what toughness means for them.
A partner should fit the plan and be understood, even if we're only together briefly.
A grand search whose practical beginning is likely to involve reading several move lists.
The toughest choice may be the choosing itself. Convenient theme.
We should assess combinations rather than rank each offered partner in isolation.
Strength can hide in the way two unfamiliar things meet.
I'd look past the first impressive outline. Useful qualities don't all announce themselves.
I'd ask an experienced visitor what they learned to notice after their first few rentals.

contexts.subject: The sign marks the entrance to Victory Road.

replies.text: Victory Road. A very confident name for a place before we've walked through it.
A destination marker, not a statement that the journey has already succeeded.
Check supplies before entering. The name doesn't make it a short walk.
It feels like a threshold even before taking the next step.
I'd make sure everyone is ready instead of letting the name hurry us.
An encouraging title placed strategically before the inconvenient work.
A road named after the thing it has no obligation to provide.
We should review the team's condition before committing to the route.
A hopeful name can wait at the mouth of a very demanding path.
It's a strong introduction. I'd let the actual route teach us what it means.
I'd want to remember how this entrance felt before knowing what waited beyond it.

contexts.subject: The sign identifies the Pokemon League center gate.

replies.text: The League entrance. Even the ordinary act of walking through a gate has dressed up for the occasion.
The marker identifies the League approach. Admission and readiness remain separate questions.
We're at the gate. Take a breath and check the team.
It looks official in a way that makes every little sound feel clearer.
I'd like a quiet moment before going from the journey to the challenge itself.
A short sign with an impressively large amount of expectation waiting behind it.
The gate is ordinary architecture doing extraordinary psychological work.
This is a useful point to review preparations before proceeding.
A boundary can make all the road behind it feel suddenly present.
The simple wording gives the place its own weight. It doesn't need much decoration.
I'd ask what everyone thought this entrance would feel like before we reached it.

contexts.subject: The Fallarbor Battle Tent sign calls great teams to gather.

FallarborTown_Text_BattleTentSign.text: BATTLE TENT FALLARBOR SITE\n“May the Greatest Teams Gather!”$

replies.text: A tent with a very ambitious guest list. I wonder if the pegs know how important the visitors are.
The invitation emphasizes teams. We'd need the guide to explain the actual event rules.
A strong team needs more than a strong introduction. Check the format.
Gathering sounds friendly. I'd like it to feel that way to somebody entering for the first time.
I'd want a team comfortable working together before worrying about being called great.
A lightweight building making a heavyweight invitation. Admirable confidence in the canvas.
A gathering of greatness, presumably subject to available tent space.
We should ask which team skills this particular site evaluates.
A small shelter can hold an intention much larger than its roof.
I like the focus on the whole team. I'd hope the experience follows through on it.
I'd ask a participant what made their teammates work better together here.

contexts.subject: The sign advertises a house where Pokemon can learn new moves.

FallarborTown_Text_MoveTutorSign.text: MOVE TUTOR'S HOUSE\n“New moves taught to POKéMON.”$

replies.text: A house full of new ideas for Pokemon. I hope the furniture has learned to keep up.
A local source of instruction. We'd need to ask which moves and conditions apply.
Useful lead. Ask before making a plan around a particular lesson.
I like places where learning something new is the whole reason for opening the door.
A new move should be something that suits the partner, not just something impressive to collect.
A modest house advertising the possibility of leaving with a considerably less modest technique.
An educational address with potentially severe consequences for the furniture.
We can compare the lesson options with the current team before committing.
An old room can hold the beginning of a new habit.
The plain sign does a useful job. I'd rather learn the details from the teacher.
I'd ask what they enjoy most about seeing a Pokemon understand a new move.

contexts.subject: The herb shop sign advertises bitter-tasting remedies.

replies.text: The sign has bravely put the bad taste right in the invitation. Honest shopkeeping.
Bitterness is a stated property, not proof of greater effectiveness by itself.
Ask what each remedy does. Don't choose only by the slogan.
I'd want our partners to know we're trying to help, even if the taste isn't pleasant.
Bitter isn't a virtue on its own. I'd ask about the intended use before buying anything.
An unusually candid advertisement, allowing one's tongue to object before entering.
A shop confident enough to warn the taste buds in advance.
We should compare the actual item effects and the partner's response.
A helpful thing can still be unpleasant to receive. That deserves noticing.
I appreciate the honesty. I'd still want more than a neat phrase before making the choice.
I'd ask the shopkeeper how they advise trainers choosing between the remedies.

contexts.subject: The department store sign promises abundant merchandise and excitement.

LilycoveCity_Text_DepartmentStoreSign.text: LILYCOVE DEPARTMENT STORE\p“Overflowing with great merchandise\nand excitement!\p“A great place to find that something\nyou need!”$

replies.text: Overflowing excitement sounds fun. I hope they've left enough room for the stairs.
The promise of abundance is promotional. A specific need will make the selection easier.
Decide what we're looking for before the displays do it for us.
That much choice can make me want a quiet corner before I buy anything.

An enormous collection of things waiting to explain why we need them.

replies.text: Cove Lily, Lilycove. The name has put on its shoes backward and decided it looks splendid.

A name with enough symmetry to give a tired traveler a brief argument with their own memory.
An establishment that has rearranged the town and installed beds inside the result.

A borrowed name turned gently around can feel like a place of its own.

contexts.subject: A harbor notice says the S.S. Tidal is still being built in Slateport before service begins.

replies.text: The ferry is coming. At the moment it's taking the longer route through being assembled.

contexts.subject: A house sign advertises removing unwanted Pokemon moves.

LilycoveCity_Text_MoveDeletersHouseSign.text: MOVE DELETER'S HOUSE\p“Unwanted POKéMON moves deleted.”$

replies.text: A house for letting go of moves. I hope the old techniques get a polite little farewell.

Letting go can be useful, but I'd want a good reason first.

contexts.subject: The sign identifies Professor Birch Pokemon laboratory.

replies.text: Professor Birch's lab. A small sign for a building with a lot of questions inside.

Right place to find Birch or someone who knows his work.

contexts.subject: The house sign identifies Wally home.

replies.text: A familiar name makes an ordinary house feel a little easier to approach.

Wally's house. We should knock before going farther.

contexts.subject: A sign marks Wanda house.

replies.text: Wanda's house. A nice straightforward answer to the wandering-about-looking-for-Wanda problem.

replies.text: Anything about Pokemon is an enormous syllabus. I hope the chalk gets holidays.

contexts.subject: Devon sign claims a wide range of products for everyday living.

RustboroCity_Text_DevonCorpSign.text: DEVON CORPORATION\p“For all your living needs, we make\nit all.”$

replies.text: All our living needs? That's a bold sign. I wonder if it can manufacture a quiet afternoon.

A large promise rests on many small things doing their work reliably.

contexts.subject: The sign identifies the Cutter house.

replies.text: The Cutter's house. I hope the hedges don't feel personally threatened by the address.

contexts.subject: Rydel Cycles advertises riding over gravel with an energetic slogan.

replies.text: The sign promises gravel for the wheels and something much harder to repair for the soul.

Choose the bike for the ground, not the size of the promise.

contexts.subject: The Game Corner sign advertises a play spot for everyone.

contexts.subject: The Name Rater sign advertises Pokemon nickname assessments.

replies.text: An official opinion on nicknames. My imaginary name committee suddenly feels underqualified.

contexts.subject: A Cable Car attendant politely accepts a declined ride.

contexts.subject: Lanette recommends organizing storage boxes so their Pokemon are easy to identify.

Knowing rain well may teach a person how much remains beyond reach.
A strong claim should come with more than confidence and a dramatic pose.

contexts.subject: The treasure hunter cannot complete a shard trade because the players bag is full.

Check the outgoing and incoming items before making the trade.
Leave a small empty place for what comes next.
A successful exchange needs more than a good choice of treasure.

A little hesitation is allowed when choosing what to keep.

contexts.subject: A Safari attendant wishes the player enjoyment after their assistance.

replies.text: A helpful stop and a cheerful send-off. Back to the little wild surprises.

An encouraging farewell suits a place full of new sights.

contexts.subject: A Safari attendant wishes luck and remains available for help.

SafariZone_South_Text_GoodLuck.text: Good luck!\pIf you need anything, don't hesitate\nto tell me, please!$

replies.text: Luck AND someone to ask. That is a good combination for wandering.

A known path is not the same as a finished discovery.

Route121_SafariZoneEntrance_Text_FirstTi.text: When you enter the SAFARI ZONE, you\nstart with 30 SAFARI BALLS for\lcatching POKéMON.\pThe SAFARI Game is over when you run\nout of SAFARI BALLS, or when you've\lwalked 500 steps.\pCome in and enjoy the SAFARI ZONE!$

An adventure with a very specific allowance of footwear and ambition.

A useful gift from people who clearly care about their practice.
The defeated household has responded with an admirably practical tribute.
A family heirloom, apparently designed to make exercise more inconvenient.
Interesting to try the equipment behind their training routine.
A loss can still leave room for respect and generosity.
A thoughtful gift, even with that little doubt about whether we need it.
I would ask how each family member uses it in practice.

contexts.subject: The glassworker hands over the finished ash-made item on successful collection.

Route113_GlassWorkshop_Text_IveFinishedG.text: Ah, I've finished your {STR_VAR_1}.\nTake it, huff-puff.$

replies.text: Our dusty walking has become an actual thing! A very satisfying transformation.
A fine example of collected material finding a useful finished form.
Good work. Keep the new glass secure.
It is lovely seeing the result after all that gathering.
There is something satisfying about taking home work made from what we brought.
The humble ash has completed its surprising transformation.
Our footsteps have acquired a tangible and much less dusty ending.
I would like to look at the finish and how the shape was made.
Something gathered softly from the road has taken a new form.
A finished piece makes the whole collecting trip feel well chosen.
I would ask how long that particular piece took to shape.

contexts.subject: The shop owner explains replanting berries and asks for help filling the world with flowers.

Route104_PrettyPetalFlowerShop_Text_Berr.text:
BERRIES grow on trees that thrive
only in soft, loamy soil.\pIf you take some BERRIES, be sure to
plant one in the loamy soil again.\pA planted BERRY will soon sprout,
grow into a plant, flower beautifully,\lthen grow BERRIES again.\pI want to see the whole wide world
filled with beautiful flowers.\lThat's my dream.\pPlease help me, {PLAYER}{KUN}. Plant BERRIES
and bring more flowers into the world.$

replies.text: One berry back in the ground. A tiny thank-you that grows its own flowers.
Replanting keeps the cycle going while allowing a harvest.
Take some, plant some. Good habit.
I like a dream that lets us help in small ways.
Leaving a berry to grow means there will be more to share.
A beautiful ambition built from very ordinary acts of planting.
A grand dream with an unusually sensible first instruction.
A system that replenishes its own materials deserves care.
A little fruit returned can become a patch of beauty later.
A flower-filled world begins with remembering the next planting.
I would enjoy finding a blooming tree we planted on an earlier visit.

contexts.subject: The shop owner says flowers bring happiness.

Route104_PrettyPetalFlowerShop_Text_Flow.text: Flowers bring so much happiness to\npeople, don't they?$

replies.text: They do. Even a tiny flower can make a whole patch look pleased.
A small visible change can make a familiar place more pleasant.
A bit of color helps a place feel cared for.
A little flower by a window can change a room.
A few flowers on the table make an ordinary day feel special.
A brief argument for beauty, supported by a great many windowsills.
They are remarkably effective for something that says so little.
A small growing thing can improve a space without much machinery.
They ask little of a passerby and still offer something lovely.
Color, shape, and a little life. A very good combination.
I like noticing which flowers people choose to keep near them.

contexts.subject: A Mauville man ends his television explanation with a casual question about watching TVs.

MauvilleCity_Text_BeenCheckingOutTV.text: Hi, have you been checking out TVs?$

replies.text: The televisions are getting checked on very thoroughly around here.
He seems interested in whether we noticed the local broadcasts.
We have seen a few. He is keen on them.
I wonder which program he wanted us to notice.
A good show can give people something pleasant to talk about.
Our viewing habits have acquired an unusually persistent local correspondent.
The television has apparently become a civic obligation.
I would ask which program he thinks is worth watching.
A familiar screen can hold a little shared window for a town.
His enthusiasm makes me curious what he has been seeing.
I would like to know which broadcast first caught his attention.

contexts.subject: A bystander near Sterns interview excitedly wonders whether they are on television.

SlateportCity_Text_AmIOnTV.text: Hey! Are you watching?\nAm I on TV?$

replies.text: The camera found one interview and several people hoping to be the background.
The field of view may include bystanders. Recognition is another matter.

I would suddenly forget what to do with my hands.
They seem pleased just to be part of the moment.
An extra has discovered the possibility of an entirely accidental debut.
The fame has not arrived yet, but the waving appears ready.
It depends where the camera is pointed. Quite a practical question.
A small chance of being seen can make a person wonderfully lively.
Background presence can still make someone's whole afternoon.
I love noticing people who suddenly realize the camera is there.

contexts.subject: A Devon researcher eagerly accepts a fossil to begin their work.

RustboroCity_DevonCorp_2F_Text_HandedFos.text: Excellent!\nLet's do this right away.\p{PLAYER} handed the {STR_VAR_1} to\nthe DEVON RESEARCHER.$

replies.text: Our old little fossil has found somebody very excited to give it a future.
A promising specimen has reached someone equipped to investigate it.
Good. Let the researcher get to work.
They sound so pleased to have something new to study.
We brought it to someone who seems ready to care for the task.
A piece of the distant past has entered an unexpectedly energetic appointment.
The fossil has traded a quiet bag for a very busy desk.
I would love to see the equipment they use for this work.
An old shape may be ready to tell us something new.
That enthusiasm makes the handoff feel very well placed.
I would ask what they examine first before we leave them to it.

contexts.subject: A contest receptionist holds a prize for later collection.

LilycoveCity_ContestLobby_Text_ComeBackF.text: Please come back for your prize\nlater on.$

replies.text: Our prize has a safe place to wait. The victory is already ours.
The collection is deferred, rather than the result being lost.
We can come back. Remember to collect it.
It is reassuring that they will keep it for us.
A reward can wait until we are ready to carry it.
The award ceremony has encountered a very manageable scheduling note.
Our winnings have been granted temporary accommodation.
Good to know the prize can be collected after we sort things out.
The pleased feeling need not wait beside the physical prize.
A patient little arrangement for something already earned.
I would make a point of returning before the day gets away from us.

contexts.subject: The receptionist explains that G-Mode needs a cable rather than a wireless adapter.

LilycoveCity_ContestLobby_Text_NoWireles.text: I'm terribly sorry.\pG-MODE does not function\nwith Wireless Adapters.\pPlease select E-MODE or try\nagain using a GBA Game Link cable.$

replies.text: The mode and the connector disagree. At least they told us which one to change.
A specific compatibility requirement. We need the appropriate connection or mode.
Wrong setup. Change the mode or use the cable.
That is much easier than guessing why it will not start.
A little clear guidance saves everyone another frustrating try.
Our grand linked entrance has been delayed by an exceptionally small connector.
The invisible connection has failed to satisfy a very visible rule.
Clear fault report, clear alternatives. I appreciate that.
Some doors open only when the little pieces match.
An awkward mismatch with a pleasantly straightforward explanation.
I would check the setup before asking them to try again.

contexts.subject: A minigame attendant accepts a canceled game and invites another visit.

replies.text: No game this time. We can save our heroic button presses for later.
A canceled attempt need not make the next visit awkward.
Another time. We can leave it there.
I like a place that lets you change your mind.
An outing can still be good without doing every activity.
Our planned diversion concludes before requiring a score.
We have narrowly escaped having our coordination quantified.
A later try might suit us better. Simple enough.
An open invitation can be left gently for another day.
A pleasant goodbye makes returning easy.
I would come back when everyone actually wants to play.

contexts.subject: A minigame attendant explains small grounded Pokemon skipping Vine Whip together in time.

MossdeepCity_GameCorner_1F_Text_PokemonJ.text:
“POKéMON JUMP”\pMake your POKéMON skip the VINE WHIP
rope with the A Button.\pOnly mini POKéMON around 28 inches
or less may participate.\pPOKéMON that only swim, burrow,
or fly are not good at jumping.\pAs a result, those POKéMON may not
participate.\pGood things happen if everyone
jumps in time.$

replies.text: Tiny jumpers, one rope, many chances to discover who was daydreaming.
Size and movement restrictions make sense for a synchronized jumping game.
Choose someone suited to jumping. Watch the timing.
That sounds fun once everyone finds the same rhythm.
A little coordination can turn a simple game into a lovely group activity.
A tiny ensemble of jumpers faces one extremely punctual vine.
A very small contest with excellent opportunities for public mistiming.
Shared timing is the interesting challenge, beyond just getting airborne.
A little leap feels different when everyone rises together.
Small participants deserve a game made for their own scale.
I would watch a round to see how they keep one another in time.

contexts.subject: An attendant explains directing Dodrios three heads to catch falling berries.

MossdeepCity_GameCorner_1F_Text_DodrioBe.text:
“DODRIO BERRY-PICKING”\pCommand DODRIO's three heads to
catch falling BERRIES.\pPress right, up, or left on the
{PLUS} Control Pad to move the heads.\pTo play this game, you must have
a DODRIO.$

replies.text: Three hungry heads and one person trying to organize lunch. Good luck.
A three-direction response task should be an interesting coordination test.
Watch the berries. Give each head a clear direction.
I would probably apologize to the head I forgot.
Three heads at snack time sounds like a very busy kitchen.
A culinary drama in which all three leading roles share one body.
An entire argument about berries, now available as a game.
Three controlled inputs and moving targets. I would enjoy trying that.
Each head gets its own little moment to notice and reach.
Three competing appetites are a remarkable challenge to coordinate.
I would love to see how differently the heads react to a missed berry.

contexts.subject: A helper directs prospective minigame players to the old man beside them.

MossdeepCity_GameCorner_1F_Text_TalkToOl.text: If you want to play a game,\nplease tell the old man beside me.$

replies.text: We asked the explanation person. The starting person is one person over.
A helpful distinction between information and arranging the game.
Talk to the old man next. Clear enough.
That was a kind way to point us in the right direction.
A little guidance can save a lot of standing around.
Our inquiry has been transferred a very manageable distance.
An impressively short referral through the local bureaucracy.
The instructions and the controls have different caretakers.
One small direction can make an unfamiliar place easier.
A clear next step is always a useful finishing touch.
I would thank the helper before speaking to the old man.

contexts.subject: The minigame attendant says the wireless adapter must be connected before returning.

MossdeepCity_GameCorner_1F_Text_AdapterN.text: The Wireless Adapter isn't connected.\nCome back when it's hooked up!$

replies.text: The wireless part still needs a piece attached. That is a sneaky detail.
The required adapter must be present before the connection can work.
Connect the adapter first. Then try again.
At least there is a clear reason it would not start.
We can sort the equipment before asking for another try.
Our wireless adventure has encountered a decidedly physical missing piece.
The connection has declined to transcend the need for its own hardware.
A missing component is a nice straightforward problem to identify.
A little gap in the arrangement can stop the whole thing.
One small accessory has turned out to be the essential one.
I would check everything is fitted before we return.

contexts.subject: The game designer encourages continuing the Pokedex and returning when complete; terminal on incomplete-Dex branch.

LilycoveCity_CoveLilyMotel_2F_Text_ShowM.text:
I'm the GAME DESIGNER.\pOh, is that right?
You're working on a POKéDEX?\pIt's tough trying to complete it,
but don't give up.\pIf you do complete it, please come
show me.$

replies.text: A big project, and someone interested in seeing the finish. That helps.
A long observational task benefits from patience and consistent records.
Keep at it. No need to finish everything today.
I like having someone who wants to see the work when it is ready.
A little progress on an ordinary day still counts.
The unfinished collection has acquired an encouraging future reviewer.
Completion can take its time. The world has many small moving subjects.
A good record grows through careful observations, not just a rushed count.
A patient curiosity can carry us a very long way.
A complete collection begins with noticing each individual well.
I would enjoy showing them the discoveries that surprised us most.

contexts.subject: The Day-Care Woman accepts a Pokemon for care; terminal only when this fills the second care slot.

Route117_PokemonDayCare_Text_WellRaiseYo.text: Fine, we'll raise your {STR_VAR_1}\nfor a while.\pCome back for it later.$

replies.text: Our friend has a place to stay. We should remember to come check on them.
The care arrangement is in place. A later visit will let us assess the stay.
They have our partner. We come back for them.
I hope the stay gives them something pleasant to do.
It is good to know someone will be watching over them.
A brief separation begins with a clear promise of a return.
Our partner has acquired temporary accommodation and a very important reservation.
We should keep track of the arrangement and plan the return visit.
Leaving gently includes remembering to return.
A little stay should end with a proper, cheerful reunion.
I would like to hear how our partner settles in.

contexts.subject: A former traveling trainer now takes pleasure in watching younger trainers battle.

SootopolisCity_MysteryEventsHouse_1F_Tex.text: When I was young, I traveled the world\nas a POKéMON TRAINER.\pNow that I've become an old buzzard,\nmy only amusement is watching young\lTRAINERS battle.$

replies.text: He has plenty of old adventures and still enjoys seeing new ones happen.
Watching can remain rewarding after a long career of participating.
He earned a seat. Hope he sees a good match.
I would like to hear one of his own travel stories.
Sharing the excitement can still make for a lovely afternoon.
The old adventurer has become an appreciative audience for the next generation.
He has found the comfortable side of competitive battling.
Experience must make certain little choices especially interesting to watch.
A journey can change shape without losing all its joy.
A good spectator brings a lifetime of appreciation to the room.
I wonder what he notices now that he missed as a young trainer.

contexts.subject: The older host is disappointed when the player declines a visiting-trainer battle.

SootopolisCity_MysteryEventsHouse_1F_Tex.text: You won't battle? I'm disappointed\nthat I can't see you battle…$

replies.text: He wanted a good match. We can still choose when we are ready.
The spectator's disappointment does not obligate a participant.

contexts.subject: A July fifth diary records discovering a new Pokemon deep in a Guyana jungle.

PokemonMansion_1F_Text_NewMonDiscoveredI.text: Diary: July 5\nGuyana, South America\pA new POKéMON was discovered deep\nin the jungle.$

replies.text: They must have been so excited when they wrote this. I wonder what happened after that.
The entry gives a date and a location, but little about the observation itself.
An exciting discovery. It still deserved careful handling.
You can almost hear someone trying to fit an enormous day onto a small page.
I hope their first thought included whether the Pokemon was all right.
A confident beginning, found in a house that makes us uneasy about the rest.
The beginning sounds so much brighter than the room it was left in.
A field discovery needs records detailed enough for someone else to check.
A living thing existed before someone arrived to call it a discovery.
They found something new to them. That does not mean it became theirs.

contexts.subject: A July tenth diary records naming the newly discovered Pokemon Mew.

PokemonMansion_1F_Text_ChristenedDiscove.text: Diary: July 10\nWe christened the newly discovered\lPOKéMON, MEW.$

replies.text: Mew. A tiny name for a day somebody clearly wanted to remember.
Assigning a name helps a record, but is only the beginning of understanding the subject.

A short name, preserved long after the hand that wrote it left.

A name placed beside a mystery, without making the mystery smaller.

This feels like the sort of entry that once made its writer smile.

contexts.subject: A February sixth diary records Mew giving birth and naming the newborn Mewtwo.

PokemonMansion_1F_Text_MewGaveBirthToMew.text: Diary: Feb. 6\nMEW gave birth.\pWe named the newborn MEWTWO.$

replies.text: A newborn should have had someone looking out for it, however extraordinary it was.

A new life needed care. Power would not change that.

New life means responsibility, not just an exciting result.
A newborn enters the record already defined in relation to someone else.
A name with a number in it can carry a very heavy expectation.

contexts.subject: A September first diary calls Mewtwo too powerful and says attempts to curb its vicious tendencies failed.

PokemonMansion_B1F_Text_MewtwoIsFarTooPo.text: Diary: Sept. 1\nMEWTWO is far too powerful.\pWe have failed to curb its vicious\ntendencies…$

Whatever happened, a living creature needed more than people becoming afraid of their own responsibility.
The record has turned from discovery to control. That change deserves our attention.
The page names the creature dangerous. It leaves its own authors curiously unexamined.
A failed attempt at control needs investigation, including conditions and treatment.
A frightened page can preserve fear without preserving the whole truth.

I want to know what happened between the hopeful entries and this one.

contexts.subject: The exhibit identifies a rare ancient Aerodactyl fossil.

PewterCity_Museum_1F_Text_AerodactylFoss.text: AERODACTYL Fossil\nA primitive and rare POKéMON.$

replies.text: That once belonged to something that could move through the sky. Hard to picture it being still.

An entrance preserved for ages after its performer left.
A long silence, shaped like something that once crossed the sky.
Physical remains can answer some questions and make entirely new ones.
Stone keeping the outline of a life the sky no longer remembers.

contexts.subject: The exhibit identifies a rare ancient Kabutops fossil.

PewterCity_Museum_1F_Text_KabutopsFossil.text: KABUTOPS Fossil\nA primitive and rare POKéMON.$

replies.text: I am glad we can admire those sharp bits from this side of history.

An old life, with edges the years have not made gentle.

Something from very far away, ending up close enough for a child to point at.

A celestial arrival, followed by the much slower business of figuring out what arrived.
A long fall, ending in a small label with an honest uncertainty.

The sky left something behind, and the mountain gave it a place to land.

contexts.subject: The museum display is labelled Space Shuttle.

replies.text: Someone looked all the way up and decided walking would not be enough.

A journey that makes packing lunch look wonderfully straightforward.
The largest possible answer to wanting to get out of the house.
An enormous machine built around a very old habit of looking up.

A vessel built for a place where no ordinary road can be made.

contexts.subject: A club member looks forward to hearing more about the player on another visit.

Text_TellMoreNextTime.text: Please tell me more about\nyourself next time!$

replies.text: We have left a little room in the conversation for the next hello.
An open-ended invitation encourages a future visit without requiring immediate disclosure.

contexts.subject: A club member calls the player fickle for cancelling a profile entry.

A cancel option ought to remain an acceptable outcome.

contexts.subject: A club member accepts the choice to leave the current profile unchanged.

A small unchanged thing can be an entirely deliberate decision.

contexts.subject: A club member pushes for a profile after the player declines to share one.

An optional profile should remain optional after the first refusal.

contexts.subject: A club member feels better acquainted with the player after receiving a profile.

contexts.subject: A club member says the profile reminds them of something a distant cousin used to say.

contexts.subject: A League checkpoint guard recognizes the required Badge and allows passage.

contexts.subject: A League guard refuses passage because the required Badge has not been earned.

contexts.subject: Oak's aide explains that an Everstone can prevent a Pokemon from evolving.

contexts.subject: The old woman accepts a declined visiting-trainer battle and invites the player to return.

contexts.subject: The minigame attendant reports that the required Wireless Adapter is not connected.

contexts.subject: The Tower receptionist thanks the returning player for competing.
