It is a small way of preparing with the team rather than only for them.
The right thing within reach is often more useful than a lot of things somewhere else.
The supporting cast has been granted its own practical wardrobe of equipment.
A small carried thing can quietly change the shape of a difficult moment.
Matching equipment to the job is more effective than assigning it at random.
A little object can become part of how a companion meets the road.
Useful is a better standard than giving everyone something merely to fill a place.
I wonder which item each trainer first learns to check without needing a reminder.

contexts.subject: A public notice asks for information about fossil thefts at Mt Moon.

PewterCity_Text_CallPoliceIfInfoOnThieve.text: NOTICE!\pThieves have been stealing POKéMON\nfossils from MT. MOON.\pPlease call the PEWTER POLICE if\nyou have any information.$

replies.text: Those fossils should be things people learn from, not things everyone has to worry about losing.
A report of theft deserves useful observations rather than speculation presented as evidence.
If we learn something definite, pass it to the people investigating.
It is sad to see something old and remarkable become the subject of an ordinary ugly theft.
Keeping a place's discoveries safe matters beyond the people who first found them.
An ancient history has been interrupted by a depressingly modern sort of greed.
The mountain has survived ages and still needs protection from somebody wanting a quick profit.
Specific facts will help more than turning every unfamiliar visitor into a suspect.
Old things have already endured enough without becoming prizes for careless hands.
Concern should make us attentive without making us reckless.
I wonder what details a hurried traveller might have noticed without realizing they mattered.

contexts.subject: A posted tip describes learning through participation in battle.

PewterCity_Text_TrainerTipsEarningEXP.text: TRAINER TIPS\pAll POKéMON that appear in battle,\nhowever briefly, earn EXP Points.$

replies.text: Even a short turn can leave somebody knowing a little more than before.
Experience is useful when the task gives the Pokemon a reasonable chance to learn safely.
Give the team practice they can handle. Nobody needs to be thrown in unprepared.
It is nice to think the brief attempts count, too.
A small chance to try something can matter without turning every lesson into an ordeal.
The supporting appearance has been granted some of the educational value of the main role.
A little time in the difficult part can still be time that teaches something.
We should judge readiness rather than treat participation itself as a complete plan.
A short step on an unfamiliar path can leave a lasting shape in the memory.
Improvement is easier to enjoy when every small beginning is allowed to matter.
I wonder which tiny first attempt each team member would choose to remember.

contexts.subject: A sign explains how to rearrange items in the Bag.

Route13_Text_SelectToSwitchItems.text: TRAINER TIPS\pUse SELECT to switch items in the\nITEMS window.$

replies.text: The Bag has a tidying option. I may need a separate sign explaining how to remember to use it.
A consistent arrangement can reduce the time spent searching when an item is needed.
Keep important supplies easy to find. Simple habit, useful later.
A little order can make an awkward moment feel much less hurried.
Put the things we use often where our hands expect them to be.
A practical note for preventing the dramatic search through an overambitious packing list.
A tidy bag is a small mercy for the future tired version of ourselves.
Clear ordering is useful precisely when there is less time to think about it.
An ordinary arrangement can become a quiet kind of reassurance.
Knowing where something is matters nearly as much as remembering to bring it.
I wonder which object always finds its way to the wrong end of the Bag despite our best plans.

contexts.subject: A sign playfully tells readers to look left of a nearby post.

Route13_Text_LookToLeftOfThatPost.text: TRAINER TIPS\pLook, look!\nLook to the left of that post!$

replies.text: A sign has stopped being a sign and started pointing excitedly like a person with a small secret.
A clear local direction is useful, provided we actually check which post it refers to.
Take a look without stomping through everything around it.
It is a friendly little way to make someone slow down and notice the roadside.
A small nudge of curiosity can turn an ordinary walk into a better afternoon.
The signwriter has supplied stage directions and an unusually enthusiastic cue.
A public notice has briefly become a conspirator.
Specific landmarks make a clue much more useful than vague encouragement.
A familiar post has acquired a little space worth looking toward.
I like the unembarrassed eagerness of somebody wanting a stranger to notice something.
I wonder how many people look exactly where they were told and smile at being guided there.

contexts.subject: A Cycling Road sign explains holding position on a slope.

Route17_Text_PressBToStayInPlace.text: TRAINER TIPS\pPress the B Button to stay in place\nwhile on a slope.$

replies.text: Excellent advice for discovering that the hill has its own travel plans.
Controlling movement on a slope is more useful than trying to correct excessive speed afterward.
Know how to stop before taking the slope fast.
I like a route that explains how to pause instead of assuming everyone wants to hurry.
A steady stop is a good chance to check where the next stretch leads.
The downhill adventure has wisely included a note about declining the downhill part.
Gravity is a very persistent travelling companion when nobody tells it to wait.
A reliable brake gives the rider more choice about the pace.
A slope is less demanding when we know how to ask it for a still moment.
Control is much more attractive than hoping to look confident while gathering speed.
I wonder how many riders learn to appreciate that little instruction after the first steep stretch.

contexts.subject: A tip emphasizes individual differences between Pokemon of the same species and level.

Route17_Text_SameSpeciesGrowDifferentRat.text: TRAINER TIPS\pAll POKéMON are unique.\pEven POKéMON of the same species\nand level grow at different rates.$

replies.text: Matching names do not make matching little lives. That seems worth putting on a sign.
A broad category cannot capture every difference between individuals. Observation remains important.
Learn the companion in front of us instead of expecting it to match a chart perfectly.
It is comforting to know that being different is part of being ordinary, too.
Two things can share a name and still need a different amount of time and attention.
The cast has declined to be manufactured from a single reusable character sheet.
A tidy label has once again failed to contain an entire living thing.
Adjust the plan to actual results instead of forcing the results to fit the plan.
Two seeds of the same kind need not reach toward the light in exactly the same way.
Comparison is useful until it makes us stop noticing the individual.
I wonder which small difference a caring trainer learns to recognize before anyone else does.

contexts.subject: A Safari Zone tip explains how to check the remaining allowance.

SafariZone_Center_Text_PressStartToCheck.text: TRAINER TIPS\pPress START to check\nremaining time.$

replies.text: A little reminder to ask the clock how the adventure is actually going.
Checking the remaining allowance supports planning instead of relying on a vague sense of time.
Know what we have left before choosing a longer route.
It feels calmer to check once than keep worrying without knowing.
Leave enough of the visit for getting back comfortably.
The excursion has included a discreet invitation to consult its less romantic accounting.
An honest number is sometimes kinder than an optimistic guess.
A visible limit makes it easier to compare the route with the remaining opportunity.
A little measure can keep the day from slipping away entirely unnoticed.
Planning is more pleasant than being surprised by the end.
I wonder how many visitors only remember that instruction when they wish they had read it earlier.

contexts.subject: A Safari sign explains that the visit's allowance is spent by walking.

SafariZone_East_Text_TimeDeclinesOnlyWhi.text: TRAINER TIPS\pThe remaining time declines only\nwhile you walk.$

replies.text: Thinking has been given a rather generous discount compared with wandering in circles.
The notice makes route choice important. A considered pause can prevent unnecessary travel.
Decide where we are going before spending steps getting there.
I like an invitation to stop and look carefully rather than hurry past everything.
A brief plan can save enough wandering to make the visit more enjoyable.
The expedition has discovered that contemplation is its most economical mode of travel.
A rare institution that appears willing to subsidize standing thoughtfully.
Check the map and make each stretch purposeful instead of repeatedly backtracking.
A still moment can hold more of the place than a hurried lap around it.
There is something pleasant about being allowed to pause without losing the afternoon to haste.
I wonder what visitors notice when they finally stop counting the path and actually look around.

contexts.subject: Safari Zone notices encourage searching for the Secret House.

SafariZone_North_Text_SecretHouseStillAh.text: TRAINER TIPS\pThe SECRET HOUSE is still ahead.$

SafariZone_West_Text_SearchForSecretHous.text: TRAINER TIPS\pZone Exploration Campaign!\nThe Search for the SECRET HOUSE!$

replies.text: A secret house with an advertising campaign. I admire the confidence of that secret.
The notices establish an intended destination, but we still need to navigate the actual route.
Keep track of the route as we search. No need to wander blindly.
A little destination can make a large unfamiliar area feel easier to approach.
A search is more pleasant when we leave ourselves a sensible way back.
The hidden location has secured unusually enthusiastic publicity.
A secret can remain elusive while being astonishingly bad at staying unmentioned.
Use the landmarks instead of treating the whole area as equally likely.
A little house has become a question at the far edge of the path.
The promise gives the walk some direction without taking away all the curiosity.
I wonder how many people remember the search more fondly than arriving at the house.

contexts.subject: A Safari tip recommends exploring tall grass to find hidden Pokemon.

SafariZone_North_Text_ZigzagThroughTallG.text: TRAINER TIPS\pPOKéMON hide in tall grass.\pZigzag through grassy areas to\nflush them out.$

replies.text: The grass contains more neighbours than it puts on the path's welcome committee.
Searching suitable habitat is more informative than expecting every Pokemon to appear in the open.
Watch our footing and do not rush through the whole patch.
It is nice to remember that the quiet grass can be full of lives we have not seen.
A careful look is better than trampling everything in a hurry to find something.
The notice recommends meeting the supporting cast where they actually live.
An apparently empty patch has refused to be summarized by the first glance.
A varied search path covers more ground than repeatedly checking the same edge.
The green has kept little spaces that our eyes cannot see from the road.
Curiosity should still leave the habitat in decent condition behind it.
I wonder which rustle belongs to the Pokemon and which is simply the grass making its own noise.

contexts.subject: A notice offers an HM for finding the Safari Secret House.

SafariZone_North_Text_WinFreeHMFindSecre.text: TRAINER TIPS\pWin a free HM for finding the\nSECRET HOUSE.$

replies.text: A walk with a useful prize waiting at the end. The house has a very effective invitation.
The reward is conditional on reaching the destination. Reading the notice does not award it.
A useful goal, if we are ready for the route.
I like when a challenge rewards looking around instead of only winning a battle.
The promised gift is worth planning for rather than rushing blindly toward.
The hidden house has added a practical epilogue to its adventure pitch.
A prize can make an old-fashioned walk suddenly acquire much more plot.
We should navigate carefully and verify the actual condition on arrival.
A little destination has hung a promise where the path can see it.
The reward should add to enjoying the visit, not turn it into a frantic obligation.
I wonder whether people arrive more pleased with the prize or with finally finding the way.

contexts.subject: A notice requests the Warden's lost Gold Teeth and offers a reward.

SafariZone_West_Text_PleaseFindWardensLo.text: REQUEST NOTICE\pPlease find the SAFARI WARDEN's\nlost GOLD TEETH.\lThey're around here somewhere.\pReward offered!\nContact: WARDEN$

replies.text: A very personal rescue mission has been printed in remarkably official lettering.
The notice identifies a specific lost object and an owner to return it to. Useful information.
If we find them, get them back to him. He clearly needs them.
It must have taken a little courage to make that problem so public.
Helping him get through an ordinary day seems a good enough reason to look.
The administrative notice has unexpectedly become an intimate tale of missing dental equipment.
A small public embarrassment may be hiding a very inconvenient private day.
A clear description and contact make a lost-item notice much easier to act on.
A person has put a small vulnerable part of the day into strangers' care.
The reward is less important than not turning his difficulty into a joke at his expense.
I wonder how relieved he will be when somebody walks in with what he thought was lost.

contexts.subject: A sign recommends Great Balls for difficult wild Pokemon captures.

SaffronCity_Text_GreatBallImprovedCatchR.text: TRAINER TIPS\pThe new GREAT BALL offers improved\ncatching rates.\pTry it on those hard-to-catch\nPOKéMON.$

replies.text: The helpful sign would like us to know there is a fancier answer to a very persistent escape artist.
A better capture chance is useful, though it remains a probability rather than a promise.
Prepare before the encounter. Do not count on any single throw.
It is nice to have options when repeated attempts are becoming frustrating.
We can choose supplies that suit the trip without buying only the most expensive answer.
The shop has offered a more distinguished container for our uncertain hopes.
A little improvement in chance need not become a certainty in the retelling.
Compare the situation and the cost instead of assuming one item is always the right choice.
A better net still leaves the world some say in what stays.
A clear benefit is useful; an advertising promise deserves its own careful look.
I wonder which encounter makes people finally appreciate the difference between possible and likely.

contexts.subject: A posted tip recommends Full Heal for several kinds of status trouble.

SaffronCity_Text_FullHealCuresStatus.text: TRAINER TIPS\pFULL HEAL cures all ailments like\nburns, paralysis, poisoning,\lfreezing, and sleep.\pIt costs a bit more, but it's more\nconvenient than buying other items.$

replies.text: One bottle trying to solve several different bad afternoons. A useful sort of ambition.
The convenience is covering several status conditions with one item, not replacing every other kind of care.
Useful supply. Still check what the team actually needs.
It is reassuring to have an answer ready before a companion is struggling.
A simpler supply list can help, provided we remember what the item does not cover.
A versatile supporting player, advertised with commendable confidence.
Convenience is valuable when it prevents confusion rather than replacing attention.
A flexible tool can reduce packing complexity, but understanding its limits still matters.
One small preparation can soften several different ways a day turns difficult.
Practical convenience is worth considering alongside the price.
I wonder which item experienced travellers learn to check before they leave town.

contexts.subject: A warning marks water with a dangerous fast current.

TwoIsland_Text_DangerFastCurrent.text: DANGER! FAST CURRENT!\nFishing and surfing prohibited!$

replies.text: The water has supplied a moving argument, and somebody was kind enough to add a written one.
A fast current can exceed the control a swimmer or rider expects to have. The warning deserves respect.
Do not test that current for fun. Find the safe route.
I am glad someone thought to warn the next person before the danger became obvious too late.
Getting through safely is worth more than saving a few steps.
The scenery has posted a rather firm objection to becoming our shortcut.
Water does not need to look angry to be stronger than us.
Observe the flow and follow the warning instead of treating ability as immunity.
A bright surface can carry a hard pull beneath it.
Confidence is less useful here than accepting good information.
I wonder how much trouble that plain little sign has prevented without anyone ever knowing.

contexts.subject: A police notice warns of a possible sleeping-Pokemon blockage and suggests a detour through Rock Tunnel.

VermilionCity_Text_SnorlaxBlockingRoute1.text: NOTICE!\pROUTE 12 may be blocked off by a\nsleeping POKéMON.\pDetour through ROCK TUNNEL to\nLAVENDER TOWN.\pVERMILION POLICE$

replies.text: The police have found a very official way to say that a nap may be controlling the traffic.
The notice offers an alternative route for a possible obstruction, not confirmation of the route's current state.
Check the situation before committing to the longer way. Prepare properly if we take the tunnel.
A detour feels less frustrating when somebody explains why it might be needed.
The suggested route deserves its own supply check, not just a quick change of direction.
A sleeping obstacle has become large enough to acquire a police-authored travel advisory.
An entire journey can be revised by someone else's very committed nap.
A useful alternate route still needs evaluating for our team's readiness.
A small sheet of words is helping the road find a way around a great sleeping shape.
It is considerate to offer another option instead of merely announcing a problem.
I wonder how many travellers changed their whole afternoon after stopping to read that notice.

contexts.subject: A forest tip recommends avoiding encounter areas when the team is tired.

ViridianForest_Text_AvoidGrassyAreasWhen.text: TRAINER TIPS\pIf your POKéMON are weak and you\nwant to avoid battles, stay away\lfrom grassy areas!$

replies.text: The grass is still full of challenges even when our companions would rather be full of rest.
Reducing avoidable encounters is sensible when the team's current condition is poor.
Get the team rested before looking for another battle.
A quiet way back can be a kindness after a difficult stretch.
Being prepared includes knowing when the next useful stop is a place to recover.
The adventure has recommended an intermission instead of another unnecessary confrontation.
A tired team should not have to argue with every rustling patch on the way home.
Choose a route that fits the team's condition rather than the route that fits our impatience.
The path can ask less of us if we stop asking too much of those beside us.
Good judgment is more attractive than insisting we always have another fight in us.
I wonder which trainer first learned that a careful retreat can be the kindest decision of the day.

contexts.subject: A posted tip explains that Oak can evaluate the Pokedex through a PC.

ViridianForest_Text_ContactOakViaPCToRat.text: TRAINER TIPS\pContact PROF. OAK via a PC to\nget your POKéDEX evaluated!$

replies.text: A progress report without making the notebook walk all the way back to the professor. Handy.
Remote evaluation makes an ongoing research task easier to review between field visits.
We can check the record when we reach a suitable place to stop.
It is nice that somebody remains interested in what we are noticing along the way.
A little outside perspective can help us plan the next part of the trip.
The travelling researcher can submit the current chapter without delivering the author in person.
A small convenience for a task that involves rather a lot of walking.
Regular feedback can help turn a large collection goal into manageable next steps.
A distant familiar voice can still put a little light on the path ahead.
A useful assessment should help the journey, not make every quiet day feel graded.
I wonder which discovery we would be most eager to tell him about instead of merely count.

contexts.subject: A forest notice explains that another trainer's Pokemon cannot be caught.

ViridianForest_Text_CantCatchOwnedMons.text: TRAINER TIPS\pYou can't catch a POKéMON that\nbelongs to someone else.\pThrow POKé BALLS only at wild\nPOKéMON to catch them!$

replies.text: Meeting a wonderful Pokemon does not make its entire existing life available for us to pack up.
The notice distinguishes a wild encounter from somebody else's established partnership.
Respect the companion and the person it came with.
It would feel awful to have a stranger treat a friend as something to collect.
Admiring someone else's team is not the same as being entitled to it.
An appealing character does not become ours simply because we have decided we like the role.
Wanting something is a poor argument for erasing everyone already attached to it.
A clear boundary saves us from treating every encounter as the same kind of opportunity.
A life already walking beside someone is not an empty place in our own story.
A little admiration can remain perfectly pleasant without becoming possessive.
I would rather hear how a trainer and Pokemon met than imagine taking the place between them.

contexts.subject: A forest tip recommends weakening wild Pokemon before attempting capture.

ViridianForest_Text_WeakenMonsBeforeCapt.text: TRAINER TIPS\pWeaken POKéMON before attempting\ncapture!\pWhen healthy, they may escape!$

replies.text: A practical tip, with the important bit being not to let excitement run the whole encounter.
Improving capture conditions can help, though the trainer still needs control over the encounter.
Plan carefully. Do not let a promising encounter become a careless scramble.
I hope people remember there is a living creature in the situation, not only an empty Ball.
A calm approach makes it easier to notice when to stop.
The would-be collector has been advised to prepare the scene rather than improvise every cue.
Enthusiasm is not famous for measuring its own strength accurately.
Choose an approach that offers control rather than relying on a forceful guess.
A new meeting deserves more care than the hurry to make it ours.
Getting what we wanted should not be the only measure of whether we handled the encounter well.
I wonder which small choice experienced trainers learn to make before the excitement takes over.

contexts.subject: A notice recommends packing Antidotes for poisoning.

ViridianForest_Text_UseAntidoteForPoison.text: For poison, use ANTIDOTE!\nGet it at POKéMON MARTS!$

replies.text: A small practical item is much nicer to remember before the forest makes it relevant.
Matching a remedy to the specific status condition avoids relying on an unsuitable item.
Check our supplies before heading farther in.
It is reassuring to know there is something ready when a companion needs help.
A modest bit of preparation can make a rough stretch much less unpleasant.
An unglamorous supporting item has received a thoroughly deserved piece of publicity.
A small bottle may be the least exciting and most welcome thing in a bag.
A clear label helps when the situation is already distracting.
Some kinds of care begin quietly before anybody is hurting.
Useful preparation need not be impressive to be worth doing.
I wonder which supply every experienced forest traveller checks twice before leaving the shop.

contexts.subject: A Safari Zone sign identifies a rest house.

replies.text: An excellent destination for feet that have developed a persuasive argument against further enthusiasm.
A designated rest point makes the visit easier to pace sensibly.
A good place to pause and check the team.
I like seeing a route make room for being tired.
A proper pause can make the rest of the visit feel new again.
The excursion has thoughtfully provided a setting for its intermission.
A small shelter can become the most attractive exhibit in the park.
We can use the stop to consider the next route instead of wandering without a plan.
A place to be still belongs on a map of a good journey.
Rest looks much better when nobody has to pretend it was not needed.
I wonder how many visitors arrive only wanting a seat and leave ready to look around again.

contexts.subject: Binoculars reveal a large Pokemon asleep on a road.

Route11_EastEntrance_2F_Text_BigMonAslee.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pA big POKéMON is asleep on a road!$

replies.text: From here the roadblock looks rather peaceful. I expect the people walking around it disagree.
The distant view confirms a sleeping obstacle without telling us how best to resolve it.
Useful to know before choosing the route. Do not rush there without a plan.
It is strange how something inconvenient can look so calm from far away.
We can prepare an alternative route rather than arrive annoyed at a sleeping creature.
The distant landscape has acquired a very substantial resting protagonist.
A magnificent nap is quietly rearranging several people's afternoons.
A view from above can reveal a route problem before we commit to it.
The road has been borrowed by a little island of sleep.
It is better to notice the obstruction now than blame the sleeper when we reach it.
I wonder how many people have looked through here and recognized the reason for their detour.

contexts.subject: The gatehouse binoculars offer a breathtaking view.

Route11_EastEntrance_2F_Text_WhatABreath.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pWhat a breathtaking view!$

replies.text: The world was doing all of that while we were busy looking at our own shoes.
A broader view can make relationships between familiar landmarks much easier to see.
Worth stopping for. We have time to look.
Some views make me want to be quiet without feeling shy about it.
A little pause can be a proper part of the journey, not merely a delay.
The scenery has earned its extravagant establishing shot.
A large enough view gives an ordinary worry a little less room.
I like seeing how the separate pieces of the route fit together.
The distance has made a little space inside the afternoon.
It is lovely to find something that holds attention without demanding it.
I would like to notice what changes in the scene while we stand still.

contexts.subject: The binocular view suggests Rock Tunnel as a route between Cerulean and Lavender.

Route11_EastEntrance_2F_Text_RockTunnelG.text:
Let's see what the binoculars have
to show…\pTo get to LAVENDER TOWN from
CERULEAN CITY…\pROCK TUNNEL appears to be a good
route to take.$

replies.text: A distant route can look wonderfully simple until you remember it goes through a mountain.

We should plan for the tunnel itself, not only the towns it connects.
The landscape has provided the outline of a chapter while discreetly withholding its difficult middle.
A line between two places can contain a surprising amount of darkness.
A useful overview needs closer practical information before becoming a complete plan.
The mountain is a bridge in the map's language and a mountain in ours.
Distance makes almost every route look tidier than it feels underfoot.
I wonder which landmark will look familiar from the road after seeing it from here.

contexts.subject: The binoculars show a man fishing.

Route12_NorthEntrance_2F_Text_TheresManF.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pThere's a man fishing!$

replies.text: A whole person somewhere is having a very different pace of afternoon from us.
A distant ordinary activity can be as interesting as a dramatic landmark.

A patient afternoon by the water sounds like a perfectly good plan.
A small human scene has taken precedence over the grand landscape.
Someone else's unhurried day has briefly entered ours.
It is useful to remember the landscape is lived in, not just travelled across.
A still figure has made the distant shore feel less empty.
The ordinary little moment gives the view something warm to settle around.

Route12_NorthEntrance_2F_Text_ItsPokemon.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pIt's POKéMON TOWER!$

replies.text: The tower is easy to spot from here. A landmark can carry more than directions.

The tower keeps its place on the horizon and many other places in memory.
Not every striking landmark is simply scenery for visitors.

contexts.subject: A large shining bird is seen flying toward the sea through the binoculars.

Route15_WestEntrance_2F_Text_LargeShinin.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pA large, shining bird is flying\ntoward the sea.$

replies.text: Oh! That is a very impressive piece of the sky to catch moving past.

A surprise like that can make the whole walk feel richer.
The scenery has briefly admitted a guest far too striking to remain background.
A bright shape has crossed the distance and improved the afternoon without staying for applause.
The glimpse is worth remembering carefully before excitement adds details we did not see.
The sky has let a small bright secret pass where we could notice it.
Some things are lovelier for not stopping to belong to the person watching.

contexts.subject: A small island can be seen on the horizon.

Route15_WestEntrance_2F_Text_SmallIsland.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pIt looks like a small island on\nthe horizon!$

contexts.subject: The Celadon Department Store can be seen through the binoculars.

Route16_NorthEntrance_2F_Text_ItsCeladon.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pIt's the CELADON DEPT. STORE!$

contexts.subject: A long path over the water is visible in the distance.

Route16_NorthEntrance_2F_Text_LongPathOv.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pThere's a long path over water far\naway.$

replies.text: Somebody looked at all that water and decided the walk should continue anyway.

contexts.subject: The binocular view places Pallet Town to the west.

Route18_EastEntrance_2F_Text_PalletTownI.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pPALLET TOWN is in the west.$

replies.text: A familiar name has found a small place on a very large view.

contexts.subject: People can be seen swimming in the distance.

Route18_EastEntrance_2F_Text_PeopleSwimm.text: Let's see what the binoculars have\nto show…\pThere are people swimming.$

contexts.subject: A fisherman's chart records the largest Magikarp measured so far.

Route12_FishingHouse_Text_MostGiganticMa.text: The most gigantic MAGIKARP\nI have ever witnessed…\p{STR_VAR_3}!$

contexts.subject: A new bicycle gleams in the shop display.

contexts.subject: Damage left by Team Rocket provides a way out of the robbed house.

CeruleanCity_House2_Text_TeamRocketLeftW.text: TEAM ROCKET left a way out!$

contexts.subject: The player leaves the vending machine without buying a drink.

contexts.subject: The slot machine cannot be used without a Coin Case.

No game here right now. Plenty of other ways to spend the afternoon.
A practical pause gives us room to decide whether we actually wanted to play.
We do not have to turn every missing requirement into an urgent shopping errand.
The entertainment has been postponed before it could become an expensive commitment.
An absent little container has briefly become excellent financial advice.
The access requirement is clear. It does not make participation necessary.
A closed small door can leave a more peaceful path open beside it.
It is all right to let this remain an activity we walked past.
I wonder how different the room feels once we stop treating every bright machine as an invitation.

contexts.subject: The player decides not to press the Mansion's secret switch yet.

replies.text: An unknown button has been asked to wait until we have thought past the satisfying click.
Deferring an unfamiliar mechanism is reasonable while its effects remain unclear.
Look at the surroundings before pressing it.
I like that not yet can be a thoughtful answer instead of a failure of curiosity.
A little patience can prevent a lot of wandering back to fix an avoidable choice.
The dramatic mechanism has been denied its cue pending a closer reading of the scene.
A mysterious switch is not owed the pleasure of being pushed immediately.
Try to understand what might move before deciding to activate it.
A small dormant thing can keep its promise of movement a little longer.
A measured pause looks better than treating every mechanism as a dare.
I wonder which detail nearby will tell us most about what that switch controls.

contexts.subject: The player presses a secret Mansion switch and changes the mechanism's state.

replies.text: The temptation has won. I hope we were paying attention to what the rooms looked like before.
The switch changes a mechanism state. We should compare the surroundings rather than assume every change helps.
Check what moved before choosing the next route.
A familiar room feels less certain once something inside it has changed.
Worth remembering the way back while we work out the new arrangement.
The concealed control has received its cue and rearranged the practical scenery.
A click is a small sound for something that can make a whole route unfamiliar.
Observe the result carefully so the change becomes information instead of only surprise.
An old house has shifted one of its quiet little choices.
Curiosity is more useful when it remembers to inspect the result.
I wonder which doorway will make the effect clearest when we look around again.

contexts.subject: The hideout elevator cannot be used without its key.

RocketHideout_Elevator_Text_AppearsToNee.text: It appears to need a key.$

replies.text: The elevator has declined to go anywhere until a very particular small object joins us.
A missing key is the indicated obstacle. The control panel alone cannot resolve it.
Find the key. Stay alert while we look.
It helps to have a clear next question when the whole place feels unfamiliar.
We can check the route systematically instead of wearing ourselves out searching the same corner.
The building's vertical progress has been withheld pending a minor but essential prop.
A surprisingly small piece of absence can immobilize a large machine.
Look for the intended access method rather than experiment with the mechanism.
The lower places remain where they are while the threshold asks for its little tooth.
At least the problem is more specific than an unhelpful refusal to move.
I wonder who was meant to keep track of the key before our visit made that inconvenient.

contexts.subject: The two required passwords are entered and the warehouse door opens.

FiveIsland_Meadow_Text_EnteredPasswordDo.text: {PLAYER} entered two passwords.\p“GOLDEEN need log.”\n“Yes, nah, CHANSEY.”\p… …  … …  … …\pThe WAREHOUSE's door opened!$

replies.text: Two very peculiar phrases have persuaded a very serious door. Language is doing odd work today.
Both credentials have been supplied and the mechanism has confirmed access.
Open now. Stay prepared for what is inside.
It is a relief to finish the puzzle, even if the place beyond still feels uncertain.
A clear entrance is a good moment to check we are ready rather than rush.
The guarded threshold has accepted its two absurdly memorable lines of dialogue.
A secret can sound ridiculous and still do an effective job of keeping a door shut.
A completed two-part check has produced the intended mechanical response.
A little knot of words has loosened the place's outer boundary.
A successful entry is progress, not a reason to stop paying attention.
I wonder whether anyone choosing those passwords ever imagined a stranger patiently putting them together.

contexts.subject: A hint suggests that boulders may alter the flow of water.

SeafoamIslands_B4F_Text_BouldersMightCha.text: Hint: Boulders might change the\nflow of water.$

replies.text: The water may be asking for a much larger conversation piece than we first expected.
An obstruction can alter a current, but we should examine the geometry before moving anything.
Work out where the water will go before shifting a boulder.
It is a little daunting to realize the path and the problem are the same moving water.
A careful plan matters when a change can affect the whole route.
The cavern has supplied a stage direction for rearranging a rather forceful piece of scenery.
An inconvenient stone may be less inconvenient somewhere else. A dangerous amount of optimism, perhaps.
Watch the channels and compare possible routes for the flow. Movement should follow understanding.
The mountain may lend one of its still things to quiet a moving one.
A useful hint still deserves patience before being treated as a complete plan.
I wonder which small detail makes the intended flow visible once somebody knows to look for it.

contexts.subject: A canyon entrance notice asks trainers not to damage the plants.

SevenIsland_SevaultCanyon_Entrance_Text_.text: SEVAULT CANYON ENTRANCE\pTRAINERS are asked to refrain from\ndamaging plants in the CANYON.$

replies.text: A canyon visit should not leave the plants wishing the path had stayed less popular.
Plants can be damaged by repeated small disturbances even when no one visitor notices the cumulative effect.
Watch our feet and leave the plants where they are.
It is nice to see a welcome that remembers the things already living here.
We can enjoy the place without treating every growing thing as something to push through.
The destination has included a modest request that the audience not destroy the scenery.
A plant does not become disposable merely because it is standing beside a useful shortcut.
Choosing a sensible route reduces unnecessary damage before anyone has to repair it.
The green small lives have no other canyon to go home to.
A good visit should not make the next person's view worse.
I wonder which delicate little plant people miss when they only look up at the cliffs.

contexts.subject: A Green Path sign asks visitors to keep nature clean.

SixIsland_GreenPath_Text_RightRouteSign.text: GREEN PATH\nThink Green, Keep Nature Clean!$

replies.text: An excellent agreement: the path supplies the green, and we refrain from supplying the litter.
Leaving nothing behind is a practical way to avoid adding harm to the habitat.
Carry our rubbish out. Simple enough.
I like when a place asks for care without needing to make a grand speech.
Anything we brought in can make the return trip with us.
The sign has proposed a very reasonable bargain with the visiting cast.
The woods are under no obligation to become our discarded packaging department.
Preventing a mess takes much less work than collecting it afterward.
The path should keep only the brief shape of our footsteps.
Leaving a beautiful place beautiful is a rather basic form of good manners.
I wonder how different the path looks after a busy day when every visitor follows that little request.

contexts.subject: A forest notice warns that wild Pokemon are drawn to Berries.

replies.text: A Berry forest attracts Berry enthusiasts. We should probably have allowed for that in the guest list.
A food-rich habitat gives a clear reason to expect Pokemon in the area.
Stay aware and keep the team ready. We are not the only visitors here.
It helps to remember that a lovely place can also be somebody else's busy feeding ground.
We should notice what the local Pokemon are doing before reaching for everything that looks ripe.
The setting has warned us that its most attractive props come with an interested resident cast.
The forest has a pantry, and we are hardly its only customers.
Food availability influences where animals gather. That makes the warning practical.
A patch of sweetness can gather more footsteps than the ones we see.
A warning is useful when it reminds us to share a place rather than act as though we own it.
I wonder which small movement in the leaves will be the first clue to who else is enjoying the Berries.

contexts.subject: The Berry Forest welcome asks visitors to share with other people and Pokemon.

ThreeIsland_BerryForest_Text_WelcomeToBe.text: Welcome to the BERRY FOREST\pBe friendly and share BERRIES with\nothers and POKéMON.$

replies.text: A forest welcome that includes the important instruction not to become the entire Berry supply's owner.
Sharing the resource helps a pleasant place remain useful to more than the first person through it.
Take reasonably and leave enough for the others.
I like a welcome that makes us part of the company rather than the centre of it.
A sweet thing is often nicer when somebody else gets some, too.
The hospitality is generous enough to include both the visiting and resident cast.
A modest reminder that finding something first is not the same as needing all of it.
A shared resource works better when each visitor considers what remains after them.
A little sweetness can travel between several lives without becoming smaller in memory.
Good company begins with remembering there are others in the place.
I wonder which ordinary shared Berry becomes somebody's favourite memory of the walk.

contexts.subject: A Bond Bridge sign asks people to cross quietly on the way toward Berry Forest.

ThreeIsland_BondBridge_Text_BondBridgeSi.text: BOND BRIDGE\nPlease be quiet when crossing.\pBERRY FOREST AHEAD$

replies.text: The bridge has requested that we arrive in the forest with our voices still on their indoor setting.
Reducing noise can make the crossing less disruptive to the surrounding habitat.
Keep it quiet. We can listen while we walk.
A quiet crossing sounds like a lovely way to notice what is around the path.
There is something pleasant about a group deciding it does not need to fill every silence.
The entrance to the next setting has requested a gentler opening performance.
A little restraint is an excellent travelling companion near a forest.
Less noise gives us better information about the surroundings as well.
A bridge can carry footsteps without needing to carry a whole argument.
It is a considerate request, and an easy way to be a good visitor.
I wonder what small sounds become noticeable once nobody is talking over the crossing.

contexts.subject: A notice advertises a search for the ultimate horn.

replies.text: Somebody has given a very particular bug obsession the magnificent title it clearly feels it deserves.
An ambitious superlative needs a clear measurement if people are expected to compare examples.
A very specific interest. We can read it without taking on a new obligation.
I like how boldly someone has let a favourite subject occupy a little piece of the path.
A hobby can make a whole ordinary island feel full of promising encounters.
The quest announcement has selected the grandest possible title for a remarkably specialized subject.
A small notice has put a very large hat on an enthusiast's question.
I would ask what makes a horn ultimate before treating it as an engineering specification.
A single unusual shape has become someone's bright little horizon.
That is a person who knows exactly which detail catches their eye.
I wonder whether the search is more fun to them than ever declaring the final winner.

contexts.subject: A Cycling Road notice warns riders about discarded items.

Route17_Text_WatchOutForDiscardedItems.text: It's a notice.\pWatch out for discarded items.$

replies.text: Things left on a cycling route are a much less charming surprise when the ground is moving quickly past.
Loose objects can become hazards when riders have limited time to react.
Watch the path and keep control of the bike.
It is frustrating when one person's forgotten rubbish becomes another person's sudden problem.
Anything we bring should stay securely packed until there is a proper place for it.
The scenic route has acquired an unfortunate scattering of unscheduled obstacles.
Somebody else's carelessness has a remarkable talent for appearing under our wheels.
Good visibility and a manageable pace help us respond without a sudden dangerous correction.
The path should not have to keep catching what people failed to carry.
A little care with belongings would spare everyone else this warning.
I wonder how many riders have learned to scan the road because of one small object in the wrong place.

contexts.subject: A playful notice tells readers to throw Poke Balls rather than throw the game.

Route17_Text_DontThrowGameThrowBalls.text: It's a notice!\pDon't throw the game, throw POKé\nBALLS instead!$

replies.text: A notice has wandered onto the cycling road specifically to make a pun. I respect the dedication.
Wordplay is a useful way to make a short message memorable, even if it supplies little practical detail.
A harmless joke. At least the sign is trying.
I like finding a little silliness in the middle of ordinary directions.
A small joke can make a long stretch of road feel more human.
The signwriter has delivered a compact double meaning and retired before the reviews arrive.
A public notice has been briefly relieved of its duty to sound important.
A memorable phrase can work better than a long instruction nobody remembers reading.
A little twist of words has been left beside the road for passing minds to catch.
It is charming that someone spent time making a routine notice playful.
I wonder who first laughed enough at that line to decide it needed a permanent sign.

contexts.subject: Many trainers have scribbled their names on the Fan Club sign.

SaffronCity_Text_TrainerFanClubSign.text: POKéMON TRAINER FAN CLUB\pMany TRAINERS have scribbled their\nnames on this sign.$

replies.text: The sign has become a guest book with rather more confidence than available space.
The accumulated names suggest people want to leave evidence of having been part of the place.
No need to add ours just because the surface is already crowded.
It is sweet in a slightly untidy way that people wanted to be remembered here.
A shared interest can make a little doorway feel like somewhere people belong.
The audience has collectively promoted itself into the credits.
A small sign has been asked to carry an unnecessarily ambitious amount of identity.
A designated guest book might do the job without making the directions harder to read.
A crowd of little names has gathered around one ordinary entrance.
Wanting a trace of yourself in a favourite place is understandable, though the sign could use some mercy.
I wonder which name belongs to somebody who still stops and smiles every time they walk past.

contexts.subject: An advertisement announces a forthcoming Silph product without a release date.

SaffronCity_Text_SilphsLatestProduct.text: SILPH's latest product!\nRelease to be determined…$

replies.text: A bold announcement that has thoughtfully left the part where it happens blank.
The notice states intent, not a confirmed release schedule or demonstrated result.
We can wait for real details before getting attached to the promise.
There is a little excitement in something unfinished, as long as nobody mistakes it for ready.
A future possibility does not need money or worry from us today.
The premiere has been announced with impressive confidence and no date whatsoever.
A promise has taken a very comfortable seat where a fact might eventually arrive.
I would rather hear what has been tested than how impressive the announcement is.
A bright blank space has been put on display before anything has grown into it.
Anticipation is pleasant; vague advertising is not the same as useful information.
I wonder how different the finished thing will be from what people imagine after reading that little notice.

contexts.subject: A museum caption praises the pictured Pokemon as endlessly cool and inestimable.

replies.text: Nonstop coolness sounds tiring. Does it get a little blanket during closing hours?
Inestimable is a convenient assessment. It spares the curator from specifying units.
The caption's impressed. I'll let the painting make its own case.
That's a lot of confidence for a small card under a picture.
Even cool Pokemon deserve an occasional warm lunch.
The curator has abolished moderation. A bold editorial decision.
Endlessly cool. At last, an occupation suited to a drafty museum.
I'd enjoy comparing what each painter chooses to make a Pokemon look cool.
Perhaps coolness stays longer when someone puts a frame around it.
A confident caption can help a portrait. This one gives it an entire entourage.
I'd ask the curator which detail made that description feel right.

contexts.subject: The museum caption greets viewers and compliments the Pokemon good looks.

replies.text: A painting that says hello first! Very considerate of the wall.
An informal greeting makes the display unusually approachable.
Friendly caption. No need to stand stiffly just because it's a museum.
It almost feels like being introduced to someone. That's rather sweet.
A welcome and a compliment. The little card has good manners.
The portrait's publicist appears to be an enthusiastic friend.
A cheerful greeting from a still image. I've met less welcoming living people.
That opening draws you closer before you even study the picture. Clever.
A small hello has been left here for every visitor.
Looking good and making people comfortable. That's an excellent combination.
I like a gallery label that sounds as though someone actually enjoyed meeting its subject.

contexts.subject: The museum caption heaps marvelous, wonderful and great praise on the Pokemon.

replies.text: Three compliments! That Pokemon has won the adjective buffet.
The description offers three positive judgments and remarkably little measurement.
Someone really liked this Pokemon. Hard to miss that part.
Whoever wrote the label sounds delighted. I like finding that in a museum.
They didn't ration the praise. An admirably generous serving.
One adjective entered the draft. Two friends followed it through the door.
Occasionally excessive praise is simply someone having a good day.
The enthusiasm comes through perfectly. Now I want to examine what inspired it.
A small card can hold a surprisingly large fondness.
The label has dressed the portrait in every compliment it owns.
I'd be curious whether the artist or the curator chose those words. Both sound proud.

contexts.subject: A museum caption likens the beautiful Pokemon to the century last Venus.

replies.text: The last one this century? I'd better appreciate it before the calendar gets ideas.
That is a sweeping historical claim for a portrait label. Beautifully ambitious.
Quite a title to put under a picture. No pressure on the subject.
They wanted the beauty to feel rare. The words make you slow down a little.
Someone gave this portrait the grandest compliment they could find.
The curator has declared the century's remaining beauty contest closed.
An extravagant title. Even museums occasionally get carried away by a pretty face.
I'd compare the framing and lighting before deciding what makes this portrait stand out.
The century can keep counting. The picture has its own quiet time.
That label promises something extraordinary. It certainly knows how to draw attention.
I wonder how visitors from different years would respond to that same claim.

contexts.subject: The caption celebrates the Pokemon dazzling smile.

replies.text: A smile saved in paint. Useful for days when everyone outside is being a raincloud.
A fleeting expression becomes available for repeated observation. A lovely use of portraiture.
A good smile can carry a whole picture.
I like that they noticed its smile, rather than only calling it beautiful.
That sounds like the sort of expression that makes strangers smile back.
The caption chooses one small expression and lets it outshine the room.
A glittering smile. I can appreciate that without becoming personally glittery.
Capturing a smile before it changes must take careful observation.
A brief kindness can leave a long reflection. Even in paint.
An expression gives beauty somewhere to live. Otherwise it's just a list of features.
Smiles change so quickly. I like thinking the artist caught one worth keeping.

contexts.subject: The caption calls its Pokemon an incomparable Pokemon Center idol.

replies.text: A Pokemon Center idol! Does the waiting room have a fan club under the chairs?
An interesting setting for celebrity. Regular visitors would certainly recognize a familiar face.
Nice to have something cheerful around a place people visit when they're worried.
A familiar Pokemon could make a Center feel less strange. I understand the affection.
A little local celebrity at the Center. That sounds like a pleasant regular to have.
From Center favorite to museum subject. An impressive expansion of the audience.
An idol with a practical venue. Admirers can recover while being overwhelmed.
The caption gives this portrait a connection to an everyday place. I like that.
Some faces become part of a place before anyone notices.
Local affection makes a different kind of fame. Usually a warmer one.
I'd love to hear which visitors first started calling it the Center's idol.

contexts.subject: The museum caption describes a lovely sweet Pokemon.

replies.text: Sweet without being sticky. A very convenient sort of portrait.
A brief description, but the intended affection is quite clear.
Simple praise. It doesn't need to shout to work.
That label feels gentle. It leaves room to enjoy the picture.
Lovely and sweet. Two things that don't require a complicated explanation.
A modest caption has slipped past the museum's supply of superlatives.
A small, uncomplicated kindness on a wall. I approve.
A short label lets the expression and pose do more of the work.
Some pictures ask for very little beyond a soft moment.
The caption knows when to stop accessorizing. A useful skill.
I'd be interested in what different visitors notice as sweet about the same portrait.

contexts.subject: The museum identifies the pretty Pokemon winning portrait.

replies.text: A winning portrait! I wonder whether the frame gets to share a tiny bit of the pride.
The caption identifies a winning work without giving us its whole contest history.
Good to see the result displayed where people can enjoy it.
A prize can pass quickly. A portrait gives the proud moment somewhere to stay.
Someone must have been pleased to see that portrait hanging here.
A victory has acquired a frame and visiting hours. Rather civilized.
A win preserved without requiring anyone to keep clapping forever.
I'd enjoy comparing the choices that made this portrait stand out to the judges.
The busy day has settled into a quiet picture.
A winning look has to read beyond the first glance. A gallery gives it that chance.
Seeing a winning work up close gives you time to notice what a quick announcement misses.

contexts.subject: The caption playfully asks the cute Pokemon for a wink.

gMuseumPaintingCaption_Cute2.text: Give us a wink!\nThe cutie POKéMON {STR_VAR_1}

replies.text: We'll be waiting a while for that wink. Paint is famously stubborn about blinking.
The request makes the subject feel responsive, despite the obvious limitations of paint.
Cheerful label. We'll spare the portrait a staring contest.
Asking a portrait to wink is a little silly. I smiled anyway.
If it actually winks, I'm checking how much sleep we've had.
The caption requests audience participation from the least mobile person in the room.
An unanswered wink request. At last, a social difficulty I share with a painting.
A playful line can make a still picture feel lively. No moving parts needed.
Perhaps the wink waits until everyone looks away.
Cute, direct, and just cheeky enough. The label understands its assignment.
That's exactly the sort of thing someone says a moment before a subject refuses to cooperate.

contexts.subject: The caption praises the Pokemon wisdom and mastery of smartness.

replies.text: A master of smartness! I still occasionally lose arguments to doors marked pull.
Wisdom and quick thinking aren't identical. The caption seems pleased to credit both.
A clever Pokemon deserves recognition too. Strength isn't the whole story.
I like seeing a quiet quality given a place on the wall.
Being wise might include knowing when to stop showing off. A useful talent.
Smartness has acquired a maestro. I await the appointment of a deputy.
A wise portrait would probably let us finish our observations without correcting us.
I'd like to know how the artist makes intelligence visible in a still image.
Wisdom can be hard to paint. You mostly see what someone does with it.
An intelligent expression is more interesting than simply adding a serious pose.
I'd ask what the subject did that made people think of wisdom in the first place.

contexts.subject: The museum caption gives its Pokemon singular praise as chosen above all others.

replies.text: Above all Pokemon is a very tall compliment. I hope the frame has sturdy hooks.
An absolute claim, with no selection method attached. Clearly this is praise, not a census.
Someone chose a favorite and committed to it.
That's a grand thing to say about one Pokemon. It must mean a lot to someone.
Favorites have a way of becoming the best in the whole world to their people.
The caption has politely dismissed every other contender on the planet.
Universal supremacy. Museums occasionally have remarkably enthusiastic handwriting.
I'd want to hear what set this subject apart for whoever chose it.
One Pokemon can fill someone's whole view for a moment.
A dramatic claim catches attention. The portrait still has to hold it.
That sounds like a story someone would tell with a lot of pride. I'd listen.

contexts.subject: The caption preserves a moment of elegance for an excellent Pokemon.

replies.text: A moment of elegance. Good thing nobody painted the moment just after a sneeze.
Selecting one moment is part of the portrait's interpretation, not merely its timing.
A good moment to keep. They don't all announce themselves beforehand.
I like the word moment there. It lets the Pokemon have other moods too.
Nobody has to be graceful all day to have a graceful moment.
The caption wisely limits perfection to a manageable interval.
A moment of elegance is plenty. Sustained elegance sounds exhausting.
The artist had to choose the pose that would make that brief quality last.
Something passing has found a place to rest.
Elegance often depends on restraint. The caption leaves a little breathing room.
One good instant can tell a story without pretending it was the subject's whole day.

contexts.subject: The caption praises a muscular fast Pokemon.

replies.text: Muscles and speed! Even its compliments have somewhere urgent to be.
Power and speed are distinct attributes. An effective portrait can suggest both.
Strong and quick is a useful combination. The picture gets to stand still, at least.
Trying to show speed in something still must be an interesting challenge.
That sounds like a Pokemon with a healthy appetite after practice.
The caption promises momentum while the frame heroically prevents any escape.
A speedster obliged to remain on a wall. A quiet little irony.
I'd study how the pose carries motion without actually moving.
A moving strength, caught briefly between one place and the next.
A powerful pose needs a clear shape. Otherwise all that energy gets lost.
A still portrait of a fast subject makes me curious about the moments on either side.

contexts.subject: The museum caption escalates its praise from strong to strongest.

replies.text: Strong, stronger, strongest! The label has done three little push-ups.
A complete progression of comparison, though the comparison group remains unspecified.
We understood strong the first time. The extra two make their point.
It sounds like the writer got more excited as the sentence went on.
That's three helpings of strong. Nobody's leaving this label hungry.
The adjective climbed its own podium before the sentence ended.
A very short escalation. Considerably tidier than most arguments about strength.
Repeating the word with increasing force is a surprisingly efficient bit of emphasis.
The picture stays still while its description keeps growing.
Even the praise has layers. This label arrived fully styled.
I'd enjoy hearing the writer read that aloud. I suspect the last word gets some volume.

contexts.subject: The museum caption enthusiastically calls its Pokemon mighty tough and hyper.

replies.text: Hyper and mighty! I suddenly appreciate the fence a picture frame provides.
The caption conveys intensity very clearly, even without a precise definition of hyper.
Plenty of energy in that description. The gallery's managing to contain it.
A lively subject in a quiet room. That contrast is rather nice.
That caption sounds ready for an afternoon run. I am ready for an afternoon snack.
The label has burst through three adjectives and is approaching the wall.
So much energy preserved somewhere it cannot rearrange the furniture. Thoughtful.
I'd like to see which visual details match all that force in the wording.
A fierce little weather system, held inside a rectangle.
That description needs a bold portrait beside it. Subtlety has already left the room.
It sounds like a subject people remember. I'd ask the artist how sitting for it went.

contexts.subject: A contest hall painting caption identifies its contest, rank, trainer and Pokemon.

replies.text: A name, a Pokemon, and a place in the contest's story. A tidy little proud corner.
The caption records category, rank, and participants. Useful context for the portrait.
Good to give the trainer and Pokemon credit together.
Seeing the names beneath it makes the picture feel more personal.
It's nice that the display remembers the pair behind the performance.
A compact credit for a partnership. No oversized speech required.
Names under a picture keep admiration from becoming entirely anonymous.
The category and rank help explain the setting without crowding out the subject.
Two names share the space beneath one remembered moment.
A clear caption lets the portrait have its personality and its proper credit.
Now there's enough context to ask a good question about the Pokemon's contest experience.

contexts.subject: A sign explains gaining battle experience by participating then switching out.

PetalburgWoods_Text_TrainerTipsExperienc.text:
TRAINER TIPS\pAny POKéMON that appears even once
in a battle is awarded EXP Points.\pTo raise a weak POKéMON, put it at the
left of the team list.\pAs soon as a battle starts, switch it
out. It will earn EXP Points without\lbeing exposed to any harm.$

replies.text: A tiny turn at the front, then back to safety. Like testing a puddle with one toe.
Participation can provide experience without requiring the weakest member to finish the battle.
Give them a chance to learn. Have a safe switch ready first.
A brief turn can still count. That's a comforting way to start learning.
Small portions of practice are easier to manage than being thrown in all at once.
An entrance needn't last long to become part of the story.
Brief exposure, followed by a sensible retreat. I respect this educational model.
That takes planning the team order before the battle starts. A useful detail.
You can leave the difficult place and still carry something learned from it.
A little confidence looks better than being pushed far past your limits.
I'd pay attention to how the new Pokemon responds to those first short turns.

contexts.subject: The sign explains move PP as well as HP and recommends a Pokemon Center.

PetalburgWoods_Text_TrainerTipsPP.text: TRAINER TIPS\pIn addition to Hit Points (HP), POKéMON\nhave Power Points (PP) that are used to\lmake moves during battle.\pIf a POKéMON runs out of PP, it must be\ntaken to a POKéMON CENTER.$

replies.text: Being healthy and having moves left are two different cupboards. Better check both.
Physical condition and remaining move uses are separate limits. Both need monitoring.
Don't judge readiness by health alone. An empty move list can end a plan quickly.
You can look fine and still have nothing left to give. It's good the sign mentions it.
A Center stop is useful before the last useful move runs dry.
Even an excellent move cannot be asked for an unlimited encore.
A reminder that looking alive is not the same as being prepared.
Two indicators, two possible shortages. Checking both avoids a very preventable problem.
Strength can run out along a quieter path than injury.
There's more to readiness than what you can see at a glance.
I'd ask a new trainer to check both before we headed farther into the woods.

contexts.subject: A sign explains Double Battles and the importance of the first two team positions.

Route104_Text_TrainerTipsDoubleBattles.text: TRAINER TIPS\pIn the HOENN region there are pairs\nof TRAINERS who challenge others\lfor 2-on-2 POKéMON battles called\lDOUBLE BATTLES.\pIn a DOUBLE BATTLE, the TRAINER must\nsend out two POKéMON, the one at the\lleft of the list and the top one.\lWatch how POKéMON are lined up.$

replies.text: The first two are a pair! Better introduce them before somebody starts calling orders.
Team arrangement determines the opening pair. Compatibility matters before the first move.
Check the first two positions now. Better here than after the challenge starts.
Two Pokemon need room to work together. I'd think about both before choosing.
Like sending out two dishes together. Timing and a sensible pairing help.
A partnership begins with a very practical casting decision. Who goes first?
Two at once. Twice as much reason to avoid improvising the entire plan.
The list order is doing real work here. A small adjustment can change the opening.
Being beside someone changes what either one can do alone.
A good pair needs more than two individually impressive members.
I'd be curious which two seem most comfortable taking the field together.

contexts.subject: A sign tells anglers to respond with A when something bites.

Route106_Text_TrainerTips.text: TRAINER TIPS\pAdvice on catching POKéMON with a ROD:\nPress the A Button if you get a bite.$

replies.text: The fish gives the cue. We provide the very small burst of panic.
Fishing combines waiting with a short response window. Quite a change of pace.
Stay ready when the line moves. That's the part you can't do afterward.
The waiting seems peaceful. I'd probably still jump when something bites.
Patience first, quick hands second. A familiar combination.
The rod offers a long pause followed by an extremely urgent punctuation mark.
A quiet activity with a surprise deadline. How considerate.
Keeping your hand ready seems more useful than staring harder at the water.
Something below notices you before you can see it.
Relaxed, but prepared. Fishing appears to have a very specific posture.
That first tug must feel different once you've learned what you're waiting for.

contexts.subject: A sign explains that equal levels need not mean identical stats and training matters.

Route109_Text_TrainerTipsSign.text: TRAINER TIPS\pPOKéMON at the same level may not\nalways have identical stats.\pPOKéMON raised by TRAINERS are said\nto grow stronger than wild POKéMON.$

replies.text: Same level, different strengths. So the number isn't the whole Pokemon after all.
Level is a useful summary, not a complete description of individual capability.
Know the Pokemon you've got. Don't rely on matching numbers.
I like that two Pokemon can reach the same level in different ways.
Training leaves its own mark. Time spent together isn't just a number.
The tidy label conceals a rather untidy collection of individual differences.
A reassuring warning against treating everyone with the same number as interchangeable.
Comparing the individual stats will tell us more than the level alone.
Two paths can reach the same marker without being the same path.
A matching size tag never promised a matching fit. This makes sense to me.
I'd ask about the training behind the numbers. That's where the interesting differences begin.

contexts.subject: A sign explains sleep and paralysis as battle techniques.

Route110_Text_TrainerTipsPrlzSleep.text: TRAINER TIPS\pThe foe can be made helpless by\nparalyzing it or causing it to sleep.\pIt is an important technique for\nPOKéMON battles.$

replies.text: A battle plan can involve fewer attacks rather than bigger ones. Sneaky little sign.
Restricting an opponent's actions changes the battle even without immediate damage.
Remember status effects when planning. Power won't solve every situation.
A battle can turn on who gets the chance to act. That makes me pay attention.
It's useful advice. I'd keep the recovery supplies where we can find them too.
The sign suggests depriving the opponent of their next contribution. Efficiently rude.
Sleep as a tactic. Finally, a battle concept with a familiar appeal.
Controlling the opponent's opportunities gives the rest of the plan room to work.
Sometimes the most important move changes the space between the others.
An opening can matter more than an impressive display of strength.
I'd want to learn the signs of both conditions before trying to build a plan around them.

contexts.subject: A sign explains reorganizing items inside the bag.

Route110_Text_TrainerTipsRegisterItems.text: TRAINER TIPS\pThe items in the BAG can be reorganized\nby pressing SELECT.$

replies.text: An organized bag! A place where a Potion doesn't have to introduce itself to every pocket.
Reducing search time is a modest improvement that becomes valuable through repetition.
Put the useful things where your hand finds them first.
Knowing where something is makes a hurried moment feel a little less loud.
The same rule as a good cupboard: often-used things within easy reach.
At last, a victory over the small chaos living at the bottom of a bag.
Order inside the bag. A limited but achievable ambition.
A simple reordering saves repeated effort later. Excellent small-scale design.
Things are easier to find when they aren't hiding behind everything else.
A useful arrangement should suit the person carrying it. Make it yours.
Everyone organizes a bag differently. I'd be interested in what you put first.

contexts.subject: The sign expands the Special Attack and Special Defense abbreviations.

Route111_Text_TrainerTipsSpAtkSpDef.text: TRAINER TIPS\pOne of the indicators of a POKéMON's\npowerfulness is SP. ATK. It stands for\l“SPECIAL ATTACK.”\pLikewise, SP. DEF stands for “SPECIAL\nDEFENSE.”$

replies.text: Good. Two mysterious little labels have agreed to use their full names.
Abbreviations are efficient once defined. Before that, they're merely compact obstacles.
Useful to know which number you're looking at before trusting it.
It's easier to ask about something once you know what it's called.
A small explanation saves a lot of pretending you already understood.
The sign generously unpacks two very tightly folded words.
An abbreviation explained without another abbreviation. A rare courtesy.
Clear labels make the whole set of information easier to use.
A name made shorter can still need a longer introduction.
A compact label works best when everyone knows what it means.
This is the kind of basic question people hesitate to ask. Glad the sign answers it.

contexts.subject: The sign explains assigning a key item to SELECT for convenient use.

Route113_Text_TrainerTipsRegisterKeyItem.text: TRAINER TIPS\pYou may register one of the KEY ITEMS\nin your BAG as SELECT.\pSimply press SELECT to use\nthe registered item conveniently.$

replies.text: One favorite tool gets a shortcut. The rest will have to queue politely in the bag.
A dedicated shortcut is most useful for the item with the highest repeated use.
Choose something you reach for often. That's what makes the shortcut worth it.
One less thing to search for when you're already concentrating. That sounds useful.
Keep the regular tool close. The occasional one can stay packed.
A frequently used item has been promoted to a very convenient address.
One shortcut. Naturally, choosing it may take longer than using it.
Saving a few steps on a repeated action adds up quickly. I like this feature.
A familiar thing becomes easier to call when you give it a place.
Convenience is personal. The best choice is the one that suits your routine.
I'd ask which item keeps coming out of your bag. There's your likely answer.

contexts.subject: The sign explains stopping an evolution with B.

Route116_Text_TrainerTipsBToStopEvolutio.text: TRAINER TIPS\pIf you want to stop a POKéMON from\nevolving, press the B Button while it\lis trying to evolve.\lThe startled POKéMON will stop.\pThis is called an evolution cancel.$

replies.text: You can interrupt it! That's a big change to leave with no little pause button.
Evolution can be interrupted during the process. Timing is essential to that choice.
Good to know before it happens. That's a decision to make with care.
A big change can arrive suddenly. Knowing there's a way to pause it is comforting.
Being able to stop doesn't make it a choice to rush. Pay attention to your Pokemon.
A transformation has a moment in which the ending can still be reconsidered.
Even a dramatic transformation permits an interruption. More considerate than most speeches.
It's an important control to know before the process starts, rather than during it.
A change can be near without having to happen this instant.
Keeping a familiar form is a decision too. The sign makes that option clear.
I'd want to know how the Pokemon felt about the change, not just how it looked.

contexts.subject: A sign explains the bag separate pockets and automatic item placement.

Route116_Text_TrainerTipsBagHasPockets.text: TRAINER TIPS\pYour BAG has several POCKETS.\pItems you obtain are automatically\nplaced in the appropriate POCKETS.\pNo TRAINER can afford to be without\na BAG of their own.$

replies.text: Pockets with jobs! Finally, some reliable employees in this traveling collection of lumps.
Sorting items by category reduces confusion as the collection grows. A sensible system.
Different pockets for different uses. Learn where things go before you need them.
It's reassuring to know something small won't disappear among everything else.
Separate the supplies and finding one won't mean unpacking your whole life.
An entire organizational philosophy disguised as a bag with extra pockets.
A bag that sorts its contents. It has outperformed several desks I've encountered.
Built-in categories save a lot of manual sorting. A good piece of everyday design.
Everything has a small place to wait until it is needed.
Practical pockets are a design feature I will always defend.
A well-used bag says a lot about someone's journey. The pocket system helps it stay readable.

contexts.subject: The sign gives the sixteen-item Secret Base decoration limit.

Route119_Text_TrainerTipsDecoration.text: TRAINER TIPS\pUp to sixteen decorations and\nfurniture items can be placed in\la SECRET BASE.\pPick your favorite items and create\nyour very own SECRET BASE exactly the\lway you want.$

replies.text: Sixteen decorations! Seventeen would apparently be an interior-design emergency.
A fixed limit makes selection part of the design. Each addition has an opportunity cost.
Leave room to walk. A base should still be usable after it's decorated.
A few things chosen carefully could make the place feel familiar.
Somewhere to sit ought to survive the first fifteen exciting choices.
Sixteen objects with which to explain your taste to anyone who wanders in.
A decorating limit. A small mercy for both visitors and the floor.
I'd sketch the arrangement first. Then the sixteen pieces can actually work together.
A hidden place can become yours through a handful of chosen things.
Sixteen is plenty for a strong idea. Decide what you want the room to feel like first.
I'd enjoy visiting bases with the same limit and seeing how differently people use it.

contexts.subject: A sign explains that PokeBlocks reduce the likelihood of Safari Pokemon fleeing.

Route121_SafariZoneEntrance_Text_Trainer.text: SAFARI ZONE TRAINER TIP!\pThrow {POKEBLOCK}S at wild POKéMON to make\nthem less likely to flee.$

replies.text: A snack can persuade someone to stay a little longer. I respect this discovery.
The sign describes a change in fleeing probability, not a guarantee of capture.
Useful to know. Keep the difference between better odds and a sure thing clear.
Giving it a reason to stay seems gentler than simply hoping it won't leave.
A well-timed treat has helped plenty of awkward meetings along.
Hospitality enters the encounter with a surprisingly practical effect.
Food reduces the urge to leave. Not an exclusively Pokemon observation.
I'd compare how long encounters last with and without a block. Carefully, of course.
An offered sweetness gives a wild moment a little more time.
Making the first meeting pleasant can change its direction. A useful social principle.
I'd pay attention to whether different Pokemon linger over different blocks.

contexts.subject: The department store directory lists services and merchandise on each floor.

LilycoveCity_DepartmentStore_1F_Text_Flo.text: 1F: SERVICE COUNTER\n    LOTTERY CORNER\p2F: TRAINER'S ZONE\p3F: BATTLE COLLECTION\p4F: TM CORNER\p5F: POKé DOLL FLOOR\pROOFTOP: ROOFTOP PLAZA$

replies.text: A whole floor for dolls! The directory has successfully endangered my concentration.
A floor directory prevents a great deal of unnecessary searching. Particularly in a building this large.
Pick the floor before climbing. Saves a few trips.
It's nice to know where we're going before the stairs get involved.
Useful things downstairs, dolls upstairs, and somewhere to pause on the roof. Sensible trip.
An entire shopping expedition reduced to a few well-placed lines.
A guide to ascending through increasingly optional purchases.
Grouping each department by floor makes the route much easier to plan.
Several little destinations stacked beneath one roof.
A directory is part of the welcome. Nobody should need detective skills to find a department.
I'd ask which floor people head for first. That probably tells you plenty about them.

contexts.subject: The adventure notebook lists menu and saving rules before blank pages.

PlayersHouse_2F_Text_Notebook.text: {PLAYER} flipped open the notebook.\pADVENTURE RULE NO. 1\nOpen the MENU with START.\pADVENTURE RULE NO. 2\nRecord your progress with SAVE.\pThe remaining pages are blank…$

replies.text: Two rules, then all that blank paper. The notebook is leaving room for us to get interesting.
A short operational guide followed by space for records. A practical beginning.
Good basics. The rest can be written as you go.
Blank pages can feel inviting when nobody has decided what belongs on them yet.
Two useful reminders and plenty of room for whatever happens next.
A remarkably restrained opening chapter. The remaining pages have confidence in you.
An unfinished notebook is less intimidating when the first two rules are manageable.
Essential instructions first, then room to extend the record. I like that arrangement.
The empty pages haven't become memories yet.
A clear beginning and generous space. That's a good notebook design.
I like seeing what someone chooses to put on the first blank page.
